Text: .** Phase fluctuations in elongated Bose-Einstein condensates (BECs) limit the spatial coherence of matter waves, posing challenges for high-precision interferometry. A quasi-one-dimensional ({87})Rb condensate is split by a pulsed optical lattice and recombined after a variable evolution time. By tuning the axial confinement and temperature, we systematically vary the phase-correlation length (L_{phi}). Interference fringes are recorded with absorption imaging and analyzed via Fourier filtering to extract visibility as a function of (L_{phi}) and propagation time. Complementary numerical simulations based on the stochastic Gross-Pitaevskii equation validate the experimental data. .** Fringe visibility decays exponentially with the ratio of the interferometer arm separation to (L_{phi}), confirming that local phase coherence governs interference contrast. We observe that, for (L_{phi}) exceeding the arm separation, visibility remains above 70 % even after 5 ms of free evolution, whereas for shorter (L_{phi}) the contrast drops below 20 %. Moreover, the visibility exhibits a weak dependence on the mean-field interaction strength, indicating that phase-fluctuation dynamics dominate over interaction-induced dephasing in the parameter regime studied. Crucially, these establish a quantitative link between phase-fluctuation length scales and interferometric performance, providing a pathway to optimize matter-wave sensors based on low-dimensional BECs.

Text: The observed scatter in the Galactic interstellar deuterium‑to‑hydrogen ratio (D/H) remains a central puzzle for cosmology and Galactic chemical evolution. One leading hypothesis attributes part of this variation to deuterium depletion onto dust grains, yet direct empirical evidence is limited. Titanium, a refractory element whose gas‑phase abundance (Ti/H) reliably traces dust‑related depletion, offers a promising diagnostic when measured alongside D/H along the same sight lines. We assembled an expanded sample of 58 sight lines spanning a broad range of Galactic environments (local bubble, warm neutral medium, and dense clouds). High‑resolution ultraviolet spectra from *HST*/STIS and *FUSE* provided precise D I and H I column densities, while ground‑based echelle observations yielded Ti II λ3384 and λ3242 absorption profiles. Uniform Voigt‑profile fitting and Bayesian hierarchical modeling were employed to derive Ti/H and D/H with rigorous uncertainty propagation. Correlation analyses incorporated Monte‑Carlo simulations to assess the significance of any Ti/H–D/H relationship while controlling for metallicity and ionization effects. We detect a statistically significant anti‑correlation (Pearson ρ = ‑0.62, p < 0.001) between Ti/H and D/H, indicating that sight lines with higher dust depletion exhibit lower gas‑phase deuterium. The best‑fit linear relation, D/H = (2.0 ± 0.2) × 10⁻⁵ − (1.5 ± 0.3) × 10⁻⁶ [Ti/H]⁻¹, accounts for ~38 % of the observed D/H variance. After correcting D/H for dust depletion using the Ti/H proxy, the intrinsic Galactic deuterium abundance converges to (2.1 ± 0.1) × 10⁻⁵, consistent with primordial values inferred from CMB measurements. These substantiate dust depletion as a major contributor to D/H scatter and provide a calibrated for recovering the true interstellar deuterium abundance.

Lattice strain that affects bandwidth gives rise to limited variations in the superconducting and normal state properties. Microstructural disorder such as antiphase boundaries that give rise to Ti network disorder can reduce the critical temperature, but Ti network disorder combined with Mg interdiffusion can affect the superconducting state much more dramatically. Thickness dependent transport studies indicate a superconductor-insulator transition as a function of film thickness regardless of lattice strain and microstructure. Text: In most classical fluids, shock waves are strongly dissipative, their energy being quickly lost through viscous damping. But in systems such as cold plasmas, superfluids, and Bose-Einstein condensates, where viscosity is negligible or non-existent, a fundamentally different type of shock wave can emerge whose behaviour is dominated by dispersion rather than dissipation. Dispersive shock waves are difficult to study experimentally, and analytical solutions to the equations that govern them have only been found in one dimension (1D). By exploiting a well-known, but little appreciated, correspondence between the behaviour of superfluids and nonlinear optical materials, we demonstrate an all-optical experimental platform for studying the dynamics of dispersive shock waves. This enables us to observe the propagation and nonlinear response of dispersive shock waves, including the interaction of colliding shock waves, in 1D and 2D. Our system offers a versatile and more accessible means for exploring superfluid-like and related dispersive phenomena.

This dichotomous relationship underscores the pivotal role of the electron-phonon interaction in governing the CO behavior in strongly correlated materials. Text: This paper establishes a novel mean value theorem for systems of integrals, providing a generalization of the classical mean value theorem to the realm of multivariate functions. Text: We present measurements of the two-point galaxy angular correlation function w(\theta) in the COSMOS field. Despite having significantly different masks, these three determinations agree well. The exception is that our result is at the upper end of the expected cosmic variance scatter for \theta > 10 arcmin, which we attribute to a particularly rich structure known to exist at z~0.8. For fainter samples, however, the level of clustering is somewhat higher than reported by some previous studies: in all three catalogues we find w(\theta=1')~0.014 at a median IAB magnitude of 24. At these very faintest magnitudes, our measurements agree well with the latest determinations from the Canada-France Legacy Survey. This level of clustering is approximately double what is predicted by the semi-analytic catalogs (at all angles). Text: The domino problem in the hyperbolic plane, a fundamental problem in geometric group theory, concerns the existence of a domino tiling for a given finite set of tiles in the hyperbolic plane. The problem has been shown to be undecidable, yet various partial have been established under specific conditions. Our research aims to contribute to this ongoing study. We employ a novel approach, combining techniques from geometric group theory and symbolic dynamics, to develop a new solution to the domino problem in the hyperbolic plane. Our approach involves the use of a specific type of tiling, which we term the "complementary tiling." This tiling is constructed using a set of fundamental domains and their corresponding group actions. We prove the existence of a domino tiling for any finite set of tiles in the hyperbolic plane, assuming the tiles satisfy a specific set of geometric conditions. Our solution relies on the complementary tiling and its associated group actions, providing a general framework for tackling the domino problem in the hyperbolic plane. This result has significant implications for the study of geometric group theory and its applications.

Text: Disclinations, dislocations, and continuous defects constitute the fundamental non-crystalline irregularities that dictate mechanical, electronic, and optical properties of solids. Classical Volterra-type treatments treat these defects as singularities in discrete lattices, yet recent experimental evidence suggests that many real materials exhibit smoothly distributed curvature and torsion fields. A unified continuum description that reconciles discrete singularities with continuous distributions is therefore required to predict defect interactions and guide defect-engineering strategies. We formulated a differential-geometric framework in which the material manifold is endowed with a metric and an independent affine connection. Curvature and torsion tensors encode disclinations and dislocations, respectively, while their smooth parts represent continuous defects. The elastic energy is expressed as a quadratic functional of these tensors, and the equilibrium equations are derived via variational principles. Analytical solutions for isolated defects and finite-element simulations for complex defect networks were performed, and were benchmarked against high-resolution transmission electron microscopy and X-ray diffraction data. The theory reproduces classical singular solutions in the appropriate limits and predicts new coupling terms between curvature and torsion that drive defect migration and annihilation. Continuous defect fields are shown to regularize the core energy, eliminating the need for ad hoc cut-offs. Numerical experiments reveal that defect-defect interactions are governed by a unified Green-function kernel, providing quantitative predictions for stress fields and strain-induced phase transformations. This reappraisal establishes a coherent, geometrically grounded description of all defect types, offering a robust foundation for defect-controlled material design.

Text: The separability of a family of one parameter W and GHZ multiqubit states is investigated using the Abe-Rajagopal q-conditional entropy approach, which provides a novel framework for analyzing the quantum correlations present in these states. The implications of these are discussed in the context of quantum information processing and the development of novel quantum technologies, highlighting the potential of the Abe-Rajagopal q-conditional entropy approach as a powerful tool for characterizing and quantifying quantum correlations in multiqubit systems. Text: Magnetic avalanches are a complex phenomenon in magnetic materials where a small perturbation can trigger a rapid, non-linear response. Text: The evolution of mass‑loss rates during the thermally pulsing asymptotic giant branch (TP‑AGB) phase critically shapes the circumstellar environments of low‑ and intermediate‑mass stars, yet the physical mechanisms that generate the observed detached shells remain incompletely understood. Synthetic CO and far‑infrared dust emission maps are produced for direct comparison with high‑resolution interferometric observations of a sample of carbon‑rich and oxygen‑rich TP‑AGB stars exhibiting detached shells. Our demonstrate that abrupt enhancements in the mass‑loss rate, by factors of 3–5 over ≈200 yr, naturally arise from the interplay between increased luminosity during a thermal pulse and the consequent shift in dust condensation radius, leading to a dense, thin shell that expands ballistically once the pulse subsides. The modeled shell thicknesses (ΔR/R≈0.1) and expansion velocities (10–20 km s⁻¹) reproduce the observed diversity, while the predicted temporal spacing between shells provides a diagnostic of the inter‑pulse period. Text: TeV J2032+4130 was the first Galactic very-high-energy (VHE) gamma-ray source discovered without a clear counterpart at lower wavelengths. Situated on the periphery of the massive Cygnus OB2 association, its nature-whether a pulsar wind nebula, supernova remnant, or collective stellar wind interaction-remains debated. X-ray observations are crucial for discriminating among these scenarios by probing non-thermal particle populations and possible synchrotron counterparts. We performed a deep (∼120 ks) observation of the TeV J2032+4130 field with XMM-Newton's EPIC-MOS and PN cameras. After standard flare filtering, we generated exposure-corrected images in the 0.5-10 keV band and constructed a point-source catalog using a maximum-likelihood algorithm. To isolate diffuse emission, detected point sources were excised and the residual maps were smoothed. Spectral properties of the extended component were derived via simultaneous fitting of MOS and PN spectra with absorbed power-law and thermal models, and the X-ray morphology was compared with the TeV excess map from HEGRA/VERITAS. We detect a faint, ≈12′-diameter X-ray nebula spatially coincident with the TeV centroid. Its spectrum is well described by an absorbed power law (photon index Γ = 2.1 ± 0.3, N_H ≈ 1.2 × 1022 cm⁻²) with an unabsorbed 2-10 keV flux of (3.4 ± 0.5) × 10⁻¹³ erg cm⁻² s⁻¹. No bright point source capable of powering the VHE emission is present. The X-ray to TeV flux ratio and spectral slope favor a leptonic origin, consistent with a pulsar wind nebula powered by an as-yet undetected pulsar, while a hadronic scenario would require unrealistically high ambient densities. These provide the first robust X-ray counterpart to TeV J2032+4130 and significantly narrow the range of viable emission mechanisms.

Text: Here, we investigate the stability of Salpeter solutions, which describe the distribution of matter in spherically symmetric, isothermal, polytropic gas spheres with a constant specific entropy. We derive the Salpeter equation, a differential equation governing the mass distribution of these systems, and examine the conditions under which the solutions remain stable. By applying the Rayleigh criterion for stability, we analyze the behavior of small perturbations to the Salpeter solutions, focusing on the effects of the gas's adiabatic index and the polytropic index on the stability of the system. Our results demonstrate that, for certain ranges of the adiabatic index and polytropic index, the Salpeter solutions exhibit a stable oscillatory behavior, while for other ranges, they exhibit a stable monotonic behavior. We also identify the boundary between these regimes and provide a quantitative estimate of the stability threshold. These findings have implications for our understanding of the structure and evolution of self-gravitating gas spheres, such as globular clusters and dwarf galaxies, and highlight the importance of considering the stability of Salpeter solutions in astrophysical contexts.

Text: The earliest phases of clustered star formation and the origin of the stellar initial mass function (IMF) are currently much debated. In order to constrain the origin of the IMF, we investigated the internal and relative motions of starless condensations and protostars previously detected by us in the dust continuum at 1.2mm in the L1688 protocluster of the Ophiuchus molecular cloud complex. The starless condensations have a mass spectrum resembling the IMF and are therefore likely representative of the initial stages of star formation in the protocluster. We carried out detailed molecular line observations, including some N2H+(1-0) mapping, of the Ophiuchus protocluster condensations using the IRAM 30m telescope. We measured subsonic or at most transonic levels of internal turbulence within the condensations, implying virial masses which generally agree within a factor of ~ 2 with the masses derived from the 1.2mm dust continuum. This supports the notion that most of the L1688 starless condensations are gravitationally bound and prestellar in nature. We measured a global one-dimensional velocity dispersion of less than 0.4 km/s between condensations. This small relative velocity dispersion implies that, in general, the condensations do not have time to interact with one another before evolving into pre-main sequence objects. Our observations support the view that the IMF is partly determined by cloud fragmentation at the prestellar stage. Competitive accretion is unlikely to be the dominant mechanism at the protostellar stage in the Ophiuchus protocluster, but it may possibly govern the growth of starless, self-gravitating condensations initially produced by gravoturbulent fragmentation toward an IMF, Salpeter-like mass spectrum.

Text: This paper presents a comprehensive analysis of the Hopf-Schur group of a field, a fundamental concept in the study of algebraic K-theory and its connection to the arithmetic of fields. We provide a detailed investigation of the structure and properties of KS(F), including its relationship to the algebraic K-theory and the Brauer group of F. Specifically, we establish a precise connection between KS(F) and the Picard group of the category of finite-dimensional projective modules over the group ring of the Galois group of F. Furthermore, we provide a new criterion for determining the vanishing of KS(F) in terms of the arithmetic properties of F, such as the presence of a finite residue field or the existence of a non-trivial unramified extension. Our have significant implications for the study of algebraic K-theory and its applications in number theory and algebraic geometry. The techniques employed in this paper rely on a combination of homotopy theory, algebraic geometry, and Galois cohomology.

Text: We present a novel application of the AdS/CFT correspondence to investigate the viscosity and jet quenching phenomena in high-energy nuclear collisions. By evaluating the holographic dual of the Wilson loop, we compute the jet quenching parameter, quantifying the extent to which the parton energy is dissipated as it propagates through the plasma. Text: Acoustic solitons-self-localized, nondispersive wave packets-have been studied in fluids, solids, and metamaterials, yet conventional classifications (bright, dark, gap) do not capture recent observations in nonlinear phononic lattices with tailored dispersion. We employed a combined analytical-numerical approach. Starting from the generalized nonlinear Schrödinger equation augmented with higher-order dispersion and nonlocal nonlinear terms, we derived exact solutions using the inverse scattering transform and variational techniques. Parallel finite-difference time-domain simulations were performed on 1-D and 2-D phononic-crystal waveguides with engineered band-gaps. Experimental validation employed laser-ultrasonic excitation of micro-fabricated silicon-nitride membranes, with interferometric detection of the resulting pressure fields. Two previously unreported families of acoustic solitons were identified: (i) hybrid bright-dark solitons that coexist within a single band gap, exhibiting a phase-locked core-tail structure, and (ii) topological acoustic solitons that inherit a quantized vortex charge from the underlying lattice symmetry. Both families demonstrate robust propagation over >10⁴ wavelengths with negligible radiation loss and can be dynamically switched by modest changes in excitation amplitude. Crucially, these expand the taxonomy of acoustic solitary waves and suggest new routes for information transport in phononic devices.

Text: A comprehensive theoretical examination of the motional frequency shifts of ions confined within the Lamb-Dicke regime is presented, where the translational motion of the ion is effectively localized to a diminutive spatial domain within its wave function. By integrating perturbation theory with numerical simulations, we have formulated an analytical expression for the frequency shift of the ion's vibrational mode, which comprehensively accounts for the influences of both the confining potential and the ion's inherent dynamics. Notably, our indicate a direct proportionality between the frequency shift and the square of the Lamb-Dicke parameter, a characteristic that quantifies the extent of overlap between the ion's wave function and the confining potential. Furthermore, a critical Lamb-Dicke parameter is identified, below which the frequency shift becomes vanishingly small, thereby demarcating the onset of the Lamb-Dicke regime. The implications of our are far-reaching, holding significant relevance for the design and operation of trapped ion systems, particularly in the contexts of quantum computing and precision spectroscopy, where precise control over the ion's vibrational modes is of paramount importance. Notably, the accuracy of our analytical expression is substantiated through a comparative validation with numerical simulations, thereby underscoring its utility for generating quantitative predictions of motional frequency shifts in trapped ion systems.

Text: This study presents an extensive investigation into the environmental context of TW Hya, a paradigmatic low-mass young star situated approximately 60 parsecs from Earth. High-resolution, mid-infrared imaging has enabled us to unveil a multifaceted environment surrounding TW Hya, characterized by the presence of a circumstellar disk, outflows, and possibly a jet structure. Mid-infrared images have revealed a distinct disk feature, corroborating earlier obtained through near-infrared and submillimeter observations. The implementation of high-contrast imaging techniques, such as adaptive optics and spatial filtering, has facilitated the detection of faint disk structures and potential companions. Spectral energy distribution (SED) analysis of the mid-infrared regime indicates an abundance of dust emission, potentially indicative of dust processing and grain growth within the disk. Furthermore, our investigations suggest the presence of a hot disk component, likely associated with the processes of active accretion and star-disk interactions. Consequently, our study provides novel insights into the morphology, composition, and dynamics of the TW Hya disk system. The high spatial resolution of our mid-infrared observations has significantly contributed to a deeper understanding of the initial stages of star formation, underscoring the crucial role that low-mass young stars play in shaping their surrounding environments. Ultimately, the of this research enhance our comprehension of the complex interplays governing the evolution of these stellar systems. **Keywords:** TW Hya, low-mass young star, mid-infrared imaging, circumstellar disk, outflows, star-disk interactions.

Text: The de Haas‑van Alphen (dHvA) effect in quasi‑one‑dimensional conductors provides a unique probe of electronic structure under simultaneous spatial confinement and magnetic quantization. Taken together, here we introduce a comprehensive evaluation of dHvA oscillations in metallic nanowires whose transverse dimensions method the electronic Fermi wavelength, thereby inducing size‑quantized subbands that coexist with Landau levels generated by a longitudinal magnetic field. By contrast, using a self‑consistent semiclassical quantization scheme that incorporates both the transverse confinement potential and the orbital magnetic response, we derive analytic expressions for the oscillatory magnetization, revealing a hierarchy of frequency components given by linear combinations of the fundamental bulk cyclotron frequency and the subband spacing, while numerical evaluation for Au and Cu nanowires (diameters 5–30 nm) demonstrates a pronounced modulation of amplitude and phase as a function of field strength, temperature, and wire diameter, including beat patterns arising from inter‑subband interference. The crossover from bulk‑like dHvA behavior to a regime dominated by size quantization occurs when the magnetic length becomes comparable to the wire radius, a condition verified by low‑temperature torque magnetometry, while our results elucidate the interplay of Landau and size quantizations, offering design criteria for nanostructured devices where quantum oscillatory phenomena can be engineered through dimensional control.

These have implications for our understanding of high-energy phenomena and the behavior of particles in extreme environments, such as those found in early universe cosmology or near black hole event horizons. Text: Several luminosity indicators have been found for Gamma-Ray Bursts (GRBs) wherein measurable light curve and spectral properties are well-correlated with the peak luminosity. Several papers have each applied one different luminosity relation to find redshifts for BATSE GRBs and claim to identify specific bursts with z>8. The existence of such high redshift events is not surprising, as BATSE has enough sensitivity to see them and GRBs are expected out to the redshift of the first star formation. To improve we used five luminosity relations with updated calibrations to determine redshifts with error bars. Combining these relations, we calculated the redshifts of 36 BATSE GRBs with claimed z>8. Our include 13 bursts with our derived best redshift z_best>8, which looks promising at first. But the calculated redshift uncertainties are significantly large in these selected cases. With only one exception, all of our bursts have z_1siglow<9. The one exception (BATSE trigger 2035) is likely a short duration burst at z>~4. Our best case for a very high redshift event is BATSE trigger 3142 with z_best>20 and z_1siglow=8.9, however we can only say z>4.1 at the two-sigma confidence level. In all, we cannot point toward any one BATSE burst as confidently having z>8. One implication is to greatly weaken prior claims that GRBs have a steeply rising rate-density out to high redshifts.

Text: Peer pressure is the social force that pushes individuals to conform to the behaviors, attitudes, and choices of their peer group, often at the expense of their own values, judgment, or wellbeing. Understanding peer pressure requires understanding the fundamental human need for belonging, which is so powerful that most people will compromise their own preferences to preserve it. By employing a systematic expansion in the inverse Planck length $1/\ell_{\mathrm{P}}$, the total entropy is expressed as a power series, including logarithmic and polynomial corrections that deviate from semi-classical predictions. This calculation leverages a framework consistent with effective field theory, ensuring ultraviolet finiteness at each order through dimensionful coupling constants. The derived entropy formula aligns with known semi-classical in the limit $\ell_{\mathrm{P}} \to 0$ while introducing novel terms such as $\ln(A/\ell_{\mathrm{P}}^2)$ and $1/\ell_{\mathrm{P}}^2$ contributions, which encode information about the quantum geometry of spacetime. These corrections are crucial for resolving ambiguities in black hole thermodynamics at the Planck scale and provide a bridge between classical general relativity and quantum gravity, underscoring the necessity of all-order analyses to address the holographic principle and the microscopic degrees of freedom governing black hole entropy. This work advances theoretical understanding of gravitational entropy and offers testable predictions for future high-precision astrophysical observations in regimes where quantum gravity effects may manifest.

Text: Single‑spin asymmetries (SSAs) in hadronic reactions provide a unique window onto the transverse spin structure of the nucleon and the dynamics of color interactions beyond the leading‑twist approximation. While sizable SSAs have been observed in inclusive processes such as semi‑inclusive deep‑inelastic scattering (SIDIS) and Drell–Yan production, their origin in exclusive channels—where the final state is fully constrained—remains less explored. Reconciling these phenomena within a unified QCD framework is essential for a comprehensive picture of spin‑orbit correlations and the role of gauge‑invariant transverse‑momentum‑dependent (TMD) distributions and generalized parton distributions (GPDs). We performed a combined phenomenological analysis of high‑precision SSA measurements from COMPASS, Jefferson Lab, and RHIC, employing a factorized description that incorporates TMD evolution for inclusive observables and a collinear twist‑3 formalism for exclusive meson electro‑production. Theoretical inputs include the Sivers and Collins functions extracted from global fits, and the chiral‑odd GPD \(H_T\) constrained by lattice QCD. Consistency checks were carried out via a matching procedure linking the TMD and collinear regimes. The analysis demonstrates that the same underlying quark–gluon correlation functions generate SSAs across inclusive and exclusive processes, with the Sivers mechanism dominating the inclusive sector and the interference of chiral‑odd GPDs driving asymmetries in exclusive \(\pi^0\) and \(\rho^0\) production. Quantitative agreement with the measured asymmetries is achieved within systematic uncertainties, supporting a unified description of transverse spin phenomena in QCD.

Text: This study systematically examines the geometric and arithmetic characteristics of multiplicative constructs derived from Brauer–Severi surfaces, which are algebraic manifolds generalizing projective planes over non-algebraically closed fields. These surfaces are distinguished by their nontrivial Galois twists and their systematic parameterization via the Brauer group of the underlying field. The structural attributes of these multiplicative constructs are scrutinized through an analytical framework integrating étale cohomology and descent theory, with particular emphasis on invariants including the cohomological Brauer group, field extensions facilitating decomposition, and the existence of rational structures. These contributions significantly advance the comprehension of algebraic surfaces within birational geometry, with profound ramifications for the investigation of central simple algebras and their corresponding geometric realizations. The research synthesizes classical algebraic geometry with contemporary cohomological methodologies, providing novel perspectives on the categorization of algebraic manifolds across arbitrary ground fields.

Text: The behavior of scalar fields on black-hole spacetimes is central to the stability analysis of general relativity. We consider the Cauchy problem for the scalar wave equation □_g ψ = 0 on the maximally extended De Sitter-Schwarzschild manifold (M,g). Using a combination of spectral decomposition, microlocal analysis, and vector-field multiplier techniques, we construct a hierarchy of energy currents adapted to the red-shift region near the event horizon and to the cosmological horizon. Quasimode constructions are employed to exhibit resonant states associated with the photon sphere. The analysis is carried out in weighted Sobolev spaces that capture both the near-horizon and asymptotic de Sitter regimes. We prove that for generic smooth, compactly supported initial data the local energy decays exponentially in time, with a rate determined by the surface gravities of the two horizons. Conversely, we exhibit a family of non-trivial initial data leading to persistent local energy due to trapped null geodesics, establishing sharp thresholds for decay versus non-decay. These reconcile earlier conflicting predictions and provide a rigorous foundation for further nonlinear investigations.

Text: This article delves into the investigation of a class of bounded linear operators on a complex Hilbert space, specifically those that satisfy the \((\alpha ,\beta )\)-normality condition, \(\alpha\,T^{*}T\le TT^{*}\le \beta\,T^{*}T\), where \(0<\alpha \le \beta\), thereby encompassing and generalising the properties of normal, hyponormal, and co-hyponormal operators. Notably, this area of study has garnered significant attention in recent times due to its potential for elucidating the geometric and spectral characteristics of these operators. The primary objective of this paper is to establish a suite of sharp norm and numerical-radius inequalities that explicitly incorporate the parameters \(\alpha\) and \(\beta\), thus providing a nuanced understanding of the operator's properties. Specifically, it is demonstrated that \(\|T\|^{2}\le \beta\,w(T)^{2}\) and \(w(T)^{2}\le \frac{\alpha +\beta }{2}\,\|T\|^{2}\), where \(w(T)\) denotes the numerical radius, thereby establishing a fundamental relationship between the norm and the numerical radius of the operator. Furthermore, this study extends the existing literature by deriving bounds for the spectral radius \(r(T)\), specifically \(r(T)\le \sqrt{\beta}\,\|T\|\) and \(r(T)\ge \sqrt{\alpha}\,\|T\|\), and providing conditions for equality, thus shedding light on the operator's eigenvalue distribution. Additionally, this research provides perturbation estimates for \((\alpha ,\beta )\)-normal operators and demonstrates their stability under additive compact perturbations, thereby underscoring their significance in the context of operator equations and spectral approximation in infinite-dimensional settings.

Text: Carbon Nanotube Field-Effect Transistors (CNTFETs) have garnered significant attention due to their exceptional electrical properties. The n+-i-n+ CNTFET configuration, in particular, has shown great promise for high-speed and low-power applications. However, the impact of dispersion on the ballistic transport in these devices remains poorly understood. We employed a self-consistent quantum mechanical simulation framework to investigate the effects of dispersion on the performance of ballistic n+-i-n+ CNTFETs. The simulations took into account the electron-phonon interactions, as well as the acoustic and optical phonon modes. Our indicate that dispersion significantly affects the on-state current and transconductance of the CNTFETs. The acoustic phonon modes were found to dominate the dispersion-induced degradation, resulting in a reduction of up to 20% in the on-state current. Furthermore, the optical phonon modes were observed to introduce additional scattering mechanisms, leading to a decrease in the device's switching speed. These provide valuable insights into the optimization of CNTFET performances and highlight the importance of considering dispersion effects in the design of future nanoscale devices.

Text: Through a novel theoretical framework, we have formulated a class number formula for real quadratic number fields, thereby offering a paradigmatic approach to the computation of class numbers and the ascertaining of the parity of the number of ideal classes in such fields. By capitalizing on the discriminant function's inherent properties and the behavior of the reduced discriminant, we have elucidated a symbiotic relationship between the class number and the critical values of the L-function associated with the real quadratic field, thereby enabling the computation of the class number as a sum of critical values. This relationship, in turn, facilitates the determination of the parity of the number of ideal classes, thereby underscoring the utility of our formula. Notably, our class number formula is applicable to a broad spectrum of real quadratic fields and provides an efficient computational framework for determining class numbers and ideal class group structures, with far-reaching implications extending to various areas of number theory, including the study of L-functions and the arithmetic of quadratic fields.

Text: This investigation examines the interplay between final-state interactions (FSI) and hadron suppression in cold nuclear matter (CNM), elucidating their collective influence on the attenuation of high-transverse-momentum hadron yields in nuclear collisions. By integrating advanced theoretical frameworks—such as parton cascade simulations and coherence-based FSI models—with empirical datasets from JLab, RHIC, and fixed-target experiments, this analysis deciphers the relative contributions of FSI-driven coherence phenomena and parton energy dissipation to quenching mechanisms. demonstrate that FSI, characterized by coherent multiple scattering and rescattering processes within the nuclear medium, predominantly attenuates hadron production at intermediate transverse momenta (1–3 GeV/c), whereas energy loss effects dominate quenching at higher momentum thresholds (>3 GeV/c). Comparative analyses of deuteron-gold collisions against proton-proton benchmarks reveal a momentum-dependent transition between FSI-dominated suppression and energy-loss-driven quenching, with the former prevailing below 2 GeV/c and the latter above. These challenge prevailing models that isolate energy loss as the sole contributor to hadron suppression, underscoring the necessity of incorporating FSI effects to accurately characterize nuclear matter dynamics. Additionally, the study identifies a correlation between FSI-induced quenching and the nuclear mass dependence of the Cronin effect, implying that coherent rescattering amplifies suppression in larger nuclei. This work provides a comprehensive framework for disentangling FSI and energy loss phenomena in CNM, offering critical insights into partonic system evolution under dense nuclear conditions and informing future experimental programs at facilities such as FAIR and the Electron-Ion Collider (EIC).

Text: We examine the applicability of multivariate normal approximation in geometric probability, particularly in the context of Poisson point processes. Text: Array‑OL is a high‑level, array‑oriented language designed to express data‑parallel algorithms for heterogeneous architectures. While its expressive power simplifies algorithmic development, systematic optimization requires a rigorous understanding of the elementary transformations (e.g., reshaping, permuting, slicing, and fusing) that preserve semantic equivalence. Existing work on transformation correctness is fragmented, lacking a unified analytical framework that can be applied automatically to large‑scale Array‑OL programs. We develop a formal calculus of elementary transformations based on an extended polyhedral model that captures both index‑affine and non‑affine array accesses typical of Array‑OL. The calculus is expressed as a set of inference rules implemented in a static analysis tool that performs interpretation of loop nests, dependence graphs, and data‑layout descriptors. Transformation candidates are generated, validated for dependence‑preserving legality, and ranked using a cost model that incorporates memory‑traffic, parallel granularity, and target‑specific constraints. The approach is evaluated on a benchmark suite comprising 28 kernels from image processing, linear algebra, and machine‑learning domains. The analysis identifies an average of 3.7 legal elementary transformations per kernel, enabling automatic generation of 12 %–28 % reduction in memory bandwidth and 15 %–34 % speed‑up on a CPU‑GPU heterogeneous platform. Moreover, the calculus proves transformation equivalence for all tested kernels, confirming its soundness and demonstrating its utility as a foundation for higher‑level Array‑OL optimizers.

We show that the distribution of future phylogenetic diversity converges to a normal distribution as the number of species grows (under mild conditions, which are necessary). Text: The response of dense granular assemblies to localized excitations is investigated through a combined experimental–numerical study aimed at elucidating the mechanisms governing unjamming, stability, and the spatial decay of induced displacements. Two-dimensional packings of frictional disks are prepared at volume fractions spanning the jamming transition and are subjected to controlled perturbations generated by a calibrated intruder that imposes a prescribed displacement or force at a single grain. High‑resolution photoelastic imaging and discrete element simulations reveal that unjamming initiates when the perturbation exceeds a critical threshold that depends non‑monotonically on the initial coordination number and interparticle friction coefficient. Above this threshold, the displacement field exhibits a robust power‑law decay, \(u(r)\sim r^{-\alpha}\), with an exponent \(\alpha\) that varies from 1.0 to 1.5 as the system approaches marginal stability. The temporal evolution follows a stretched‑exponential relaxation, indicating a broad spectrum of relaxation times associated with heterogeneous force chain rearrangements. Scaling analyses demonstrate that the critical perturbation magnitude and decay exponent collapse onto universal curves when expressed in terms of the distance to the jamming point. These provide quantitative criteria for predicting the onset of flow in granular media and underscore the role of local perturbations in destabilizing otherwise jammed configurations.

Text: **Photogalvanic effects in HgTe quantum wells** .** HgTe quantum wells (QWs) are model systems for two-dimensional topological insulators, exhibiting strong spin-orbit coupling and inverted band structures. Their unique band topology makes them promising platforms for spin-photonic devices, yet the mechanisms of light-induced charge transport-photogalvanic effects (PGE)-remain incompletely understood. .** We fabricated high-mobility HgTe QWs (8-12 nm thick) on CdTe substrates and patterned Hall bars for electrical detection. The samples were illuminated with tunable mid-infrared and terahertz lasers (λ = 4-100 µm) under controlled linear and circular polarization. Time-resolved photocurrent measurements were performed at 4-300 K, while gate voltages tuned the Fermi level across the bulk gap. Symmetry analysis and microscopic modeling were employed to disentangle linear and circular PGE contributions. .** We observed pronounced linear and circular PGEs whose amplitudes scale linearly with light intensity and vary strongly with polarization angle, confirming their symmetry-allowed origin. The circular PGE exhibits a reversal of sign upon switching the helicity, evidencing spin-dependent asymmetric scattering of photoexcited carriers. Temperature dependence reveals a crossover from bulk-dominated to edge-state dominated transport at low temperatures, with the circular PGE persisting in the topological regime. Crucially, these demonstrate that HgTe QWs provide a tunable platform for generating spin-polarized photocurrents, advancing the understanding of light-matter interactions in topological semiconductors and informing the design of optically controlled spintronic devices.

Text: This study presents a comprehensive theoretical framework for understanding the role of fission cycling in the nucleosynthesis of heavy elements during the explosive phase of a supernova, specifically in the context of rapid neutron capture processes (r-process). Our calculations reveal that fission cycling, where fissioning nuclei undergo repeated cycles of neutron capture and subsequent fission, significantly enhances the production of heavy elements, particularly those with atomic masses A > 250. This process is shown to be crucial for the formation of the heaviest r-process nuclei, which are thought to be primarily synthesized in supernovae. Our indicate that fission cycling can increase the yields of these elements by factors of up to 5, compared to models that neglect this process. Text: In this study, we investigate the effects of crystal grinding on the specific heat of PrOs$_4$Sb$_{12}$, a heavy fermion superconductor with a complex electronic structure. Our suggest that the two transitions arise from the presence of two distinct superconducting phases, corresponding to the A and B crystallographic sites in the PrOs$_4$Sb$_{12}$ crystal structure. These are consistent with a scenario in which the crystal grinding process introduces defects and strain into the crystal lattice, which in turn affect the superconducting properties of PrOs$_4$Sb$_{12}$. Text: Two versions of a fast, purely reflective Paul-Baker type telescope are discussed, each with an 8.4-m aperture, 3 deg diameter flat field and f/1.25 focal ratio. Text: The double shuffle relations of Euler sums have garnered significant attention in recent years due to their profound implications in number theory and algebraic geometry. Euler sums, which are defined as the summation of products of harmonic numbers and zeta values, have been found to satisfy a plethora of intriguing relations, including the double shuffle relations. These relations, which involve the interplay between the shuffle product and the stuffle product, have been shown to be intimately connected to the combinatorial and algebraic structures underlying Euler sums. Through a combination of algebraic manipulations and combinatorial arguments, we demonstrate that the double shuffle relations of Euler sums can be used to derive a wide range of identities and congruences, including those involving the Riemann zeta function and the multiple zeta functions. Our have far-reaching implications for the study of Euler sums and their connections to other areas of mathematics, and provide a foundation for further research into the properties and applications of these enigmatic objects. Furthermore, the double shuffle relations have been found to be closely related to the study of motivic Galois groups and the Grothendieck-Teichmüller group, highlighting the deep connections between Euler sums and the broader landscape of algebraic geometry and number theory.

Text: We present the observation of Very High Energy (VHE) gamma-ray emission from Cassiopeia A (Cas A), a supernova remnant located at a distance of approximately 3.4 kiloparsecs, using the MAGIC telescope array. Text: The nuclear pore complex (NPC) is the sole conduit for macromolecular exchange between the nucleus and cytoplasm, yet the physical principles governing passive diffusion of diverse cargos through its intrinsically disordered FG‑repeat meshwork remain incompletely resolved. Clarifying how size, shape, and surface chemistry modulate translocation rates is essential for elucidating cellular homeostasis and for designing nucleocytoplasmic delivery vectors. We combined high‑speed single‑molecule fluorescence microscopy with quantitative photobleaching analysis to track fluorescently labeled proteins and polysaccharide probes ranging from 2 kDa to 150 kDa in live HeLa cells. Diffusion coefficients were extracted using Bayesian hidden‑Markov modeling of trajectories captured at 1 kHz. Parallel coarse‑grained molecular dynamics simulations of the NPC scaffold incorporated experimentally derived FG‑repeat interaction potentials, enabling direct comparison between observed transport kinetics and theoretical predictions. Passive diffusion exhibited a sharp size‑dependent cutoff at ~40 kDa (hydrodynamic radius ≈ 2.5 nm), beyond which transport rates declined exponentially (τ ∝ e^{αR}). Positively charged cargos displayed a 2‑fold increase in dwell time relative to neutral counterparts, implicating electrostatic coupling with FG repeats. Simulations reproduced these trends and identified transient “hydrogel‑like” regions that selectively retard larger, charged molecules. The integrated experimental‑computational framework thus delineates quantitative limits of NPC‑mediated diffusion and provides a mechanistic basis for selective permeability.

Text: The phase‑time (or Wigner‑time) formulation remains a cornerstone for quantifying the duration of quantum tunnelling, yet discrepancies between its predictions and high‑precision attosecond experiments suggest the presence of overlooked contributions. Small corrections arising from the finite spatial extent of the barrier, non‑parabolic dispersion, and relativistic mass‑renormalisation may reconcile theory with observation. Starting from the one‑dimensional time‑independent Schrödinger equation, we perform a systematic perturbative expansion of the transmission amplitude for a generic smooth barrier \(V(x)\). The stationary‑phase approximation is applied to the exact wave‑packet integral, retaining terms up to second order in the barrier‑gradient parameter \(\epsilon = \hbar k_0^{-1}\partial_x V/V\). Transfer‑matrix techniques yield analytic expressions for the corrected phase shift, from which the modified tunnelling time \(\tau = \tau_{\mathrm{W}} + \delta\tau\) is derived. Numerical simulations employing split‑operator propagation validate the analytical across a range of barrier heights, widths, and incident energies. The correction \(\delta\tau\) scales as \(\epsilon^2\) and can reach up to 5 % of the conventional Wigner time for sub‑nanometre barriers with steep edges. Inclusion of these terms eliminates the apparent super‑luminal tunnelling predictions and aligns the theoretical phase time with recent attosecond streaking measurements within experimental uncertainty. The underscore the necessity of higher‑order phase‑time corrections for accurate temporal characterisation of quantum tunnelling phenomena.

Text: We investigated the inhomogeneous electronic properties at the surface and interior of VO_{2} thin films that exhibit a strong first-order metal-insulator transition (MIT). The temperature dependence of the p$^{XRD}$ was very closely correlated with the dc conductivity near the MIT temperature, and fit the percolation theory predictions quite well: $\sigma$ $\sim$ (p - p_{c})^{t} with t = 2.0$\pm$0.1 and p_{c} = 0.16$\pm$0.01. This agreement demonstrates that in our VO$_{2}$ thin film, the MIT should occur during the percolation process. We also used surface-sensitive scanning tunneling spectroscopy (STS) to investigate the microscopic evolution of the MIT near the surface. Similar to the XRD , STS maps revealed a systematic decrease in the metallic phase as temperature decreased. However, this rate of change was much slower than the rate observed with XRD, indicating that the electronic inhomogeneity near the surface differs greatly from that inside the film. We investigated several possible origins of this discrepancy, and postulated that the variety in the strain states near the surface plays an important role in the broad MIT observed using STS. Text: Although both electron-ion and electron-electron bremsstrahlung contribute to the hard X-ray emission from solar flares, the latter is normally ignored. Such an omission is not justified at electron (and photon) energies above $sim 300$ keV, and inclusion of the additional electron-electron bremsstrahlung in general makes the electron spectrum required to produce a given hard X-ray spectrum steeper at high energies. Unlike electron-ion bremsstrahlung, electron-electron bremsstrahlung cannot produce photons of all energies up to the maximum electron energy involved. The maximum possible photon energy depends on the angle between the direction of the emitting electron and the emitted photon, and this suggests a diagnostic for an upper cutoff energy and/or for the degree of beaming of the accelerated electrons. We analyze the large event of January 17, 2005 observed by RHESSI and show that the upward break around 400 keV in the observed hard X-ray spectrum is naturally accounted for by the inclusion of electron-electron bremsstrahlung. Indeed, the mean source electron spectrum recovered through a regularized inversion of the hard X-ray spectrum, using a cross-section that includes both electron-ion and electron-electron terms, has a relatively constant spectral index $delta$ over the range from electron kinetic energy $E = 200$ keV to $E = 1$ MeV. However, the level of detail discernible in the recovered electron spectrum is not sufficient to determine whether or not any upper cutoff energy exists.

Our results reveal notable variations in the total transmission profiles across the different filter bands, with the U and V filters exhibiting the highest transmission levels. Conversely, the J, H, and K filters exhibit reduced transmission efficiency due to the presence of atmospheric absorption lines and the increased sensitivity of the grism substrates to these filters' wavelengths. The derived transmission profiles were then compared to the nominal filter transmission curves provided by the ESO, highlighting discrepancies that can impact the accuracy of photometric measurements. These findings underscore the importance of accurate filter transmission profiles in ensuring reliable astronomical observations and suggest that updates to the ESO's filter calibration data may be necessary to reconcile our outcomes with nominal values.

Text: In a comprehensive analysis of 429 million B-meson decays garnered by the BaBar experiment at the PEP-II B-factory, we have undertaken a precise measurement of the Cabibbo-Kobayashi-Maskawa (CKM) angle gamma, a pivotal parameter in the Standard Model of particle physics. The investigation specifically focused on the B-+- to D*([K0s pi- pi+])K*-[K- pi0 pi+] decay mode, wherein the D* and K* mesons were reconstructed in their respective final states, thereby enabling the determination of the measured branching fraction of this process to be (1.44 +/- 0.15 +/- 0.09)*10^-4. Leveraging the isospin relationship between the D* and K* decay channels, we effectively extracted the relative weak phase gamma from the ratio of the time-dependent CP asymmetries in the B-+- to D*([K0s pi- pi+])K*- and B-+- to D*([K- pi0 pi+])K* decays, yielding a value of gamma = (85 +/- 13 +/- 5) degrees, where the first uncertainty constitutes the statistical component and the second pertains to the systematic errors inherent in this measurement. Notably, this result signifies a substantial advancement over previous determinations of gamma in this decay mode, thereby contributing to the ongoing endeavors aimed at establishing the CKM angle gamma with a high degree of precision.

Text: Supermassive black holes have generally been recognized as the most destructive force in nature. But in recent years, they have undergone a dramatic shift in paradigm. Possibly half of all the radiation produced after the Big Bang may be attributed to them, whose number is now known to exceed 300 million. The most accessible among them is situated at the Center of Our Galaxy. In the following pages, we will examine the evidence that has brought us to this point, and we will understand why many expect to actually image the event horizon of the Galaxy's central black hole within this decade.

Text: The accelerating expansion of the universe, first observed in the late 1990s, has been attributed to a mysterious entity known as dark energy. However, the underlying mechanism driving this phenomenon remains poorly understood. Recent studies have suggested that the Casimir force, a quantum fluctuation-induced effect, may play a role in the acceleration of the universe. We employed a theoretical framework combining quantum field theory and cosmology to investigate the potential impact of the Casimir force on the universe's expansion. Our model considered the Casimir force as a negative pressure component, which was incorporated into the Friedmann-Lemaître-Robertson-Walker (FLRW) equations. Our indicate that the Casimir force can indeed contribute to the acceleration of the universe, particularly at large scales. The calculated acceleration matches the observed value of the cosmological constant, providing a potential alternative explanation for the acceleration of the universe. Furthermore, our model predicts a scale-dependent behavior, which may be tested through future observations of the cosmic microwave radiation and large-scale structure. These offer a new perspective on the role of quantum fluctuations in shaping the evolution of the universe.

Text: We investigate the role of gauged discrete symmetries in safeguarding proton stability within a broad class of grand‑unified and supersymmetric extensions of the Standard Model. By promoting traditionally global discrete symmetries (e.g., matter parity, baryon‑triality) to gauge symmetries, we enforce exact conservation laws that survive quantum gravitational effects, which are expected to violate global charges. We formulate a systematic anomaly‑cancellation criterion for discrete gauge groups $\mathbb{Z}_N$ embedded in continuous gauge factors, and we classify all viable $\mathbb{Z}_N$ charge assignments that simultaneously forbid all dimension‑four and dimension‑five baryon‑number‑violating operators while allowing realistic Yukawa couplings and neutrino mass generation. The resulting models predict proton lifetimes exceeding current experimental bounds by several orders of magnitude, with characteristic decay channels dictated by the residual unbroken symmetry. We further explore the phenomenological signatures of the associated discrete gauge bosons and domain‑wall dynamics, demonstrating consistency with cosmological constraints. Our analysis establishes gauged discrete symmetries as a robust, model‑independent mechanism for proton protection, offering concrete targets for forthcoming proton‑decay searches and collider probes of exotic discrete gauge sectors.

Text: The observed baryon number density (n_B) and the cosmological constant (Λ) represent two of the most puzzling parameters in contemporary cosmology. While Λ governs the accelerated expansion of the Universe, n_B encodes the net matter–antimatter asymmetry generated during baryogenesis. Both quantities are extraordinarily small in natural units, prompting speculation that a common underlying mechanism may link them. This work investigates whether a quantitative interrelation can arise within standard ΛCDM cosmology augmented by plausible extensions of particle physics. We adopt a multi‑pronged theoretical approach. First, we derive consistency conditions from the Friedmann equations, expressing Λ in terms of the present critical density and n_B via the baryon‐to‑photon ratio η. Second, we construct an effective field theory wherein a dynamical vacuum energy couples to a conserved baryon current through a dimension‑six operator, and we evaluate its impact on the evolution of Λ during the electroweak epoch. Third, we confront the resulting parameter space with observational constraints from cosmic microwave anisotropies, big‑bang nucleosynthesis, and Type Ia supernovae. The analysis reveals that, under generic assumptions, any direct proportionality between n_B and Λ is severely limited: the induced vacuum energy contribution is at most 10⁻⁴⁰ of the observed Λ. However, a weak logarithmic dependence emerges in models with a time‑varying scalar field that simultaneously drives baryogenesis and dark energy. Consequently, while a strict linear interrelation is ruled out, a subtle correlation mediated by high‑scale physics remains viable and motivates further exploration of unified frameworks for matter–antimatter asymmetry and dark energy.

Text: This paper investigates two situations in which the forward kinematics of planar 3-RPR parallel manipulators degenerates. These situations have not been addressed before. The first degeneracy arises when the three input joint variables r1, r2 and r3 satisfy a certain relationship. This degeneracy yields a double root of the characteristic polynomial in t, which could be erroneously interpreted as two coalesce assembly modes. But, unlike what arises in non-degenerate cases, this double root yields two sets of solutions for the position coordinates (x, y) of the platform. In the second situation, we show that the forward kinematics degenerates over the whole joint space if the base and platform triangles are congruent and the platform triangle is rotated by 180 deg about one of its sides. For these "degenerate" manipulators, which are defined here for the first time, the forward kinematics is reduced to the solution of a 3rd-degree polynomial and a quadratics in sequence. Such manipulators constitute, in turn, a new family of analytic planar manipulators that would be more suitable for industrial applications.

Text: We present the first installment of a comprehensive panchromatic study of the Globular Cluster NGC 1904, focusing on the characteristics and evolution of its blue straggler population. Utilizing a combination of photometric and spectroscopic observations from the Hubble Space Telescope, the Kepler Space Telescope, and ground-based facilities, we have compiled a dataset of 2,500 cluster members spanning a wide wavelength range from the ultraviolet to the near-infrared. Our analysis reveals a diverse blue straggler population, comprising 120 objects, which exhibit a range of properties indicative of varying formation mechanisms. We find that the blue straggler distribution within the cluster is consistent with a mixture of mass-transfer and merger scenarios, with a significant fraction of objects displaying characteristics of recent stellar interactions. Our outcomes also suggest that the blue straggler population in NGC 1904 is not in a state of equilibrium, with ongoing stellar dynamics and evolution contributing to the observed distribution. we provide a foundation for further investigation into the complex dynamics and physics governing the evolution of globular cluster populations.

Text: This study explores the interplay between carbon-enhanced metal-poor (CEMP) stars, the cosmic microwave (CMB), and the stellar initial mass function (IMF) in the early universe. We employ a combination of simulations, observations, and theoretical modeling to investigate the role of CEMP stars in shaping the chemical evolution of the universe. Our suggest that CEMP stars, which are thought to be the descendants of massive stars that underwent explosive nucleosynthesis, played a significant role in enriching the interstellar medium with carbon and other heavy elements during the early universe. By comparing our simulations with observations of the CMB, we find that the IMF in the early universe was likely top-heavy, with a higher fraction of massive stars than observed in the present day. This implies that the early universe underwent a period of rapid star formation, which in turn influenced the thermal and density fluctuations in the universe, leaving a lasting imprint on the CMB. Our have significant implications for our understanding of the early universe and the chemical evolution of galaxies.

Text: Within the framework of stochastic systems, boundary-driven zero-range processes in random media exhibit a distinctive paradigm, wherein particles undergo exchange between neighboring sites in a randomly configured network, characterized by zero-range interactions and the non-conservation of particle numbers at each site. This investigation elucidates the role of random media in modulating the dynamic behavior of these processes, specifically the manner in which spatial disorder influences the emergent macroscopic behavior, manifesting as a non-trivial interplay between local and global dynamics. Employing a synergistic combination of analytical and numerical , we derived a set of mean-field equations that capture the evolution of particle density and current in the system, thereby providing a comprehensive framework for understanding the underlying mechanisms. Notably, our indicate that the presence of random media gives rise to anomalous transport phenomena, marked by a non-linear dependence of the particle current on the particle density, thereby deviating from the standard paradigm of Fickian diffusion. Furthermore, we observe a breakdown of the ergodic regime, accompanied by a crossover to a non-ergodic regime, wherein the particle distribution becomes effectively frozen in certain regions of the network, underscoring the intricate interplay between spatial disorder and emergent behavior. The implications of our extend to the realm of complex systems in disordered environments, potentially shedding light on the behavior of granular flow, traffic flow, and other stochastic systems, thereby underscoring their relevance to a broad range of disciplines.

Text: Resistive switching (RS) in complex oxides is a promising route toward next‑generation non‑volatile memory devices, yet the microscopic origin of the switching‐induced electronic rearrangements remains debated. Chromium‑doped strontium titanate (SrTiO₃:Cr) exhibits pronounced bipolar RS, suggesting that the dopant may modulate the local Ti–O network and create conductive filaments, but direct spectroscopic evidence linking structural changes to the resistive states is lacking. Thin‑film heterostructures of SrTiO₃:Cr (0.5 at % Cr) were fabricated by pulsed laser deposition on Nb‑doped SrTiO₃ substrates. Electrical biasing cycles generated distinct high‑resistance (HRS) and low‑resistance (LRS) states. In‑situ X‑ray absorption spectroscopy (XAS) at the Cr K‑edge, Ti K‑edge, and O K‑edge was performed at beamline 8‑ID of the Advanced Photon Source under controlled bias. Linear combination fitting and extended X‑ray absorption fine‑structure (EXAFS) analysis quantified oxidation‑state variations and bond‑length distortions. Complementary conductive atomic‑force microscopy mapped filamentary pathways. XAS reveals a reversible Cr³⁺→Cr⁴⁺ oxidation shift concomitant with a ~0.03 Å contraction of the Cr–O bond in the LRS, while Ti retains a Ti⁴⁺ valence but shows a subtle elongation of Ti–O bonds (≈0.02 Å). The O K‑edge pre‑edge intensity increases in the LRS, indicating enhanced Ti‑3d–O‑2p hybridization. These spectroscopic signatures correlate spatially with conductive filaments identified by AFM, supporting a model wherein Cr‑mediated redox activity nucleates oxygen‑vacancy‑rich filaments that dominate the RS behavior in SrTiO₃:Cr.

Text: A thorough examination of the radio afterglow phenomena exhibited by the gamma-ray burst GRB 030329 over a period of three years, commencing approximately 5 hours subsequent to the cataclysmic event, reveals an anomalous evolutionary trend. By virtue of sustained monitoring endeavors conducted utilizing the Very Large Array (VLA) and the Australia Telescope Compact Array (ATCA) at frequencies spanning 4.9 GHz to 8.6 GHz, we elucidate the radio afterglow's complex dynamics. Notably, our indicate that the radio afterglow of GRB 030329 demonstrates a non-conformist trajectory, characterized by an attenuated deceleration rate in flux density. Furthermore, the observed spectral flux densities during early epochs are found to be incongruous with a purely synchrotron self-absorbed (SSA) emission paradigm, suggesting the inculcation of inverse Compton scattering processes. To elucidate the observed afterglow evolution, we employ a synchrotron self-Compton (SSC) model incorporating a density gradient. The derived parameters, including the electron power-law index and the magnetic field strengt, correlate well with the predictions emanating from the SSC model, thereby providing substantial evidence for the preponderant role of SSC processes in the radio afterglow of GRB 030329. Our investigation underscores the significance of prolonged monitoring campaigns in probing the diverse emission mechanisms that regulate the comportment of gamma-ray burst afterglows.

Text: Clothing trends are the cyclical movements of style preference that sweep through consumer culture, shifting what is perceived as desirable, contemporary, and appropriate within particular social groups and market segments. They emerge from a complex interplay of forces: the creative decisions of designers, the editorial influence of fashion media, the adoption patterns of cultural figures and celebrities, the economic calculations of manufacturers and retailers, and increasingly the organic spread of aesthetic ideas through social media. Trend cycles have historically operated on seasonal rhythms tied to fashion industry calendars, but fast fashion and social media have accelerated and fragmented these cycles dramatically — trends can now emerge, peak, and become overexposed within weeks rather than seasons. This acceleration has been criticized for its environmental consequences and its effect on the quality of design, creating enormous pressure to produce novelty continuously rather than investing in enduring quality. The counter-trend of buying fewer, better-made pieces and developing personal style independent of seasonal dictates has gained cultural traction in response.

Text: We study the hydrodynamic limit for some conservative particle systems with degenerate rates, namely with nearest neighbor exchange rates which vanish for certain configurations. These models belong to the class of {\sl kinetically constrained lattice gases} (KCLG) which have been introduced and intensively studied in physics literature as simple models for the liquid/glass transition. Due to the degeneracy of rates for KCLG there exists {\sl blocked configurations} which do not evolve under the dynamics and in general the hyperplanes of configurations with a fixed number of particles can be decomposed into different irreducible sets. As a consequence, both the Entropy and Relative Entropy method cannot be straightforwardly applied to prove the hydrodynamic limit. In particular, some care should be put when proving the One and Two block Lemmas which guarantee local convergence to equilibrium. We show that, for initial profiles smooth enough and bounded away from zero and one, the macroscopic density profile for our KCLG evolves under the diffusive time scaling according to the porous medium equation. Then we prove the same result for more general profiles for a slightly perturbed dynamics obtained by adding jumps of the Symmetric Simple Exclusion. The role of the latter is to remove the degeneracy of rates and at the same time they are properly slowed down in order not to change the macroscopic behavior. The equilibrium fluctuations and the magnitude of the spectral gap for this perturbed model are also obtained.

Here we report the discovery of a new co-moving (13 sigma) stellar companion 17.8 arcsec (350 AU in projected separation) north of the nearby star HD141272 (21 pc). With EMMI/NTT optical spectroscopy we determined the spectral type of the companion to be M3+-0.5V. The derived spectral type as well as the near infrared photometry of the companion are both fully consistent with a 0.26+-0.07 Msol dwarf located at the distance of HD141272 (21 pc). Text: We present a comprehensive theoretical analysis of the Dark Particle, a hypothetical particle postulated to explain the observed phenomena of dark matter in the universe. By contrast, utilizing a combination of cosmological and particle physics constraints, we perform a global fit of the Dark Particle's mass and coupling to other Standard Model particles. Our approach is based on the Dark Sector model, where the Dark Particle is a scalar boson interacting with the Standard Model via a mediator particle. We derive the Dark Particle's relic density and abundance, taking into account the effects of annihilation, co-annihilation, and scattering processes. More broadly, our results reveal a degenerate solution space, where the Dark Particle's mass and coupling are highly correlated, with a narrow range of allowed values that satisfy both cosmological and particle physics constraints. We find that the Dark Particle's mass is constrained to be within the range of 5-20 GeV, while its coupling to the Standard Model is found to be in the range of 10^-4 to 10^-3 — these findings have significant implications for the search for dark matter at future particle colliders and direct detection experiments.

Text: Fluctuations of the number of condensed atoms in a finite-size, weakly interacting Bose gas confined in a box potential are investigated for temperatures up to the critical region. The canonical partition functions are evaluated using a recursive scheme for smaller systems, and a saddle-point approximation for larger samples, that allows to treat realistic size systems containing up to $N sim 105$ particles. We point out the importance of particle-number constrain and interactions between out of condensate atoms for the statistics near the critical region. For sufficiently large systems the crossover from the anomalous to normal scaling of the fluctuations is observed. The excitations are described in a self-consistent way within the Bogoliubov-Popov approximation, and the interactions between thermal atoms are described by means of the Hartree-Fock method.

Text: The present study demonstrates existence and robustness properties for Fokker-Planck equations governed by log-concave reference measures, employing advanced analytical frameworks to characterize asymptotic behavior of associated probability distributions. Utilizing the inherent convexity characteristics of log-concave potentials, we derive a priori estimates for Markov semigroups, thereby establishing global well-posedness within weighted Sobolev spaces. Stability is rigorously examined through hypocoercivity theory and entropy dissipation principles, revealing exponential contraction of solutions toward equilibrium states in both relative entropy and Wasserstein metrics. Central to our analysis is the application of the Bakry-Émery Γ₂ formalism, which quantifies curvature-induced decay mechanisms, enabling precise characterization of spectral gaps proportional to the convexity modulus. These extend classical hypocoercivity paradigms to encompass non-degenerate diffusions with singular coefficients, offering explicit convergence rates contingent on the reference measure's logarithmic concavity. The theoretical implications are substantiated through applications in statistical physics and computational statistics, where log-concave reference measures underpin overdamped Langevin dynamics and Bayesian inference. By integrating functional inequalities with probabilistic methodologies, this work provides a cohesive framework for analyzing existence, uniqueness, and exponential stabilization of Fokker-Planck systems, even under high-dimensional regimes. Numerical experiments further validate the efficacy of log-concave reference measures in accelerating sampling algorithms, underscoring their practical utility in modern stochastic modeling.

Text: In the vicinity of glass and jamming transitions, the dynamics of particulate systems exhibit distinct characteristics that are often linked to the emergence of non-ergodic behavior and the breakdown of fluidity. Our studies have revealed a universal feature of particle displacements in these regimes, where the distribution of local displacements can be described by a power-law function with an exponent that depends on the packing fraction and the thermal energy of the system. This behavior is observed in both two-dimensional and three-dimensional systems, across a range of particle sizes and shapes, and is insensitive to the specific details of the interaction potential. By analyzing the spatial correlations of displacements, we have identified a characteristic length scale that diverges as the jamming transition is approached, indicating a growing spatial coherence of particle motions. These results suggest that the dynamics of particulate systems near glass and jamming transitions are governed by a common underlying mechanism, which may be exploited to design novel materials and systems that exhibit optimal properties at the transition point.

Text: We present a search for the lightest scalar top quark (stop) in proton-antiproton collisions at a center-of-mass energy of 1.96 TeV using the CDF II detector at the Fermilab Tevatron. The search is based on a dataset of 9.7 fb^-1 of integrated luminosity and focuses on events containing two leptons, a bottom quark jet, and significant missing transverse energy, which are characteristic of stop pair production. Events are categorized into two main signatures based on the lepton flavor and number of jets. Our analysis employs a likelihood-based discriminant to separate signal from and employs a neural network to improve the separation of signal and events. We searched for the lightest stop quark with a mass ranging from 40 to 160 GeV, and assuming a 100% branching fraction to a bottom quark and a chargino, we found no evidence for stop pair production. Our are interpreted in the context of the minimal supersymmetric standard model, and we set limits on the stop mass and the chargino mass. The most stringent limit is obtained for a stop mass of 130 GeV, where we exclude the stop-chargino hypothesis at 95% confidence level.

Text: The South Pole has emerged as a prime location for cosmic microwave background research since the early 1990s, boasting minimal atmospheric interference, consistent weather patterns, and a frigid, arid climate conducive to sub-millimetre observations. Pioneering experiments such as DASI and Boomerang leveraged these conditions to chart temperature fluctuations and identify acoustic peak structures, while subsequent initiatives like CBI and BICEP expanded the scope to include polarization and preliminary detection of primordial B-mode signals. The South Pole Telescope and its successors, SPTpol and SPT-3G, have yielded high-resolution temperature and polarization maps, refined cosmological parameters, and precisely measured CMB lensing. Ongoing endeavors, including the BICEP/Keck Array and Simons Observatory, strive to enhance foreground separation, target the tensor-to-scalar ratio, and map the small-scale power spectrum with unprecedented accuracy. Future ventures, such as CMB-S4 and next-generation polarimeters, will harness the South Pole's unique advantages to achieve sub-microkelvin sensitivity, validate inflationary theories, and determine neutrino mass sums with precision, thereby solidifying the region's status as a premier hub for precision cosmology.

Text: This study presents a novel, unified information metric that integrates Shannon's concept of probabilistic entropy with Popper's idea of epistemic falsifiability, effectively bridging the gap between traditional communication theory and the philosophy of science. By expanding on the Shannon information of an event, a falsification weight is incorporated to quantify the degree to which an observation disproves competing hypotheses. The resulting generalized metric, expressed as I_G = –log P + λ·F, where P is the outcome probability and F is the normalized falsification score, adheres to both Shannon's additivity axioms and Popper's criteria for maximizing informational value. Analytical demonstrations show that I_G converges to Shannon entropy when falsification is negligible and transforms into an epistemic information measure under uniform probability distributions. Simulation experiments on dynamic Bayesian networks reveal that agents utilizing I_G achieve faster convergence to factual truth than those relying solely on conventional entropy, indicating that this generalized formula provides a foundational framework for developing learning algorithms that prioritize hypothesis testing, with significant implications for machine learning, scientific inference, and knowledge acquisition.

Text: The secure and robust functioning of a network relies on the defect-free implementation of network applications. From a Zebu specification, a compiler automatically generates stubs to be used by an application to parse network messages. Zebu is easy to use, as it builds on notations used in RFCs to describe protocol grammars. Zebu is also efficient, as the memory usage is tailored to application needs and message fragments can be specified to be processed on demand. Finally, Zebu-based applications are robust, as the Zebu compiler automatically checks specification consistency and generates parsing stubs that include validation of the message structure. Text: Quantum entanglement, a fundamental feature of quantum mechanics, has garnered significant interest in the field of quantum information processing. Our demonstrate the successful production of a GHZ state (Greenberger-Horne-Zeilinger state) in a three-spin system, characterized by a high degree of entanglement and a long coherence time. Our provide a significant step towards the realization of large-scale quantum information processing in quantum dot systems.
