Text: The Shifman-Vainshtein-Zakharov sum rules serve as a crucial link between quantum chromodynamics and hadronic phenomena, establishing a relationship between correlation function moments and non-perturbative condensates. Nevertheless, the determination of bound-state properties, such as mass and decay constants, is hindered by systematic errors stemming from operator product expansion truncation, continuum modeling, and Borel window selection. To investigate these error sources, a numerical analysis was conducted using a solvable quantum-mechanical potential model that replicates QCD dynamics, allowing for the isolation of each approximation's impact on extracted parameters. The findings indicate that continuum modeling is the primary source of error, contributing uncertainties of approximately 10-15%, whereas operator product expansion truncation and Borel parameter dependence introduce errors below 5%. A refined dual-threshold approach is proposed to mitigate continuum bias, demonstrating its effectiveness in both a toy model and realistic QCD sum-rule applications for light-meson and heavy-quark systems, highlighting the importance of systematic error quantification for reliable phenomenological predictions based on SVZ sum rules.

Text: This study presents a novel approach for estimating mass loss rates of above-ground biomass (AGB) from radio frequency data, leveraging the relationship between biomass decay and radio wave attenuation. We employed a combination of field measurements and radio wave propagation modeling to validate a new method for calculating AGB mass loss rates based on radio data. Our approach involves the transmission of radio signals through tree canopies and the subsequent analysis of signal attenuation, which is influenced by the biomass density and decay rate. By utilizing a comprehensive dataset comprising radio frequency measurements and corresponding AGB mass loss rates from controlled experiments, we developed a regression model that accurately predicts mass loss rates from radio signal attenuation. Our demonstrate a strong correlation between radio signal attenuation and AGB mass loss rates, with a coefficient of determination (R²) of 0.88. This method offers a non-invasive and cost-effective alternative for monitoring AGB mass loss rates, particularly in remote or inaccessible areas, and has significant implications for forest ecology and carbon cycle research.

Text: The vacuum dependence on boundary conditions in quantum field theories is analysed from a very general viewpoint. From this perspective the renormalization prescriptions not only imply the renormalization of the couplings of the theory in the bulk but also the appearance of a flow in the space of boundary conditions. For regular boundaries this flow has a large variety of fixed points and no cyclic orbit. The family of fixed points includes Neumann and Dirichlet boundary conditions. In one-dimensional field theories pseudoperiodic and quasiperiodic boundary conditions are also RG fixed points. Under these conditions massless bosonic free field theories are conformally invariant. Among all fixed points only Neumann boundary conditions are infrared stable fixed points. All other conformal invariant boundary conditions become unstable under some relevant perturbations. In finite volumes we analyse the dependence of the vacuum energy along the trajectories of the renormalization group flow providing an interesting framework for dark energy evolution. On the contrary, the renormalization group flow on the boundary does not affect the leading behaviour of the entanglement entropy of the vacuum in one-dimensional conformally invariant bosonic theories.

Text: Extracting relevant information, causally inferring and predicting the future states with high accuracy is a crucial task for modeling complex systems. The endeavor to address these tasks is made even more challenging when we have to deal with high-dimensional heterogeneous data streams. Such data streams often have higher-order inter-dependencies across spatial and temporal dimensions. We propose to perform a soft-clustering of the data and learn its dynamics to produce a compact dynamical model while still ensuring the original objectives of causal inference and accurate predictions. To efficiently and rigorously process the dynamics of soft-clustering, we advocate for an information theory inspired approach that incorporates stochastic calculus and seeks to determine a trade-off between the predictive accuracy and compactness of the mathematical representation.

Text: - YTiO₃ is a prototypical Mott insulator that orders ferromagnetically below 30 K. Its optical spectrum encodes the interplay of strong electron correlations, crystal-field splitting, and spin ordering, yet systematic temperature-dependent data are scarce. - High-quality single crystals were probed by variable-angle spectroscopic ellipsometry over 0.5-6 eV at 10-300 K. The complex dielectric function was extracted using a Drude-Lorentz fit constrained by Kramers-Kronig consistency. Temperature-dependent spectra were analyzed for anisotropy along the orthorhombic a, b, and c axes. - A pronounced absorption edge appears at 2.0 eV, corresponding to the Mott gap, with a 0.1 eV red-shift upon cooling below Tc. An excitonic resonance at 2.4 eV shows strong spin-dependent intensity, indicating coupling between optical transitions and ferromagnetic order. Polarization-resolved data reveal significant anisotropy: the a-axis exhibits a higher oscillator strength than the b-axis. First-principles calculations confirm the orbital-ordered ground state and reproduce the observed spectral features. Crucially, these demonstrate that spectral ellipsometry is a sensitive probe of spin-correlated electronic structure in YTiO₃, offering insights into the coupling between magnetism and charge dynamics in transition-metal oxides.

Text: The Galactic ridge emits soft γ-rays (20-200 keV) whose origin remains debated; previous missions lacked the sensitivity for detailed spatial and spectral characterization. We analyzed 12 Ms of INTEGRAL/SPI data collected between 2003 and 2015. Using a maximum-likelihood imaging algorithm combined with a sophisticated model based on detector count rates, we produced sky maps and extracted spectra for the ridge region. The emission was decomposed into point sources and a residual diffuse component, and the spatial distribution was compared with CO and HI gas templates. The ridge emission is dominated by a diffuse component with a power-law spectrum (photon index 1.78 ± 0.05) extending to 200 keV. The diffuse flux accounts for 70 % of the total 20-200 keV emission, while discrete sources contribute the remainder. Spatial correlation with molecular gas is weak, suggesting a dominant contribution from inverse Compton scattering of cosmic-ray electrons on the interstellar radiation field, supplemented by bremsstrahlung. These clarify the spectral and morphological properties of the soft γ-ray ridge and constrain models of Galactic high-energy processes.

Text: We establish a convexity theorem for real projective structures on closed surfaces, providing a fundamental topological constraint on the geometry of such structures. Given a closed surface Σ, a real projective structure on Σ is defined by a maximal atlas of charts to the real projective line RP^1, where the transition functions are projective transformations. Our theorem states that if Σ carries a real projective structure with an anisotropic projective metric, then the convex core of Σ is a convex subset of Σ, which is a fundamental region for the action of the projective holonomy group on Σ. The convex core is defined as the closure of the union of all projective geodesic triangles in Σ, and its convexity is shown to be equivalent to the anisotropy of the projective metric. This result has far-reaching implications for the study of real projective structures, particularly in the context of geometric assessment and topology. It provides a geometric characterization of the convexity of the convex core, which is a key ingredient in the work of the geometry and topology of real projective manifolds.

Text: This comprehensive investigation into the effect of vibrational modes on the low-temperature properties of molecular conductors, a class of materials distinguished by their singular electronic and structural attributes, has been conducted through a synergistic approach combining theoretical simulations and experimental measurements. Furthermore, a significant impact of the phonon modes on the low-temperature thermal expansion and specific heat capacity of these materials has been observed, with anomalies in the thermal properties manifesting at temperatures corresponding to the activation of specific vibrational modes, thereby underscoring the crucial role of vibrational effects in shaping the low-temperature properties of molecular conductors and holding important implications for the design and optimization of these materials for applications in electronic devices and thermoelectric energy conversion, where their unique properties could be leveraged to enhance performance.

Text: - Cascading phenomena, whereby a piece of information propagates through successive blog posts, constitute a primary mechanism for collective attention and opinion formation on the Web. While prior work has examined diffusion on small-scale or platform-specific networks, the structural and temporal determinants of cascades in truly large-scale blog graphs remain poorly understood. - We assembled a directed, time-stamped blog graph comprising 4.2 M nodes and 12.7 M hyperlinks collected over a 24-month period (2018-2020). Cascades were identified by tracing citation chains and extracting maximal acyclic subgraphs rooted at original posts. We characterized cascade properties (size, depth, breadth) and employed survival analysis, hierarchical Bayesian modeling, and motif-based community detection to quantify the influence of node centrality, topical similarity (via Latent Dirichlet Allocation), and temporal posting patterns. All computations were performed on a distributed Spark cluster, and were validated against synthetic cascade models. - Cascade size follows a truncated power-law (α ≈ 2.1) with a heavy tail accounting for <1 % of cascades that generate >50 % of total reposts. Depth is limited (median = 3 hops), yet hubs with high eigenvector centrality disproportionately initiate deep cascades (p < 0.001). Temporal alignment between source and responder activity windows amplifies cascade growth by 27 % on average. Moreover, topical homophily increases cascade breadth by 15 % but reduces depth, suggesting a trade-off between breadth-driven diffusion and hierarchical propagation. Crucially, these illuminate the multi-scale mechanisms governing information spread in extensive blog ecosystems.

Text: This study presents a distinctive method to decision tree modeling by integrating relational views, which are graphical representations of complex relationships between entities, into the decision tree learning process. The put forward method, termed Relational Decision Trees (RDTs), utilizes a hybrid approach that combines the strengths of both decision trees and entity-relationship modeling. By incorporating relational views, RDTs enable the discovery of intricate patterns and relationships between attributes, resulting in more accurate and robust decision models. Notably, our approach leverages graph-based algorithms to identify key relationships and dependencies between entities, which are then used to construct the decision tree structure. In particular, the effectiveness of RDTs is evaluated through a comprehensive simulation study using both synthetic and real-world datasets, demonstrating significant improvements in classification accuracy and model interpretability compared to traditional decision tree methods. The results of this research have important implications for various applications, including data mining, knowledge discovery, and business analytics, where the ability to capture complex relationships and dependencies is crucial for informed decision-making, while the RDT approach offers a promising alternative to traditional decision tree methods, particularly in domains where relational data is prevalent.

Text: We present a novel approach for observing high redshift galaxy clusters by leveraging the gravitational lensing of the Ostriker-Vishniac effect, a cosmological phenomenon arising from the interplay between large-scale structure and the linear growth of density fluctuations. By exploiting the subtle distortions induced by foreground galaxy clusters on the anisotropic distribution of cosmic microwave (CMB) polarization, we demonstrate the feasibility of detecting these high-redshift systems. Our involves analyzing the CMB polarization patterns in the vicinity of identified galaxy clusters, with a focus on the subtle imprint of the Ostriker-Vishniac effect on the CMB polarization power spectra. We utilize advanced numerical simulations and a novel statistical framework to quantify the lensing-induced distortions and reconstruct the high-redshift galaxy cluster distributions. Our indicate that this novel approach offers a powerful means for probing the high-redshift universe, enabling the study of galaxy cluster formation and evolution in unprecedented detail. The technique holds significant potential for advancing our understanding of the cosmic web and the underlying cosmological parameters governing large-scale structure formation.

Text: This investigation elucidates the critical behavior inherent in irreversible reaction systems, which underpins the emergence of phase transitions and scaling phenomena in nonequilibrium chemical kinetics. By scrutinizing a class of lattice-based models governed by irreversible reaction-diffusion processes, it is demonstrated that these systems undergo continuous phase transitions characterized by power-law scaling of reaction rates and spatial correlation lengths, thereby diverging from equilibrium thermodynamic properties. Employing a combination of mean-field theory and Monte Carlo simulations, critical exponents are identified that deviate from equilibrium Ising universality classes, highlighting the distinct nature of nonequilibrium criticality and underscoring the significance of classifying irreversible reaction systems into novel universality classes. Furthermore, the analysis reveals that reaction order, diffusion asymmetry, and activation thresholds play pivotal roles in determining the system's criticality, with higher-order reactions promoting stronger long-range correlations and the interplay between kinetic constraints and spatial coherence giving rise to the emergence of distinct nonequilibrium universality classes. Conversely, comparisons with reversible counterparts demonstrate that unidirectional processes suppress certain critical modes while enhancing others, thereby underscoring the essential role of irreversibility in shaping the critical behavior of these systems. The of this study have profound implications for understanding self-organization in catalytic networks, polymerization dynamics, and ecological systems, where irreversibility is a defining characteristic, and offer insights into the design of materials and processes where critical behavior is harnessed for functional control.

Text: We present a comprehensive X-ray spectroscopic analysis of the gravitationally-lensed blazar PKS1830-211, revealing complex variable X-ray absorption patterns. Our indicate that PKS1830-211 serves as a unique laboratory for studying the interactions between the interstellar and intergalactic media in the context of gravitational lensing, offering valuable insights into the physical processes governing the X-ray absorption in distant active galactic nuclei. Text: The Berezinskii‑Kosterlitz‑Thouless (BKT) transition, driven by the unbinding of vortex–antivortex pairs, underlies the critical behavior of two‑dimensional superfluids and superconducting films; yet a comprehensive analytical framework for the influence of a perpendicular magnetic field remains lacking. Here we develop a systematic sine‑Gordon representation of the BKT Hamiltonian that incorporates the coupling of the phase field to an external vector potential, thereby encoding magnetic‑field‑induced vortex proliferation within a unified field‑theoretic formalism. By performing a duality transformation we map the XY model with Peierls substitution onto a compact scalar field theory with a cosine perturbation whose amplitude acquires a field‑dependent renormalization. Employing perturbative renormalization‑group analysis we derive flow equations for the vortex fugacity and the stiffness, revealing a field‑controlled crossover from the conventional BKT fixed point to a vortex‑liquid regime characterized by a finite correlation length scaling as \(\xi\sim \exp\!\bigl[c/(H-H_{c})^{1/2}\bigr]\). Numerical integration of the flow confirms the predicted shift of the universal jump in superfluid density and yields quantitative predictions for magnetization and I‑V characteristics that agree with recent transport measurements on ultrathin NbN and graphene‑based superconductors. Our sine‑Gordon approach thus furnishes a versatile analytical tool for exploring finite‑field BKT physics and can be extended to incorporate disorder and anisotropy effects.

Text: H13CN J=8-7 sub-millimetre line emission produced in the circumstellar envelope around the extreme carbon star IRC+10216 has been imaged at sub-arcsecond angular resolution using the SMA. Supplemented by a detailed excitation analysis the average fractional abundance of H13CN in the inner wind (< 5E15 cm) is estimated to be about 4E-7, translating into a total HCN fractional abundance of 2E-5 using the isotopic ratio 12C/13C=50. Multi-transitional single-dish observations further requires the H13CN fractional abundance to remain more or less constant in the envelope out to a radius of about 4E16 cm, where the HCN molecules are effectively destroyed, most probably, by photodissociation. The large amount of HCN present in the inner wind provides effective line cooling that can dominate over that generated from CO line emission. It is also shown that great care needs to be taken in the radiative transfer modelling where non-local, and non-LTE, effects are important and where the radiation field from thermal dust grains plays a major role in exciting the HCN molecules. The amount of HCN present in the circumstellar envelope around IRC+10216 is consistent with predicted photospheric values based on equilibrium chemical models and indicates that any non-equilibrium chemistry occurring in the extended pulsating atmosphere has no drastic net effect on the fractional abundance of HCN molecules that enters the outer envelope. It further suggests that few HCN molecules are incorporated into dust grains.

The findings of this study provide new insights into the behavior of the energy-momentum tensor near the event horizon of a black hole and have implications for our understanding of the nature of black hole singularities.

Text: We have imaged the central 1kpc of the circumnuclear starburst disk in the galaxy NGC253 in the HCN(1-0), HCO+(1-0), and CO(1-0) transitions at 60pc resolution using the Owens Valley Radio Observatory Millimeter-Wavelength Array (OVRO). We have also obtained Atacama Pathfinder Experiment (APEX) observations of the HCN(4-3) and the HCO+(4-3) lines of the starburst disk. We find that the emission from the HCN(1-0) and HCO+(1-0) transitions, both indicators of dense molecular gas, trace regions which are non-distinguishable within the uncertainties of our observations. Even though the continuum flux varies by more than a factor 10 across the starburst disk, the HCN/HCO+ ratio is constant throughout the disk, and we derive an average ratio of 1.1+/-0.2. From an excitation analysis we find that all lines from both molecules are subthermally excited and that they are optically thick. This subthermal excitation implies that the observed HCN/HCO+ line ratio is sensitive to the underlying chemistry. The constant line ratio thus implies that there are no strong abundance gradients across the starburst disk of NGC253. This finding may also explain the variations in L'(HCN)/L'(HCO+) between different star forming galaxies both nearby and at high redshifts.

Text: Our examination investigatees the impact of self-citation corrections on Egghe's g index, a bibliometric measure of an author's productivity and impact. Egghe's g index is a variant of the h index that accounts for the distribution of an author's publications across different productivity levels, providing a more nuanced characterization of an author's contribution to their field. However, the incorporation of self-citations in the calculation of Egghe's g index has been criticized for inflating the index value. To address this issue, we have developed a correction technique that subtracts the proportion of self-citations from the total citations to an author's publications. We apply this correction to a dataset of publications from a large academic database and compare the adjusted Egghe's g indices to the original values. The results show that the self-citation correction significantly reduces the index value for a substantial proportion of authors, particularly those with considerable self-citation rates. These outcomes suggest that the inclusion of self-citations in Egghe's g index can lead to inflated estimates of an author's productivity and impact, and that the correction method presented in this analysis offers a more accurate representation of an author's contribution to their field.

Text: Likewise, when drivers hear loud, fast music, they unconsciously step a bit harder on the gas pedal. Walking at our own pace creates an unadulterated feedback loop between the rhythm of our bodies and our mental state that we cannot experience as easily when we're jogging at the gym, steering a car, biking, or during any other kind of locomotion. When we stroll, the pace of our feet naturally vacillates with our moods and the cadence of our inner speech; at the same time, we can actively change the pace of our thoughts by deliberately walking more briskly or by slowing down. Because we don't have to devote much conscious effort to the act of walking, our attention is free to wander-to overlay the world before us with a parade of images from the mind's theatre. This is precisely the kind of mental state that studies have linked to innovative ideas and strokes of insight. Earlier this year, Marily Oppezzo and Daniel Schwartz of Stanford published what is likely the first set of studies that directly measure the way walking changes creativity in the moment. They got the idea for the studies while on a walk. "My doctoral advisor had the habit of going for walks with his students to brainstorm," Oppezzo says of Schwartz. "One day we got kind of meta." In a series of four experiments, Oppezzo and Schwartz asked a hundred and seventy-six college students to complete different tests of creative thinking while either sitting, walking on a treadmill, or sauntering through Stanford's campus. These constraints enhance the precision of prior estimates by 20%, thereby refining the uncertainty margins in cosmic structure formation dynamics. While the corroborate the ΛCDM model's gravitational paradigm, they also underscore the necessity for advanced-resolution datasets to interrogate potential discrepancies in high-redshift domains or modified gravity frameworks. This investigation exemplifies the utility of multi-probe observational campaigns in calibrating cosmological parameters and validating foundational physical theories.

Text: It was the recordings made by New Orleans musicians in the Chicago region from 1923 to 1928 that became the basis for widespread recognition of jazz as an American art form. Continuing the pragmatism that had characterized their musical experiments back home, these musicians employed diverse strategies, while also remaining true to the community cultures on which New Orleans-style jazz was based. In 1923, King Oliver's Creole Jazz Band (featuring Louis Armstrong) relied exclusively on "head" arrangements (tunes worked out in advance and learned by rote) to prepare for its recording sessions, including titles like "Canal Street Blues," "Snake Rag," and "New Orleans Stomp." Beginning in 1925, Louis Armstrong and his Hot Five supplemented the occasional use of sheet music with head arrangements and spontaneous ideas generated in the studio to achieve an identifiable sound, leading to recordings like "Heebie Jeebies" (1926), "Struttin' with Some Barbecue" (1927), and especially "West End Blues" (1928), which were acclaimed as jazz masterpieces. Jelly Roll Morton's Red Hot Peppers rehearsed with scores but added improvised passages, insinuating individual voices where Morton wanted them, as heard in "Black Bottom Stomp" (1926), "Jungle Blues" (1927), and "Georgia Swing" (1928). Each group had its own sound, but they were also working together to advance the idiom, especially evident in the transition from collective to solo improvisation driven primarily by Louis Armstrong. Back in New Orleans, recordings made after 1924 by the Halfway House Orchestra, the Original Tuxedo Jazz Orchestra, Sam Morgan's Jazz Band, the New Orleans Owls, John Hyman's Bayou Stompers, and the Jones & Collins Astoria Hot Eight illustrated a parallel variegation among bands that did not travel, and none of them sounded like the New Orleans-derived bands in Chicago.

These soft modes manifest as singularities in the gluon propagator, which we show to be a consequence of the decoupling of low-energy degrees of freedom from the high-energy modes of the theory. Employing a combination of analytical and numerical techniques, we derive a set of gauge-invariant equations that describe the dynamics of these soft modes, and demonstrate their connection to the phenomenon of confinement, which is a fundamental aspect of strong-interaction physics. Our provide new insights into the infrared behavior of Yang-Mills theory and have implications for the development of effective field theories that can be used to describe hadronic physics in the non-perturbative regime.

Text: Temporal segmentation is a crucial aspect in understanding complex temporal patterns in various fields, such as signal processing and time-series analysis. Traditional approaches to temporal segmentation often rely on fixed thresholding or heuristic , which may not generalize well to unseen data. Recent advances in deep learning have led to the development of Recurrent Neural Networks (RNNs) that can learn to segment temporal sequences effectively. However, the fixed architecture of RNNs can limit their adaptability to diverse temporal patterns. In this study, we propose a novel model that combines a mixture of RNN experts with adaptive variance to segment temporal sequences effectively. Our model consists of multiple RNN experts, each with a distinct architecture and learning rate, which are combined using a weighted sum. The weights are adapted based on the variance of the RNN experts' predictions, allowing the model to adapt to changing temporal patterns. We evaluate our model on several benchmark datasets, including the Berkeley Gesture Dataset and the UCI Human Activity Recognition Dataset. Interestingly, we observed that the proposed model outperforms state-of-the-art in terms of segmentation accuracy and adaptability to changing temporal patterns. The adaptive variance mechanism enables the model to learn from its mistakes and adjust its predictions accordingly, resulting in improved performance in challenging scenarios.

Text: This research endeavor undertakes a comprehensive investigation into the fundamental processes governing magnetic reconnection in high energy plasmas. Through the development of a new theoretical framework, we provide a coherent and predictive explanation for the complex dynamics involved in this phenomenon. Our work draws upon recent advancements in nonlinear plasma physics and leverages quantitative simulations to elucidate the intricate interplay between magnetic field lines, plasma flows, and energy dissipation. We demonstrate that the reconnection process can be effectively described within the context of a two-fluid magnetohydrodynamic model, incorporating the effects of particle gyro-motion and Hall currents. Our results reveal that the reconnection rate is strongly influenced by the plasma temperature and magnetic field strength, with considerable implications for understanding the behavior of high energy plasmas in a variety of astrophysical contexts, including solar flares, magnetospheric substorms, and stellar coronae. By providing a unified theoretical description of magnetic reconnection, our research facilitates a deeper understanding of the underlying physics and enables the development of more accurate models for predicting plasma behavior in these complex systems.

Text: The ATIC-2 experiment reported an anomalous excess of high-energy gamma-ray events that could be attributed to various astrophysical or particle physics sources. To better understand the observed gamma-ray flux, it is essential to accurately calculate the atmospheric muon flux, which can mimic gamma-ray signals in ground-based experiments. We employed a combination of Monte Carlo simulations and atmospheric propagation models to calculate the atmospheric muon flux. We used the GEANT4 simulation toolkit to simulate the production and propagation of muons in the atmosphere, taking into account the effects of geomagnetic field, atmospheric density, and nuclear interactions. The were then propagated through the atmosphere using the FLUKA code, which accounts for the attenuation of muons due to interactions with air nuclei. Our calculations indicate that the atmospheric muon flux is significantly higher than previously reported, particularly in the energy range of 1-10 GeV. Crucially, this result has important implications for the interpretation of the ATIC-2 experiment, suggesting that a substantial portion of the observed gamma-ray excess could be attributed to atmospheric muons rather than exotic astrophysical sources.

Text: Deforestation refers to the large-scale removal of forest cover, whether through clearing for agricultural expansion, urban development, commercial logging, extractive industries, or infrastructure construction, resulting in the permanent loss of forested ecosystems and the ecological functions and biodiversity they support. Tropical deforestation in regions including the Amazon Basin, the Congo Basin, and Southeast Asia represents among the most environmentally damaging processes currently occurring globally, as tropical forests harbor approximately half of all terrestrial species and fulfill critical roles in regulating the global climate by sequestering substantial quantities of carbon dioxide. The destruction of forest ecosystems releases large quantities of stored carbon into the atmosphere, making a significant contribution to greenhouse gas emissions and climate change. Deforestation also disrupts local and regional hydrological cycles, contributes to soil erosion and land degradation, displaces indigenous communities from their traditional territories, and reduces the availability of forest-based resources. Addressing deforestation effectively requires strengthened governance frameworks, adoption of sustainable agricultural practices, financial incentives for forest conservation, and meaningful international policy commitments.

Text: This investigation proposes an additive approximation algorithm for edge-deletion problems, a paradigmatic class of graph modification problems wherein the objective is to transform a stipulated input graph into a target graph through the deletion of edges. Our algorithm operates by iteratively selecting edges for deletion from the input graph, utilizing a synergistic combination of local search and linear programming techniques to minimize the additive error, with the pivotal innovation residing in the design of a novel LP relaxation that effectively captures the fundamental structure of the edge-deletion problem, thereby allowing us to derive precise bounds on the additive error. Through a series of experiments conducted on benchmark instances, we demonstrate the efficacy of our algorithm in achieving high-quality solutions with commensurately low additive error, with far-reaching implications for diverse applications, including network design, graph clustering, and data analysis.

Text: we investigate the elastic relaxation mechanisms that occur during the two-dimensional (2D) epitaxial growth of thin films, focusing on the oscillations of in-plane lattice spacing. Our results demonstrate that the in-plane lattice spacing exhibits periodic oscillations, which are directly correlated with the elastic strain relaxation in the film. The observed oscillations are attributed to the formation of misfit dislocations at the film-substrate interface, leading to an alternating increase and decrease in lattice spacing. By analyzing the periodicity and amplitude of these oscillations, we have derived a new model that describes the elastic relaxation mechanisms in 2D epitaxial growth, providing a fundamental understanding of the underlying physics. Central outcomes encompass the derivation of robust consistency conditions governing bulk-boundary operator product expansion (OPE) coefficients, the analytical characterization of logarithmic partner fields as composite bulk entities, and the formulation of generalized Cardy-like relations that accommodate logarithmic contributions. The integrates modular transformation properties of boundary partition functions with bulk entanglement entropy analyses, unveiling previously uncharted constraints on the spectrums of bulk LCFTs. These demonstrate how logarithmic structures inherently subvert conventional holographic prescriptions akin to AdS/CFT, thereby establishing a theoretical scaffold for constructing bulk duals of LCFTs exhibiting non-unitary or non-rational symmetry algebras. Text: The Accardi complementarity principle is a fundamental concept in the theory of generalized probabilistic structures, also known as generalized probability theories. This principle has far-reaching implications for our understanding of the foundations of quantum mechanics and its potential generalizations. However, the principle has been rigorously established only for μ ≥ 0, leaving a gap in the understanding of the complementary relation for negative values of the parameter μ. We employ a novel approach based on the theory of generalized stochastic processes to derive the Accardi complementarity principle for the range -1/2 < μ < 0. Our involves the construction of a family of generalized probability measures, which are shown to satisfy the required properties of complementarity. We establish the Accardi complementarity principle for the range -1/2 < μ < 0, providing a complete characterization of the complementary relation for all values of μ. Our demonstrate the existence of a generalized probabilistic structure for the range -1/2 < μ < 0, which is consistent with the Accardi complementarity principle. The implications of these are discussed in the context of generalized quantum mechanics and the search for new foundations of quantum theory.

Our research reveals that the $\lambda$-transition is accompanied by a precipitous increase in the formation of S8 rings, which serve as the fundamental building blocks of the liquid Sulphur network, thereby substantiating their pivotal role in the thermodynamic behavior of this molecular liquid. Furthermore, we observed a pronounced shift in the dynamics of Sulphur atoms, characterized by a transition from a diffusive motion, where the atoms exhibit a high degree of mobility, to a more localized motion, where the atoms are confined to a relatively smaller spatial region. These pivotal observations are corroborated by the analysis of the pair distribution functions and the mean squared displacements of Sulphur atoms, thereby underscoring the significance of these kinetic and structural metrics in understanding the $\lambda$-transition. The of this study provide novel insights into the underlying mechanisms governing the $\lambda$-transition in liquid Sulphur, with far-reaching implications for our comprehension of the thermodynamic and kinetic behavior of molecular liquids, and shed light on the intricate interplay between molecular structure and dynamics in determining the phase behavior of Sulphur, thus advancing our understanding of the complex relationships governing the phase transitions of molecular liquids.

Text: An investigation of the possible inflation of stimulated Brillouin backscattering (SBS) due to ion kinetic effects is presented using electromagnetic particle simulations and integrations of three-wave coupled-mode equations with linear and nonlinear models of the nonlinear ion physics. Systematic scans of the laser intensity have been undertaken with both one-dimensional particle simulations and coupled-mode-equations integrations, and two values of the electron-to-ion temperature ratio (to vary the linear ion Landau damping) are considered. Text: The semi-classical dilaton cosmology is a well-known extension of the Einstein's general relativity theory, incorporating the dilaton field and its interactions with gravity. The model has been extensively used to study the early universe, particularly during the inflationary era. However, the inclusion of non-commutative parameters has been a topic of recent interest, as it may lead to new insights into the cosmological evolution. Here, we investigate the effects of two non-commutative parameters on the regular cosmological phase transition in the semi-classical dilaton cosmology. Using the semi-classical dilaton cosmology framework, we derive the effective action that includes the two non-commutative parameters. We then apply the Hartle-Hawking no-boundary proposal to obtain the quantum cosmological dynamics. The regular cosmological phase transition is studied by analyzing the behavior of the scale factor and the dilaton field as a function of the non-commutative parameters. We find that the inclusion of the two non-commutative parameters leads to a novel solution of the semi-classical dilaton cosmology, exhibiting a regular cosmological phase transition. The transition is characterized by a non-trivial behavior of the scale factor and the dilaton field, which are significantly influenced by the non-commutative parameters. Our suggest that the two non-commutative parameters may play a crucial role in the early universe evolution, particularly during the inflationary era.

Text: The uni-directional pulse propagation approximation (UPPA) has been widely employed in the analysis of optical and acoustic wave propagation in various media, providing a computationally efficient yet simplified framework to model complex wave dynamics. This study aims to investigate the limits of the UPPA by systematically analyzing its breakdown in scenarios where backscattered waves become dominant. A numerical framework based on the parabolic equation method is developed to simulate wave propagation in both the UPPA and full-wave regimes. indicate that the UPPA exhibits significant deviations from full-wave predictions at high incidence angles, strong scattering media, and long propagation distances, leading to overestimation of wave intensities and altered spectral signatures. The of this study provide critical insights into the applicability and limitations of the UPPA, highlighting the need for caution in its application to complex wave propagation scenarios where backscattered waves may be significant. By establishing the boundaries of the UPPA, this research contributes to the development of more accurate and robust models for wave propagation in various fields.

Text: Field theories in extra dimensions have garnered significant attention in recent years, driven by the quest to reconcile quantum mechanics and general relativity within a unified theoretical framework. However, the computational complexity associated with these theories often hinders progress. To address this challenge, we explore a renormalizable 1/N_f expansion as a viable approach for simplifying the analysis of field theories in extra dimensions. We employ the 1/N_f expansion, a well-established technique for perturbatively analyzing field theories in the large-N limit. By applying this expansion to field theories in extra dimensions, we derive a systematic and computationally tractable framework for calculating physical observables. Specifically, we consider a five-dimensional Yang-Mills theory with a gauge group of rank N, coupled to matter fields in the fundamental representation. Our demonstrate that the 1/N_f expansion provides an effective means of renormalizing field theories in extra dimensions. By evaluating the one-loop corrections to the gauge coupling and matter self-energies, we find that the expansion yields accurate predictions for physical observables, even for finite values of N. This approach offers a novel and computationally efficient method for investigating the properties of field theories in extra dimensions, thereby facilitating further research into the underlying physics of these systems.

The symmetry score is shown to be a reliable indicator of symmetry, allowing for the identification of symmetric components in the mixture distribution. Moreover, the incorporation of a warped metric leads to a substantial modification of the Casimir force, which becomes increasingly attractive as the compactification radius decreases. These findings offer significant insights into the interplay between geometry, gravity, and quantum fluctuations, and may have profound implications for our understanding of braneworld scenarios and moduli stabilization in string theory. Text: Recently, much research has been carried out on Hamiltonians that are not Hermitian but are symmetric under space-time reflection, that is, Hamiltonians that exhibit PT symmetry. Investigations of the Sturm-Liouville eigenvalue problem associated with such Hamiltonians have shown that in many cases the entire energy spectrum is real and positive and that the eigenfunctions form an orthogonal and complete basis. Furthermore, the quantum theories determined by such Hamiltonians have been shown to be consistent in the sense that the probabilities are positive and the dynamical trajectories are unitary. However, the geometrical structures that underlie quantum theories formulated in terms of such Hamiltonians have hitherto not been fully understood. This paper studies in detail the geometric properties of a Hilbert space endowed with a parity structure and analyses the characteristics of a PT-symmetric Hamiltonian and its eigenstates. A canonical relationship between a PT-symmetric operator and a Hermitian operator is established. It is shown that the quadratic form corresponding to the parity operator, in particular, gives rise to a natural partition of the Hilbert space into two halves corresponding to states having positive and negative PT norm. The indefiniteness of the norm can be circumvented by introducing a symmetry operator C that defines a positive definite inner product by means of a CPT conjugation operation.

Text: A comprehensive, theoretically-driven examination of the characteristics of crypto-Hermitian Hamiltonians, a subset of non-Hermitian Hamiltonians distinguished by the property of possessing real eigenvalues and a well-defined spectrum, is presented in this investigation. The concept of cryptogauge symmetry is formulated, which serves as an extension of the notion of gauge symmetry to the realm of crypto-Hermitian operators, thereby generalizing its applicability. It is demonstrated that cryptogauge symmetry constitutes an indispensable component in the construction of crypto-Hermitian Hamiltonians and assumes a pivotal role in the elucidation of their spectral properties. In addition, the notion of cryptoghosts is introduced, denoting the complex conjugate of the eigenstate of a crypto-Hermitian Hamiltonian. The relationship between cryptoghosts and their corresponding eigenstates is systematically explored, revealing a profound connection between the two. A novel analytical framework for the study of crypto-Hermitian Hamiltonians is developed, which exploits the interplay between cryptogauge symmetry and cryptoghosts to derive non-trivial constraints on the eigenvalues and eigenvectors of these operators. This research provides a fundamental comprehension of the properties and behavior of crypto-Hermitian Hamiltonians, casting new light on the intricate relationship between symmetry, unitarity, and reality in quantum mechanics.

Text: The couplings $g_{\rho HH}$ of the $\rho$ meson with any hadron H are calculated in a holographic dual of QCD where the Regge trajectories for mesons are manifest. The resulting couplings grow linearly with the exciting number of H, thus are far from universal. A simple argument has been given for this behavior based on quasi-classical picture of excited hadrons. It seems that in holographic duals with exact Regge trajectories the $g_{\rho HH}$ universality should be violated. The $\rho$-dominance for the electromagnetic form factors of H are also strongly violated, except for the lowest state, the pion. Quite unexpected, the form factor of the pion is completely saturated by the contribution of the $\rho$. The asymptotic behavior of the form factors are also calculated, and are found to be perfectly accordant with the prediction of conformal symmetry and pertubative QCD.

Text: The orbits of stars close to a massive black hole are nearly Keplerian ellipses. Such orbits exert long term torques on each other, which lead to an enhanced angular momentum relaxation known as resonant relaxation. Under certain conditions, this process can modify the angular momentum distribution and affect the interaction rates of the stars with the massive black hole more efficiently than non-resonant relaxation. The torque on an orbit exerted by the cluster depends on the eccentricity of the orbit. In this paper, we calculate this dependence and determine the resonant relaxation timescale as a function of eccentricity. In particular, we show that the component of the torque that changes the magnitude of the angular momentum is linearly proportional to eccentricity, so resonant relaxation is much more efficient on eccentric orbits than on circular orbits.

Text: We establish a criterion for the transience of multidimensional branching random walk in random environment (BRWRE), a stochastic process describing the spatial dynamics of a population subject to environmental fluctuations and local competition. The BRWRE is characterized by a branching mechanism and a random movement of particles, and its behavior is influenced by the spatial heterogeneity of the environment. We derive a sufficient condition for the transience of the BRWRE by considering the asymptotic growth rate of the population and the rate of decay of the spatial correlations of the environment. Specifically, we show that if the expected logarithmic growth rate of the branching mechanism exceeds the expected rate of return to the origin in the random environment, the process is transient, meaning that the population eventually disappears. Our result yields a clear and tractable criterion for predicting the long-term behavior of the BRWRE in various settings, and its implications can be applied to the study of population dynamics, epidemic spread, and resource allocation in complex systems.

Conversely, the turbulent flow is seen to induce complex, non-linear responses in the polymer dynamics, including enhanced stretching and relaxation rates. Text: We have identified perhaps the largest major galaxy merger ever seen. While analysing Spitzer IRAC images of CL0958+4702, an X-ray selected cluster at z=0.39, we discovered an unusual plume of stars extending $\gtrsim$110 kpc outward from the bright central galaxy (BCG). Three galaxies 1-1.5 mag fainter than the BCG lie within 17 kpc (projected) of the BCG and are probably participating in the merger. The plume is detected in all four IRAC channels and at optical wavelengths in images from the WIYN telescope; the surface brightness is remarkably high ($\mu_r\approx$24.8 mag arcsec$^{-2}$ at 50 kpc). The optical and infrared colors are consistent with those of other BCGs, suggesting that the plume is composed of old stars and negligible recent star formation (hence a "dry merger"). The luminosity in the plume is at least equivalent to a 4L^* galaxy. A diffuse halo extending 110 kpc from the BCG in one IRAC image suggests the total amount of diffuse light is L_r\sim 1.3x10^{11}h^{-2} L_sun. A Chandra observation shows an X-ray image and spectrum typical of moderate-mass clusters. We use MMT/Hectospec to measure 905 redshifts in a 1 deg^2 region around the cluster. The velocities of two of the BCG companions indicate a merger timescale for the companion galaxies of $\sim$110 Myr and $\sim$0.5-1 Gyr for the plume. We conclude that the BCG and intracluster light of CL0958 is formed by major mergers at moderate redshifts. After the major merger is complete, CL0958 will likely become a fossil cluster.

Text: Using three-dimensional hydrodynamic simulations, we investigate heating and turbulence driving in an intracluster medium (ICM) by orbital motions of galaxies in a galaxy cluster. We consider Ng member galaxies on isothermal and isotropic orbits through an ICM typical of rich clusters. An of the galaxies immediately produces gravitational wakes, providing perturbations that can potentially grow via resonant interaction with the gas. When Ng^{1/2}Mg_11 < 100, where Mg_11 is each galaxy mass in units of 10^{11} Msun, the perturbations are in the linear regime and the resonant excitation of gravity waves is efficient to generate kinetic energy in the ICM, resulting in the velocity dispersion sigma_v ~ 2.2 Ng^{1/2}Mg_11 km/s. When Ng^{1/2}Mg_11 > 100, on the other hand, nonlinear fluctuations of the ICM destroy galaxy wakes and thus render resonant excitation weak or absent. In this case, the kinetic energy saturates at the level corresponding to sigma_v ~ 220 km/s. The angle-averaged velocity power spectra of turbulence driven in our models have slopes in the range of -3.7 to -4.3. With the nonlinear saturation of resonant excitation, none of the cooling models considered are able to halt cooling catastrophe, suggesting that the galaxy motions alone are unlikely to solve the cooling flow problem.

Text: The consistent coupling of multiple massless spin‑2 fields (gravitons) remains a central challenge in higher‑spin gauge theory, owing to the severe restrictions imposed by gauge invariance and the absence of a universally accepted interaction vertex. In particular, a massless \(p\)-form provides a natural conduit for exchanging quantum numbers between distinct graviton sectors without violating the no‑ghost condition. We employ the antifield–BRST deformation framework to systematically explore all local, Lorentz‑invariant deformations of the free action describing a collection of \(N\) linearized spin‑2 fields coupled to a massless Abelian \(p\)-form in \(D\) spacetime dimensions (\(D>p+2\)). The analysis is carried out to second order in the deformation parameter, with cohomological techniques used to isolate non‑trivial elements of the BRST cohomology \(H^0(s|d)\). Consistency conditions such as the master equation, gauge‑algebra closure, and the absence of higher‑derivative ghosts are imposed throughout. The cohomological investigation reveals a unique class of cubic vertices in which the \(p\)-form field mediates cross‑interactions among the spin‑2 fields via terms of the form \(B_{\mu_1\ldots\mu_p}\,h^{\mu\nu}_a\,\partial_{[\mu}h_{\nu]\rho}^b\). These vertices are gauge‑invariant up to total derivatives and survive the second‑order consistency check, leading to a deformed gauge algebra that remains Abelian for the \(p\)-form but acquires field‑dependent structure constants for the graviton sector. No additional higher‑derivative or non‑local terms are required. Consequently, a consistent, ghost‑free interaction scheme for a multiplet of spin‑2 fields mediated by a massless \(p\)-form is established, opening new avenues for constructing multi‑graviton models and exploring their phenomenological implications.

Text: .** BiMnO₃ is a prototypical multiferroic perovskite that exhibits ferromagnetic order below 100 K and has attracted intense scrutiny because of its controversial magnetic structure and the interplay between magnetism and ferroelectricity. Muon-spin relaxation (µSR) offers a sensitive, local probe of both static magnetism and dynamic fluctuations, making it ideal for disentangling the magnetic ground state of BiMnO₃. .** Zero-field and longitudinal-field µSR spectra were collected on polycrystalline BiMnO₃ from 2 to 150 K using a pulsed muon source. Time-dependent asymmetry was fitted with a stretched-exponential relaxation function, allowing extraction of the relaxation rate λ(T) and stretching exponent β(T). Complementary magnetization and heat-capacity data were used to corroborate the transition temperature. The temperature dependence of λ was analyzed within a critical-scaling framework to assess the nature of spin dynamics near the Curie temperature. .** A sharp increase in λ at T_C = 103(2) K signals the onset of long-range ferromagnetic order, with β≈1 below T_C indicating homogeneous relaxation. Above T_C, λ follows a power-law λ∝(T-T_C)-n with n≈1.1, evidencing critical slowing down of Mn³⁺ spin fluctuations. No additional low-temperature anomalies were detected, ruling out spin-glass behavior. The µSR data thus confirm a conventional ferromagnetic transition in BiMnO₃, with well-defined static internal fields below T_C and critical spin dynamics above it. This local-probe insight clarifies the magnetic ground state and provides a benchmark for theoretical models of coupled ferroelectric-magnetic order in BiMnO₃.

Building upon the thermodynamic definition of free energy, our method leverages the statistical properties of nonequilibrium work data to infer the underlying free energy landscape. Specifically, we employ a Bayesian formulation that incorporates a prior distribution over the free energy surface, allowing for flexible modeling of the instrument noise and its impact on the measured work data. Our framework utilizes a Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) algorithm to sample from the posterior distribution of the free energy surface, enabling robust estimation in the presence of noise. We demonstrate the efficacy of our approach using simulated data generated from a variety of systems, including a simple harmonic oscillator and a more complex biomolecular system. Our outcomes show that the Bayesian estimates of the free energy surface exhibit improved accuracy and reduced uncertainty compared to traditional maximum likelihood methods, particularly in the presence of high levels of instrument noise. This work has significant implications for the examination of nonequilibrium work data in a range of fields, including biophysics, materials science, and thermodynamics.

Text: The Constrained Minimal Supersymmetric Standard Model (CMSSM) is a widely studied framework for beyond the Standard Model physics. Naturalness arguments suggest that the model parameters should be distributed according to specific priors, which can significantly impact the inference of model parameters from experimental data. We employ a Bayesian approach to analyze the CMSSM, adopting natural priors for the model parameters. We use a Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) algorithm to sample the parameter space and constrain the model using a combination of LHC and other experimental data. The MCMC chain is then used to generate predictions for LHC observables, effectively providing a "weather forecast" for the LHC experiments. Interestingly, we observed that natural priors can significantly alter the preferred regions of the CMSSM parameter space, leading to distinct predictions for LHC observables. We find that the natural priors favor specific ranges of the CMSSM parameters, which can be tested in future LHC runs. Our analysis provides a framework for reconciling theoretical naturalness with experimental constraints, and highlights the importance of careful consideration of prior distributions in beyond the Standard Model phenomenology.

Text: Granular materials are pervasive in both natural and industrial contexts, displaying intricate collective behavior that deviates significantly from equilibrium. This study presents a kinetic theory framework that describes the linear response properties of a dense hard-sphere granular fluid subject to inelastic collisions. By modifying the Enskog equation to account for velocity-dependent restitution and utilizing the Chapman-Enskog expansion, we obtain explicit formulas for the time-dependent correlation functions of density, momentum, and temperature in a homogeneous cooling state. Notably, our theory reveals a strong interplay between thermal and momentum modes, resulting in a complex sound propagation dispersion relation that is heavily attenuated by collisional dissipation. Validation of our analytical findings against molecular dynamics simulations yields quantitative concurrence for a range of packing densities and restitution coefficients, particularly in the intermediate time domain. This kinetic theory provides a rigorous methodology for calculating transport coefficients and fluctuation spectra, shedding light on the underlying mechanisms governing clustering and segregation in driven granular systems, and ultimately serving as a foundational tool for predicting the behavior of granular fluids under external perturbations.

Text: We demonstrate that eavesdropping on the continuous-variable quantum cryptographic protocol with no basis switching is limited by the Heisenberg uncertainty principle, rendering it impossible to achieve an arbitrary level of information gain. In our examination, we consider the most general attack scenario, where an eavesdropper has complete control over the environment and can perform arbitrary operations on the quantum states of the communication channel. We show that the Heisenberg uncertainty principle imposes a fundamental bound on the minimum variance of the eavesdropper's measurement outcomes, which in turn limits the maximum information gain achievable through eavesdropping. Specifically, we derive a tight lower bound on the eavesdropper's information gain, which is a function of the quantum channel's noise properties and the eavesdropper's measurement strategy. Our results reveal that even with no basis switching, the Heisenberg-limited eavesdropping bound provides an insurmountable barrier to achieving perfect security in continuous-variable quantum cryptography. The implications of our findings have significant implications for the development of secure quantum communication protocols.

Text: In a seminal investigation of the fundamental principles governing the gravitational collapse of a pressureless fluid in spherically symmetric spacetime, we elucidate the intricate process by which black holes emerge from the dynamics of matter under extreme gravitational conditions. Building upon the foundational framework of general relativity, our theoretical framework commences with an examination of the Einstein field equations and their application to the Schwarzschild metric, which provides a precise description of the exterior spacetime geometry in the vicinity of the collapsing fluid. A novel mathematical framework is subsequently formulated, predicated on the Israel's formalism of a sharp interface between the collapsed matter and the exterior Schwarzschild solution, thereby allowing for a well-defined and tractable analysis of the gravitational collapse phenomenon. Through the manipulation of the Einstein field equations, we derive the Tolman-Oppenheimer-Volkoff (TOV) equation, a pivotal differential equation governing the intricate interplay between the radial pressure, mass density, and radius of the collapsing fluid. The resulting temporal evolution of these fundamental quantities reveals a profound relationship between the collapse trajectory and a critical density threshold, beyond which a singularity emerges in the core of the fluid, accompanied by a precipitous divergence in curvature and the appearance of a trapped surface. This pivotal insight is further substantiated by the application of the Penrose-Hoyle criterion and the trapped surface theorem, which collectively demonstrate that the formation of a black hole is an inevitability once the collapse exceeds a critical density threshold. Notwithstanding the complexity of the spacetime dynamics at play, our analysis provides a rigorous and comprehensive foundation for understanding the ontological transition from a regular, matter-dominated universe to a spacetime characterized by a singularity and a black hole. The theoretical framework developed in this study thus offers significant contributions to the broader understanding of black hole formation, with implications extending to the collapse of massive stars, galaxy interactions, and the evolution of the universe as a whole. This comprehensive study is a testament to the profound power and insight afforded by the application of mathematical and theoretical physics to the complex dynamics of gravitational collapse, yielding novel and profound understanding of the fundamental processes governing the emergence of black holes in the cosmos.

Text: This analysis undertakes an in-depth examination of the properties and characteristics of corners in normal matrices, a class of matrices that commute with their conjugate transpose. Our findings provide new understanding into the algebraic and geometric properties of normal matrices, shedding light on the intricate relationships between their eigenvalues, singular values, and eigenvectors. Text: We show that a liquid mixture in the thermodynamically stable homogeneous phase can undergo a phase-separation transition when rotated at sufficiently high frequency $omega$. This phase-transition is different from the usual case where two liquids are immiscible or where the slow sedimentation process of one component (e.g. a polymer) is accelerated due to centrifugation. For a binary mixture, the main coupling is due to a term $propto Deltarho(omega r)2$, where $Deltarho$ is the difference between the two liquid densities and $r$ the distance from the rotation axis. Below the critical temperature there is a critical rotation frequency $omega_c$, below which smooth density gradients occur. When $omega>omega_c$, we find a sharp interface between the low density liquid close to the center of the centrifuge and a high density liquid far from the center. These may be relevant to various separation processes and to the control of chemical reactions, in particular their kinetics.

Text: In this paper we propose several strategies for the exact computation of the determinant of a rational matrix. First, we use the Chinese Remaindering Theorem and the rational reconstruction to recover the rational determinant from its modular images. Then we show a preconditioning for the determinant which allows us to skip the rational reconstruction process and reconstruct an integer result. We compare those approaches with matrix preconditioning which allow us to treat integer instead of rational matrices. This allows us to introduce integer determinant algorithms to the rational determinant problem. In particular, we discuss the applicability of the adaptive determinant algorithm of [9] and compare it with the integer Chinese Remaindering scheme. We present an analysis of the complexity of the strategies and evaluate their experimental performance on numerous examples. This experience allows us to develop an adaptive strategy which would choose the best solution at the run time, depending on matrix properties. All strategies have been implemented in LinBox linear algebra library.

Text: Tverberg’s theorem is a cornerstone of combinatorial geometry, guaranteeing that any set of \((r-1)(d+1)+1\) points in \(\mathbb{R}^{d}\) can be partitioned into \(r\) subsets whose convex hulls intersect. In many applications, however, the admissible partitions are subject to additional geometric or combinatorial restrictions, a situation not addressed by the classical statement. We investigate Tverberg-type results under a broad class of constraints, including prescribed colorings, forbidden configurations, and affine subspace containment requirements. By extending the configuration space/test map scheme and employing equivariant obstruction theory for the symmetric group \(\mathfrak{S}_{r}\), we derive new existence theorems that quantify the minimal number of points needed to achieve constrained Tverberg partitions. In particular, we prove that for any integer \(k\ge1\) and any coloring of the point set with at most \(k\) colors, a Tverberg partition respecting the coloring exists provided the number of points exceeds \((r-1)(d+1)+k\). Moreover, we establish sharp bounds for partitions avoiding a given family of forbidden simplices and for partitions whose intersecting point lies in a prescribed affine subspace of codimension \(c\). These results unify and generalize numerous recent constrained Tverberg theorems, and they open pathways for applications in data clustering, fair division, and topological combinatorics.

Text: This investigation examines the inherent characteristics of the geometric potential within the invariant adiabatic theoretical framework, a paradigm elucidating the behavior of dynamical systems undergoing gradual parameter modulations. Through rigorous analytical methodologies and symmetry-informed computational techniques, the geometric potential is demonstrated to emerge as an invariant quantity, fundamentally contingent upon the curvature of the system's configurational manifold and the topological attributes of the adiabatic subspace. Notably, the potential's dual functionality in mitigating non-adiabatic couplings and encapsulating quantum geometric contributions is quantified, with its intensity directly proportional to the eigenstate curvature and inversely correlated to the adiabatic parameter variation rate. Theoretical derivations further establish the geometric potential's invariance under gauge transformations of the adiabatic basis, thereby ensuring its reliability in characterizing physical invariants. Computational simulations of archetypal quantum systems validate these properties, showcasing enhanced precision in predicting adiabatic dynamics. These delineate the geometric potential as a cornerstone of adiabatic theory, offering a cohesive framework for analyzing energy localization, dissipation, and topological robustness in multi-scale systems. By elucidating the geometric potential's role in mediating long-range inter-subsystem interactions, this study advances theoretical paradigms for quantum control applications, topological material design, and the exploration of emergent phenomena in constrained Hamiltonian systems. The work underscores the critical nexus between geometric fidelity and dynamical invariance, providing a robust foundation for engineering stable quantum and classical systems across diverse physical contexts.

Text: We examine the possibility of distinguishing a supersymmetric gluino from a Kaluza-Klein gluon of universal extra dimensions (UED) at the Large Hadron Collider (LHC). Text: Nuclear quantum phase transitions (NQPTs) refer to the abrupt changes in nuclear properties as a function of a control parameter, such as temperature or magnetic field, that exhibit non-classical behavior. Despite their significance in nuclear physics, the microscopic mechanisms underlying NQPTs remain poorly understood. We employed a combination of ab initio calculations and density functional theory to investigate the microscopic origins of NQPTs in a series of nuclear systems. Our calculations involved solving the many-body Schrödinger equation using a realistic nuclear potential and accounting for correlations between nucleons using a variety of many-body forces. We also employed a novel numerical to extract the critical exponents and scaling behavior of the systems. Our calculations reveal a clear microscopic signature of NQPTs, characterized by a sudden change in the nuclear wave function and a corresponding change in the occupation of single-particle states. We find that the critical behavior of the systems is accurately described by a conformal field theory approach, with critical exponents that are consistent with experimental observations. Our provide a new understanding of the microscopic origins of NQPTs and have important implications for the development of new nuclear theories.

Text: We present a method for the direct and continuous separation of red and white blood cells from plasma at the microscale. The method is implemented in a microfluidic system with magnetic functionality. The fluidic structure within the microsystem consists of an inlet and a single microfluidic channel with multiple outlets. The magnetic functionality is provided by an array of integrated soft-magnetic elements that are embedded transverse and adjacent to the microchannel. The elements are magnetized using an external field, and once magnetized they produce a magnetic force on blood cells as they flow through the microchannel. In whole blood, white blood cells (WBCs) behave as diamagnetic microparticles, while red blood cells (RBCs) exhibit diamagnetic or paramagnetic behavior depending on the oxygenation of their hemoglobin. We study the motion of blood cells through the microchannel using a mathematical model that takes into account the magnetic, fluidic and gravitational forces on the cells. We use the model to study blood cell separation, and our analysis indicates that the microsystem is capable of separating WBC-rich plasma, deoxygenated RBC-rich plasma and cell-depleted plasma into respective outlets.

Text: This study presents a novel, adaptive numerical procedure for solving the Vlasov equation, a fundamental kinetic equation in plasma physics and astrophysics. Numerical experiments demonstrate the efficacy of the proposed method in accurately capturing the evolution of the Vlasov equation across a range of test cases, including one-dimensional and two-dimensional scenarios. Text: Strichartz estimates are fundamental tools in the analysis of linear and nonlinear Schrödinger equations, providing space-time integrability properties of solutions. However, sharpness of these bounds in higher dimensions and for rough initial data remains an open problem. We employ a refined decomposition of the Schrödinger propagator into localized frequency pieces and apply bilinear restriction theory together with time-frequency analysis. By interpolating between improved local smoothing estimates and dispersive bounds, we derive a family of mixed-norm estimates that extend the admissible range. In particular, we establish endpoint Strichartz inequalities for dimensions (dge4) and for initial data in weighted Sobolev spaces. The new estimates sharpen the known space-time integrability properties, yielding better control of nonlinear interactions. They enable the proof of global well-posedness for energy-critical NLS with rough data and improve scattering criteria in the mass-critical regime. Crucially, our also provide a framework for extending Strichartz theory to variable-coefficient Schrödinger operators.

Text: Non-backtracking random walks (NBRWs) are a type of random walk on graphs where the probability of revisiting a node is reduced by imposing a constraint on the adjacency matrix. This process has been shown to exhibit anomalous diffusion characteristics in certain regimes. However, the analysis of NBRWs is often hindered by the lack of a tractable approximation for the probability distribution of the walk. In this study, we investigate the applicability of a Poisson approximation to NBRWs on large graphs. Text: We have successfully conceived and fabricated a paradigmatic fully permanent magnet atom chip optimized for the generation of Bose-Einstein condensates (BECs), a phenomenon characterized by the macroscopic occupation of a single quantum state. Text: The Carleson estimate, a fundamental concept in harmonic analysis, provides a necessary condition for the boundedness of the Hilbert transform on the real line. Text: The partition function pertaining to finite--temperature decoding of a (typical) randomly chosen code is known to have three types of behavior, corresponding to three phases in the plane of rate vs. temperature: the {\it ferromagnetic phase}, corresponding to correct decoding, the {\it paramagnetic phase}, of complete disorder, which is dominated by exponentially many incorrect codewords, and the {\it glassy phase} (or the condensed phase), where the system is frozen at minimum energy and dominated by subexponentially many incorrect codewords. We show that the statistical physics associated with the two latter phases are intimately related to random coding exponents. In particular, the exponent associated with the probability of correct decoding at rates above capacity is directly related to the free energy in the glassy phase, and the exponent associated with probability of error (the error exponent) at rates below capacity, is strongly related to the free energy in the paramagnetic phase. In fact, we derive alternative expressions of these exponents in terms of the corresponding free energies, and make an attempt to obtain some insights from these expressions. Finally, as a side result, we also compare the phase diagram associated with a simple finite-temperature universal decoder for discrete memoryless channels, to that of the finite--temperature decoder that is aware of the channel statistics.

Using a combination of coupling arguments, logarithmic Sobolev inequalities, and representation-theoretic decomposition of the Laplacian, we derive explicit bounds on the total variation distance to the Haar measure. A novel "matrix-valued coupling" is constructed by synchronizing the two-dimensional rotations across all subspaces, which yields a contractive metric in expectation. .** Our analysis establishes that the mixing time of Kac's random walk on ( mathrm{SU}(n) ) scales as ( Theta(n{2}log n) ), matching the spectral gap lower bound up to a logarithmic factor. Moreover, we prove that after ( O(n{2}log n) ) steps the distribution is within ( varepsilon ) of equilibrium in total variation for any fixed ( varepsilon>0 ). Crucially, this result sharpens previous estimates and confirms the conjectured polynomial rate of convergence, providing a rigorous foundation for the use of Kac's walk in modeling quantum equilibration.

Text: The validity of Newtonian dynamics and General Relativity in regimes of extremely low acceleration remains an open question, with alternative theories such as Modified Newtonian Dynamics (MOND) and emergent gravity predicting measurable deviations. Globular clusters (GCs), being dark‑matter–free, pressure‑supported stellar systems that span a wide range of internal accelerations (down to ≲10⁻¹¹ m s⁻²), provide an ideal laboratory for probing the weak‑acceleration limit of gravitation. We selected a homogeneous sample of 28 Milky Way GCs with high‑precision proper motions from *Gaia* EDR3 and line‑of‑sight velocities from extensive spectroscopic surveys. For each cluster we constructed spherical Jeans models under both Newtonian and MONDian frameworks, incorporating realistic anisotropy profiles and external field effects. Bayesian model comparison was performed using Markov Chain Monte Carlo sampling to derive posterior distributions of the mass‑to‑light ratio, anisotropy parameter, and the MOND acceleration scale a₀. Systematic uncertainties from distance, binary contamination, and tidal heating were quantified through Monte‑Carlo resampling. The majority of clusters are well described by Newtonian dynamics with mass‑to‑light ratios consistent with stellar population synthesis predictions (⟨Υ_V⟩ = 1.9 ± 0.3 M_⊙ L_⊙⁻¹). MONDian models do not provide a statistically significant improvement; the inferred a₀ values are broadly compatible with the canonical MOND value but exhibit large scatter (a₀ = (1.1 ± 0.7) × 10⁻¹⁰ m s⁻²). No systematic trend of residuals with internal acceleration is observed, placing stringent constraints on deviations from Newtonian gravity at accelerations ≲10⁻¹¹ m s⁻². These reinforce the applicability of standard gravity in the weak‑acceleration regime probed by Galactic globular clusters.

Recent advances link these bodies to test sets of integer programming, yet a systematic exploration of this relationship and its algorithmic implications remains incomplete. By employing Gröbner basis techniques, we derive explicit test sets for the corresponding integer programs and prove that these test sets generate all minimal infeasible vectors. The construction is implemented via a polyhedral decomposition that respects the underlying lattice structure, enabling efficient enumeration of maximal lattice‑free bodies. We then translate the geometric data into a finite algorithm for solving the Frobenius problem in arbitrary dimension. The proposed framework yields a polynomial‑time algorithm for enumerating all maximal lattice‑free bodies associated with a given integer generating set, and consequently produces a complete test set for the Frobenius problem. Empirical on benchmark instances demonstrate a substantial reduction in computational complexity compared with classical algorithms, and the naturally extends to provide tight bounds on the Frobenius number in higher dimensions. This work bridges convex geometry, combinatorial optimization, and number theory, offering new tools for longstanding problems in integer programming.

Third, we construct explicit families of diffeomorphisms using Dehn-twist-like "Nielsen-Thurston" models and analyze their iterates via renormalization arguments. Text: We consider a new approach to power control in decentralized wireless networks, termed fractional power control (FPC). Intuitively, s=1/2 balances between helping disadvantaged users while making sure they do not flood the network with interference.

Text: Healthy eating is a topic surrounded by more noise, confusion, and conflicting advice than almost any other area of personal health. Several spectral lines show intrinsic variations with orbital phase. Text: The principle that "quantization commutes with reduction" (QCR) underlies much of modern symplectic geometry and mathematical physics, asserting that the reduced quantum Hilbert space obtained after symplectic reduction coincides, up to unitary equivalence, with the invariant subspace of the unreduced quantization.
