Text: This study puts forward a detailed analysis of fuzzy fluid mechanics in three-dimensional (3D) environments, extending the theoretical approach of fuzzy set theory to the complex dynamics of fluid flows. By incorporating fuzzy logic and fuzzy numbers into classical fluid mechanics, we develop a novel mathematical structure that accounts for the inherent uncertainties and ambiguities associated with fluid behavior. The suggested methodology enables the representation of fluid properties, such as velocity and pressure, as fuzzy numbers, thereby allowing for a more accurate and realistic modeling of turbulent flows and multi-phase systems. Our 3D fuzzy fluid mechanics model is formulated using the modified Navier-Stokes equations, which incorporate fuzzy operators and membership functions to capture the uncertainty and non-linearity of fluid flows. Quantitative simulations of various 3D fluid flow scenarios, including turbulent channel flows and vortex dynamics, establish the effectiveness of our approach in predicting fluid behavior with improved accuracy and precision, particularly in regions of elevated uncertainty and complexity. The results of this analysis have significant implications for the development of advanced turbulence models, multi-phase flow simulations, and computational fluid dynamics (CFD) applications in engineering and environmental sciences.

Text: The present study undertakes an intensive examination of the global existence and potential finite-time blow-up of solutions to quantum hydrodynamic (QHD) models, specifically within the confines of bounded spatial domains. By virtue of its genesis as the non-relativistic limit of quantum field theories, the QHD system serves as a mathematical representation of the dynamics of quantum fluids, thus warranting a comprehensive investigation of its numerical and analytical behavior. This inquiry is centered around the one-dimensional QHD system, whose dynamics unfold according to a pair of coupled equations of motion for the quantum velocity and density fields. Leveraging the analytical toolkits of functional analysis and partial differential equations, we establish the existence of global solutions on bounded intervals and uncover a novel instability mechanism that facilitates the finite-time blow-up of solutions. Notably, the ensuing blow-up phenomenon arises as an emergent consequence of nonlinear interactions between the quantum pressure and quantum velocity, culminating in an unbounded increase in the solution's local energy norm. Our research have profound implications for the development of computational and the physical interpretation of QHD models, particularly within the contexts of nanoscale and mesoscale fluid dynamics. Our mathematical investigation centers on the one-dimensional QHD system, a dynamical system described by the following pair of coupled equations of motion: ∂u/∂t + ∂p/∂x = 0 ∂p/∂t + ∂(up)/∂x = -∂/∂x (∂u/∂x) - ∂V/∂x Here, u(x,t) represents the quantum velocity, p(x,t) embodies the quantum pressure, and V(x) signifies the external potential, which can be safely neglected under the assumption of a constant or zero external potential. This mathematical formulation provides a precise articulation of the intricate dynamics of quantum fluids, thus underscoring the significance of our investigation into the global existence and potential finite-time blow-up of solutions to the one-dimensional QHD system.

Text: This investigation details an exhaustive exploration of Dirac magnetic monopoles, characterized by quantized magnetic charges (±g_D, where g_D = e/2α_em), within the framework of e⁺e⁻ collisions at the Large Electron-Positron Collider (LEP2), employing the OPAL detector's sophisticated instrumentation. Utilizing a dataset amassed between 1996 and 2000, spanning a center-of-mass energy range of 161–209 GeV and an integrated luminosity of 650 pb⁻¹, the study focused on identifying monopole candidates via their anomalous ionization profiles, which manifest as elevated energy deposition within the tracking system relative to conventional minimum-ionizing particles. Candidate selection criteria incorporated high-transverse-momentum tracks exhibiting ionization signatures consistent with monopole hypotheses, alongside compatibility with magnetic field interactions specific to hypothetical monopole charges. Despite comprehensive analysis of these signatures, no statistically significant excess events were discerned beyond Standard Model predictions, thereby establishing stringent 95% confidence level upper bounds on the monopole production cross-section. These constraints effectively exclude monopole masses within the range of approximately 105 GeV/c², contingent on the production mechanism, thereby refining the parameter space of models positing Dirac monopoles, including grand unified theories and other extensions of the Standard Model. The absence of observed monopoles not only advances current experimental benchmarks for such particles in e⁺e⁻ collision environments but also underscores the pivotal role of LEP2-era experiments in interrogating fundamental symmetries and probing the viability of physics beyond the Standard Model.

Text: We report a novel approach to amplify plasmons at terahertz frequencies in graphene by harnessing stimulated emission, a phenomenon that enables efficient energy transfer between excited states. Our theoretical framework, supported by first-principles simulations, demonstrates that the unique electronic properties of graphene enable the creation of a self-sustaining feedback loop, where plasmons emitted by a stimulating source can, in turn, stimulate further emission of plasmons. This process is facilitated by the high carrier mobility and Fermi level tunability of graphene, allowing for precise control over the plasmon frequency and amplitude. Our simulations predict that this stimulated emission process can enhance the plasmon amplitude by several orders of magnitude, leading to the potential for high-power terahertz sources with unprecedented efficiency and tunability. Furthermore, the scalability and flexibility of graphene make this approach an attractive candidate for integration into various devices, including photonic and optoelectronic systems, with potential applications in fields such as medical imaging, spectroscopy, and quantum computing.

Text: In a groundbreaking endeavor to elucidate the primordial evolution of the universe, we develop an innovative hybrid simulation paradigm designed to efficaciously investigate the nascent structure formation and reionization processes. By synergistically integrating cutting-edge hydrodynamical solvers with semi-analytical models, our framework is adept at capturing the intricate, multi-scale interactions that govern the evolution of the intergalactic medium, thereby facilitating a comprehensive understanding of the cosmological large-scale structure. Leveraging the efficacy of machine learning algorithms to dynamically optimize the computational expenditure, our framework achieves a substantial reduction in simulation time, thereby enabling the investigation of larger volumes and higher resolutions. Based on the Planck 2018 cosmological constraint set, our simulations account for the formation of dark matter halos, gas collapse, and the reionization process, thereby culminating in a self-consistent portrayal of the early universe. Notably, our simulations reveal the emergence of the first stars, quasars, and the resultant reionization of the intergalactic medium, providing novel insights into the fundamental processes that shaped the early universe. Our paves the way for an in-depth comprehension of structure formation, reionization, and the cosmic dawn, enabling the exploration of the universe's primeval evolution. The synergy between our hybrid simulations and machine learning-based optimization strategy presents a paradigmatic shift in the field of cosmological simulations, thereby opening up avenues for research that seek to elucidate the complex mechanisms governing the early universe's evolution. By providing a robust framework for simulating large-scale structure and reionization, our approach has far-reaching implications for our understanding of the cosmos and its fundamental constituents. This work presents an innovative paradigm for studying the structure formation, reionization, and the cosmic dawn, providing a novel framework that integrates hydrodynamical simulations, semi-analytical models, and machine learning algorithms. By leveraging the synergy between these methodologies, we unlock a previously inaccessible regime of cosmological simulations, thereby illuminating the complex processes that governed the evolution of the early universe. This study is a testament to the potential of interdisciplinary approaches in advancing our understanding of the cosmos, with far-reaching implications for the study of cosmological large-scale structure, reionization, and the origins of the universe.

Text: We have mapped the starless core TMC-1C in a variety of molecular lines with the IRAM 30m telescope. High density tracers show clear signs of self-absorption and sub-sonic infall asymmetries are present in N2H+ (1-0) and DCO+ (2-1) lines. The inward velocity profile in N2H+ (1-0) is extended over a region of about 7,000 AU in radius around the dust continuum peak, which is the most extended ``infalling'' region observed in a starless core with this tracer. The kinetic temperature (~12 K) measured from C17O and C18O suggests that their emission comes from a shell outside the colder interior traced by the mm continuum dust. The C18O (2-1) excitation temperature drops from 12 K to ~10 K away from the center. This is consistent with a volume density drop of the gas traced by the C18O lines, from ~4x10^4 cm^-3 towards the dust peak to ~6x10^3 cm^-3 at a projected distance from the dust peak of 80" (or 11,000 AU). The column density implied by the gas and dust show similar N2H+ and CO depletion factors (f_D < 6). This can be explained with a simple scenario in which: (i) the TMC-1C core is embedded in a relatively dense environment (H2 ~10^4 cm^-3), where CO is mostly in the gas phase and the N2H+ abundance had time to reach equilibrium values; (ii) the surrounding material (rich in CO and N2H+) is accreting onto the dense core nucleus; (iii) TMC-1C is older than 3x10^5 yr, to account for the observed abundance of N2H+ across the core (~10^-10 w.r.t. H2); and (iv) the core nucleus is either much younger (~10^4 yr) or ``undepleted'' material from the surrounding envelope has fallen towards it in the past 10,000 yr.

Text: Within the internal shock scenario we consider different mechanisms of high energy ($>1$ MeV) photon production inside a Gamma Ray Burst (GRB) fireball and derive the expected high energy photon spectra from individual GRBs during the prompt phase. The photon spectra of leptonic and hadronic origins are compared within different sets of parameter regimes. Our suggest that the high energy emission is dominated by the leptonic component if fraction of shock energy carried by electrons is not very small (e.g. $\epsilon_e > 10^{-3}$). For very small values of $\epsilon_e$ the hadronic emission component could be comparable to or even exceed the leptonic component in the GeV-TeV regime. However, in this case a much larger energy budget of the fireball is required to account for the same level of the observed sub-MeV spectrum. The fireballs are therefore extremely inefficient in radiation. For a canonical fireball bulk Lorentz factor (e.g. $\Gamma=400$), emissions above $\sim 10$ GeV are attenuated by two-photon pair production processes. For a fireball with an even higher Lorentz factor, the cutoff energy is higher, and emissions of 10 TeV - PeV due to $\pi^0$-decay can also escape from the internal shocks. The flux level is however too low to be detected by current TeV detectors, and these photons also suffer attenuation by external soft photons.

Text: It is widely believed that the perovskite Sr$_2$RuO$_4$ is an unconventional superconductor with broken time reversal symmetry. It has been predicted that superconductors with broken time reversal symmetry should have spontaneously generated supercurrents at edges and domain walls. We have done careful imaging of the magnetic fields above Sr$_2$RuO$_4$ single crystals using scanning Hall bar and SQUID microscopies, and see no evidence for such spontaneously generated supercurrents. We use the from our magnetic imaging to place upper limits on the spontaneously generated supercurrents at edges and domain walls as a function of domain size. For a single domain, this upper limit is below the predicted signal by two orders of magnitude. We speculate on the causes and implications of the lack of large spontaneous supercurrents in this very interesting superconducting system.

Text: This comprehensive investigation delves into the intricate dynamics governing the interrelation between relative states and their environmental context, thereby integrating fundamental principles derived from quantum mechanics, notably einselection, envariance, and quantum Darwinism, within the theoretical paradigm of the existential interpretation. The process of einselection, wherein the system's environment preferentially selects a specific basis, substantiates the pivotal role of relative states in delineating the system's intrinsic properties, thereby underscoring the significance of an environment-mediated selection process. Conversely, envariance, a concept elucidating the symbiotic relationship between disparate branches of the wave function, underscores the paramount influence of the environment on a system's ontological existence, thereby highlighting the intricate interdependence between a system and its environmental surroundings. Furthermore, quantum Darwinism, a theoretical framework positing that the interaction between the environment and a system precipitates the emergence of classical properties, underscores the pivotal role of the environment in shaping the system's state, thereby facilitating a nuanced understanding of the environmental contributions to the system's classical behavior. The existential interpretation, which posits the veracity of all branches of the wave function, provides a theoretical framework for elucidating the interplay between relative states and their environmental context, thereby enabling a more comprehensive understanding of the complex relationships between a system's properties, its environmental surroundings, and the emergence of classical behavior in quantum systems, ultimately contributing to a deeper comprehension of the fundamental nature of reality.

Text: Supporting students with learning disabilities means going beyond just following rules, embracing cognitive diversity. Dyslexia, dyscalculia, and executive functioning deficits are distinct neurological variations in processing information, not reflections of intelligence. And when schools provide early screenings, they can deploy targeted interventions before learning gaps become too big, which makes sense. Schools can use assistive technologies like text-to-speech software, graphic organizers to help students demonstrate their understanding without being held back by their deficits - this way students with deficits can show what they know, despite their deficits. But teachers need training to differentiate instruction, break tasks into smaller steps, offer multiple paths to mastery, using technology in a way that supports learning. By reframing accommodations as essential tools for equity, we create classrooms where neurodivergent students thrive, and that's a good thing, because every student deserves to succeed.

Text: The enumeration of complex plane curves with singularities is a fundamental problem in algebraic geometry, with significant implications for our understanding of the topology and geometry of these curves. In this study, we focus on the specific case of complex plane curves with two singular points, providing a comprehensive analysis of their enumeration and classification. Utilizing a combination of algebraic and geometric techniques, we derive a novel formula for counting the number of such curves with prescribed singularities, taking into account the intricate relationships between the curve's degree, genus, and singularity type. Our shed new light on the intricate structure of complex plane curves with multiple singularities, revealing subtle patterns and connections that have hitherto gone unnoticed. The of this research have far-reaching implications for the study of algebraic curves, moduli spaces, and the topology of singularities, and are expected to stimulate further research in these areas, ultimately deepening our understanding of the complex and fascinating world of algebraic geometry.

Text: We present a comprehensive investigation into the spin polarization of the magnetic semiconductor EuS via a nuanced application of zero-field and Zeeman-split Andreev reflection spectroscopy, a technique that capitalizes on the spin-dependent scattering of electrons at superconducting interfaces to elucidate the spin polarization of the semiconductor in question. EuS, a paradigmatic half-metallic ferromagnet with a Curie temperature of 16.5 K, exhibits a singular spin-polarized conduction band, rendering it an exemplary system for probing the intricacies of spin-dependent electronic properties. The spin polarization of EuS was meticulously investigated using Andreev reflection spectroscopy, which exploits the dichotomy in spin-dependent electron scattering at superconducting interfaces to interrogate the spin polarization of the semiconductor. Our experimental apparatus comprised a EuS thin film deposited on a superconducting Al substrate, thereby enabling us to measure the spin polarization of the semiconductor in both zero-field and Zeeman-split conditions. Under zero-field conditions, we observed a spin polarization of 72% at the Fermi level, consistent with previous reports and corroborative of the semiconductor's inherent spin-polarized characteristics. Conversely, upon the application of a magnetic field, the Zeeman splitting of the Andreev reflection spectrum revealed a marked increase in spin polarization, achieving a value of 92% at 2 T, thereby underscoring the capacity of Andreev reflection spectroscopy to probe the spin polarization of magnetic semiconductors and shed novel insights into the spin-dependent electronic properties of EuS.

Text: This study undertakes a comprehensive analysis of 3R manipulators featuring orthogonal axes, a configuration commonly employed in industrial robotics and mechanical systems. By developing a rigorous mathematical framework, we derive closed-form solutions for the inverse kinematics and Jacobian matrices of these manipulators, thereby facilitating the evaluation of their kinematic performance. A comparative analysis of various 3R manipulator configurations is conducted, including those with fixed and variable joint offsets, to elucidate the effects of these design parameters on the manipulator's workspace, dexterity, and singularity characteristics. The demonstrate that the choice of joint offset significantly influences the manipulator's performance, with variable joint offsets offering improved workspace and dexterity, albeit at the expense of increased complexity and reduced robustness to singularity formation. Our provide valuable insights for the design and optimization of 3R manipulators with orthogonal axes, enabling the development of more efficient and effective robotic systems for a wide range of applications.

Text: We describe a Monte Carlo method to approximate the maximum likelihood estimate (MLE), when there are missing data and the observed data likelihood is not available in closed form. This method uses simulated missing data that are independent and identically distributed and independent of the observed data. Our Monte Carlo approximation to the MLE is a consistent and asymptotically normal estimate of the minimizer $theta*$ of the Kullback--Leibler information, as both Monte Carlo and observed data sample sizes go to infinity simultaneously. Plug-in estimates of the asymptotic variance are provided for constructing confidence regions for $theta*$. We give Logit--Normal generalized linear mixed model examples, calculated using an R package.

Comparative studies across high- and low-income settings indicate significant disparities in implementation fidelity and outcome achievement. These findings challenge the assumption that evidence-based approaches developed in resource-rich environments are directly transferable. Tailored implementation strategies that account for local constraints are essential for maximizing the impact of quantum computing initiatives on cryptographic security.

Text: This article presents a comprehensive study of the symplectic cohomology of certain classes of Weinstein manifolds, revealing a previously overlooked bias in the conventional approach to this subject. By systematically applying the theory of Floer homology, we demonstrate that the symplectic cohomology of these manifolds exhibits a dependence on the choice of Morse function used in the construction of the Floer complex. Furthermore, through a detailed analysis of the action filtration and the Novikov ring, we identify a subtle relationship between the symplectic cohomology and the cohomology of the underlying manifold. Our suggest that the symplectic cohomology of Weinstein manifolds is not as robust as previously thought, and that the choice of Morse function can significantly impact the resulting cohomology groups. We provide explicit examples to illustrate this phenomenon, and discuss the implications of our for the broader field of symplectic geometry and topological quantum field theory. Our work highlights the need for a more nuanced understanding of the symplectic cohomology, and provides a framework for further research in this area.

Text: Quasi-conformal actions were introduced in the physics literature as a generalization of the familiar fractional linear action on the upper half plane, to Hermitian symmetric tube domains based on arbitrary Jordan algebras, and further to arbitrary Freudenthal triple systems. In the mathematics literature, quaternionic discrete series unitary representations of real reductive groups in their quaternionic real form were constructed as degree 1 cohomology on the twistor spaces of symmetric quaternionic-Kahler spaces. These two constructions are essentially identical, as we show explicitly for the two rank 2 cases SU(2,1) and G_{2(2)}. We obtain explicit for certain principal series, quaternionic discrete series and minimal representations of these groups, including formulas for the lowest K-types in various polarizations. We expect our to have applications to topological strings, black hole micro-state counting and to the theory of automorphic forms.

Text: This paper establishes a deep connection between the derived category of quasi-coherent sheaves and axiomatic stable homotopy theory. We demonstrate that the derived category of quasi-coherent sheaves over a smooth variety can be equivalently viewed as a stable infinity category, thereby providing an intrinsic framework for studying the derived geometry of algebraic varieties. Furthermore, we show that this construction gives rise to a functor from the category of smooth varieties to the category of stable infinity categories, which we conjecture to be a universal object in the sense of axiomatic stable homotopy theory. Our main result involves establishing a canonical equivalence between this functor and the stable infinity category of motivic spectra, thereby providing a new perspective on the motivic stable homotopy theory of algebraic varieties. This equivalence has far-reaching implications for the study of algebraic cycles, Chow groups, and motivic cohomology, and sheds new light on the deep connections between derived algebraic geometry and stable homotopy theory. The of this paper have significant implications for the development of a unified theory of stable homotopy and motivic cohomology.

Text: We investigate the consistency of a modified $f(R)$ gravity theory, specifically $f(R)=\sqrt{R^{2}-R_{0}^{2}}$, with cosmological observations in the Palatini formalism. This theory introduces a nonlinear function of the Ricci scalar $R$, where $R_{0}$ is a free parameter representing a dark energy component. By adopting the Palatini formalism, we derive the modified Einstein-Hilbert action and subsequently, the field equations. We then apply the modified theory to the late-time cosmology, focusing on the expansion history of the universe. Our analysis reveals that the $f(R)=\sqrt{R^{2}-R_{0}^{2}}$ theory can successfully reproduce the observed accelerating expansion of the universe, as indicated by the Supernovae Type Ia data and the Cosmic Microwave (CMB) measurements. Furthermore, we find that the model is consistent with the large-scale structure (LSS) observations, including the matter power spectrum and the galaxy clusters distribution. The of this study demonstrate that the $f(R)=\sqrt{R^{2}-R_{0}^{2}}$ theory, in the Palatini formalism, provides a viable alternative to the $\Lambda$CDM model, suggesting that this modified gravity theory can be a promising candidate for explaining the dark energy phenomenon.

Text: This study further explores the integrable lattices and their sublattices, building upon the previously established connections between the B-quadrilateral lattice and its associated self-adjoint schemes. By using the algebraic structures inherent to the B-quadrilateral lattice, we derive novel self-adjoint schemes on the triangular and honeycomb lattices, thereby extending the scope of integrable models to these two fundamental lattice geometries. Our research reveals that the B-quadrilateral lattice serves as a unifying model for the construction of self-adjoint schemes on the triangular and honeycomb lattices, highlighting the intrinsic relationships between these lattices. The derived self-adjoint schemes exhibit a rich algebraic structure, with the potential to provide new perspective into the dynamics of integrable systems on these lattices. This work thus contributes to a deeper insight into of the connections between different lattice geometries and their associated integrable models, with potential applications in the fields of statistical mechanics, quantum field theory, and condensed matter physics. The resulting self-adjoint schemes offer a promising platform for further investigation into the properties and behavior of integrable systems on the triangular and honeycomb lattices.

The Calabi-Yau manifold, characterized by a non-trivial holomorphic volume form, serves as a repository of information regarding the spatial orientations, types, and configurations of D-branes in the , thereby encoding a multifaceted topological landscape. Our approach hinges on the application of the Calabi-Yau condition within a higher-dimensional framework, wherein the Calabi-Yau metric is determined by the distribution of D-branes, thus allowing for a nuanced exploration of the intricate relationships between the Calabi-Yau manifold and the D-branes it contains. Text: The dynamics of the outer Solar System, characterized by intricate celestial mechanics, poses a compelling enigma as it relates to the formation of trans-Neptunian object (TNO) binaries, a phenomenon hitherto not thoroughly understood in scientific circles. In our research, we propose a novel theoretical paradigm for the genesis of TNO binaries through chaos-assisted capture, a process leverages the extreme sensitivity of chaotic systems to initial conditions. A comprehensive numerical model was developed to simulate the long-term evolution of the Solar System, taking into account the perturbative effects of adjacent giant planets as well as the inherent orbital instabilities in the chaotic dynamics of the outer Solar System. Our model demonstrates that the confluence of gravitational perturbations and orbital instabilities can facilitate the capture of small TNOs into stable binary orbits around larger primary bodies. Leveraging both analytical and numerical techniques, we show that chaos-assisted capture can operate efficaciously over a broad spectrum of initial conditions, thereby enabling the formation of TNO binaries with properties consistent with observational data. Notably, our simulations predict the ejection of small TNOs from originally single-object orbits and their subsequent gravitational capture by larger primary bodies, resulting in the creation of stable binary systems. These have profound implications for our comprehension of the evolution and demographics of the TNO population, as well as the prospect for discovering new binary systems through future surveys of the outer Solar System.

Text: Structural fluctuations in the thermal equilibrium of the kinesin motor domain are studied using a lattice protein model with Go interactions. By means of the multi-self-overlap ensemble (MSOE) Monte Carlo method and the principal component analysis (PCA), the free-energy landscape is obtained. It is shown that kinesins have two subdomains that exhibit partial folding/unfolding at functionally important regions: one is located around the nucleotide binding site and the other includes the main microtubule binding site. These subdomains are consistent with structural variability that was reported recently based on experimentally-obtained structures. On the other hand, such large structural fluctuations have not been captured by B-factor or normal mode analyses. Thus, they are beyond the elastic regime, and it is essential to take into account chain connectivity for studying the function of kinesins.

Text: In the present study, we employ advanced laser spectroscopy techniques to investigate the hyperfine structure in highly-charged ions, with a primary focus on the implications for Quantum Electrodynamics (QED) at high-field strengths. The hyperfine structure, resulting from the interaction between the nuclear spin and the orbital angular momentum of the electrons, provides a sensitive probe of the relativistic corrections to the energy levels of these ions. Our experimental approach involves the precise measurement of the hyperfine splittings in highly-charged ions, such as hydrogen-like and helium-like systems, using a state-of-the-art laser setup and high-resolution spectroscopy. By comparing our experimental results with state-of-the-art QED calculations, we aim to assess the accuracy of QED predictions at high-field strengths, which have significant implications for our grasp of of atomic physics and the behavior of matter at extreme conditions. Our findings will contribute to the ongoing efforts to refine the QED structure and improve the precision of atomic energy level calculations, with potential applications in fields such as atomic physics, particle physics, and materials science.

Text: .** The Fokker-Planck equation (FPE) governs the time evolution of probability densities for stochastic processes and is central to nonequilibrium statistical physics. While most FPEs are analytically intractable, a subset admits exact solutions, typically through mapping to a Schrödinger operator with a solvable potential. Recent developments in quasi-exactly solvable (QES) quantum mechanics suggest that a broader class of FPEs may possess a finite set of analytically accessible eigenstates, providing valuable benchmarks for numerical schemes and insight into the spectral structure of stochastic dynamics. .** We construct QES FPEs by imposing that the associated differential operator preserves a finite-dimensional polynomial subspace. This is achieved by embedding the drift and diffusion coefficients in a representation of the sl(2,ℝ) algebra and employing a gauge transformation to a Schrödinger-like form. The resulting FPEs are parametrized by a set of algebraic constraints that guarantee the existence of an invariant subspace spanned by orthogonal polynomials. We then solve the corresponding eigenvalue problem explicitly for the lowest-lying modes, yielding closed-form stationary distributions and relaxation spectra. .** The analysis uncovers two infinite families of QES FPEs characterized by polynomial drift terms of degree two or three and constant diffusion. For each family, we provide explicit expressions for the stationary density and the first few non-zero eigenvalues, illustrating how the algebraic structure controls the spectral gaps. Crucially, these extend the catalog of analytically tractable stochastic models, offering new testbeds for stochastic simulation algorithms and shedding light on the interplay between drift, diffusion, and spectral properties in nonequilibrium systems.

Text: This paper presents a novel approach to tropical implicitization, a fundamental problem in computational algebraic geometry and tropical geometry. We introduce the concept of mixed fiber polytopes, a class of polytopes that arise as the Minkowski sum of tropical varieties and fiber polytopes. Our main result is a tropical implicitization theorem, which establishes a one-to-one correspondence between mixed fiber polytopes and tropical polynomials of a given degree. This correspondence is facilitated by a novel algorithm that computes the mixed fiber polytope associated with a given tropical polynomial. We demonstrate the applicability of our approach by applying it to the implicitization of tropical curves and surfaces, as well as the computation of tropical Milnor numbers. Our have significant implications for the study of tropical geometry, algebraic geometry, and computer-aided geometric design, and provide a powerful tool for the analysis and computation of tropical varieties. The mixed fiber polytope framework offers a new perspective on the geometric structure of tropical polynomials, and opens up new avenues for research in tropical geometry and its applications.

Our theoretical framework and numerical simulations show that nonlocal correlations can be harnessed to generate frequency-dependent signals with high spectral resolution and accuracy. Text: We present a comparative work of dust-to-gas ratios in a sample of luminous, ultraluminous, and hyperluminous infrared galaxies, leveraging high-resolution spectroscopic data from the Atacama Large Millimeter/submillimeter Array (ALMA) and the Hubble Space Telescope. Our analysis indicates distinct trends in the dust-to-gas ratios among these extreme infrared emitters, which are characterized by intense star formation activity and substantial galaxy-scale gas reservoirs. At the same time, the luminous infrared galaxies exhibit a narrow range of dust-to-gas ratios, indicative of efficient gas consumption and dust production through star-forming processes. In contrast, the ultraluminous infrared galaxies display a wider dispersion in dust-to-gas ratios, suggesting the presence of additional dust enrichment mechanisms, such as active galactic nuclei (AGN) activity or mergers. As a result, the hyperluminous infrared galaxies, meanwhile, show the lowest dust-to-gas ratios, implying a dominant role for gas stripping or outflows in regulating their dust content. These findings have notable implications for our insight into of the complex interplay between gas, dust, and star formation in extreme galaxy populations, and further investigation of these trends is essential for refining galaxy evolution models and shedding light on the mechanisms driving the formation of the most luminous galaxies in the universe.

Text: When a charge is held static near a constant density spherical star, it experiences a self-force which is significantly different from the force it would experience when placed near a black hole of the same mass. The force is found to be repulsive. A similar calculation of the self-force is also performed for a conducting star. This calculation is valid for any static, spherically conducting star, since the result is independent of the interior metric. When the charge is placed very close to the conducting star, the force is found to be attractive but when the charge is placed beyond a certain distance (2.95M for a conducting star of radius 2.25M), the force is found to be repulsive. When the charge is placed very far from the star (be it conducting or insulating), the charge experiences the same repulsive force it would experience when placed in the spacetime of a black hole with the same mass as the star.

Text: **On the superstrings-induced four-dimensional gravity, and its applications to cosmology** The emergence of four-dimensional gravity remains an open problem in theoretical physics, with various approaches attempting to reconcile the principles of general relativity with the requirements of quantum mechanics. In the context of superstring theory, the compactification of extra dimensions can give rise to four-dimensional effective field theories. We investigate the superstrings-induced four-dimensional gravity, exploring its potential applications to cosmology. Employing a top-down approach, we compactify ten-dimensional superstring theory on a Calabi-Yau manifold, resulting in a four-dimensional effective field theory. We then use the resulting Lagrangian to derive the Einstein field equations, incorporating the effects of superstring-induced corrections. Our analysis focuses on the cosmological implications of these corrections, including their potential impact on the early universe. Our demonstrate that the superstrings-induced four-dimensional gravity exhibits novel features, such as a non-trivial cosmological constant and modified Friedmann equations. These modifications lead to interesting cosmological scenarios, including accelerated expansion and alternative models of dark energy. Our have significant implications for the study of the early universe and the nature of gravity at high energies.

Text: The development of generalized kinetic equations for charge carriers in graphene is a crucial step towards understanding the unique transport properties of this two-dimensional material. Graphene's remarkable electronic properties, such as high carrier mobility and anomalous quantum Hall effect, are influenced by the interactions between charge carriers and the lattice vibrations, as well as other quasiparticles. To capture these complex interactions, we have derived a set of generalized kinetic equations that take into account the non-equilibrium distribution of charge carriers, phonons, and other excitations. Our approach is based on the nonequilibrium Green's function formalism, which allows us to incorporate the effects of electron-phonon, electron-electron, and electron-impurity interactions on the charge carrier dynamics. The resulting kinetic equations provide a comprehensive description of the transport coefficients, such as conductivity, Seebeck coefficient, and thermal conductivity, and enable the study of various nonequilibrium phenomena, including hot carrier relaxation, thermoelectric effects, and nonlinear transport. By applying these generalized kinetic equations to graphene, we can gain deeper insights into the underlying physics of charge carrier transport in this material and explore its potential applications in nanoelectronics and optoelectronics.

Text: In this investigation we scrutinize the kernel of the norm homomorphism within a restricted class of unramified extensions of number fields; more precisely, we focus on extensions of the form \(K/F\) where the base field \(F\) is a quadratic extension of \(\mathbb{Q}\) and \(K\) constitutes an unramified extension of \(F\) of degree \(n\). Our central objective is to ascertain the precise structure of the kernel of the norm map \(N_{K/F}\colon K^{\times}\to F^{\times}\), and we succeed in deriving sharp, explicit criteria under which this kernel collapses to the trivial subgroup. To achieve this, we deploy a multifaceted arsenal of algebraic and analytic tools—including Galois cohomology, the apparatus of class field theory, and the arithmetic of cyclotomic fields—to forge a rigorous link between the kernel’s constitution and the underlying arithmetic invariants of the extension \(K/F\). The ramifications of our reverberate across several domains: they refine our comprehension of class groups and ideal class groups, illuminate the internal architecture of the field extensions under consideration, and, more broadly, shed fresh light on the intricate interplay between the norm map and the arithmetic of unramified number field extensions, thereby deepening the theoretical understanding of these kernels in the unramified setting.

Text: The study of orthogonal complex structures on domains in R^4 has garnered significant attention in recent years due to its profound implications in geometry, topology, and theoretical physics. Our research reveals that the presence of orthogonal complex structures on a domain in R^4 imposes stringent conditions on the domain's curvature and topology, leading to a rich and intricate relationship between the complex and Riemannian geometries of the domain. Specifically, we demonstrate that the existence of orthogonal complex structures on a domain in R^4 is intimately tied to the domain's Kahler-Einstein metric, and that the topology of the domain plays a crucial role in determining the existence and uniqueness of such structures. Text: In this investigation, we undertake a comprehensive examination of the non-Hermitian von Roos Hamiltonian, a quantum mechanical system characterized by $\eta$-weak-pseudo-Hermiticity, a distinctive property that enables the Hamiltonian's energy spectrum to remain real despite its non-Hermitian nature. This peculiarity arises from the of an anti-Hermitian operator $\eta$, through which the von Roos Hamiltonian is derived and its $\eta$-weak-pseudo-Hermiticity is demonstrated, exemplified by the condition $\eta \hat{H} \eta^{-1} = \hat{H}^\dagger$, which serves as a defining characteristic of this phenomenon. Notably, we establish that the von Roos Hamiltonian exhibits isospectrality with its Hermitian counterpart, a consequence of which is that the energy spectra of the non-Hermitian and Hermitian systems coincide identically. Furthermore, by exploiting the isospectrality and $\eta$-weak-pseudo-Hermiticity of the von Roos Hamiltonian, we demonstrate its exact solvability, thereby facilitating the exact solution of the Schrödinger equation for this system and allowing us to obtain the eigenvalues and eigenstates, which are shown to be real and orthogonal. Text: In this work, we investigate the emergence of toroidal magnetic fields in type II superconducting neutron stars, a phenomenon that has significant implications for our understanding of these enigmatic objects. Text: RNA motifs typically consist of short, modular patterns that include base pairs formed within and between modules. Estimating the abundance of these patterns is of fundamental importance for assessing the statistical significance of matches in genomewide searches, and for predicting whether a given function has evolved many times in different species or arose from a single common ancestor. In this manuscript, we review in an integrated and self-contained manner some basic concepts of automata theory, generating functions and transfer matrix that are relevant to pattern analysis in biological sequences. We formalize, in a general framework, the concept of Markov chain embedding to analyze patterns in random strings produced by a memoryless source. This conceptualization, together with the capability of automata to recognize complicated patterns, allows a systematic analysis of problems related to the occurrence and frequency of patterns in random strings. The applications we present focus on the concept of synchronization of automata, as well as automata used to search for a finite number of keywords (including sets of patterns generated according to base pairing rules) in a general text.

Text: This work presents a novel non-linear symmetry-preserving observer design on Lie groups, providing a framework for estimating the state of complex dynamical systems that exhibit Lie group structure. The performance of the observer is demonstrated through simulations and experiments on a variety of Lie group-valued systems, including a robotic manipulator on SE(3) and a quantum system on SU(2). Text: The Yukawa-Higgs model is a fundamental theory in particle physics describing the interaction between fermions and scalar bosons. However, the fermion doubling problem associated with lattice discretization of fermions necessitates the use of Ginsparg-Wilson (GW) fermions, which preserve chiral symmetry. This presents a study of the perturbative spectrum of the Yukawa-Higgs model with GW fermions. We employ a lattice discretization of the Yukawa-Higgs model with GW fermions and perform a perturbative analysis in the strong coupling regime. The GW fermion action is implemented using the overlap formalism, and the scalar boson action is discretized using a standard Wilson action. We calculate the fermion and boson propagators in the perturbative regime and analyze the mass spectrum of the model. Interestingly, we observed that the perturbative spectrum of the Yukawa-Higgs model with GW fermions exhibits a characteristic pattern of degenerate mass eigenstates, consistent with the expected behavior of a chirally symmetric theory. We observe a suppression of the fermion mass in the presence of the scalar boson, indicating a significant effect of the Yukawa interaction. Our provide insights into the properties of the Yukawa-Higgs model in the strong coupling regime and have implications for lattice simulations of the standard model.

Text: The zero-temperature limit of Gibbs measures constitutes a central problem in statistical mechanics and dynamical systems, linking thermodynamic formalism with the selection of ground-state configurations. While one-dimensional lattice models with short-range interactions admit explicit solutions at positive temperature, the behavior of the corresponding Gibbs states as the inverse temperature β → ∞ remains only partially understood, especially concerning uniqueness, convergence, and the role of sub-exponential energy barriers. We consider a broad class of one-dimensional lattice systems defined by Hölder-continuous potentials on the full shift Σ = {0,1}ℤ. Using the Ruelle-Perron-Frobenius operator, we derive precise asymptotics for the leading eigenvalue and eigenfunction as β grows. A variational analysis based on the Dobrushin-Lanford-Ruelle equations is combined with renewal-type estimates to control the contribution of rare excitations. Moreover, we implement a coupling-construction that yields explicit bounds on the total variation distance between finite-volume Gibbs measures at temperature T = 1/β and the set of invariant measures minimizing the potential. We prove that, for generic Hölder potentials, the family of Gibbs measures converges weak-∗ to a unique ground-state measure supported on the set of minimizing configurations. In contrast, for a dense subset of non-generic potentials we exhibit non-uniqueness and a temperature-dependent selection mechanism, characterized by a hierarchical ordering of minimizing periodic orbits. These delineate the precise conditions under which the zero-temperature limit is well-behaved in one dimension and illuminate the interplay between regularity of the interaction and the emergence of multiple ground-state phases.

Text: This research article presents a comprehensive analysis of the anisotropic piezoresistive phenomena observed in two-dimensional hole systems localized within (311)A-oriented gallium arsenide (GaAs) substrates under cryogenic operational conditions. Through the application of magneto-transport characterization techniques coupled with precise strain calibration methodologies, the study establishes that the piezoresistive coefficients exhibit pronounced directional variability, contingent upon the crystallographic orientation of the (311)A plane. At sub-5 K temperatures, where thermal noise-induced perturbations are minimized, the measured piezoresistive response demonstrates a marked in-plane anisotropy, with divergent magnitudes along [110] and [1-10] crystallographic axes, attributed to the asymmetric interaction between applied strain and the valence band structure of the quantum-confined hole ensemble. Theoretical modeling, integrating deformation potential formalism and k·p perturbation theory, provides a rigorous framework to rationalize these directional dependencies, emphasizing the role of valence band hybridization and the interplay between surface anisotropy and effective mass dispersion. Notably, the low-temperature regime amplifies the system's sensitivity to strain-mediated modulation of carrier density, yielding a piezoresistive gauge factor surpassing previously documented values for (001) GaAs configurations. These not only elucidate the fundamental interplay among crystal symmetry, quantum confinement, and mechanical strain in anisotropic semiconductor heterostructures but also underscore the (311)A GaAs platform's potential for next-generation strain-sensing technologies, offering enhanced performance metrics through tailored crystallographic engineering.

Text: Periodic travelling waves are fundamental solutions of the shallow‑water equations and play a central role in coastal and oceanic dynamics. While classical linear theory predicts neutral stability for such waves, nonlinear effects—particularly those captured by Newton’s second‑order ordinary differential equation governing the wave profile—can induce modulational and subharmonic instabilities. A rigorous stability assessment that integrates the underlying Hamiltonian structure with modern spectral techniques remains lacking. We reformulate the travelling‑wave problem as a Hamiltonian system derived from Newton’s equation for the free‑surface elevation, employing a phase‑plane reduction to obtain a one‑parameter family of periodic orbits. Floquet theory is then applied to the linearised perturbation equations, and the associated monodromy matrix is computed analytically for small‑amplitude waves and numerically for finite amplitudes using a spectral collocation scheme. The Krein signature of eigenvalues is evaluated to distinguish between spectrally stable and unstable regimes, and continuation trace stability boundaries in the parameter space defined by wave steepness and depth‑to‑wavelength ratio. The analysis reveals two distinct instability mechanisms: (i) a Benjamin‑Feir‑type modulational instability emerging beyond a critical steepness threshold, and (ii) a subharmonic bifurcation linked to resonances with the underlying Newtonian potential. For shallow depths (h ≪ λ) the modulational band shrinks, rendering long‑wave periodic solutions spectrally stable, whereas deeper configurations exhibit pronounced instability islands. These provide a comprehensive map of stability domains for periodic travelling shallow‑water waves, offering predictive insight for both theoretical studies and engineering applications.

Text: We introduce an enhanced negative type for finite metric trees, providing a novel framework for the characterization and classification of such structures. Text: For a finitely generated group G and a banach space X let \alpha^*_X(G) (respectively \alpha^#_X(G)) be the supremum over all \alpha\ge 0 such that there exists a Lipschitz mapping (respectively an equivariant mapping) f:G\to X and c>0 such that for all x,y\in G we have \|f(x)-f(y)\|\ge c\cdot d_G(x,y)^\alpha. In particular, the Hilbert compression exponent (respectively the equivariant Hilbert compression exponent) of G is \alpha^*(G)=\alpha^*_{L_2}(G) (respectively \alpha^#(G)= \alpha_{L_2}^#(G)). Text: The descent algebra of the symmetric group, introduced by Solomon, encodes the combinatorial structure of permutation descents and has been extensively studied over fields of characteristic 0. Moreover, we establish that 𝔇ₙ(𝔽ₚ) is a quasi‑hereditary algebra with a heredity chain governed by the dominance order on p‑cores. Text: The Maximum Weighted Edge Biclique (MWEB) problem—selecting a complete bipartite subgraph of a weighted bipartite graph that maximizes the sum of its edge weights—captures the combinatorial core of numerous data‑mining, bioinformatics, and network‑analysis tasks. Despite its centrality, the approximability landscape of MWEB remains poorly understood, especially when edge weights can be both positive and negative. Establishing strong hardness is essential for guiding algorithm design and for delineating the limits of tractable special cases. We employ a reduction framework based on the Gap‑Exponential Time Hypothesis (Gap‑ETH) and the PCP theorem to construct gap‑preserving reductions from well‑studied label‑cover and densest‑k‑subgraph instances to MWEB. By carefully encoding weight signs and magnitudes, we prove that any polynomial‑time algorithm achieving an approximation ratio better than \(2^{\log^{1-\epsilon} n}\) (for any constant \(\epsilon>0\)) would violate Gap‑ETH. The reductions are further refined to preserve bipartiteness and to apply to weighted variants with bounded integer weights, yielding tight inapproximability bounds across a spectrum of weight regimes. We demonstrate that MWEB is not only NP‑hard but also **strongly inapproximable**: no polynomial‑time algorithm can achieve a sub‑exponential approximation factor unless widely believed complexity assumptions fail. These hardness immediately imply similar limits for a suite of applications, including community detection in signed networks, bicluster mining with mixed relevance scores, and optimal design of cross‑modal recommendation systems. Consequently, any practical approach to these domains must rely on heuristics, parameterized algorithms, or restrictive structural assumptions rather than generic approximation schemes.

Text: Quantified constraints and Quantified Boolean Formulae are typically much more difficult to reason with than classical constraints, because quantifier alternation makes the usual notion of solution inappropriate. In this paper, we show that most of the properties that are used by solvers for CSP can be generalized to quantified CSP. We propose a systematic study of the relations which hold between these properties, as well as complexity regarding the decision of these properties. Text: When we experience that unmistakable shiver down our spines, as if a cold breeze has swept through our veins, we know that music has reached a place deep within us. It's as if the notes and melodies have somehow tapped into our emotional core, sending a resonance through every fibre of our being. The sensation is both exhilarating and humbling, a reminder that music has the power to transcend the rational and speak directly to our soul. We might attribute this phenomenon to the emotional intensity of a particular song, but the truth is more complex. It's not just the lyrics or the melody that move us - it's the intricate web of memories, associations, and personal experiences that we've woven around the music. A particular tune might evoke the smell of our childhood home, the sight of a loved one's smile, or the feeling of standing on a mountaintop, gazing out at an endless horizon. As we listen, our minds are flooded with these memories, and the music becomes a kind of emotional anchor, securing us to a particular moment in time. In this way, music gives us chills not just because of its beauty or its power, but because it reminds us of the messy, beautiful tapestry of our own lives - and the ways in which music has been there to weave it all together. As we experience that shiver, we're not just responding to the music - we're responding to ourselves.
Label: AW

Text: The accelerated expansion of the universe, driven by the enigmatic dark energy, has long been a subject of intense scientific investigation. One promising avenue for understanding the nature and evolution of dark energy lies in the time-dependent behavior of cosmological redshift, a phenomenon directly observable in the light emitted by distant sources over cosmic time. By analyzing the redshift drift signal, a direct consequence of the temporal evolution of redshifts, we have assessed the potential of this probe to discriminate between different dark energy models and constrain their underlying parameters. Our findings indicate that the redshift drift signal can indeed provide valuable insights into the equation of state of dark energy, thereby shedding light on its properties and evolution over cosmic scales. Moreover, our analysis of future spectroscopic surveys, including those enabled by the Extremely Large Telescope, reveals that these forthcoming facilities will be capable of detecting the redshift drift signal with exceptional precision, thereby offering a promising route for testing dark energy models and refining our understanding of the universe's expansion history.
Label: AWP

Text: We present a comprehensive dynamical model of the Andromeda galaxy (M 31), focusing on the distribution of visible matter and dark matter. Utilizing a suite of hydrodynamic simulations, we have developed a multi-component model that accurately reproduces the observed morphological and kinematic features of M 31. Our model incorporates a range of physical processes, including stellar and gas dynamics, star formation, and feedback mechanisms. The visible matter distribution is represented by a combination of stellar and gas components, while the dark matter is treated as a diffuse, collisionless fluid. By fitting the model to a range of observational constraints, including photometric, spectroscopic, and kinematic data, we have derived a detailed dark matter density distribution for M 31. Our indicate that the dark matter halo is a triaxial, oblate system with a density profile that is well-represented by a Navarro-Frenk-White (NFW) profile. The dark matter fraction within the optical radius of M 31 is found to be approximately 70%, with a mass-to-light ratio that is consistent with the expectations of cold dark matter cosmology. Our model provides a robust framework for understanding the complex interplay between visible and dark matter in the Andromeda galaxy.

Text: This study presents a comprehensive analysis of near-infrared (near-IR) spectral features of red supergiants and giants, with a focus on the effects of surface abundance ratios on their spectral properties. We developed a set of theoretical models that incorporate both solar and mixing-induced surface abundance ratios, allowing us to examine the impact of these ratios on the near-IR spectra of these stars. Our models demonstrate that the near-IR spectra of red supergiants and giants are sensitive to the surface abundance ratios of key elements such as carbon, nitrogen, and oxygen. The models with mixing-induced surface abundance ratios exhibit distinct spectral features, including altered molecular band strengths and shifted spectral line profiles, compared to those with solar abundance ratios. By comparing our theoretical models with observed near-IR spectra of red supergiants and giants, we aim to constrain the surface abundance ratios of these stars and gain insights into their evolutionary histories and internal mixing processes. The of this study have significant implications for our understanding of the formation and evolution of massive stars and the role of internal mixing in shaping their spectral properties.

Text: We investigate the physical interpretation of the Riemann zeta function as a FZZT brane partition function associated with a matrix/gravity correspondence. The Hilbert-Polya operator in this interpretation is the master matrix of the large N matrix model. Using a related function $\Xi(z)$ we develop an analogy between this function and the Airy function Ai(z) of the Gaussian matrix model. The analogy gives an intuitive physical reason why the zeros lie on a critical line. Using a Fourier transform of the $\Xi(z)$ function we identify a Kontsevich integrand. Generalizing this integrand to $n \times n$ matrices we develop a Kontsevich matrix model which describes n FZZT branes. The Kontsevich model associated with the $\Xi(z)$ function is given by a superposition of Liouville type matrix models that have been used to describe matrix model instantons.

Text: This study presents a comprehensive analysis of self-similar solutions for the non-strictly hyperbolic Whitham equations, a system of partial differential equations that arise in the context of the Korteweg-de Vries (KdV) hierarchy. We derive a general framework for obtaining self-similar solutions by employing a similarity transformation approach, which yields a set of ordinary differential equations that govern the behavior of the solutions. Our demonstrate that the Whitham equations admit a rich family of self-similar solutions, including solitary waves, cnoidal waves, and periodic waves, which are characterized by their spatial and temporal evolution. By examining the properties of these self-similar solutions, we uncover interesting connections between the Whitham equations and the underlying KdV hierarchy, shedding new light on the dynamics of nonlinear dispersive waves. Furthermore, our provide a deeper understanding of the role of non-strict hyperbolicity in the behavior of the Whitham equations, highlighting its implications for the development of wave patterns and the emergence of singularities. The of this study have significant implications for the study of nonlinear waves and the development of new mathematical models for understanding their behavior.

Text: **Precision Measurement of the Casimir-Lifshitz Force in a Fluid: Unraveling the Complex Interplay between Quantum Fluctuations and Fluid Dynamics using Advanced Nanoscale Characterization Techniques.** In a pioneering effort to elucidate the intricacies of the Casimir-Lifshitz force, a fundamental electromagnetic phenomenon arising from the quantization of the photon field, a multidisciplinary team of researchers has successfully measured this force in a fluidic system with unprecedented precision. The experiment leveraged cutting-edge nanoscale characterization techniques, including atomic force microscopy and ellipsometry, to elucidate the precise dynamics of the force in a fluidic environment. Two parallel plates made of a transparent material were situated in a fixed separation, enabled by a microelectromechanical system that provided meticulous control over the gap distance, thus circumventing a longstanding challenge in accurately quantifying this phenomenon. The measurement protocol involved a synergistic combination of numerical simulations and experimental data, thereby validating the accuracy of the and revealing the profound influence of fluid dynamics on the behavior of the Casimir-Lifshitz force. A thorough investigation of the interplay between the plate material properties, fluid viscosity, and force magnitude was also conducted, shedding valuable light on the underlying physics of this complex phenomenon. The outcomes of this research hold significant implications for the development of novel applications of the Casimir effect in fluid-based systems, thereby illuminating opportunities for novel technological innovations. The precision measurement protocol used in this study exemplifies the convergence of advanced nanoscale characterization techniques and sophisticated control of the experimental environment, thereby providing a comprehensive understanding of the Casimir-Lifshitz force in a fluidic environment. As a consequence, this research contributes to the enrichment of our understanding of quantum fluctuations in complex environments, paving the way for further investigations into the intricacies of this enigmatic phenomenon. **Relevant Keywords:** Casimir-Lifshitz force, fluid dynamics, precision measurement, nanoscale characterization, atomic force microscopy, ellipsometry.

Text: We present spectroscopic observations of the AndXII dwarf spheroidal galaxy using DEIMOS/Keck-II, showing it to be moving rapidly through the Local Group (-556 km/s heliocentric velocity, -281 km/s relative to Andromeda from the MW), falling into the Local Group from 115 kpc beyond Andromeda's nucleus. AndXII therefore represents a dwarf galaxy plausibly falling into the Local Group for the first time, and never having experienced a dense galactic environment. From Green Bank Telescope observations, a limit on the H{I} gas mass of <3000 Msun suggests that AndXII's gas could have been removed prior to experiencing the tides of the Local Group galaxies. Orbit models suggest the dwarf is close to the escape velocity of M31 for published mass models. AndXII is our best direct evidence for the late infall of satellite galaxies, a prediction of cosmological simulations.

Text: This work deals with the effects of an anharmonic trap on an interacting two-boson system in one dimension. Our primary focus is on the role of the induced coupling between the center of mass and the relative motion as both anharmonicity and the (repulsive) interaction strength are varied. The ground state reveals a strong localization in the relative coordinate, counteracting the tendency to fragment for stronger repulsion. To explore the quantum dynamics, we study the system's response upon (i) exciting the harmonic ground state by continuously switching on an additional anharmonicity, and (ii) displacing the center of mass, this way triggering collective oscillations. The interplay between collective and internal dynamics materializes in the collapse of oscillations, which are explained in terms of few-mode models.

Text: Let $ X: M \hook S^5$ be a compact Legendrian surface in pseudoconformal(CR) 5-sphere. We introduce a pseudoconformally invariant Willmore type second order functional $ \W(X)$, and study its critical points called Willmore Legendrian surfaces. The fifth order structure equations show that Willmore dual can be defined for a class of Willmore Legendrian surfaces. Moreover when this dual is constant, Willmore Legendrian surface admits a Weierstra\ss type representation in terms of immersed meromorphic curve in $ \C^2$ satisfying an appropriate real period condition via pseudoconformal stereographic projection. We show that every compact Riemann surface admits a generally one to one, conformal, Willmore Legendrian immersion in $ S^5$ with constant Willmore dual. As a corollary, every compact Riemann surface can be conformally immersed in $ \C^2$ as an exact, algebraic Lagrangian surface.

Text: This study investigates the intricate relationship between probabilities and quantum fluctuations, shedding new light on the fundamental principles governing the behavior of microscopic systems in quantum mechanics. We examine the probabilistic nature of quantum states, where the uncertainty principle implies that certain properties, such as position and momentum, cannot be precisely known simultaneously. By employing a mathematical framework based on the Feynman path integral formulation, we illustrate that quantum fluctuations arise from the superposition of multiple probabilistic outcomes, leading to the emergence of characteristic features such as entanglement and non-locality. Our analysis reveals that the probabilistic nature of quantum mechanics is intricately linked to the inherent fluctuations, with the latter serving as a manifestation of the former. The outcomes of this study contribute to a deeper grasp of of the probabilistic foundations of quantum mechanics and have implications for the development of novel quantum technologies, including quantum computing and quantum metrology. The findings presented here offer a novel perspective on the interplay between probability and quantum fluctuations.

Text: This study offers a theoretical investigation of electron transport phenomena in a gate-all-around silicon nanowire, employing the Green's function formalism to systematically analyze the interplay between charge carrier confinement and scattering-induced decoherence under the influence of impurity-induced perturbations. The computational framework is grounded in the non-equilibrium Green's function formalism, which systematically incorporates spatial heterogeneity in both the electrostatic potential and the scattering potential arising from impurity distributions. The nanowire architecture under scrutiny features a gate-all-around configuration, wherein the semiconductor channel is enveloped by metallic gates on all lateral and axial surfaces, thereby enabling precise modulation of the electrostatic environment. Through this approach, we elucidate the manner in which impurity scattering modulates the conductance characteristics of the nanowire, culminating in a diminished transmission probability across the device. Additionally, the energy-dependent behavior of transmission coefficients is scrutinized in relation to the magnitude of the impurity scattering potential, revealing critical correlations between electron energy levels and scattering efficiency. These not only provide profound insights into the transport dynamics of gate-all-around silicon nanowires but also underscore their significance for the rational design and optimization of nanoscale electronic systems, particularly in contexts where scattering effects dominate device performance.

Text: This study explores the properties and behavior of non-real zeros of linear differential polynomials, which are a fundamental class of objects in algebraic and differential geometry. By extending the of previous research on real zeros, we develop a comprehensive framework for understanding the distribution and asymptotic behavior of non-real zeros of linear differential polynomials. Our approach is based on a novel application of the method of majorized sequences, which enables us to derive sharp bounds on the number of non-real zeros and their distribution in the complex plane. We also establish a link between the non-real zeros of linear differential polynomials and the topology of their associated algebraic curves, providing new insights into the geometric structure of these curves. Our have significant implications for various fields, including differential equations, algebraic geometry, and theoretical physics, where linear differential polynomials play a crucial role in modeling complex systems and phenomena. The of this study lay the groundwork for further research in this area and provide a deeper understanding of the underlying mathematical structures governing the behavior of non-real zeros of linear differential polynomials.

Text: The control of quantum dynamics via specially tailored laser pulses is a long-standing goal in physics and chemistry. Partly, this dream has come true, as sophisticated pulse shaping experiments allow to coherently control product ratios of chemical reactions. The theoretical design of the laser pulse to transfer an initial state to a given final state can be achieved with the help of quantum optimal control theory (QOCT). This tutorial provides an to QOCT. It shows how the control equations defining such an optimal pulse follow from the variation of a properly defined functional. We explain the most successful schemes to solve these control equations and show how to incorporate additional constraints in the pulse design. The algorithms are then applied to simple quantum systems and the obtained pulses are analyzed. Besides the traditional final-time control , the tutorial also presents an algorithm and an example to handle time-dependent control targets.

Text: This study investigates the phenomenon of symmetry breaking in few layer graphene films, a topic of significant interest in the field of two-dimensional materials research. Through a combination of experimental and computational techniques, we demonstrate that the symmetry breaking in these films arises from the intrinsic stacking disorder and layer bending, which induce strain fields that disrupt the otherwise perfect hexagonal lattice structure of graphene. Our experiments, utilizing scanning tunneling microscopy and atomic force microscopy, reveal the emergence of local symmetry breaking in few layer graphene films, manifesting as the formation of pentagonal and heptagonal defects. Theoretical simulations, based on density functional theory and continuum mechanics, corroborate these , predicting the formation of strain-induced defects and their impact on the electronic structure of the material. Our have important implications for the understanding of the unique properties of few layer graphene films, and highlight the need for careful consideration of structural imperfections in the design and application of these materials in emerging technologies, such as nanoelectronics and energy storage devices.

Text: This study explores the phenomenon of lepton flavor violating (LFV) photoleptonic effect, a hypothetical process in which a high-energy photon is absorbed by a lepton, resulting in the emission of a different lepton flavor. We propose a novel theoretical framework to describe this process, incorporating recent advances in quantum field theory and particle physics. Our model predicts the existence of a new, dimension-5 effective operator responsible for the LFV photoleptonic effect, which arises from the interaction between the photon and a lepton with a virtual lepton flavor-changing boson. We derive a set of constraints on the model parameters, focusing on the muon-electron flavor-violating channel, and confront them with existing experimental data from high-energy particle colliders, such as the LHC and B-factories. Our indicate that the LFV photoleptonic effect may be accessible to future experimental searches, particularly in the context of the electron-muon flavor-violating process. Furthermore, we discuss the implications of our on the Standard Model of particle physics and potential new physics beyond the Standard Model.

Text: This study investigates the properties of conserved matter superenergy currents in the context of orthogonally transitive Abelian G2 isometry groups, which are ubiquitous in various gravitational and cosmological scenarios. By employing a covariant and tetrad-based approach, we derive an explicit expression for the superenergy current, which is found to be intimately connected to the intrinsic geometry of the spacetime manifold. Our analysis reveals that the conserved current is determined by the interplay between the matter fields and the spacetime geometry, with the Abelian G2 isometry group playing a pivotal role in constraining the possible configurations. We demonstrate that the superenergy current satisfies a set of conservation equations, which can be used to impose constraints on the matter fields and the spacetime geometry. Furthermore, our show that the conserved current can be expressed as a sum of contributions from the matter fields and the spacetime geometry, providing a novel insight into the interplay between matter and geometry in the presence of orthogonally transitive Abelian G2 isometry groups, and shedding new light on the underlying structure of the theory. The implications of our are discussed in the context of various astrophysical and cosmological applications.

Text: This study investigates the phenomenon of tunneled crystals in the context of sphere packings, with a focus on elucidating the structural characteristics that emerge as the packing approaches the jamming threshold, and by employing advanced computational methods and machine learning techniques, we simulated and analyzed the behavior of monodisperse hard spheres under various compressions, thereby capturing the intricate dynamics of the system as it transitions from a fluid-like to a solid-like state. Our results reveal the emergence of tunneled crystals, which are characterized by the presence of crystalline domains with periodically arranged tunnel-like structures. These features are shown to be indicative of a metastable state, wherein the system is poised to undergo a phase transition to a fully jammed crystal. Through a detailed analysis of the structural and kinematic properties of the system, we illustrate that the formation of tunneled crystals is a hallmark of the approach to the jamming threshold, and that these structures play a crucial role in mediating the transition to full crystallization. These findings contribute significantly to our understanding of the complex dynamics of soft matter systems and have implications for the design of innovative materials with unique properties.

Text: Luminous Compact Galaxies (LCGs) are a rare, high-surface-brightness population that dominates the star-formation budget at intermediate redshift (0.5 < z < 1.5). Their small physical sizes (r ≲ 2 kpc) and intense star-forming activity suggest that they may be the progenitors of present-day spheroids, yet their internal structures and evolutionary pathways remain poorly constrained. We selected 312 LCGs from the HST/ACS GOODS-North and GOODS-South fields using a combined magnitude (M_B < -20) and half-light radius (r_e < 2 kpc) criterion. Multi-band ACS imaging (F435W, F606W, F775W, F850LP) was processed with the GALFIT package to obtain Sérsic indices, effective radii, and axial ratios. Complementary non-parametric diagnostics (Gini, M20, asymmetry) were measured to quantify morphological disturbance. Stellar masses and star-formation rates were derived from SED fitting to the GOODS photometric catalogues, and spectroscopic redshifts were incorporated where available. The majority (≈ 68 %) of LCGs exhibit high asymmetry (A > 0.35) and elevated Gini-M20 signatures consistent with major mergers or violent disk instabilities. Approximately 22 % possess disk-like Sérsic indices (n ≈ 1-2) and low asymmetry, indicating a subset of compact, rotationally supported systems. The remaining objects show high Sérsic indices (n > 3) and smooth light profiles, characteristic of nascent spheroids. Stellar masses span 109.5-1011 M_⊙, with specific star-formation rates an order of magnitude above the main sequence. Crucially, these imply that LCGs are a heterogeneous class, where merger-driven bursts dominate at higher redshifts while a minority evolve into compact early-type galaxies, contributing significantly to the buildup of the red-sequence population.
