Text: we explore the intersection of neutrino physics and cosmological selection, delving into the theoretical framework of growing neutrinos as a solution to the Hubble tension. By reevaluating the current understanding of neutrino mass and the cosmological constant, we put forward a original cosmological model where neutrinos are allowed to grow in mass over time. This paradigm shift enables a reconciliation of the observed value of the Hubble constant with the predictions of the Planck satellite. We demonstrate that a growing neutrino model can accommodate the observed features of the cosmic microwave background, large-scale structure, and type Ia supernovae, thereby providing a viable alternative to the standard LCDM cosmology. Furthermore, our analysis reveals that the growth of neutrino mass can lead to a selection effect in the observable universe, where regions with a higher neutrino density are preferentially selected, influencing the observed distribution of galaxies and galaxy clusters. The implications of this work extend beyond cosmology, shedding light on the fundamental nature of neutrinos and their role in shaping the universe. This investigation provides a new perspective on the interplay between neutrino physics and cosmological evolution.

Text: we examine the complete phenomenological lifecycle of microscopic black holes that could be produced in high‑energy particle collisions under scenarios of TeV‑scale gravity with large extra dimensions. Employing semiclassical Hawking‑radiation theory combined with state‑of‑the‑art parton‑distribution functions, we simulate black‑hole formation at center‑of‑mass energies accessible to the Large Hadron Collider and prospective 100 TeV machines, tracking the subsequent balding, spin‑down, Schwarzschild, and Planck phases. The assessment quantifies evaporation spectra, multiplicities, and angular distributions of Standard‑Model quanta, emphasizing distinctive high‑multiplicity, high‑transverse‑momentum signatures and missing‑energy patterns arising from graviton emission into the bulk. Constraints from recent LHC data are recast to set lower bounds on the fundamental Planck scale, while Monte‑Carlo studies evaluate detector efficiencies for the most promising channels. We also discuss safety considerations, confirming that rapid Hawking evaporation precludes any catastrophic growth. The results delineate the parameter space where black‑hole events remain experimentally observable, outline strategies for their identification in upcoming collider runs, and highlight the implications of a potential discovery for quantum‑gravity phenomenology.
Label: AWH

Text: In a dull and colorless village, a poor artist quietly chose to brighten the lives of others through a secret act of kindness. Each night, while everyone slept, he carried his simple brushes and leftover paint to the cracked walls of the town square, covering them with lively scenes of nature, flying birds, and blooming fields. He never signed his work or looked for recognition. Every morning, the villagers awoke to fresh bursts of color that lifted their spirits and brought the community together, though no one knew who was responsible. The paintings slowly transformed the town's atmosphere, inspiring hope and warmth among its people, while the artist remained satisfied working unnoticed. Years later, after he died alone in his small shack, the villagers discovered stacks of worn brushes and sketches identical to the murals. Only then did they understand that the quiet man they had ignored was the one who had filled their village with life and beauty. To honor him, they turned his modest home into a public gallery, remembering him as proof that true greatness does not depend on fame or applause, but on the lasting impact of one's contributions.

Text: This investigation critically examines a contemporary empirical validation of Bell inequality violations, thereby substantiating the non-local correlations inherent in quantum mechanics and challenging classical notions of locality. Utilizing entangled photon pairs produced through spontaneous parametric down-conversion, the experimental design incorporated polarization measurements at spatially non-commuting detectors, synchronized via relativistically constrained protocols to preclude causal influence between measurement events. The implementation employed high-fidelity superconducting nanowire single-photon detectors in conjunction with dynamically randomized measurement bases, effectively mitigating detection and locality loopholes that have historically compromised the robustness of prior Bell tests. Analysis of 1.5 × 10^9 photon pairs yielded a CHSH-Bell parameter value of S = 2.82 ± 0.04, which markedly exceeded the classical threshold of 2 by 19 standard deviations, thereby demonstrating a statistically indubitable deviation from local hidden variable theories. Quantum-theoretical predictions, derived from the formalism of entangled state superposition, exhibited precise concordance with the observed data, affirming the intrinsic non-separability of quantum systems. The experimental protocol further incorporated temporal coincidence counting and Bayesian error analysis to quantify the resilience of the observed violations against potential systematic biases, including detector dead-time effects and temporal drift. These not only consolidate the empirical foundation of quantum non-locality but also establish a paradigmatic framework for future investigations into quantum information architectures, secure communication protocols, and the ontological interpretation of quantum theory.
Label: AWP

Text: We present dynamical mean field theory (DMFT) for the local spectral densities of the one- and two-particle response functions for the infinite dimensional Hubbard model in a magnetic field. We look at the different regimes corresponding to half-filling, near half-filling and well away from half-filling, for intermediate and strong values of the local interaction $U$. The low energy are analyzed in terms of quasiparticles with field dependent parameters. The renormalized parameters are determined by two different , both based on numerical renormalization group (NRG) calculations, and we find good agreement. Away from half-filling the quasiparticle weights, $z_sigma(H)$, differ according to the spin type $sigma=uparrow$ or $sigma=downarrow$. Using the renormalized parameters, we show that DMFT-NRG for the local longitudinal and transverse dynamic spin susceptibilities in an arbitrary field can be understood in terms of repeated scattering of these quasiparticles. We also check Luttinger's theorem for the Hubbard model and find it to be satisfied in all parameter regimes and for all values of the magnetic field.

Text: In Vogue' s 1969 Christmas issue, Vladimir Nabokov offered some advice for teaching James Joyce's "Ulysses": "Instead of perpetuating the pretentious nonsense of Homeric, chromatic, and visceral chapter headings, instructors should prepare maps of Dublin with Bloom's and Stephen's intertwining itineraries clearly traced." He drew a charming one himself. Several decades later, a Boston College English professor named Joseph Nugent and his colleagues put together an annotated Google map that shadows Stephen Dedalus and Leopold Bloom step by step. The Virginia Woolf Society of Great Britain, as well as students at the Georgia Institute of Technology, have similarly reconstructed the paths of the London amblers in " Mrs. Dalloway." Such maps clarify how much these novels depend on a curious link between mind and feet. Joyce and Woolf were writers who transformed the quicksilver of consciousness into paper and ink. To accomplish this, they sent characters on walks about town. As Mrs. Dalloway walks, she does not merely perceive the city around her. Rather, she dips in and out of her past, remolding London into a highly textured mental landscape, "making it up, building it round one, tumbling it, creating it every moment afresh." Since at least the time of peripatetic Greek philosophers, many other writers have discovered a deep, intuitive connection between walking, thinking, and writing.

Text: This study explores the evolution of large scale curvature fluctuations during the perturbative decay of the inflaton, a process that is fundamental to our understanding of the origin and evolution of the universe. We examine the impact of the inflaton's decay on the primordial fluctuation spectrum, focusing on the interplay between the decay rate, the inflaton's potential, and the curvature perturbation amplitude. Utilizing a hybrid approach that combines analytical calculations with numerical simulations, we investigate the evolution of curvature fluctuations during the decay process, including the effects of non-perturbative corrections. Our reveal that the decay of the inflaton significantly influences the curvature fluctuation spectrum, leading to enhanced power at large scales and a departure from the standard slow-roll prediction. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the decay process introduces a novel scale dependence in the curvature perturbation amplitude, which may have implications for the interpretation of future cosmic microwave and large-scale structure observations. These highlight the importance of considering the perturbative decay of the inflaton in the study of primordial cosmology.

Text: Braided doubles provide a unifying framework for classical and quantum universal enveloping algebras and rational Cherednik algebras. They are a class of algebras with triangular decomposition, arising from a deformation problem, the solutions to which are called quasi-Yetter-Drinfeld modules. A basic family of quasi-YD modules is provided by braidings (matrices satisfying the quantum Yang-Baxter equation); these give rise to quantum versions of the Weyl algebra, where the role of polynomial rings is played by Nichols-Woronowicz algebras. Rational Cherednik algebras for t = 0 emerge as subalgebras in doubles of Nichols-Woronowicz algebras. For nonzero t, the Nichols-Woronowicz algebra is replaced with an algebra associated to the classical Yang-Baxter equation.

Text: We introduce a novel strategy to reconstructing weak values, a fundamental concept in quantum mechanics that has garnered significant attention in recent years, without relying on the traditional weak measurement protocol. Our method is based on a combination of quantum state tomography and Bayesian inference, allowing us to estimate the weak value of an observable with high precision. By capitalizing on the principles of quantum estimation theory, we reveal that it is possible to recover the weak value of a system even when the measurement process is not weak. Our approach does not require the use of post-selection or any other form of measurement that is typically associated with weak measurements. Moreover, instead, we utilize a probabilistic framework to reconstruct the weak value from a set of measured data; our results have significant implications for the study of weak values, as they open up new possibilities for experimental and theoretical investigations of this phenomenon, while we demonstrate the efficacy of our approach using a simple optical system, and our observations suggest that this procedure may be broadly applicable to a wide range of quantum systems.

Text: We quantify through high-resolution simulations the influence of spatial dimensionality on the critical exponents governing the liquid-vapor phase transition in confined geometries. Utilizing Monte Carlo within the grand-canonical ensemble, we compute the coexistence curves and interfacial properties for Lennard-Jones fluids confined to slit pores of varying widths. Our demonstrate a systematic crossover from three-dimensional Ising universality to two-dimensional behavior as the confining dimension is reduced, with the critical temperature exhibiting a monotonic suppression proportional to the inverse pore width. The calculated critical exponents are in excellent agreement with conformal field theory predictions for confined systems, providing a unified framework for understanding phase behavior in nanoscale environments relevant to microfluidic and porous media applications.

Text: People began to drink coffee because it meant something to them: a flavor for everyone, a style for every lifestyle-we have methodically been taught to socialize over coffee, to look for a boost in productivity from this drink. We're identified by the brand that we drink, by the coffee houses we frequent, and by the process by which the beans are grown and harvested. We tout words such as "Free-Trade" and organic. Roman was right-it is all about 'me.' But as Roseberry concludes, these connections have been carefully structured by the market: Coffees offer us a way to look at our relationship to the larger world and see that sometimes our choices are not really our own, to think about how brands and larger market forces can help create what appear to be stable icons in our lives. The 'me' that we have come to emphasize may be less personal than we realize. In preparation for the coming posts, tell me what you're drinking, when you started drinking coffee, or why you don't. How does coffee make you feel? Do you remember your parents or grandparents drinking coffee? How has that influenced your opinion of the drink? Roseberry, W. (1996). Text: .** Donaldson invariants have proved indispensable for distinguishing smooth structures on four-manifolds, yet their applicability to non-Kählerian complex surfaces-particularly those of class VII with (b_2=1)-remains largely unexplored. .** We extend the analytical framework of anti-self-dual Yang-Mills theory to compact complex surfaces lacking a Kähler metric, employing a refined deformation theory of holomorphic bundles and a weighted Sobolev-space analysis adapted to the non-Kähler . By constructing explicit families of reducible instantons on minimal class VII surfaces and analyzing the associated wall-crossing phenomena, we obtain a complete description of the instanton moduli space. .** The resulting Donaldson invariants are shown to vanish unless the surface admits a global spherical shell, in which case they detect the existence of a unique holomorphic line bundle with prescribed curvature. When compared to local emission-line galaxies of similar luminosity and mass (using the near-infrared luminosity-metallicity and mass-metallicity relations), we find that LIRGs and ULIRGs are under-abundant by a factor of two on average. As a corollary, LIRGs and ULIRGs also have smaller effective yields. We conclude that the observed under-abundance from the combination of a decrease of abundance with increasing radius in the progenitor galaxies and strong, interaction- or merger-induced gas inflow into the galaxy nucleus. This demonstrates that local abundance scaling relations are not universal, a fact that must be accounted for when interpreting abundances earlier in the universe's history when merger-induced star formation was the dominant mode. We use our local sample to compare to high-redshift samples and assess abundance evolution in LIRGs and ULIRGs. We find that abundances in these systems increased by ~0.2 dex from z ~ 0.6 to z ~ 0.1. Text: .* The Briot-Bouquet family of nonlinear ordinary differential equations, originally studied in the nineteenth century, admits a rich structure of meromorphic solutions when of first order. Recent progress in the theory of integrable systems suggests that higher-order extensions of these equations may also possess nontrivial meromorphic solutions, yet a systematic classification remains elusive. .* We formulate the general $n$-th order Briot-Bouquet equation [ P!left(z,;u,;u',dots ,u{(n)}right)=0, ] with $P$ a polynomial in the dependent variable and its derivatives. Employing Nevanlinna's value-distribution theory, we derive growth estimates for putative meromorphic solutions and identify their possible pole configurations. A singularity-analysis scheme reduces the problem to a finite set of algebraic constraints on the coefficients of $P$. These constraints are then solved using Gröbner-basis techniques, yielding explicit parametrizations of the admissible equations. Finally, we construct the corresponding meromorphic solutions in terms of elliptic functions, rational functions, and their degenerations. .* We establish necessary and sufficient conditions for the existence of meromorphic solutions of arbitrary order: the coefficients must satisfy a finite system of algebraic relations that generalize the classical Briot-Bouquet conditions. Under these conditions every solution is either a rational function, a periodic elliptic function, or a composition of such functions with elementary transformations. The classification includes all previously known first-order cases and reveals new families of higher-order equations admitting doubly-periodic solutions. Crucially, these provide a complete description of the meromorphic solution space for higher-order Briot-Bouquet differential equations.

We present REAS2, a Monte‑Carlo framework that couples the state‑of‑the‑art air‑shower simulation code CORSIKA with a full‑vector treatment of geosynchrotron radiation. Individual electron–positron trajectories are extracted from CORSIKA output, including realistic energy, spatial, and angular distributions as well as atmospheric density variations. The time‑dependent Liénard–Wiechert potentials are evaluated for each particle, and the resulting electric fields are summed coherently at observer locations. The code incorporates frequency‑dependent atmospheric refractivity and implements a GPU‑accelerated integration scheme to achieve sub‑nanosecond temporal resolution. REAS2 reproduces the measured lateral distribution, polarization, and frequency spectra of radio pulses from the LOPES and AERA experiments within experimental uncertainties. Sensitivity studies reveal that shower‑to‑shower fluctuations and geomagnetic field orientation dominate the intrinsic variance, while the impact of the hadronic interaction model is sub‑dominant. These validate CORSIKA‑based particle tracking as a robust tool for interpreting geosynchrotron radio data and pave the way for precision composition studies using radio observables.

Text: The perovskite oxide LaMnO₃ exhibits antiferromagnetic order and strong electron-correlation effects, yet its magnetic functionality can be dramatically altered by B-site substitution. Introducing Fe³⁺ ions is predicted to generate mixed-valence Mn³⁺/Fe³⁺ networks that foster uncompensated interfacial spins, a prerequisite for exchange-bias (EB) phenomena. Understanding how Fe concentration modulates the magnetic phase coexistence and interfacial coupling is essential for designing oxide-based spintronic devices. Polycrystalline LaMn₁₋ₓFeₓO₃ (0 ≤ x ≤ 0.30) samples were synthesized by solid-state reaction and characterized using X-ray diffraction (Rietveld refinement) to confirm phase purity and lattice evolution. Magnetic properties were probed with a SQUID magnetometer: zero-field-cooled (ZFC) and field-cooled (FC) hysteresis loops were recorded at 5-300 K after cooling in a 5 T field. The EB field (H_EB) and coercivity (H_C) were extracted, and their temperature dependence was correlated with neutron diffraction data to identify magnetic ordering. Fe substitution up to x = 0.20 preserves the orthorhombic perovskite structure while inducing a gradual transition from A-type antiferromagnetism to a ferrimagnetic ground state. A robust exchange-bias effect emerges for 0.10 ≤ x ≤ 0.20, with a maximum H_EB ≈ 210 Oe at 5 K for x = 0.15, accompanied by enhanced coercivity (H_C ≈ 1.2 kOe). The EB vanishes above the Néel temperature of the residual Mn sublattice, confirming that interfacial exchange between Mn-rich antiferromagnetic domains and Fe-induced ferromagnetic clusters underlies the observed bias. Crucially, these demonstrate that controlled Fe doping is an effective route to tailor exchange-bias in LaMnO₃-based oxides.

As we repeat the experience, the connection strengthens, making it easier to recall the memory later on. But what's fascinating is how emotions and senses play a role in solidifying these memories. The smell of those cookies, for instance, is linked to the happy feelings I associate with my grandmother's love and care. This is because our brain's emotional centers, like the amygdala, are closely tied to our memory-forming processes. As a result, memories that are emotionally charged, like my Sundays at my grandmother's, become more vivid and long-lasting. It's no wonder, then, that the smell of freshly baked cookies can transport me back to those idyllic afternoons, filled with warmth and love, in an instant. The science of memory formation may be complex, but its effects are nothing short of magical, allowing us to hold onto cherished moments from our past.

Text: We present a measurement of the top-quark mass using a dataset of 1.8 fb^-1 of proton-antiproton collisions at a center-of-mass energy of 1.96 TeV collected by the CDF II detector at Fermilab. Secondary vertex b-tagging is employed to identify the jets originating from the bottom-quark hadronization. We use a likelihood-based approach to extract the top-quark mass from the distribution of the E_T^miss and the invariant mass of the b-tagged jets. The measurement yields a top-quark mass of 173.32 ± 1.35 GeV, consistent with the world average value. Utilizing the Bethe-anstaz method, we have derived an exact analytical solution for the many-body wave function of the system, thereby enabling the calculation of the energy spectrum and the corresponding eigenstates. Notably, the Coulomb interaction plays a pivotal role in the emergence of resonant peaks in the density of states, which are intimately associated with the formation of quasiparticles characterized by anomalous properties. Through a meticulous analysis of the energy spectrum and the eigenstates, we have elucidated the conditions under which the resonant behavior manifests and have determined the attendant parameters. The obtained in this study demonstrate that the resonant peaks exhibit a sensitivity to the strength of the Coulomb interaction and the energy level spacing of the quantum dot, thereby underscoring the critical importance of these factors in modulating the system's behavior. Ultimately, this research provides a comprehensive understanding of the resonant behavior in an open quantum dot system with a Coulomb interaction, casting new light on the underlying physics of this intricate many-body system and offering significant implications for the design of electronic devices and the elucidation of transport phenomena in nanostructures.

Text: This investigation examines the structural characteristics of a non-recurrent Markov chain distinguished by a finite set of critical transition states, offering novel insights into the interplay between topological constraints and stochastic persistence in infinite-state systems. We construct an irreducible discrete-time Markov process defined on an unbounded, discrete state space, wherein transience emerges from the strategic placement of finite structural bottlenecks that partition the state space into disjoint domains of recurrence and escape. By integrating harmonic analysis with generating function methodologies, we demonstrate that these critical transition states function as probabilistic chokepoints, directing trajectory evolution toward transient asymptotic behavior while maintaining local recurrence in isolated subgraphs. A rigorous examination of the chain’s transition dynamics reveals that the finite critical states induce sub-exponential attenuation of recurrence probabilities, diverging from the canonical exponential decay observed in classical transient chains without such bottlenecks. Through spectral decomposition and potential-theoretic arguments, we establish necessary conditions for transience in this framework, underscoring how localized structural constraints can globally manipulate the chain’s ergodic properties. Theoretical implications extend to applications in population genetics and network diffusion, where heterogeneous spatial configurations govern long-term system behavior, while the proposed framework provides a robust foundation for synthesizing stochastic models with engineered transience. Text: We provide a new estimate of the local supermassive black hole mass function using (i) the empirical relation between supermassive black hole mass and the Sersic index of the host spheroidal stellar system and (ii) the measured (spheroid) Sersic indices drawn from 10k galaxies in the Millennium Galaxy Catalogue. The observational simplicity of our approach, and the direct measurements of the black hole predictor quantity, i.e. the Sersic index, for both elliptical galaxies and the bulges of disc galaxies makes it straightforward to estimate accurate black hole masses in early- and late-type galaxies alike. We have parameterised the supermassive black hole mass function with a Schechter function and find, at the low-mass end, a logarithmic slope (1+alpha) of ~0.7 for the full galaxy sample and ~1.0 for the early-type galaxy sample. Considering spheroidal stellar systems brighter than M_B = -18 mag, and integrating down to black hole masses of 10^6 M_sun, we find that the local mass density of supermassive black holes in early-type galaxies rho_{bh, early-type} = (3.5+/-1.2) x 10^5 h^3_{70} M_sun Mpc^{-3}, and in late-type galaxies rho_{bh, late-type} = (1.0+/-0.5) x 10^5 h^3_{70} M_sun Mpc^{-3}. The uncertainties are derived from Monte Carlo simulations which include uncertainties in the M_bh-n relation, the catalogue of Sersic indices, the galaxy weights and Malmquist bias. The combined, cosmological, supermassive black hole mass density is thus Omega_{bh, total} = (3.2+/-1.2) x 10^{-6} h_70. That is, using a new and independent method, we conclude that (0.007+/-0.003) h^3_{70} per cent of the universe's baryons are presently locked up in supermassive black holes at the centres of galaxies.

Text: Single-electron spins confined in semiconductor double quantum dots are a leading platform for scalable quantum processors. While electrically driven resonant pulses enable fast spin rotations, leakage of the qubit state into non-computational charge or orbital levels during rapid gate operations has emerged as a dominant source of decoherence, severely limiting gate fidelity. We perform time-resolved pulsed-gate experiments on a GaAs double dot while driving coherent spin rotations with an on-chip microwave antenna. Charge sensing via a proximal quantum point contact provides single-shot readout of both spin and leakage events. By varying interdot detuning, pulse amplitude, and rise time, we extract leakage probabilities and the corresponding dephasing rates. A Lindblad master-equation model incorporating interdot tunneling, spin-orbit coupling, and hyperfine noise is fitted to the data to quantify the leakage contribution to decoherence. Leakage probabilities up to 8 % are observed for fast π-pulses, reducing Ramsey visibility from 0.93 to 0.78, while the extracted dephasing time T₂* drops from 18 ns (no leakage) to 12 ns at maximum leakage. Optimized pulse shaping and operation at the sweet spot suppress leakage below 2 %, restoring T₂* to 16 ns. These delineate the parameter regime where leakage dominates and provide practical guidelines for achieving high-fidelity spin control in double-dot architectures.

Text: We report on observations of SN 1006 with the X-ray Imaging Spectrometers (XIS) on board Suzaku. We firmly detected K-shell emission from Fe, for the first time, and find that the Fe ionization state is quite low. The broad band spectrum extracted from the southeast of the remnant is well fitted with a model consisting of three optically thin thermal non-equilibrium ionization plasmas and a power-law component. Two of the thermal models are highly overabundant in heavy elements and, hence, are likely due to ejecta. These components have different ionization parameters: $n_et \sim 1.4\times 10^{10}$ cm$^{-3}$ s and $n_et \sim 7.7\times 10^8$ cm$^{-3}$ s and it is the later one that produces the Fe-K emission. This suggests that Fe has been heated by the reverse shock more recently than the other elements, consistent with a picture where the ejecta are stratified by composition with Fe in the interior. On the other hand, the third thermal component is assumed to be solar abundance, and we associate it with emission from the interstellar medium (ISM). The electron temperature and ionization parameter are $kT_e \sim $0.5 keV and $n_et \sim 5.8\times 10^9$ cm$^{-3}$ s. The electron temperature is lower than that expected from the shock velocity which suggests a lack of collisionless electron heating at the forward shock. The extremely low ionization parameter and extreme non-equilibrium state are due to the low density of the ambient medium.

Text: Symplectic orbifolds with isolated cyclic quotient singularities arise naturally in Hamiltonian dynamics, mirror symmetry and the study of moduli spaces. While algebraic techniques guarantee the existence of crepant resolutions for many such singularities, a parallel symplectic theory—ensuring the resolution inherits a compatible symplectic form—is less developed. Understanding when and how symplectic cyclic orbifold singularities can be resolved is essential for extending Floer‑theoretic invariants and for constructing smooth symplectic models of singular moduli spaces. We combine equivariant symplectic blow‑up, symplectic cutting, and toric degeneration techniques to construct explicit symplectic resolutions of the quotient \(\mathbb{C}^{2n}/\mathbb{Z}_{k}\) equipped with the standard symplectic form. The approach proceeds by (i) realizing the cyclic action as a Hamiltonian \(S^{1}\)-action, (ii) applying Lerman’s symplectic cut to isolate the singular stratum, and (iii) gluing a collection of weighted projective spaces along their common moment‑map fibers. Compatibility with the canonical class is verified using the symplectic version of the McKay correspondence, and the resulting manifolds are shown to be crepant in the sense that the symplectic form represents the pull‑back of the original cohomology class. We prove that every isolated symplectic cyclic quotient singularity admits a smooth symplectic resolution that is crepant and unique up to symplectomorphism when the order of the cyclic group is coprime to the dimension. The construction yields explicit models for low‑dimensional cases (e.g., \(A_{k-1}\) surface singularities) and provides a systematic procedure for higher dimensions. Moreover, the resolved spaces retain the original orbifold’s quantum cohomology and admit compatible Hamiltonian torus actions, opening new avenues for symplectic invariants on formerly singular spaces.

Text: Quintessential inflation proposes a unified description of both the early universe's inflationary epoch and the current accelerated expansion, mediated by a single scalar field. This framework has garnered significant attention due to its potential to address fundamental questions in cosmology. We employ a novel reconstruction technique, utilizing the effective field theory approach, to revisit the quintessential inflationary paradigm. Our involves parameterizing the scalar field's potential and reconstructing the model's dynamics from observational data, including cosmic microwave radiation and large-scale structure measurements. Our indicate that the reconstructed model exhibits a viable quintessential inflationary scenario, consistent with current observational constraints. The scalar field's potential is found to exhibit a steep exponential behavior at early times, followed by a shallow plateau at later times, thereby realizing a successful inflationary epoch and a subsequent quintessence-driven acceleration. The model's predictions for key cosmological parameters, such as the spectral index and tensor-to-scalar ratio, are in agreement with current observational bounds, demonstrating the viability of this reconstructed quintessential inflationary model. Further investigation of this framework may provide valuable insights into the underlying physics of the universe.

Text: This study presents a comprehensive analysis of dimensional reduction schemes arising from general covariance breaking in theories beyond the Standard Model of particle physics. Building upon the framework of effective field theory, we derive a unified set of constraints on the effective Lagrangian that captures the universal features of dimensional reduction schemes across various breaking mechanisms, including spontaneous and explicit symmetry breaking. Our approach leads to a novel classification of dimensionally reduced theories based on the irreducible representations of the spontaneously broken symmetry group. We demonstrate that this classification scheme provides a systematic framework for organizing and comparing the phenomenological implications of different dimensional reduction schemes, including those relevant to the Higgs sector and beyond. Furthermore, we investigate the implications of these universal features for the discovery prospects of new physics at the Large Hadron Collider and other future colliders, highlighting the potential for a unified understanding of the dimensional reduction paradigm in theories beyond the Standard Model. Our provide a foundation for a more comprehensive understanding of the dimensional reduction framework and its applications in particle physics.

Text: Investigations into the phenomenon of high-harmonic generation (HHG) in diatomic molecules have revealed a complex interplay between the nuclear and electronic degrees of freedom, resulting in intricate interference patterns within the HHG spectra, which are thought to emerge from the dynamic interrelationship between the molecular orbitals and the nuclear dynamics. Theoretical studies have consistently demonstrated that intense laser pulses induce the recombination of electrons with their parent ions, thereby generating high-energy photons, and recent research has underscored the pivotal role of the molecular orbitals and the nuclear vibrational modes in shaping the HHG spectra. Employing a quantum-orbit analysis, we conducted an in-depth examination of the HHG process in diatomic molecules, with a particular emphasis on elucidating the relationship between the topology of the molecular orbitals, the nuclear motions, and the attendant interference patterns. Our computational indicate that the orbital contributions to the HHG spectra are inextricably linked to the nuclear dynamics, particularly the vibrational modes, thereby substantiating the efficacy of the quantum-orbit analysis as a robust framework for understanding the intricate mechanisms underlying HHG in diatomic molecules. This study's have far-reaching implications for the control of HHG in molecular systems and may provide insight into the underlying physical mechanisms governing this phenomenon, thereby facilitating a more nuanced comprehension of the complex interplay between the nuclear and electronic degrees of freedom.

Text: The deployment of Space Time Cube (STC) as a visualization tool for elucidating spatiotemporal patterns in geographic and socio-environmental phenomena is contingent upon a nuanced understanding of the underlying trade-offs that can impede the accuracy and interpretability of . Although the STC provides a robust framework for apprehending the intricate relationships between space and time, its efficacy is subject to a series of interrelated factors that necessitate careful consideration. Specifically, the resolutions, aggregation techniques, and dimensional configurations employed in STC representation can significantly impact the detection and interpretation of spatiotemporal patterns. A systematic investigation of the trade-offs inherent to STC representation was undertaken by way of a case study examining climate-driven land cover change in a tropical ecosystem. The of this inquiry underscore the reciprocal relationship between resolution and dimensionality: increased resolution and dimensionality facilitate more accurate pattern detection, albeit at the expense of increased computational complexity and data visualization clutter. Conversely, aggregation of data serves to simplify the visualization process, yet may result in the loss of fine-scale detail and nuanced relationships inherent to the data. The outcomes of this study possess a profound impact on the application of STC in spatiotemporal analysis and visualization. It is essential that the choice of resolution, aggregation, and dimensionality is carefully calibrated in consonance with the research question and data characteristics to ensure the optimal extraction of meaningful insights. Furthermore, this research underscores the imperative need for a more refined understanding of the trade-offs inherent to STC representation, providing valuable insights into strategies for optimizing STC design to facilitate effective spatiotemporal analysis. Keywords: Space Time Cube, Spatiotemporal analysis, Visualization trade-offs, Resolution, Aggregation, Dimensionality, Climate-driven land cover change.

Text: In this study we interrogate the symmetry principles that dictate the stochastic dynamics of a paradigmatic Brownian motor subjected to a spatially periodic potential while driven far from equilibrium; by fusing a path‑integral representation with high‑resolution numerical integration of the corresponding Langevin equations, we obtain rigorous correspondences between forward and time‑reversed trajectories, thereby extending Crooks’ fluctuation theorem to encompass both spatial and temporal asymmetries inherent to the system; the ensuing analysis demonstrates that the motor’s thermodynamic efficiency and directed current are bounded by a suite of reciprocity relations that couple the likelihood of a prescribed trajectory to that of its spatially inverted counterpart when the load and driving protocol are simultaneously reversed, and these relations are analytically corroborated in the overdamped regime while being empirically substantiated through extensive Monte‑Carlo sampling, which further reveals that symmetry violations manifest exclusively when the external driving protocol forfeits time‑reversal invariance; collectively, these furnish a comprehensive theoretical scaffold for interpreting empirical observations of coherent transport in nanoscale engines and furnish actionable guidelines for engineering optimal performance by strategically modulating the symmetry characteristics of the underlying potential landscape.

Text: In metals, the emergence of Charge Density Waves (CDWs) has sparked considerable interest due to their remarkable properties and promising applications, which stem from a periodic fluctuation of electronic charge density. This unusual behavior is deeply rooted in the concept of Fermi surface nesting, where parallel sections of the metal's Fermi surface, connected by a specific wavevector, can give rise to the growth of CDW instabilities. Through a multi-faceted approach that combines theoretical modeling with experimental characterization, our research has elucidated the pivotal role of Fermi surface nesting in the formation of CDWs, while also highlighting the impact of electronic correlations and lattice dynamics. Notably, the degree of nesting can be effectively modulated by adjusting the chemical composition of the metal or applying external pressure, thereby offering a means to manipulate these states in metal systems. Our findings have provided valuable insights into the underlying mechanisms of CDW formation and underscored the potential for developing novel electronic materials and devices with tailored properties.

Text: The lecture notes describe the Delaunay Tessellation Field Estimator for Cosmic Web analysis. The high sensitivity of Voronoi/Delaunay tessellations to the local point distribution is used to obtain estimates of density and related quantities. The adaptive and minimum triangulation properties of Delaunay tessellations are utilized for interpolation to continuous volume-covering density and velocity fields. The adaptivity to the local density and geometry preserves three key characteristics of the cosmic matter distribution: 1) its hierarchical nature,2) its anisotropic weblike morphology, 3) the presence and structure of voids. The lecture notes discuss the mathematical context and of the DTFE method, in essence a first order version of Natural Neighbour , smooth and higher order spatial interpolation techniques. This is followed by an outline of the DTFE procedure. A series of tests on spatially complex point distributions provides quantitative information on its performance and noise characteristics. We conclude with a few cosmological applications. The reconstruction of the spatial weblike patterns in N-body simulations and in the 2dFGRS provide a visual impression of DTFE's performance. The analysis of the velocity divergence pdf and maps obtained of the velocity flow in the Local Universe (implied by PSCz) illustrate its promise for probing the dynamics of cosmic structure. The Watershed Void Finder (Platen et al. 2007), for the study of voids, and Multiscale Morphology Filter (Aragon-Calvo et al. 2007), for identifying and analyzing weblike networks of filaments, sheets and clusters, are based upon DTFE density fields. We also mention SimpleX, a related random lattice radiative transfer formalism (Ritzerveld & Icke 2006).

Text: The compatibility of the pure power law infrared solution of QCD and lattice data for the gluon and ghost propagators in Landau gauge is discussed. For the gluon propagator, the lattice data is well described by a pure power law with an infrared exponent $\kappa \sim 0.53$, in the Dyson-Schwinger notation. $\kappa$ is measured using a technique that suppresses finite volume effects. This value implies a vanishing zero momentum gluon propagator, in agreement with the Gribov-Zwanziger confinement scenario. For the ghost propagator, the lattice data seem not to follow a pure power law, at least for the range of momenta accessed in our simulation.

Text: In the pursuit of elucidating the intricacies of qubit dephasing precipitated by telegraph noise, a ubiquitous manifestation of stochastic processes endemic to fluctuators, a novel exact analytical solution has been derived. This formulation, rooted in a synthesis of analytical techniques and stochastic calculus, effectively yields a closed-form expression for the time-evolved density matrix of a qubit, thus rendering a comprehensive account of the dephasing effects occasioned by the telegraph noise. Underlying this development is a master equation framework, wherein the resultant partial differential equation is solved to procure an exact analytical solution for the time-evolved density matrix of the qubit as a function of the telegraph noise parameters and qubit characteristics. This achievement underscores the existence of a distinct regime of strong-qubit-telegraph noise coupling, wherein the qubit's dephasing dynamics exhibit a pronounced departure from Gaussian behavior, thereby underscoring the non-trivial nature of the telegraph noise-induced decoherence. The implications of this exact solution are far-reaching, with significant repercussions for the mitigation of telegraph noise in qubit-based quantum information processing protocols. Notably, the advent of noise-resilient quantum control strategies and the optimization of quantum gates become feasible, thus underscoring the pivotal role of stochastic noise characterization in the quest for reliable and high-fidelity quantum computing. The analytical framework thus presented serves as a reliable paradigm for modeling and analyzing the dephasing dynamics of qubits in realistic environments, thereby facilitating an in-depth exploration of the intricate interplay between qubit properties and stochastic noise. In this regard, this study contributes meaningfully to the advancement of quantum information processing, by providing a precise analytical solution to a critical problem of paramount importance in the realm of quantum computation, and, by the same token, serves as a foundation for continued research into the dynamics of qubit-dephasing in the presence of stochastic noise. Consequently, the development of novel control strategies and the enhancement of quantum processing capabilities can be achieved through an in-depth understanding of the telegraph noise-induced dephasing dynamics of qubits.

Text: This work develops novel empirical Bayes methods for controlling the false discovery rate (FDR) in the presence of dependent data. In many high-dimensional genomic studies, such as gene expression analysis and copy number variation detection, the data exhibit complex dependencies and correlations among features. Existing FDR control methods often fail to account for these dependencies, leading to excessive false positives and compromised statistical power. Our empirical Bayes approach leverages a hierarchical model to capture the underlying dependencies in the data, enabling the estimation of the local FDR for each feature. We develop a two-stage procedure that first estimates the local FDR by means of the empirical Bayes procedure, and then uses a thresholding scheme to select features with a low estimated FDR. Our simulations and real-data analyses demonstrate that the proposed procedure effectively controls the FDR and achieves improved power and accuracy compared to existing methods, particularly in scenarios with strong dependencies among features. The proposed method has potential applications in various fields where controlling FDR is vital, including genetics, neuroscience, and finance.

Text: Explicit Calabi-Yau metrics are derived that are argued to map to the Maldacena-Nu\~{n}ez AdS solutions of M-theory and IIB under geometric transitions. In each case the metrics are singular where a H^2 K\"{a}hler two-cycle degenerates but are otherwise smooth. They are derived as the most general Calabi-Yau solutions of an ansatz for the supergravity description of branes wrapped on K\"{a}hler two-cycles. The ansatz is inspired by re-writing the AdS solutions, and the structure defined by half their Killing spinors, in this form. The world-volume theories of fractional branes wrapped at the singularities of these metrics are proposed as the duals of the AdS solutions. The existence of supergravity solutions interpolating between the $AdS$ and Calabi-Yau metrics is conjectured and their boundary conditions briefly discussed.

Text: The existence of additional spatial dimensions is a cornerstone of several high-energy theories, yet empirical evidence remains elusive. Compact astrophysical objects-neutron stars, quark stars, and hybrid stars-provide extreme density and curvature regimes where the influence of extra dimensions could manifest through modifications of the equation of state (EoS), gravitational binding, and radiative properties. Identifying observable signatures in such stars therefore offers a promising avenue for testing higher-dimensional scenarios. We construct a suite of relativistic stellar models incorporating Kaluza-Klein and braneworld corrections to Einstein's field equations. The bulk-induced stress-energy tensor is parametrized by a compactification radius (R_c) and a brane tension (lambda). For each model we solve the modified Tolman-Oppenheimer-Volkoff equations using a range of microphysical EoS (nucleonic, hyperonic, and deconfined quark matter). Predicted mass-radius relations, tidal deformabilities, and surface temperature evolution are then compared with recent multimessenger observations from NICER, LIGO/Virgo, and XMM-Newton. Compact stars with masses >2 M(_odot) and radii ≤11 km can be reproduced only when (R_c lesssim 10{-19}) m and (lambda gtrsim 10{9}) MeV(4), implying strong suppression of extra-dimensional effects. However, subtle deviations in the tidal Love numbers (ΔΛ/Λ ≈ 5 %) and cooling curves emerge for (R_c) in the range (10{-18})-(10{-19}) m, providing testable signatures. Crucially, our delineate the parameter space where compact-star observations can either constrain or reveal the presence of hidden dimensions.

Text: We investigate the jamming transition and percolation behavior in particulate systems exhibiting attractive interactions, which significantly deviate from their repulsive counterparts — the incorporation of attractive forces introduces novel characteristics to the jamming transition, including the emergence of new percolation universality classes. Utilizing a combination of numerical simulations and theoretical analysis, we uncover the distinct critical exponents that govern the percolation transition in these systems. Our results reveal that the attractive interactions lead to a breakdown of the conventional percolation universality classes, resulting in the formation of two new classes: a 'soft' class characterized by a lower percolation threshold and a 'hard' class marked by a higher threshold, while we also observe a non-monotonic dependence of the percolation threshold on the strength of attractive interactions, indicating a complex interplay between packing efficiency and attractive forces. Our findings provide new insights into the behavior of particulate systems with attraction, shedding light on the rich phenomenology of jammed states and percolation transitions in such systems.

Text: By scrutinizing the architecture of complete problems for classical complexity classes through the prism of first‑order projections (FOPs)—a syntactic reduction paradigm that conserves logical definability—we delineate canonical forms for such problems and thereby demonstrate that for any class that admits a natural complete problem there exists a unique, up to logical equivalence, minimal representation which remains invariant under the action of FOPs; in particular, our principal theorem establishes that the canonical forms for the classes NP, coNP, and L align precisely with the canonical normal forms of their respective defining logics, namely existential second‑order formulas for NP, universal second‑order formulas for coNP, and first‑order formulas augmented with built‑in arithmetic for L, and furthermore we prove that any complete problem can be mapped to its canonical counterpart by means of a polynomial‑time FOP, a transformation which is also invertible within the same class; consequently, these imply that the entire space of complete problems constitutes essentially a single orbit under the group action induced by FOPs, thereby streamlining the reduction landscape, and ultimately yield novel perspectives on the robustness of completeness, the construction of canonical hard instances, and the intricate relationship between logical definability and computational intractability.

Text: This investigation seeks to elucidate discrepancies between Anti-de Sitter/Conformal Field Theory (AdS/CFT)-based predictions for heavy quark energy loss and perturbative Quantum Chromodynamics (pQCD) calculations in the context of heavy-ion collisions, leveraging the Pb+Pb collision data from the Large Hadron Collider (LHC). By capitalizing on the AdS/CFT correspondence, which provides a theoretical framework for mapping the dynamics of strongly coupled quark-gluon plasma to a dual gravitational system, we endeavored to model the phenomenon of heavy quark jet quenching in heavy-ion collisions and juxtapose these with traditional pQCD frameworks that rely on weak coupling approximations. Through a comprehensive analysis of high-precision nuclear modification factors (R_AA) and azimuthal anisotropy (v2) for heavy-flavor hadrons in Pb+Pb collisions at √s_NN = 5.02 TeV, we observed systematic discrepancies between the two approaches, particularly in the suppression of high-transverse-momentum (p_T) heavy quarkonia and charm/bottom mesons. Notably, AdS/CFT simulations predicted enhanced energy loss in the strongly coupled plasma regime, leading to steeper suppression trends in R_AA compared to pQCD estimates for p_T > 20 GeV/c. However, observed v2 data for D mesons showed better agreement with pQCD-based collective flow models, suggesting a complex interplay of transport and medium-induced effects. These underscore the necessity of refining theoretical models to account for non-conformal corrections in AdS/CFT and non-perturbative QCD dynamics, while acknowledging the limitations imposed by experimental uncertainties in jet reconstruction and subtraction. Ultimately, this study contributes to the ongoing quest to disentangle the roles of coupling strength and plasma geometry in heavy quark dynamics, providing valuable insights into the thermalization and equilibration processes of the quark-gluon plasma in extreme conditions.

Text: We demonstrate that two key theoretical objects used widely in Computational Neuroscience, the phase-resetting curve (PRC) from dynamics and the spike triggered average (STA) from statistical analysis, are closely related under a wide range of stimulus conditions. We prove that the STA is proportional to the derivative of the PRC. We compare these analytic to numerical calculations for the Hodgkin-Huxley neuron and we apply the method to neurons in the olfactory bulb of mice. This observation allows us to relate the stimulus-response properties of a neuron to its dynamics, bridging the gap between dynamical and information theoretic approaches to understanding brain computations and facilitating the interpretation of changes in channels and other cellular properties as influencing the representation of stimuli.

Text: This study delves into the investigation of weak convergence in the Prokhorov metric for numerical schemes designed to approximate Itô stochastic differential equations (SDEs) of the form $dX_{t} = \mu(X_{t})dt + \sigma(X_{t})dW_{t}$, where the stochastic process $X_t$ is governed by a drift coefficient $\mu$, a diffusion coefficient $\sigma$, and a standard Wiener process $W_t$. Notably, the drift coefficient $\mu$ encapsulates the deterministic components influencing the stochastic process, while the diffusion coefficient $\sigma$ governs the random fluctuations. Our primary focus is on the weak convergence of numerical approximations of the solution $X_t$, quantified by the probability measure $\mathbb{P}_n$ induced by the numerical scheme, to the target measure $\mathbb{P}$ defined by the original SDE. This convergence is examined in the context of the Prokhorov metric, a metric of considerable utility in assessing the convergence of probability measures. The application of the Prokhorov metric in this study enables us to establish the convergence properties of numerical approximations with respect to the underlying probability measure. Our demonstrate the weak convergence of a broad class of numerical schemes, encompassing the Euler-Maruyama method, the Milstein method, and the stochastic Runge-Kutta method, in the Prokhorov metric. Specifically, we demonstrate that these numerical schemes converge weakly to the target measure $\mathbb{P}$ as the time-step size $h$ approaches zero, underscoring the efficacy of these in approximating the underlying stochastic process. The proof of these relies on the rigorous application of Prokhorov's theorem and the utilization of the Skorohod representation theorem, a powerful tool for constructing a sequence of random variables that converges weakly to a given random variable. Furthermore, we derive a bound on the Prokhorov distance between the numerical approximation and the target measure, thereby facilitating the numerical implementation of the and providing a tangible metric for assessing the accuracy of these approximations. This study's contributions to the field of stochastic analysis and numerical for stochastic differential equations are multifaceted. Firstly, our work advances the existing understanding of weak convergence in the Prokhorov metric for numerical schemes designed to approximate Itô SDEs. Secondly, our provide a rigorous foundation for the analysis of the convergence of numerical in this setting, thereby underpinning the development of more accurate and reliable numerical schemes. Finally, these possess relevance to the broader fields of statistical analysis of stochastic processes and numerical for stochastic differential equations. In summary, this study's application of the Prokhorov metric to the analysis of numerical schemes for Itô SDEs has significant implications for the understanding of weak convergence in these systems, thereby informing the development of more effective numerical for approximating stochastic processes.

Text: In a comprehensive exploration of novel theoretical frameworks, we embark upon the development of a sophisticated for describing the intricate dynamics of compounding fields, a manifestation of the confluence of gravitational waves and curved spacetimes. Founded upon the bedrock principles of General Relativity and Quantum Mechanics, our formulation provides a paradigm for the derivation of quantum equations governing the behavior of compounding fields within spacetimes of complex geometries. By synergistically integrating a range of mathematical techniques, including differential geometric and group-theoretic formalisms, we establish a novel system of equations capable of capturing the intricate interplay between gravitational and quantum fluctuations in the presence of curvature. The pivotal innovation of our approach lies in the introduction of a geometrically-inspired Lagrangian density, which serves as the fundamental construct for encoding the interactions between Riemannian curvature, metric perturbations, and quantum fluctuations. The resulting field equations, derived through a series of systematic derivations, are characterized by a complex set of coupled partial differential equations, which seamlessly integrate linearized Einstein field equations and a set of non-commutative algebraic constraints governing the dynamics of the compounding fields. Notably, our formulation is demonstrated to be congruent with existing gravitational field theories in curved spacetimes, thereby underscoring the universality and applicability of our approach. The mathematical tools and formalisms developed within this work have profound implications for the study of gravitational wave physics, cosmological theories, and the quantum mechanics of spacetime itself. By providing a rigorous foundation for the exploration of quantum phenomena in the presence of curvature, our enable predictions and insights that may shed new light upon fundamental questions in theoretical physics, thereby facilitating a deeper comprehension of the intricate relationships between gravity, spacetime, and matter.

Text: We present the first detailed abundance analysis of M giant stars residing in the inner bulge of the Milky Way, drawing on high-resolution infrared spectroscopy obtained with the Near-Infrared Integral Field Spectrograph (NIFS) at the Keck Observatory and the Gemini Near-Infrared Integral Field Spectrograph (NIFS) at the Gemini North telescope. Our sample consists of 25 M giants located within a projected radius of 1.5 kpc from the Galactic center, providing a unique opportunity to investigate the chemical composition and kinematics of this metal-rich and dynamically complex stellar population. We derived accurate elemental abundances for 16 key species, including C, N, O, Na, Mg, Al, Si, Ca, Ti, Cr, Mn, Fe, Ni, Cu, Zn, and Ba, through a state-of-the-art spectral synthesis code that takes into account the complex line blending and non-LTE effects characteristic of the infrared region. Our results reveal a striking dichotomy between the abundance patterns of M giants in the inner bulge and those in the solar neighborhood, highlighting the complex and dynamic nature of chemical evolution in the Galactic bulge.

Text: The theoretical viability of detecting dissipative motion within the quantum vacuum through the phenomenon of superradiance, wherein a collective spontaneous emission of photons manifests in a system comprising atoms or molecules, is a subject of investigation in this study. By positing an experimental paradigm utilizing an ensemble of ultracold atoms that can be intentionally induced to exhibit dissipative motion, we establish a theoretical framework predicated upon the master equation for complex many-body systems, thereby incorporating both unitary and dissipative dynamical processes. Through a derivation of an expression for the superradiance rate, a metric that quantifies the collective emission of photons, we establish a nexus between this phenomenon and the dissipative motion of the constituent atoms. Notably, our illustrate that the superradiance rate is significantly amplified when the atoms undergo dissipative motion, thereby affording the potential for detection of this effect. Furthermore, we engage in a discussion of the experimental hurdles and requirements necessary to observe this phenomenon, including the necessity for high sensitivity and low-noise measurement capabilities. Ultimately, the successful detection of dissipative motion within the quantum vacuum via superradiance would furnish novel insights into the comportment of quantum systems and elucidate the role of dissipation within the theoretical paradigm of quantum mechanics.

Text: This investigation examines the synergistic relationship between spectral heterogeneity and orbital angular momentum (OAM) in the context of structured light fields within polychromatic rotating photon modes. Through the superposition of discrete spectral elements characterized by unique OAM values, the study introduces a previously uncharacterized class of photonic structures exhibiting temporally evolving rotational dynamics during propagation. The generation mechanism employs precisely engineered phase modulation techniques applied to spectrally broadened light sources, facilitating concurrent manipulation of both spectral and spatial modal parameters. Analytical models indicate that spectral composition directly influences azimuthal phase distributions, resulting in spatiotemporally variable OAM configurations across the beam profile. Experimental verification through vector beam characterization and spectral analysis techniques substantiates the successful synthesis of these modes, demonstrating tunable helicity parameters and spectral dispersion ranges. The research emphasizes that chromatic dispersion acts as a critical mediator between OAM states and wavelength parameters, inducing measurable spectral redshifts proportional to the topological charge. The provide a conceptual framework for multidimensional information encoding in photonic systems, with prospective applications spanning high-capacity data transmission, quantum metrology, and advanced photonics. Additionally, the capacity to fabricate spectrally resolved rotating modes facilitates novel approaches to controlling nonlinear optical processes and photonic device interactions. These outcomes not only deepen our comprehension of structured light in spectrally broadened domains but also establish a paradigm for emerging photonic technologies integrating hybrid spectral-spatial encoding schemes.

Text: We calculate the dc supercurrent through a Josephson tunnel junction consisting of an antiferromagnetic (AF) interlayer sandwiched between two d-wave superconductors (d). In this case induced magnetism near the interface can strongly diminish the critical current for 110 oriented junctions whereas no suppression is obtained for the 100 orientation. This may help resolve a long-standing puzzle of the critical current versus grain boundary angle in high-T_c superconductors.

Text: We report coincident damped Lyman alpha (DLA) and sub-DLA absorption at z = 2.66 and z = 2.94 towards the z ~ 3 13.8 arcsecond separation binary quasar SDSS 1116+4118 AB. At the redshifts of the absorbers, this angular separation corresponds to a proper transverse separation of ~ 110 kpc. A third absorber, a sub-DLA at z = 2.47, is detected towards SDSS 1116+4118 B, but no corresponding high column density absorber is present towards SDSS 1116+4118 A. We use high resolution galaxy simulations and a clustering analysis to interpret the coincident absorption and its implications for galaxy structure at z ~ 3. We conclude that the common absorption in the two lines of sight is unlikely to arise from a single galaxy, or a galaxy plus satellite system, and is more feasibly explained by a group of two or more galaxies with separations ~ 100 kpc. The impact of these on single line of sight observations is also discussed; we show that abundances of DLAs may be affected by up to a few tenths of a dex by line of sight DLA blending. From a Keck ESI spectrum of the two quasars, we measure metal column densities for all five absorbers and determine abundances for the three absorbers with log N(HI) > 20. For the two highest N(HI) absorbers, we determine high levels of metal enrichment, corresponding to 1/3 and 1/5 solar. These metallicities are amongst the highest measured for DLAs at any redshift and are consistent with values measured in Lyman break galaxies at 2 < z < 3. For the DLA at z = 2.94 we also infer an approximately solar ratio of alpha-to-Fe peak elements from [S/Zn] = +0.05, and measure an upper limit for the molecular fraction in this particular line of sight of log f(H_2)< -5.5.

Text: We include fermions to the model proposed in hep-th/0606021, and obtain a renormalizable 4-dimensional SU(N) gauge theory which spontaneously generates fuzzy extra dimensions and behaves like Yang-Mills theory on M^4 \times S^2. We find a truncated tower of fermionic Kaluza-Klein states transforming under the low-energy gauge group, which is found to be either SU(n), or SU(n_1) x SU(n_2) x U(1). The latter case implies a nontrivial U(1) flux on S^2, leading to would-be zero modes for the bifundamental fermions. In the non-chiral case they may pair up to acquire a mass, and the emerging picture is that of mirror fermions. Outcomes indicate that significant variations in EMP waveforms and intensity occur due to interactions with terrain features, including diffractive and reflective effects. These outcomes have central implications for the development of accurate EMP propagation models and the prediction of EMP effects on sensitive electronic systems in complex environments. The computational model presented in this investigation offers a robust framework for investigating EMP-terrain interactions and informing the design of more resilient electronic systems.

Text: We establish that the contour of splitting trees, a fundamental object in the analysis of random discrete structures, exhibits the properties of a Lévy process. In particular, splitting trees are rooted trees where each node has a random number of children, and the contour process is a continuous path that encodes the order in which the nodes are visited in a depth-first traversal. Our main result shows that the contour process has stationary and independent increments, is continuous in probability, and has a càdlàg (right-continuous with left limits) sample path. Building on this, furthermore, we demonstrate that the contours of splitting trees can be represented as a compound Poisson process, where the jumps are given by the lengths of the segments between the nodes in the tree, and this characterization enables us to identify the Lévy measure associated with the contour process, which we demonstrate to be a mixture of a Dirac measure and a continuous Lévy measure. Our results have implications for the study of random discrete structures, and the properties of the contour process have been used in a variety of applications, including random graphs and statistical physics.

Text: This critical analysis investigates accelerated test models (ATMs) as pivotal methodologies for forecasting product reliability and elucidating failure mechanisms through stress-induced degradation under controlled, intensified conditions, thereby facilitating economically viable reliability evaluations across diverse industrial domains, including microelectronics, polymer engineering, and pharmaceutical stability studies. While these models demonstrate efficacy in capturing distinct degradation pathways—such as thermally activated processes, mechanical wear, or cyclic fatigue—they exhibit inherent constraints, including oversimplification of non-linear stress interactions, susceptibility to inaccuracies in parameter estimation, and challenges in extrapolating to real-world operational environments. Contemporary research addresses these barriers through the development of hybrid models integrating physics-based mechanisms with data-driven algorithms, as well as advanced computational techniques, notably machine learning, to enhance predictive fidelity and adaptability to multi-stressor scenarios. Crucial considerations in ATM implementation encompass rigorous validation against empirical datasets, accounting for synergistic stress effects, and addressing uncertainties in model calibration. The synthesis underscores the imperative to select model architectures commensurate with material characteristics, stress profiles, and degradation kinetics, while advocating for the establishment of standardized validation protocols to improve cross-industry applicability. Text: .** Pattern-avoiding permutations form a central object in enumerative combinatorics, with applications ranging from sorting theory to algebraic geometry. A Gray code for a family of combinatorial objects is an ordering in which successive elements differ by a minimal, well-defined change. While Gray codes are well studied for unrestricted permutations, little is known for pattern-avoiding classes, despite their rich structural properties. .** We develop a unified constructive framework that associates each class of pattern-avoiding permutations with a generating tree and a corresponding insertion encoding. By exploiting the tree's recursive structure, we design a depth-first traversal that yields a linear-time algorithm for generating the permutations in Gray-code order. The adjacency criterion is defined via a single transposition or a bounded-length block move, guaranteeing that consecutive permutations differ by a minimal change. We prove correctness by induction on the tree depth and analyze the algorithmic complexity, showing that each step requires (O(1)) amortized time. .** The framework produces explicit Gray codes for several classical pattern-avoiding families, including 132-avoiding, 123-avoiding, and 231-avoiding permutations, as well as for the more restrictive class of permutations avoiding both 132 and 321. In each case, the generated sequence respects the pattern constraints and exhibits the desired adjacency property. The provide new tools for efficient enumeration, random sampling, and algorithmic applications in sorting and data structure design. Crucially, open questions remain for classes with multiple pattern constraints and for extending the approach to vincular and barred patterns.

Text: .** The Majorana nature of neutrinos remains one of the most profound open questions in particle physics. Text: In a paradigmatic development at the intersection of additive number theory and combinatorial mathematics, our investigation yields a pivotal theoretical finding, namely, that the Graham conjecture is an implicit precursor to the Erdős-Turan conjecture. This demonstration is predicated on the Graham conjecture, first proposed by Ronald Graham in 1970, which posits a fundamental principle that governs the behavior of prime numbers, stipulating that for any natural number k greater than unity, the sum-free condition holds fast, asserting that for any positive integers n_1, n_2, ..., n_k satisfying 0 < n_1 < n_2 < ... < n_k, there exists a nonnegative integer c, constrained by 0 ≤ c < n_2, such that the sequence of numbers c + n_2, c + n_2 + n_3, ..., c + n_2 + n_3 + ... + n_k is comprised exclusively of prime numbers. Conversely, the Erdős-Turan conjecture, formulated by Paul Erdős and Pál Turán in 1948, posits a theoretical framework for investigating the divisibility properties of k-tuples, specifically conjecturing that if the sum of the reciprocals of the terms of the k-tuple (n_1, n_2, ..., n_k) is finite and the k-tuple meets certain divisibility criteria, then at least one term is divisible by another. Our proof exploits a novel combinatorial reduction, effecting a transduction of the implications of the Graham conjecture to those of the Erdős-Turan conjecture, thereby establishing a profound theoretical connection between two of the most enduring conjectures in additive number theory. This breakthrough has far-reaching implications for additive number theory, forging a fundamental link between the Graham conjecture and the Erdős-Turan conjecture, two enigmatic conjectures that have captivated mathematicians for decades. Our finding not only sheds new light on the structural properties of prime numbers but also highlights the intricate relationships that exist between seemingly disparate concepts within additive number theory. A one-zone chemical evolution model of the Milky Way for the elemental composition of the disk combined with an evolution model for its interstellar dust component similar to that of Dwek (1998) is developed. The dust model considers dust-mass return from AGB stars as calculated from synthetic AGB models combined with models for dust condensation in stellar outflows. Supernova dust formation is included in a simple parameterized form which is gauged by observed abundances of presolar dust grains with supernova origin. For dust growth in the ISM a simple method is developed for coupling this with disk and dust evolution models. The time evolution of the abundance of the following dust species is followed in the model: silicate, carbon, silicon carbide, and iron dust from AGB stars and from SNe as well as silicate, carbon, and iron dust grown in molecular clouds. It is shown that the interstellar dust population is dominated by dust accreted in molecular clouds; most of the dust material entering the Solar System at its formation does not show isotopic abundance anomalies of the refractory elements, i.e., inconspicuous isotopic abundances do not point to a Solar System origin of dust grains. The observed abundance ratios of presolar dust grains formed in SN ejecta and in AGB star outflows requires that for the ejecta from SNe the fraction of refractory elements condensed into dust is 0.15 for carbon dust and is quite small ($\sim10^{-4}$) for other dust species.

A predictive model incorporating these two kinematic parameters explained 58 % of the variance in throwing speed (adjusted R² = 0.58). Cluster analysis identified three throwing archetypes: “Power‑dominant,” “Efficiency‑dominant,” and “Mixed,” each exhibiting unique muscle activation timing. The suggest that integrating kinematic and neuromuscular assessments provides a more nuanced evaluation of throwing ability than velocity alone, offering actionable targets for individualized training and injury mitigation.

Text: Many of the mutations accumulated by naturally evolving proteins are neutral in the sense that they do not significantly alter a protein's ability to perform its primary biological function. However, new protein functions evolve when selection begins to favor other, "promiscuous" functions that are incidental to a protein's biological role. If mutations that are neutral with respect to a protein's primary biological function cause substantial changes in promiscuous functions, these mutations could enable future functional evolution. Here we investigate this possibility experimentally by examining how cytochrome P450 enzymes that have evolved neutrally with respect to activity on a single substrate have changed in their abilities to catalyze reactions on five other substrates. We find that the enzymes have sometimes changed as much as four-fold in the promiscuous activities. The changes in promiscuous activities tend to increase with the number of mutations, and can be largely rationalized in terms of the chemical structures of the substrates. The activities on chemically similar substrates tend to change in a coordinated fashion, potentially providing a route for systematically predicting the change in one function based on the measurement of several others. Text: Marching bands that played for second-line dancers in the street, like the Onward Brass Band (a "reading" band that adapted to "faking" around 1905 when jazz became popular) and the Eureka (organized in 1920 as a jazz brass band), usually consisted of ten to twelve instruments: three trumpets, two reeds (originally clarinets; after World War II more likely saxophones), two trombones, brass bass, and snare and bass drummers. What all these bands shared was a style of playing "hot" dance music that suited the demands of a diverse, music-loving clientele, whether in cabarets, at dance halls, on riverboats, or in the streets. Solo improvisation was not common in New Orleans jazz bands until the mid-1920s, as documented on the recordings of the New Orleans Rhythm Kings, King Oliver's Creole Jazz Band, Clarence Williams's Blue Five, and Louis Armstrong and his Hot Five. Traditional New Orleans jazz entered the American entertainment mainstream in two ways between 1907 and 1917- through touring and phonograph records. Prior to the first jazz recordings by the Original Dixieland Jazz Band in New York in February 1917, New Orleans musicians had already traveled widely throughout North America. For example, the Creole pianist and composer Jelly Roll Morton left the city in 1907 and remained itinerant for most of his life; the Original Creole Orchestra worked the Pantages vaudeville circuit from 1914 to 1918, including Canada; and Tom Brown's Band from Dixieland played cabarets and theaters in Chicago and New York in 1915. Text: N-body simulations give us a rough idea of how the shape of a simulated object appears in three-dimensional space. From an observational point of view this may give us a misleading picture. Since stars are evolving in mass the stellar evolution may also influence the dynamics of the system. Hence, if one is interested in simulating what the morphology will look like through a telescope, one needs to simulate in addition evolving stars and weight them by their luminosity. Therefore we need to combine simulations of the dynamical evolution and a stellar population synthesis at the same time. For the dynamical evolution part we use a parallel version of a direct N-body code, NBODY6++. This code also includes stellar evolution. We link the parameters from this stellar evolution routine to the BaSeL 2.0 stellar library. For isolated clusters we found assimilable to standard stellar population synthesis codes such as the PEGASE code. For clusters in a tidal field we found that the integrated colors become relatively bluer due to energy equipartition effects. In the time shortly before dissolution of the cluster the stellar M/L ratio becomes lower compared to isolated clusters. We compared the of our simulations to integrated spectra of galactic globular clusters. For the cluster NGC 1851 we found good agreement between simulation and observation.
