Text: Superstatistics provides a unifying framework for describing complex systems that exhibit spatio-temporal fluctuations of an intensive parameter (e.g., inverse temperature, energy dissipation rate). By superimposing local equilibrium statistics with a slowly varying probability distribution of the controlling parameter, the approach bridges conventional Boltzmann-Gibbs statistics and non-extensive generalizations, offering insight into anomalous diffusion, turbulence, and high-energy particle spectra. We review the mathematical foundations of superstatistics, emphasizing the derivation of marginal distributions from a convolution of conditional Boltzmann factors with a priori distributions (χ², inverse-γ, log-normal). Analytical techniques-including Laplace transforms, saddle-point approximations, and renormalization-group arguments-are employed to obtain explicit forms of the resulting Tsallis-type and stretched-exponential PDFs. Numerical simulations of Langevin dynamics with stochastic temperature fields validate the theoretical predictions. Representative physical systems (Kolmogorov turbulence, granular gases, and cosmic-ray propagation) are modeled by selecting appropriate fluctuation kernels. The analysis demonstrates that superstatistical models reproduce experimentally observed heavy-tailed distributions with a minimal set of parameters, elucidating the origin of non-Gaussian statistics in diverse settings. Moreover, we identify universal scaling relations linking the variance of the intensive parameter to the entropic index, and we show that the superstatistical formalism can be systematically extended to incorporate memory effects and spatial heterogeneities, thereby broadening its applicability to emerging complex-matter phenomena.

Text: This study presents a novel analytical solution for the motion of two unequal mass particles in the post-Minkowski approximation, a framework that accounts for the effects of gravity and high-speed particles. By employing the post-Minkowski metric, which deviates from the Minkowski spacetime metric in the presence of a gravitational potential, we derive a set of coupled differential equations governing the circular motion of two particles with unequal masses. Utilizing a perturbative approach, we expand the metric in powers of the gravitational potential and retain terms up to the first order. The resulting equations are then solved numerically, yielding a set of orbital parameters that characterize the circular motion of the particles. Our indicate that the post-Minkowski approximation provides a more accurate representation of the orbital dynamics, particularly for particles with mass ratios close to unity. The obtained solution can be used to study the gravitational interactions in various astrophysical contexts, including binary star systems and compact object binaries, where the post-Minkowski approximation is expected to provide a more accurate description of the gravitational dynamics.

The resulting thermodynamic description is shown to be consistent with the classical theory of linear elasticity, yet it offers a more fundamental and comprehensive understanding of the underlying physical mechanisms. Text: The pursuit of sustainable and efficient energy sources has led to significant research into thermonuclear reactions. Traditional approaches to achieving these reactions have focused on magnetic confinement , which pose significant engineering challenges. In contrast, exploiting gravity as a means of plasma retention offers a novel and potentially more straightforward approach. This concept has been explored theoretically, but its practical feasibility remains untested. We employ a multidisciplinary approach to investigate the feasibility of a gravity-based thermonuclear reactor. Our study combines analytical modeling, numerical simulations, and experimental validation. A bespoke computational framework is developed to simulate the behavior of high-temperature plasma under the influence of gravity, accounting for key factors such as plasma density, temperature, and containment geometry. Experimental verification of key assumptions is conducted using state-of-the-art diagnostics and spectroscopic analysis. Our demonstrate the potential for gravity retention of high-temperature plasma, showing that stable confinement can be achieved through careful optimization of containment geometry and plasma conditions. Notably, our simulations predict a significant increase in plasma lifetimes and a substantial reduction in energy losses, suggesting a promising path forward for the development of a practical thermonuclear reactor.

Text: We demonstrate that cosmic microwave observations consistent with a cosmological constant universe predict in a well-defined sense that lower redshift measures will nearly automatically deliver w=-1 for the dark energy equation of state value unless they are sensitive to w(z). Thus low redshift data pointing to w=-1 does not truly argue for a cosmological constant. Even the simplest question of whether the equation of state of dark energy is equal to the cosmological constant therefore requires experiments able to sensitively constrain time variation w(z) and not merely a constant w. We also note a number of issues regarding parametrization of w(z), demonstrating that the standard form w(z)=w_0+w_a z/(1+z) is robust but use of high order polynomials and cutting off the high redshift behavior can be pathological.

Text: In a theoretical study, we explore the creation and utilization of Gaussian number-squeezed states within a symmetric double-well potential confinement of a two-mode Bose-Einstein condensate, aiming to attain sub-shot-noise sensitivity in phase estimation via atom interferometry. Our analysis, based on the Bose-Hubbard Hamiltonian with weak tunnelling and moderate on-site interactions, reveals that the ground state exhibits a Gaussian distribution of particle number differences with a variance that can be reduced by over 30% below the binomial limit without requiring strong correlations. By implementing a controlled quench of the inter-well barrier or a sequence of interaction-driven phase-shearing pulses, we achieve enhanced squeezing, resulting in a squeezing parameter as low as -12 dB for realistic atom numbers. This enables a phase-estimation precision that surpasses the standard quantum limit, scaling as 1/(N√ξ²), and relies solely on standard optical lattice techniques and time-of-flight imaging, making it experimentally feasible with current cold-atom platforms, thus paving the way for quantum-enhanced metrology and high-precision sensors.

Text: Quantum dot systems are of significant interest in the field of condensed matter physics, exhibiting unique properties that arise from the confinement of electrons within a small region. The presence of a Coulomb interaction in such systems introduces non-trivial dynamics, necessitating the development of analytical tools for their study. In this context, the Bethe-ansatz approach has proven to be a powerful for solving integrable models. We apply the Bethe-ansatz to an open quantum dot system with a Coulomb interaction, incorporating a Fermi-liquid description of the leads. The Hamiltonian is formulated in terms of an effective bosonization, allowing for the derivation of a set of Bethe-ansatz equations. These equations are solved numerically, enabling the extraction of key observables such as the density of states and the spectral function. Text: The zero‑temperature linear conductance of a parallel T‑shaped double quantum‑dot (DQD) system is investigated by combining a two‑impurity Anderson Hamiltonian with a non‑equilibrium Green’s‑function formalism and quantitative renormalization‑group calculations. In the regime of strong onsite Coulomb repulsion the system exhibits a crossover from a conventional Kondo plateau (G≈2e^2/h) to a regime of destructive interference where the conductance is suppressed to zero, reflecting the formation of a molecular‑like singlet state between the dots. Key diagnostics—PNS radius, accretion rate, BH formation time, and time‑dependent neutrino luminosities and spectra—were extracted and compared across EOSs. Inclusion of hyperonic degrees of freedom (BHBΛφ) accelerates collapse, producing a sharp truncation of the neutrino signal. These EOS‑dependent signatures provide discriminating observables for future galactic BH‑forming events and constrain the high‑density nuclear EOS.

These diagrams are equipped with a tensor product and a braiding operation, which enable us to study the composition of morphisms and the behavior of representations under tensor products. We prove that the 2-category D is a braided monoidal category, and that its representation theory is closely related to the representation theory of the quantum general linear group. We also establish a one-to-one correspondence between the objects of D and the set of isomorphism classes of finite-dimensional irreducible representations of U_q(sl_n). Our provide a powerful tool for studying the representation theory of U_q(sl_n), and we expect that they will have far-reaching implications for the study of quantum groups and their applications in physics and mathematics.

Text: What divers can teach you about learning a second language Back in 1975, researchers Godden and Baddeley did something a bit weird. They sent divers underwater and taught them a bunch of words, played through a diving communication device. They also taught them some words on dry land. 24 hours later, they tested the divers both underwater and on dry land to see how many words they could remember. Turns out, the divers forgot 40% more words when the context was different, that is, if they'd learnt the words on land and tried to recall them underwater and vice-versa. Decades of research support the very same quirk about human memory: we remember things more easily when we use them in the same situation we learnt them in, and forget them more easily in different situations. If you learn verbs by rote, you might remember them while you're going through the list in your head, but you'll probably struggle to recall them in conversation. Similarly, if you learn words and grammar on apps, they might come to mind easily when you're fiddling with your phone, but disappear as soon as you need them in real life. If you learn a language through conversations, you'll remember better when you're having conversations. If you learn by writing, you'll remember better when you're writing. If you learn by listening, you'll remember more easily when listening. If you learn by reading, you'll remember more easily when reading. Text: Lattice polynomial functions, constructed from the binary operations of join and meet, constitute a fundamental tool in algebraic aggregation and decision-theoretic modeling. However, classical formulations treat all variables symmetrically, limiting their capacity to encode heterogeneous importance or interaction among criteria. Introducing explicit weight parameters yields *weighted lattice polynomials* (WLPs), which extend the expressive power of lattice-based aggregators while preserving the underlying order-theoretic structure. We formalize WLPs on bounded distributive lattices by associating each variable (x_i) with a weight (w_iin L) and defining the function as a finite composition of weighted joins and meets. Using the Möbius transform and Birkhoff's representation theorem, we derive canonical normal forms and establish necessary and sufficient conditions for monotonicity, idempotency, and continuity. Theoretical are complemented by an algorithmic framework for constructing WLPs from given weight vectors and for evaluating them efficiently via recursive decomposition. The analysis reveals that every WLP admits a unique representation as a supremum of weighted infima (and dually as an infimum of weighted suprema), thereby generalizing the classical Sugeno integral. We prove that WLPs subsume weighted median and weighted Choquet operators, and we identify a subclass that is closed under functional composition. Crucially, applications to multi-criteria decision making and fuzzy optimization demonstrate that WLPs provide a flexible yet tractable means of modeling asymmetric importance and interaction among criteria.

Text: Understanding the binding mechanisms of many‑body bosonic systems under relativistic kinematics is essential for modeling dense quantum fluids, nuclear clusters, and exotic states of matter. While non‑relativistic treatments provide accurate low‑energy predictions, they fail to capture the momentum‑dependent mass corrections that become significant at intermediate and high densities. A systematic investigation of semirelativistic Hamiltonians for N‑boson ensembles therefore addresses a critical gap in the theoretical description of such systems. We consider a translationally invariant semirelativistic Hamiltonian \(H=\sum_{i=1}^{N}\sqrt{p_i^{2}+m^{2}}+\sum_{i<j}V(r_{ij})\) with a pairwise attractive potential \(V(r)=-\lambda\,e^{-\mu r}\). Using a combination of variational Monte‑Carlo optimization and the hyperspherical harmonics expansion, we construct trial wave functions that respect bosonic symmetry and incorporate relativistic kinetic corrections. The binding energy per particle, \(E_B(N)/N\), is extracted for particle numbers ranging from \(N=2\) to \(N=30\) and for a broad set of coupling parameters \((\lambda,\mu,m)\). Convergence is verified by benchmarking against exact diagonalization for \(N\le4\). The semirelativistic corrections increase the binding energy by up to 15 % relative to the non‑relativistic limit for moderate couplings, with the effect amplifying as \(N\) grows. A universal scaling law \(E_B(N)/N\approx a\,N^{\alpha}+b\) emerges, where \(\alpha\approx0.6\) and the coefficients depend smoothly on \(\lambda/m\) and \(\mu/m\). The delineate regimes where relativistic kinematics dominate the stability of bosonic clusters and provide quantitative benchmarks for future many‑body simulations of semirelativistic quantum systems.

Text: This investigation centres upon the rigorous formulation and analysis of multidimensional stochastic differential equations (SDEs) endowed with anticipating initial processes and reflection constraints, thereby facilitating the investigation of intricate phenomena governed by a composite array of stochastic dynamics and geometric boundaries. Specifically, the stochastic process in question assumes the form of a family of random fields that are endowed with a certain degree of predictive capability, allowing for the consideration of situations wherein outcomes of the process are known, or at least partially known, at the outset, thereby conferring an anticipatory dimension to the model. A central aspect of the problem under consideration pertains to the incorporation of a reflection mechanism within the SDE, whereby the stochastic trajectory is subject to a constraint imposed by a reflecting boundary, thereby precluding the process from straying beyond a defined spatial domain, namely, a Lipschitz domain. In this context, our primary objective is to establish the existence and uniqueness of solutions to the SDE, despite the presence of anticipating initial processes and reflection constraints, the latter of which presents a formidable analytical challenge. Our investigation employs an innovative amalgamation of advanced techniques from stochastic analysis, including the Wong-Zakai approximation and the reflection principle, to establish a rigorous criteria for the well-posedness of the SDE. Specifically, we demonstrate that a solution to the SDE exists and is determined uniquely, provided the anticipating initial process is endowed with a regularity structure as defined by the Malliavin calculus, and the diffusion coefficient is sufficiently smooth to ensure a well-defined and continuous stochastic trajectory. Furthermore, we provide a probabilistic interpretation of the anticipating initial condition by showing that the solution to the SDE converges to a reference solution as the degree of refinement of the anticipating initial process is increased. The implications of our are far-reaching and consequential, facilitating the rigorous analysis and modelling of a broad array of complex phenomena in physics and finance, characterized by anticipating initial conditions and reflection constraints. Through our work, we thus contribute to the advancement of the field by establishing a solid foundation for the mathematical analysis of SDEs with anticipating initial processes and reflection constraints, thereby opening up new avenues for the investigation of intricate stochastic phenomena and their applications in various fields of inquiry.

Text: Locally symmetric spaces associated with semisimple Lie groups are fundamental objects in geometry and analysis. The $Lp$-spectrum, a natural extension of the Laplace spectrum, has been of increasing interest in recent years due to its connections with the heat kernel, geometric analysis, and number theory. For spaces of higher rank, the $Lp$-spectrum is often difficult to compute directly, motivating the development of spectral theory in the context of rank-reducing techniques. We focus on locally symmetric spaces with $Q$-rank one, where $Q$ is a certain quadratic form associated with the underlying Lie group. Using the Selberg's Principle and the theory of Eisenstein series, we construct an orthonormal basis for the $Lp$-space of the space in question. This allows us to establish a correspondence between the $Lp$-spectrum and the spectrum of a certain transfer operator. Our main result establishes that the $Lp$-spectrum of a locally symmetric space with $Q$-rank one can be computed explicitly in terms of the spectrum of the associated transfer operator. Furthermore, we derive a geometric criterion for the existence of a spectral gap, which has significant implications for the study of the heat kernel and the geometry of the space. Our provide a significant step towards the development of an $Lp$-spectral theory for higher-rank spaces.

Text: The Mumford-Shah functional, originally devised for image segmentation, has become a prototypical variational model for free-discontinuity problems in fracture mechanics. In the context of brittle materials, its two-term structure-bulk elastic energy and surface fracture energy-captures the competition between deformation and crack creation. While absolute minimizers of the functional are well understood in static settings, the characterization of *equilibrium* (or critical) states, which satisfy only first-order optimality conditions, remains incomplete, especially when coupled to a kinetic law for crack propagation. We employ a rigorous variational framework based on Γ-convergence and the theory of functions of bounded variation (SBV). First, we derive the Euler-Lagrange conditions for equilibrium configurations of the Mumford-Shah functional under mixed Dirichlet-Neumann boundary data. Next, we introduce a notion of *absolute minimal state* as a configuration that minimizes the functional among all admissible competitors sharing the same crack set. To connect these states with fracture dynamics, we formulate a quasistatic evolution law driven by the energy release rate, and we prove existence of a global solution by a time-discretization scheme coupled with a minimizing movements approach. Equilibrium configurations satisfy a balance between the elastic stress intensity factor and the Griffith surface energy density, but they need not be absolute minima unless the crack set is locally stable. We prove that any absolute minimal state coincides with a global energy minimizer and yields a vanishing first variation of the total energy. Moreover, the quasistatic evolution constructed from absolute minimal states reproduces classical brittle fracture propagation: the crack advances only when the energy release rate reaches the material toughness, and the resulting crack paths are energetically optimal. These provide a unified variational description bridging static Mumford-Shah minimizers, equilibrium states, and dynamic fracture propagation.

Text: Current research on micro-mechanical resonators strives for quantum-limited detection of the motion of macroscopic objects. The cavity-mode structure selects a single collective vibrational mode that is measured by the cavity's optical properties, actuated by the cavity optical field, and subject to backaction by the quantum force fluctuations of this field. Text: Quantum dots interfaced with one-dimensional conductors provide a versatile platform for probing non-Fermi-liquid physics. When the leads are described by a Luttinger liquid (LL), electron-electron interactions modify the tunnelling density of states and consequently the charging characteristics of the dot, challenging the conventional picture of Coulomb blockade in metallic leads. Understanding these effects is essential for designing nanoscale devices that exploit strongly correlated electron systems. We model a single-level quantum dot capacitively coupled to two semi-infinite LL leads characterized by the interaction parameter (K) ((0<K<1)). The Hamiltonian is treated via bosonization and a perturbative renormalization-group (RG) analysis up to second order in the dot-lead tunnelling amplitude. Complementary density-matrix renormalization-group (DMRG) simulations on finite chains validate the analytical flow equations. The dot occupation (n(V_g,T)) is computed as a function of gate voltage (V_g) and temperature (T), and the differential capacitance is extracted to identify scaling regimes. We find that the charging curve exhibits interaction-dependent power-law tails, (n(V_g)-n_0propto V_g-V_0{alpha(K)}) with (alpha(K)=1/K-1), reflecting the suppressed tunnelling density of states of the LL. The Coulomb-blockade peak broadens and its height diminishes for stronger repulsion ((Krightarrow 0)), while the effective charging energy is renormalized as (E_C{ast}propto E_C K{beta}). At low temperatures, the differential capacitance follows a universal scaling form (C(V_g,T)=T{alpha(K)-1}f[(V_g-V_0)/T]). These elucidate how LL correlations control charge quantization in quantum-dot devices.

Text: Physical rest is emotional, whether you want it to be or not. Slowing down physically means the insides follow sometime after, though they cannot be rushed. This essay is part of a new Sydney Review of Books essay series devoted to the labour of writing called Writers at Work. We've asked critics, essayists, poets, artists, and scholars to reflect on how writers get made and how writing gets made in the twenty-first century. I live with depression, and I know the feeling of low mood descending, and this ache is not quite it. The ache isn't only mine, either; it goes beyond my edges and is shared by people around me. It feels widespread, not just within my local community, but perhaps distributed generationally. The immediate and personal cause of my own ache could be a number of things. One of those things is that I have finished drafting a book-length project after four years of work on it, and right now I'm in the pause of waiting to see whether it will find a place in the world. The book is part memoir, burrowing deeply into personal and family experience, as well as body politics. To have it be read sometimes feels more like a need than a desire. Having worked on one thing for a very long time is exhausting, and I'm scared by the creative pause that's fallen over my writing.

Text: A Lissajous knot is one that can be parameterized by a single cosine function in each coordinate. Lissajous knots are highly symmetric, and for this reason, not all knots are Lissajous. In particular, we systematically tabulate all Lissajous knots with small frequencies and as a result substantially enlarge the tables of known Lissajous knots. A Fourier (i, j, k) knot is similar to a Lissajous knot except that each coordinate is now described by a finite sum of i, j, and k cosine functions respectively. According to Lamm, every knot is a Fourier-(1,1,k) knot for some k. By randomly searching the set of Fourier-(1,1,2) knots we find that all 2-bridge knots up to 14 crossings are either Lissajous or Fourier-(1,1,2) knots. We show that all twist knots are Fourier-(1,1,2) knots and give evidence suggesting that all torus knots are Fourier-(1,1,2) knots. As a result of our computer search, several knots with relatively small crossing numbers are identified as potential counterexamples to interesting conjectures.

Text: The Bohm–Gadella (BG) formalism extends conventional quantum mechanics by employing rigged Hilbert spaces and Gamow vectors to describe resonant and decaying states. In his 2006 paper, Rafael de la Madrid argued that the BG theory yields contradictions with the standard Hilbert‑space framework, particularly concerning the completeness of Gamow vectors and the unitarity of time evolution. Clarifying these issues is essential for assessing whether the BG approach can be reconciled with the axioms of quantum theory. We perform a systematic re‑examination of the mathematical structure underlying the BG theory. First, we reconstruct the Gel’fand triple employed by BG and verify the domain properties of the Hamiltonian’s extensions. Second, we apply spectral deformation techniques to the Lippmann–Schwinger equation, deriving explicit conditions under which Gamow vectors constitute a basis of the dual space. Third, we test de la Madrid’s inconsistency claim by constructing explicit counter‑examples using solvable models (e.g., the Friedrichs–Lee model) and by evaluating the unitarity of the semigroup generated by the complex‑scaled Hamiltonian. Our analysis confirms that the apparent contradictions identified by de la Madrid stem from an overly restrictive interpretation of completeness and from neglecting the role of the Hardy‑space boundary conditions inherent to the BG construction. When the appropriate Hardy‑space rigging is imposed, Gamow vectors form a dense set in the dual space, and the time‑evolution semigroup remains contractive, preserving probability in the sense of rigged Hilbert spaces. Consequently, the BG formalism is mathematically consistent with quantum mechanics, provided its domain specifications are carefully adhered to.

Text: Powder snow avalanches are a significant threat to alpine regions, causing widespread damage and loss of life. Snow samples were collected from powder snow avalanche deposits in the European Alps during the 2019-2020 winter season. The samples were analyzed using a combination of laser diffraction and optical microscopy techniques to determine the size and shape of individual snow particles. The show that the size distribution of snow particles in powder snow avalanches is characterized by a high proportion of small particles (< 500 μm) and a distinct bimodal distribution. The smaller particles are found to be more prevalent in the upper layers of the avalanche deposit, while the larger particles are more abundant in the lower layers. These have significant implications for our understanding of powder snow avalanche dynamics and highlight the need for further research into the role of particle size in triggering and propagating these events.

Text: Critical curves are geometrical constructs that govern the behavior of dynamical systems, separating regions of distinct stability and bifurcation properties. Our approach involved generating ensemble trajectories and tracking their intersections with the critical curve, allowing us to compute probability distributions and statistical moments of first passage times and distances. Our reveal a power-law dependence of first passage times on the distance from the critical curve, with a universal exponent that is invariant across different parameter regimes. Additionally, we found that the distribution of first passage distances exhibits a characteristic scaling form, which can be rationalized in terms of the underlying geometrical and dynamical properties of the system. These provide new insights into the statistical mechanics of critical curves and have implications for the design and optimization of complex systems.

Text: This investigation expounds a systematic algebraic characterization of the pro-solvable étale fundamental group of smooth affine curves defined over fields of characteristic zero, synthesizing advanced techniques from profinite group theory and Galois cohomology to achieve an explicit reconstruction of its structural invariants. A pivotal theorem derived here articulates a necessary and sufficient condition for the solvable reconstruction of the fundamental group, effectively bypassing the requirement for exhaustive profinite resolution. This algebraic formulation not only provides a robust computational framework for analyzing arithmetic properties of affine curves but also delineates the intrinsic limitations of solvable group actions on their étale coverings. The significantly extend prior investigations into pro-nilpotent fundamental groups and offer novel perspectives on the classification of affine varieties through their fundamental group structures. Furthermore, the implications for moduli space theory and the study of Galois representations linked to geometric fundamental groups are discussed, highlighting the method’s potential to unify algebraic and topological paradigms in algebraic geometry. Text: Linear descriptor differential equations (LDDEs) are a fundamental class of mathematical models used to describe complex systems with time delays and nonlinearities. These systems are ubiquitous in various fields, including control theory, biology, and economics. The study of linear mappings induced by LDDEs is crucial in understanding the behavior of such systems. However, the existing literature lacks a comprehensive analysis of the properties of these mappings. In this paper, we investigate the properties of linear mappings induced by LDDEs. We employ a novel approach, combining techniques from linear algebra and differential equations to analyze the mapping's kernel, image, and invertibility. Specifically, we use the descriptor matrix representation of LDDEs to derive conditions for the mapping to be injective, surjective, and invertible. Interestingly, we observed that the properties of the linear mapping induced by an LDDE are closely related to the descriptor matrix's rank and nullity. We establish necessary and sufficient conditions for the mapping to be injective, surjective, and invertible in terms of the descriptor matrix's eigenvalues and eigenvectors. Our provide valuable insights into the behavior of complex systems modeled by LDDEs and have implications for control and analysis of such systems.

Text: The low‑energy dynamics of M2‑branes probing singular Calabi‑Yau four‑folds provide a powerful laboratory for exploring three‑dimensional \(\mathcal{N}=2\) superconformal field theories (SCFTs) and their geometric counterparts. In particular, toric Calabi‑Yau singularities admit multiple, physically equivalent quiver Chern‑Simons (CS) gauge theories—an instance of toric duality—whose precise mapping remains incompletely understood beyond the abelian regime. We employ a systematic probe analysis by placing a single M2‑brane in the of toric cones defined by convex lattice polytopes. The worldvolume theory is derived via the forward algorithm, translating toric data into CS quivers with superpotential terms dictated by brane tilings. We then implement a sequence of Seiberg‑like dualities, monopole operator deformations, and Hilbert‑series computations to generate candidate dual phases. Consistency checks include matching of global symmetries, moduli‑space Hilbert series, and supersymmetric partition functions on \(S^3\). Our confirm that distinct quiver CS theories related by the above transformations share identical mesonic moduli spaces, thereby establishing explicit instances of toric duality for a broad class of non‑compact toric Calabi‑Yau four‑folds. Moreover, we uncover a novel correspondence between the combinatorial structure of the toric diagram and the hierarchy of dualities, revealing that certain internal lattice points encode monopole‑induced superpotential terms essential for duality. These insights deepen the holographic dictionary between M2‑brane probes and toric geometry, and provide a constructive framework for classifying three‑dimensional toric dual pairs.

Text: The exotic baryon antidecuplet, predicted by chiral soliton models and lattice QCD, offers a unique laboratory for testing flavor‑SU(3) symmetry breaking and the interplay between spin‑flavor dynamics in QCD. While its mass spectrum has been extensively studied, the electromagnetic and axial‑vector transition properties remain poorly constrained, limiting our understanding of its internal structure and the mechanisms governing its decay modes. We employ the SU(3) collective quantization of the chiral quark‑soliton model (χQSM) to compute the magnetic dipole (M1) and axial‑vector (A1) transition form factors for all allowed antidecuplet‑octet and antidecuplet‑decuplet transitions. Rotational corrections up to order 1/N_c and linear strange‑quark mass corrections are incorporated. The resulting form factors are parameter‑free predictions, calibrated only by the empirical octet magnetic moments and axial charges. Finite‑momentum transfer dependence is obtained via a dipole ansatz consistent with the soliton profile functions. Our calculations reveal a pronounced hierarchy: magnetic transitions to the nucleon octet are suppressed by SU(3) symmetry breaking, while axial‑vector couplings to the decuplet are sizable (|g_A^{*}|≈0.3–0.5). The predicted radiative widths Γ(Θ^+→K^+γ)≈0.2 keV and axial decay widths Γ(Ξ_{3/2}→Ξπ)≈1.8 MeV agree with existing experimental limits and provide clear signatures for forthcoming photoproduction and weak‑decay experiments. These constitute the first comprehensive, model‑consistent set of transition observables for the baryon antidecuplet.

Text: Parton showers are a crucial component of modern particle physics simulations, describing the hadronization process of quarks and gluons into final-state hadrons. We develop a novel analytic framework to gain control over parton showers, leveraging a combination of perturbative and non-perturbative techniques. By employing a Lagrangian-based approach and a systematic expansion in the strong coupling constant, we derive an exact, perturbative solution for the parton shower evolution. This formulation is then matched to a non-perturbative description of hadronization, yielding a unified, analytic model. Our demonstrate significant improvements in the predictive power and accuracy of parton shower calculations. The developed framework enables the computation of precise, analytic distributions for parton shower observables, facilitating a deeper understanding of hadronization dynamics and high-energy collision physics. The proposed model has been validated against existing numerical simulations, showcasing its potential for applications in precision particle physics calculations.

Text: The study of open quantum systems has been a subject of considerable interest in recent years, with applications in quantum information processing, quantum thermodynamics, and quantum metrology. In these systems, interactions with the environment can lead to decoherence, loss of quantum coherence, and degradation of quantum information. Environmental monitoring has been proposed as a potential tool for controlling and mitigating these effects, but a comprehensive understanding of its consequences on open quantum dynamics remains elusive. We investigate the effects of environmental monitoring on open quantum systems using a combination of theoretical and numerical . Specifically, we employ a Lindblad master equation approach to model the dynamics of a two-level system coupled to a dissipative environment, and incorporate environmental monitoring via an additional measurement channel. Our numerical simulations focus on the impact of monitoring strength and measurement frequency on the system's dynamics. Our demonstrate that environmental monitoring can indeed exert a significant influence on open quantum dynamics, often leading to reduced decoherence and increased system coherence. However, we also identify non-trivial regimes where monitoring leads to undesirable effects, such as enhanced dissipation or non-stationary dynamics. Our provide new insights into the role of environmental monitoring in open quantum systems and highlight the need for careful consideration of system-environment interactions in the development of quantum technologies.

Text: Theoretical and Empirical Explorations of Hidden Markov Models in Continuous-Time Settings The utility of Hidden Markov Models (HMMs) in elucidating the complex dynamics underlying various engineering and scientific phenomena has garnered substantial attention in recent years. Notwithstanding the vast applications of HMMs, the preponderance of existing formulations is predicated upon discrete-time assumptions, necessitating the development of novel methodologies to accommodate the complexities inherent in continuous-time settings. This study endeavors to address this lacuna by extending the Maximum Likelihood Estimator (MLE) framework to Hidden Markov Models in continuous time, thereby enabling the estimation of model parameters from continuous time series data. Through an in-depth mathematical examination of the continuous-time state-space model, a novel algorithm is derived for the Maximum Likelihood Estimation of continuous-time HMM parameters. This proposed method incorporates the Expectation-Maximization (EM) algorithm, which iteratively updates the model parameters to maximize the likelihood of the observed data, thus ensuring optimal convergence and minimizing computational complexity. A comprehensive simulation study is conducted to validate the efficacy of the proposed algorithm, underscoring its robustness and accuracy in estimating model parameters under various scenarios. To further underscore the practical relevance of the proposed algorithm, we apply it to a real-world dataset of gene expression time series data, yielding profound insights into the patterns and relationships between hidden states and observed gene expression levels. The discernible temporal dependencies and dynamics inherent in this dataset demonstrate the potential of continuous-time HMMs in elucidating the intricacies of biological systems. This research constitutes a tripartite contribution: the establishment of a novel MLE framework for continuous-time HMMs, the development of an EM algorithm for efficient estimation of model parameters, and the application of the proposed algorithm to a real-world dataset, thereby illuminating its potential in analyzing complex systems. **Keywords:** Continuous-Time Hidden Markov Models, Maximum Likelihood Estimation, Expectation-Maximization Algorithm, Gene Expression Time Series Data. Text: The hard-X/soft-γ transient IGR J11321-5311 was first reported by the INTEGRAL/IBIS survey in 2005, but its nature and high-energy behavior remain poorly constrained. Understanding such short-lived outbursts is essential for probing accretion physics in compact binaries and for identifying new classes of transient high-energy sources. We performed a systematic re-analysis of all INTEGRAL observations covering the sky region of IGR J11321-5311 between 2003 and 2022, using the latest OSA 11.2 pipeline. Light curves were extracted in the 20-200 keV band with 0.5 s resolution, and spectra were generated for each detected flare. Timing analysis employed Lomb-Scargle periodograms and epoch-folding techniques to search for coherent pulsations. Spectral modeling utilized an absorbed cutoff power-law and thermal Comptonization (CompTT) models, with cross-calibration to simultaneous Swift/XRT data when available. Three distinct outbursts were identified, each lasting 2-5 ks and reaching peak fluxes of (3.2 ± 0.4) × 10⁻⁹ erg cm⁻² s⁻¹ (20-100 keV). The broadband spectra are best described by a cutoff power-law (photon index Γ = 1.3 ± 0.2, cutoff energy E_c = 45 ± 8 keV) or a Comptonization component with kT_e ≈ 30 keV and τ ≈ 2. No coherent pulsations were detected (upper limit 5 % rms for periods 0.1-100 s). The rapid variability, hard spectrum, and lack of a bright optical counterpart suggest a low-mass X-ray binary hosting a neutron star in a propeller regime, although a magnetar flare cannot be excluded. These refine the source classification and highlight the importance of continuous INTEGRAL monitoring for transient high-energy phenomena.

Our provide a novel perspective on the geometric and algebraic underpinnings of the Calogero-Moser correspondence, thereby illuminating the intricate and multifaceted relationships that exist between quiver representations, derived categories, and integrable systems. Moreover, our research has far-reaching implications for the study of singularities, symplectic geometry, and representation theory, and sheds new light on the complex interplay between algebraic and geometric structures in the theory of integrable systems, thereby underscoring the recollement of deformed preprojective algebras as a potent tool for navigating the intricate and multifaceted landscape of integrable systems.

By utilizing high-precision measurements of z_max and the associated ADD peak from observational datasets such as supernova surveys, cosmic microwave anisotropies, and galaxy clustering, we demonstrate that these features provide stringent constraints on the cosmological parameter space. Through Markov chain Monte Carlo simulations, we derive Ω_m ≈ 0.3 and Ω_Λ ≈ 0.7 at 68% confidence, consistent with ΛCDM, while tighter constraints emerge when combining z_max with other probes, thereby validating the ADD maximum as a complementary cosmological standard ruler that enhances our ability to test the concordance model against alternative scenarios.

Text: Cooperative wireless networks exploit spatial diversity through distributed space‑time coding (DSTC), yet conventional DSTC relies on accurate channel state information (CSI) at the receiver, which is often impractical in fast‑fading or low‑latency scenarios. Non‑coherent DSTC circumvents CSI requirements but typically suffers from severe performance loss because of insufficient training and suboptimal code design. A principled training‑based approach is needed to retain the diversity benefits of DSTC while operating without explicit CSI. We propose a training‑based distributed non‑coherent space‑time coding strategy for a half‑duplex relay network. Each source transmission is preceded by a short orthogonal pilot sequence that is relayed jointly with the data symbols using a linear amplify‑and‑forward protocol. The relays employ a unitary precoding matrix drawn from a Grassmannian codebook, ensuring constant‑modulus transmission and facilitating non‑coherent detection at the destination. An analytical framework based on the pairwise error probability (PEP) is developed to derive the achievable diversity order and to optimize the pilot length and power allocation. The scheme is evaluated through Monte‑Carlo simulations and compared with existing coherent and non‑coherent DSTC schemes. The proposed strategy attains the full cooperative diversity order of the relay network while requiring only a fraction of the training overhead of coherent DSTC. Simulation demonstrate a 2–3 dB SNR gain over state‑of‑the‑art non‑coherent schemes and performance within 1 dB of coherent DSTC at moderate mobility. The analysis confirms that the training‑based design offers a robust trade‑off between spectral efficiency and reliability for practical distributed MIMO deployments.

Text: Recently Conrey, Farmer and Zirnbauer conjectured formulas for the averages over a family of ratios of products of shifted L-functions. There are now many showing agreement between the main terms of number theory and random matrix theory; however, there are very few families where the lower order terms are known. These terms often depend on subtle arithmetic properties of the family, and provide a way to break the universality of behavior. The L-functions Ratios Conjecture provides a powerful and tractable way to predict these terms. We test a specific case here, that of the 1-level density for the symplectic family of quadratic Dirichlet characters arising from even fundamental discriminants d \le X. For test functions supported in (-1/3, 1/3) we calculate all the lower order terms up to size O(X^{-1/2+epsilon}) and observe perfect agreement with the conjecture (for test functions supported in (-1, 1) we show agreement up to errors of size O(X^{-epsilon}) for any epsilon). The incorporation of a fourth scalar family, which comprises an additional Higgs doublet and singlet, presents a promising avenue to rectify this deficiency while concurrently offering the potential to probe for new physics beyond the Standard Model. Our investigation focuses on the impact of the fourth scalar family on the Higgs signal and at the LHC, with particular emphasis on the observability of the Higgs boson in the 4b and ZH modes. Notably, our calculations reveal that the presence of the supplementary Higgs doublet gives rise to significant modifications in the Higgs production rates and decay branching ratios, which can in turn affect the Higgs reconstruction and identification at the LHC. Through an in-depth examination of the intricate relationship between the Standard Model Higgs boson and the additional scalar states, we demonstrate that a fourth scalar family can lead to a distinct phenomenological signature that can be leveraged to test the validity of the Standard Model and beyond. Our study provides a comprehensive understanding of the implications of the fourth scalar family on the Higgs observability at the LHC, laying the groundwork for future searches and discoveries that have far-reaching consequences for our understanding of the fundamental laws of physics.

Text: Our analysis investigatees the interplay between neutrino number asymmetry and cosmological birefringence, two fundamental concepts in modern cosmology and particle physics. We explore the impact of neutrino asymmetry on the polarization of the cosmic microwave background radiation (CMB), which is a sensitive probe of primordial interactions and the early universe. Our theoretical framework combines the effects of neutrino number asymmetry, neutrino oscillations, and photon-neutrino interactions within a comprehensive model. We show that a non-zero neutrino asymmetry can induce a significant birefringence in the CMB polarization patterns, which may be detectable by future CMB experiments such as CMB-S4. The resulting cosmological birefringence can be used to constrain models of neutrino number asymmetry and provide insights into the neutrino mass hierarchy and the fundamental parameters of the Standard Model of particle physics. Our results have considerable implications for our grasp of of the early universe and the properties of neutrinos, and highlight the importance of the CMB as a probe of primordial physics. The findings of this study can be tested by future observations and experiments.

Text: This study presents a comprehensive investigation into the Jacobi-metric stability criterion, a fundamental concept in the field of dynamical systems and control theory. The Jacobi-metric stability criterion is a necessary and sufficient condition for the stability of a periodic trajectory of a Hamiltonian system, and its application has far-reaching implications in various fields, including celestial mechanics, robotics, and optimal control. Building upon previous work, we derive a novel characterization of the Jacobi-metric stability criterion, which provides a more transparent and computationally efficient framework for analyzing the stability of periodic trajectories. Our demonstrate that the Jacobi-metric stability criterion can be expressed in terms of a set of matrix inequalities, which can be solved using standard optimization techniques. We illustrate the efficacy of our approach through a series of numerical examples, including a comparison with existing in the literature. The of this study have significant implications for the design and analysis of stable periodic trajectories in a wide range of applications, and provide a valuable tool for researchers and practitioners seeking to ensure the stability of complex dynamical systems.

Text: Dilute magnetic systems have garnered significant attention due to their unique magnetic properties, which arise from the interplay between localized magnetic moments and the underlying crystal lattice. Superexchange interactions, mediated by non-magnetic ions, play a crucial role in determining the magnetic behavior of these systems. We employed a combination of density functional theory and Monte Carlo simulations to investigate the magnetic properties of dilute magnets. Our calculations focused on the effects of superexchange interactions on the magnetic ordering in systems with varying concentrations of magnetic ions. Our reveal the emergence of canted ferromagnetism in dilute magnets, driven by superexchange interactions between localized magnetic moments. The canting angle, which characterizes the deviation from perfect ferromagnetic alignment, is found to be sensitive to the concentration of magnetic ions and the strength of superexchange interactions. Notably, our simulations demonstrate a transition from ferromagnetic to canted ferromagnetic ordering as the magnetic ion concentration decreases, highlighting the importance of superexchange interactions in shaping the magnetic properties of dilute magnets. Text: A general continuum theory is developed for ion intercalation dynamics in a single crystal of a rechargeable battery cathode. It is based on an existing phase-field formulation of the bulk free energy and incorporates two crucial effects: (i) anisotropic ionic mobility in the crystal and (ii) surface reactions governing the flux of ions across the electrode/electrolyte interface, depending on the local free energy difference. Although the phase boundary can form a classical diffusive "shrinking core" when the dynamics is bulk-transport-limited, the theory also predicts a new regime of surface-reaction-limited (SRL) dynamics, where the phase boundary extends from surface to surface along planes of fast ionic diffusion, consistent with recent experiments on LiFePO4. In the SRL regime, the theory produces a fundamentally new equation for phase transformation dynamics, which admits traveling-wave solutions. Rather than forming a shrinking core of untransformed material, the phase boundary advances by filling (or emptying) successive channels of fast diffusion in the crystal. By considering the random nucleation of SRL phase-transformation waves, the theory predicts a very different picture of charge/discharge dynamics from the classical diffusion-limited model, which could affect the interpretation of experimental data for LiFePO4.

Text: We present a comprehensive study of the s-wave pion-nucleus optical potential, a fundamental concept in nuclear physics that describes the interaction between a pion and a nucleus. Employing a rigorous theoretical framework, we derive the s-wave pion-nucleus optical potential by combining the relativistic mean-field model with the capable Lagrangian approach. Our calculations take into account the nucleon-nucleon interaction, the pion-nucleon interaction, and the nuclear medium effects. The resulting optical potential is expressed in terms of the pion-nucleus scattering length, the pion-nucleus efficient mass, and the nuclear density. We examine the dependence of the optical potential on the pion energy, the nuclear mass number, and the nuclear density. Our outcomes indicate that the s-wave pion-nucleus optical potential is strongly affected by the nuclear medium effects, particularly at low pion energies. We also find that the optical potential exhibits a non-trivial dependence on the nuclear mass number and density. These findings have significant implications for the grasp of of pion-nucleus interactions in various nuclear reactions and processes, including pion-nucleus scattering, pion-induced nuclear reactions, and nuclear pion production.

Text: We propose an innovative approach towards establishing a gauge invariant volume-weighted probability measure for eternal inflation, which has been a long-standing challenge in the framework of eternal inflation. This measure is constructed by leveraging the notion of a 'volume' element associated with a spacelike hypersurface, which is invariant under diffeomorphisms and provides a natural way to weight the probability of different inflationary trajectories. The resulting probability measure is shown to be consistent with the principles of eternal inflation, including the concept of a multiverse and the notion of an ensemble of universes. Our approach provides a rigorous and well-defined framework for quantifying the probability of different inflationary outcomes, enabling a more nuanced understanding of the multiverse and its implications for our understanding of the fundamental laws of physics. Text: We study the ground state energy E_G(n) of N classical n-vector spins with the hamiltonian H = - \sum_{i>j} J_ij S_i.S_j where S_i and S_j are n-vectors and the coupling constants J_ij are arbitrary. We prove that E_G(n) is independent of n for all n > n_{max}(N) = floor((sqrt(8N+1)-1) / 2) . We show that this bound is the best possible. We also derive an upper bound for E_G(m) in terms of E_G(n), for m<n. We obtain an upper bound on the frustration in the system, as measured by F(n), which is defined to be (\sum_{i>j} |J_ij| + E_G(n)) / (\sum_{i>j} |J_ij|). We describe a procedure for constructing a set of J_ij's such that an arbitrary given state, {S_i}, is the ground state.

Text: We present a comprehensive set of low resolution spectral templates for galaxies spanning the wavelength range from 0.2 to 10 microns, encompassing the ultraviolet, visible, near-infrared, and mid-infrared regimes. Our templates are based on a library of 50 galaxy spectra, carefully curated from existing observational datasets, to ensure a representative sample of galaxy types and properties. Our templates are suitable for a range of applications, including galaxy classification, star formation rate estimation, and dust attenuation modeling. We demonstrate the utility of our templates through a series of case studies, showcasing their ability to accurately reproduce the observed spectra of nearby galaxies and predict the emission properties of galaxies at considerable redshifts. Text: We investigate the dynamical instability and dispersion management of an attractive Bose-Einstein condensate (BEC) in an optical lattice. Our computational simulations, based on the Gross-Pitaevskii equation with periodic potential, reveal a rich interplay between the condensate's properties and the optical lattice parameters. Specifically, we find that the attractive interactions and the periodic potential give rise to a variety of dynamical instabilities, including collapse and fragmentation of the condensate. The optical lattice's dispersion management, achieved through careful tuning of the lattice depth and periodicity, is shown to mitigate these instabilities and maintain the condensate's stability. Our results demonstrate that the interplay between attractive interactions, optical lattice potential, and dispersion management can be controlled to achieve a stable and coherent BEC. Furthermore, our outcomes have implications for the realization of optical lattice-based quantum simulation platforms and the exploration of exotic quantum many-body systems with attractive interactions. The presented investigation provides valuable perspective into the complex physics of attractive condensates in optical lattices.

Text: In a pioneering experimental endeavor, we successfully implement a paradigmatic quantum-resonance ratchet, a cutting-edge device that capitalizes on the intrinsic dynamics of quantum fluctuations to effectuate directed transport without the need for extrinsic applied fields or gradients. This innovative system, comprising a linear chain of 30 superconducting qubits carefully designed to emulate the hallmark signatures of a quantum harmonic oscillator, showcases the intricate interconnectedness of quantum fluctuations and directed transport. By meticulously fine-tuning the inter-qubit coupling strengths, we establish a resonance condition that enables the efficient conveyance of quantum information between qubits. Through our meticulously controlled hybrid quantum-control scheme, which seamlessly integrates global and local control techniques to facilitate quantum-state engineering and the precise measurement of the system's configuration, we demonstrate the unequivocal presence of a ratchet effect. This phenomenon manifests as directed transport in response to quantum fluctuations alone, giving rise to a current-like phenomenon that underscores the potential of harnessing quantum fluctuations for practical applications in quantum information processing and quantum transportation. Our high-fidelity tomographic measurements of the qubit state conclusively reveal a striking enhancement of directed transport in the resonance regime, with transport probabilities up to 5 times greater than in the off-resonance regime. These signify the prospects of quantum-resonance ratchets as a novel platform for investigating quantum fluctuations and exploiting them for the advancement of quantum information processing and quantum transportation. The presented herein mark a significant milestone in the development of quantum resonance ratchets and underscore the transformative potential of harnessing quantum fluctuations for novel applications. **Keywords:** Quantum fluctuations, Quantum-resonance ratchet, Directed transport, Quantum harmonic oscillator, Superconducting qubits.

Text: In the realm of symplectic geometry, the existence of extremal K\"ahler metrics is a longstanding problem. A K\"ahler metric is considered extremal if its Ricci tensor is parallel. The manifold $\mathbb{CP}^2\sharp 2\bar{\mathbb{CP}^2}$, resulting from blowing up $\mathbb{CP}^2$ at two points, presents a complex scenario for the search of extremal K\"ahler metrics. Previous studies have focused on the existence of such metrics on $\mathbb{CP}^2$, but little is known about the case of $\mathbb{CP}^2\sharp 2\bar{\mathbb{CP}^2}$. This study employs a combination of analytical and numerical techniques to investigate the existence of bilaterally symmetric extremal K\"ahler metrics on $\mathbb{CP}^2\sharp 2\bar{\mathbb{CP}^2}$. The analysis is based on the equation for the extremal K\"ahler metrics and the use of the Einstein-Hilbert functional to derive a variational problem. We provide a theoretical framework and numerical evidence suggesting that bilaterally symmetric extremal K\"ahler metrics on $\mathbb{CP}^2\sharp 2\bar{\mathbb{CP}^2}$ may not exist. Our indicate that the presence of singularities and the blow-up points play a crucial role in the non-existence of such metrics. This study contributes to the ongoing research in the field of extremal K\"ahler geometry and provides new insights into the properties of K\"ahler metrics on complex manifolds.

Text: A spontaneously active neural system that is capable of continual learning should also be capable of homeostasis of both firing rate and connectivity. Experimental evidence suggests that both types of homeostasis exist, and that connectivity is maintained at a state that is optimal for information transmission and storage. This state is referred to as the critical state. We present a simple stochastic computational Hebbian learning model that incorporates both firing rate and critical homeostasis, and we explore its stability and connectivity properties. We also examine the behavior of our model with a simulated seizure and with simulated acute deafferentation. We argue that a neural system that is more highly connected than the critical state (i.e., one that is "supercritical") is epileptogenic. Based on our simulations, we predict that the post-seizural and post-deafferentation states should be supercritical and epileptogenic. Furthermore, interventions that boost spontaneous activity should be protective against epileptogenesis.

Text: A novel, computationally efficient iterative rounding algorithm has been devised to tackle the Closest String Problem (CSP), a pivotal issue within the realm of computational biology and string analysis, wherein the goal is to identify a solitary string that minimizes the maximum edit distance to a provided set of strings, each accompanied by an associated edit distance metric. By harnessing the concepts of string alignment and edit distance, our proposed iterative rounding approach systematically refines the candidate string across successive iterations, systematically eliminating strings exhibiting high edit distances and converging towards an optimal solution with each refinement. This algorithm commences by initializing a putative candidate string, which is subsequently iteratively rounded by selecting a string from the input set that exhibits the minimum edit distance to the current candidate, thereby incorporating the latter into the former; this iterative process is repeated until convergence is achieved, at which point the algorithm has yielded an optimal solution. Text: We propose a novel, remarkably compact approximate solution to the Kondo problem, a prototypical many-body problem in condensed matter physics, wherein the intricate interaction between a magnetic impurity and a Fermi gas is meticulously described. The construction is carried out explicitly for the series \(A_n,B_n,C_n,D_n\) and their super‑extensions \(A(m,n),B(m,n),C(n),D(m,n)\), revealing a unified pattern governed by the Cartan matrix and the \(\mathbb{Z}_2\)-grading. Text: .** In quantum chaos, time-reversal symmetry (TRS) governs spectral correlations and the distribution of eigenstates. While the quantum ergodicity theorem guarantees that eigenfunctions of a classically ergodic Hamiltonian become uniformly distributed in the semiclassical limit, the converse implication-whether quantum ergodicity forces classical ergodicity-remains largely unproven. Dynamical breaking of TRS, achieved through magnetic flux or non-Hermitian perturbations, provides a controlled laboratory to investigate this relationship. .** We employ a hybrid analytical-numerical approach. Semiclassical trace-formula expansions are combined with random-matrix theory (RMT) to predict spectral statistics for systems with tunable TRS breaking. Extensive diagonalization of quantum maps (kicked rotator, perturbed cat map) with adjustable symmetry-breaking parameters is performed. Husimi-function analyses quantify eigenstate delocalization, while level-spacing distributions are compared to Gaussian orthogonal (GOE) and Gaussian unitary (GUE) ensembles. Counter-examples are constructed by adding localized perturbations that preserve classical ergodicity yet generate non-ergodic quantum states. .** Our confirm that dynamical TRS breaking induces a universal GOE-GUE crossover and promotes eigenstate equidistribution in fully chaotic regimes. However, we identify robust counter-examples where quantum states remain ergodic despite underlying classical integrability, demonstrating that converse quantum ergodicity is not automatic. These delineate the precise dynamical conditions linking quantum and classical ergodicity and underscore the pivotal role of TRS in the emergence of universal quantum chaos.

Text: This treatise introduces a novel paradigm, denominated pseudo-random puncturing, aimed at optimizing the efficacy of turbo codes through the diminution of the error floor phenomenon, a pervasive issue that constrains the performance of these codes, which are ubiquitously employed in contemporary communication systems on account of their high coding gains and simplicity of implementation. Specifically, the error floor, characterized by a non-decreasing error rate at elevated signal-to-noise ratios (SNRs), constitutes a significant limitation to the performance of turbo codes, necessitating the development of novel techniques to mitigate this phenomenon. To address this pressing concern, we propose a pseudo-random puncturing method that entails the randomized selection of a subset of bits from the turbo code's parity-check matrix for transmission, effectively diminishing the decoding complexity and concomitantly enhancing the overall efficiency of the coding process. Through an exhaustive analysis of the performance of pseudo-random puncturing on diverse turbo code ensembles, we demonstrate that this technique can significantly ameliorate the error floor characteristics of turbo codes, thereby yielding a substantial reduction in bit error rates at high SNRs, thus underscoring its viability and efficiency as a paradigm for enhancing the performance of turbo codes in a wide range of communication applications.

For a given compact set $A$, the Riesz energy of $N$ points on $A$ is defined as the sum of the Riesz potentials of $N$ points on $A$, where the Riesz potential is given by $I_{\alpha}(x_{1}, \ldots, x_{N}) = \sum_{1 \leq i < j \leq N} |x_{i} - x_{j}|^{-\alpha}$. Our show that the limit distribution of the optimal points on a set of revolution, as the number of points $N$ tends to infinity, is supported on a subset of the set's surface. Specifically, for $\alpha \in (0,2)$, we establish the existence of a probability measure $\mu$ supported on the surface of the set such that the empirical measure of the optimal points converges weakly to $\mu$ as $N$ tends to infinity. Furthermore, we provide an explicit expression for the density of $\mu$ in terms of the geometry of the set and the parameter $\alpha$. These have implications for the study of optimal point configurations on sets of revolution in three-dimensional space.

Text: In the present investigation we scrutinize the impact of robust pickup‑channel coupling on proton elastic scattering from the neutron‑rich nucleus \(^{10}\)Be, employing a coupled‑reaction‑channels (CRC) formalism that explicitly incorporates the proton‑to‑deuteron pickup transition populating the bound states of \(^{9}\)Be; by performing concurrent fits to high‑precision elastic scattering measurements taken at incident energies spanning 30–80 MeV, we constrain the optical‑potential parameters through a global phenomenological fit, while the pickup‑form factors are generated from realistic overlap functions computed from shell‑model spectroscopic amplitudes; the inclusion of the pickup channel yields a pronounced suppression of the elastic cross‑section at forward angles and induces characteristic oscillations at intermediate angles, thereby achieving quantitative concordance with the measured angular distributions; sensitivity analyses further reveal that the coupling effects are dominated by the low‑lying \(5/2^{-}\) state of \(^{9}\)Be, and that omitting this channel leads to a systematic overestimation of the reaction cross‑section by as much as 15 %; consequently, these underscore that precise modeling of proton scattering on weakly bound systems mandates an explicit treatment of pickup processes, furnishing essential constraints for nuclear‑reaction theory and guiding the design of forthcoming experiments on exotic nuclei.

Text: In this document I develop a weight function theory of positive order basis function interpolants and smoothers. **In Chapter 1 the basis functions and data spaces are defined directly using weight functions. Text: This paper presents a novel discrete query quantum algorithm for evaluating NAND formulas, a fundamental problem in quantum computing. Our algorithm, dubbed NAND-Q, achieves a nearly optimal time complexity of O(sqrt(n)/epsilon^2) for evaluating an n-variable NAND formula with an error probability epsilon. This result closes a significant gap in our understanding of the query complexity of NAND formulas, which has been a longstanding open problem in quantum query complexity. Our algorithm employs a combination of quantum parallelism, interference, and amplitude amplification to efficiently evaluate the NAND formula. The core of the algorithm relies on a quantum circuit that iteratively applies a series of controlled-NOT gates and Hadamard rotations to the input qubits. We demonstrate that our algorithm outperforms previously known quantum algorithms for NAND formulas, including the original Grover algorithm and its subsequent variations. Furthermore, we prove that our algorithm is nearly optimal by providing a lower bound of Omega(sqrt(n)/epsilon^2) on the query complexity of NAND formulas. Our have significant implications for the study of quantum query complexity and its applications in quantum computing.

Text: In wireless ad hoc networks, distributed nodes can collaboratively form an antenna array for long-distance communications to achieve high energy efficiency. In recent work, Ochiai, et al., have shown that such collaborative beamforming can achieve a statistically nice beampattern with a narrow main lobe and low sidelobes. However, the process of collaboration introduces significant delay, since all collaborating nodes need access to the same information. In this paper, a technique that significantly reduces the collaboration overhead is proposed. It consists of two phases. In the first phase, nodes transmit locally in a random access fashion. Collisions, when they occur, are viewed as linear mixtures of the collided packets. In the second phase, a set of cooperating nodes acts as a distributed antenna system and beamform the received analog waveform to one or more faraway destinations. This step requires multiplication of the received analog waveform by a complex number, which is independently computed by each cooperating node, and which enables separation of the collided packets based on their final destination. The scheme requires that each node has global knowledge of the network coordinates. The proposed scheme can achieve high throughput, which in certain cases exceeds one.

Text: We examine the canonical and deformation quantization of Toda lattices associated with both simple and affine Lie algebras, emphasizing structural features that persist under generalizations of the underlying root systems. The resulting quantum integrals of motion are expressed in terms of non‑commutative symmetric functions, and their mutual commutativity is proved by means of a generalized quantum R‑matrix formalism. Text: .** Precision measurements of the Standard Model (SM) Higgs boson at hadron colliders rely on accurate theoretical predictions for production cross sections and kinematic distributions. Fixed-order perturbative QCD calculations suffer from large logarithmic corrections in the small-transverse-momentum (q_T) region and near threshold, which can compromise the reliability of signal modelling. Resummation techniques, such as transverse-momentum and threshold resummation at next-to-next-to-leading logarithmic (NNLL) accuracy, are essential to tame these logarithms and improve the description of Higgs observables. .** We implemented joint q_T-threshold resummation for gluon-fusion Higgs production at the Large Hadron Collider (LHC) and the Tevatron, matched to next-to-next-to-leading order (NNLO) fixed-order . The resummed predictions were interfaced with parton-shower generators to assess their impact on experimentally relevant observables, such as the Higgs transverse-momentum spectrum and the invariant-mass distribution of the diphoton decay channel. Uncertainties from scale variations, parton distribution functions, and non-perturbative effects were systematically evaluated. .** Resummation reduces the q_T-dependent theoretical uncertainty by up to 30 % in the low-q_T region and stabilises the total cross-section prediction at the percent level. The improved modelling shifts the diphoton invariant-mass peak by < 1 GeV and enhances the signal-to- ratio in the boosted regime by 5 %. These effects translate into a measurable improvement in the extraction of the Higgs coupling to gluons, demonstrating that NNLL resummation is indispensable for precision Higgs physics at current and future hadron colliders.

Our generalize the seminal Cartier-Rota theory of classical Spitzer-type identities for commutative Rota-Baxter algebras. In the classical, commutative, case, these identities can be understood as deriving from the theory of symmetric functions. Here, we show that an analogous property holds for noncommutative Rota-Baxter algebras. Text: Electrons in solids have been conventionally classified as either band-like itinerant ones or atomic-like localized ones depending on their properties. On the other hand, well below T*, their Fermi surfaces (FS's) have been observed by magneto-oscillatory techniques, and generally they can be explained well by the 'itinerant' f-electron model. These two models assume totally different natures of felectrons, and how they transform between localized and itinerant state as a function of temperatures has never been understood on the level of their electronic structures. Text: In many biomedical and social-science investigations the same subjects are observed under two conditions, yielding paired binary outcomes. Power comparisons reveal a consistent advantage over McNemar's test under moderate to high correlation (ρ ≥ 0.5) and when the true difference in proportions exceeds 0.10. The analysis is conducted within the theoretical framework of a high-energy $ e^+e^- $ linear collider operating at center-of-mass energies up to 3 TeV, capitalizing on its pristine experimental environment and precise energy calibration to isolate dijet events arising from contact interactions. By deriving cross-section calculations using leading-order perturbative QCD and incorporating kinematic cuts to maximize the signal-to- ratio, we demonstrate the pivotal role of jet transverse momentum and angular distributions as critical observables. Notably, our indicate that next-generation detectors can attain exclusion limits on the contact interaction energy scale exceeding 100 TeV for specific operator structures, thereby underscoring the substantial potential of linear colliders to probe short-distance physics inaccessible to hadron colliders, particularly in scenarios where contact interactions are suppressed by large energy denominators. Systematic uncertainties from parton distribution functions and hadronization effects are meticulously quantified, revealing their minimal impact on the overall sensitivity, thus substantiating the efficacy of dijet final states as a versatile tool for constraining non-Standard Model couplings and complementing existing searches for new resonances or anomalies in high-energy collisions.

Text: We present the of a comprehensive spectroscopic analysis of the X-ray burst spectra of the low-mass X-ray binary GS 1826-24, specifically targeting the detection of gravitationally redshifted absorption lines in the burst spectra. GS 1826-24 is a well-studied neutron star binary system that exhibits type-I X-ray bursts, which offer a unique opportunity to probe the strong-field gravity regime. Our analysis is based on a dataset of 15 X-ray bursts observed with the Chandra X-ray Observatory and the XMM-Newton satellite. We employed a sophisticated spectral fitting technique to model the burst spectra, incorporating a range of physically motivated models to describe the complex spectral behavior during the bursts. Despite the high sensitivity of our observations and the use of advanced spectral modeling tools, we report the non-detection of gravitationally redshifted absorption lines in the burst spectra of GS 1826-24. Our are in contrast to theoretical predictions and previous studies, highlighting the need for further investigation to resolve the tension between observations and theory. The implications of our for our understanding of strong-field gravity and the properties of neutron star atmospheres are discussed.

Text: we propose a novel approach to reconstructing the properties of Weakly Interacting Massive Particles (WIMPs), a popular candidate for dark matter, using neutrino detectors. Traditional WIMP searches rely on direct detection experiments, which often suffer from background noise and limited sensitivity. By using the unique capabilities of neutrino detectors, our approach exploits the distinct signatures of WIMP-induced neutrino production to constrain WIMP properties. We show that a high-statistics sample of neutrino events can be used to infer the WIMP mass, spin-dependent scattering cross-section, and annihilation branching ratios. Our analysis employs a Markov Chain Monte Carlo procedure to simulate WIMP-induced neutrino production and compare it with experimental data from a generic neutrino detector. The results show that the proposed approach can provide competitive constraints on WIMP properties, particularly for lighter WIMP masses. This work has implications for future neutrino detection experiments, which could offer a complementary and powerful tool for dark matter searches. We discuss the prospects of applying this method to existing and future neutrino detectors, highlighting the potential for breakthroughs in our insight into of the dark matter sector.

Text: The study of mean field equations with turbulence is a complex and multifaceted problem that has garnered significant attention in recent years due to its far-reaching implications in various fields, including physics, engineering, and mathematics. In this context, we investigate the existence of solutions to mean field equations that incorporate turbulence, which is modeled using stochastic processes and nonlinear terms. Our analysis relies on a combination of analytical and numerical techniques, including fixed point theory, stochastic analysis, and computational simulations. We establish the existence of weak solutions to the mean field equations with turbulence, and we demonstrate that these solutions satisfy certain regularity properties, such as boundedness and continuity. Furthermore, we show that the solutions exhibit a range of behaviors, including bifurcations and pattern formation, which are characteristic of turbulent systems. Our provide new insights into the mathematical structure of mean field equations with turbulence and have important implications for the study of complex systems and nonlinear phenomena.
