Text: Cosmological shock waves result from supersonic flow motions induced by hierarchical clustering of nonlinear structures in the universe. These shocks govern the nature of cosmic plasma through thermalization of gas and acceleration of nonthermal, cosmic-ray (CR) particles. We study the statistics and energetics of shocks formed in cosmological simulations of a concordance $\Lambda$CDM universe, with a special emphasis on the effects of non-gravitational processes such as radiative cooling, photoionization/heating, and galactic superwind feedbacks. Adopting an improved model for gas thermalization and CR acceleration efficiencies based on nonlinear diffusive shock acceleration calculations, we then estimate the gas thermal energy and the CR energy dissipated at shocks through the history of the universe. Since shocks can serve as sites for generation of vorticity, we also examine the vorticity that should have been generated mostly at curved shocks in cosmological simulations. We find that the dynamics and energetics of shocks are governed primarily by the gravity of matter, so other non-gravitational processes do not affect significantly the global energy dissipation and vorticity generation at cosmological shocks. Our reinforce scenarios in which the intracluster medium and warm-hot intergalactic medium contain energetically significant populations of nonthermal particles and turbulent flow motions.

Our approach is based on a perturbative analysis of the coupled oscillator equations, which enables us to derive an expression for the critical coupling strength required for the onset of complete phase synchronization. We find that the transition is characterized by a sharp increase in the degree of phase synchronization as the coupling strength exceeds a critical threshold, beyond which the oscillators become fully synchronized. The analytical are validated through numerical simulations, demonstrating excellent agreement between theory and simulation. Our work provides a fundamental understanding of the transition to complete phase synchronization, with implications for the design and control of synchronized systems in various fields, and sheds new light on the complex dynamics of coupled oscillators, enabling the development of more efficient and robust synchronization protocols.

Text: The 1987 supernova (SN 1987A) in the Large Magellanic Cloud (LMC) provided a unique opportunity to study the explosion mechanism and potential gamma-ray burst (GRB) progenitors. We analyzed archival data from the Supernova Early Warning System (SNEWS) and the Gamma-Ray Burst Monitor (GBM) aboard the Fermi Gamma-Ray Space Telescope to investigate potential correlations between SN 1987A and GRBs. Our analysis included a comprehensive review of the SN 1987A light curve and spectroscopic data, as well as a search for possible gamma-ray emission in the vicinity of the supernova. Text: A critical consideration in the realm of high-energy particle physics experiments concerns the potential impact of Cherenkov light generated by charged particles in lead tungstate (PbWO4) crystals on the accuracy and reliability of observational . Utilizing photomultiplier tubes, the temporal and amplitude distributions of the resultant signals were meticulously recorded, subsequently enabling the dissection of Cherenkov light contributions from the scintillation signals emanating from PbWO4. Our research indicate that the Cherenkov light yield from PbWO4 crystals represents approximately 2.5% ±0.5% of the total energy deposited by incident charged particles, in concert with theoretical predictions. Text: Spin-dependent transport in magnetic multilayers underpins the operation of spintronic devices such as spin valves and magnetic tunnel junctions. Understanding how spin currents propagate, scatter, and relax across ferromagnet/non-ferromagnet interfaces is essential for optimizing giant magnetoresistance (GMR) and spin-transfer torque (STT) efficiencies. We fabricated [Co(3 nm)/Cu(5 nm)]ₙ multilayers (n = 5-10) by magnetron sputtering on Si/SiO₂ substrates, followed by annealing to sharpen interfaces. Spin transport was probed via (i) four-point GMR measurements at 4-300 K, (ii) ferromagnetic resonance (FMR) spin-pumping experiments to extract spin-mixing conductance, and (iii) first-principles density-functional calculations of interfacial electronic structure and spin-dependent transmission. Spin diffusion lengths were determined by fitting the thickness dependence of the GMR amplitude to the Valet-Fert model. The multilayers exhibit a pronounced GMR ratio (> 30 % at 4 K) that decays exponentially with Cu spacer thickness, yielding a spin-diffusion length λ_Cu = 35 ± 3 nm. Spin-pumping measurements reveal a large interfacial spin-mixing conductance (G↑↓ ≈ 5 × 10¹⁴ Ω⁻¹ m⁻²), consistent with ab initio predictions of high transmission for majority spins. Temperature-dependent studies show a modest reduction in λ_Cu and a 15 % decrease in GMR at 300 K, indicating phonon-mediated spin relaxation. These provide quantitative benchmarks for spin-transport parameters in Co/Cu multilayers and demonstrate the viability of such stacks for low-power STT devices.

Text: We investigate colour selection techniques for high redshift galaxies in the UKIDSS Ultra Deep Survey Early Data Release (UDS EDR). Combined with very deep Subaru optical photometry, the depth (K_AB = 22.5) and area (0.62 deg^2) of the UDS EDR allows us to investigate optical/near-IR selection using a large sample of over 30,000 objects. By using the B-z, z-K colour-colour diagram (the BzK technique) we identify over 7500 candidate galaxies at z > 1.4, which can be further separated into passive and starforming systems (pBzK and sBzK respectively). Our unique sample allows us to identify a new feature not previously seen in BzK diagrams, consistent with the passively evolving track of early type galaxies at z < 1.4. We also compare the BzK technique with the R-K colour selection of Extremely Red Objects (EROs) and the J-K selection of Distant Red Galaxies (DRGs), and quantify the overlap between these populations. We find that the majority of DRGs, at these relatively bright magnitudes are also EROs. Since previous studies have found that DRGs at these magnitudes have redshifts of z ~ 1 we determine that these DRG/ERO galaxies have SEDs consistent with being dusty star-forming galaxies or AGN at z < 2. Finally we observe a flattening in the number counts of pBzK galaxies, similar to other studies, which may indicate that we are sampling the luminosity function of passive z > 1 galaxies over a narrow redshift range.

Text: We present a comprehensive investigation into the N=8 supersymmetric mechanics on the three-dimensional sphere S^3. By adopting a geometric approach, we derive the supersymmetric mechanics on S^3 as a Hamiltonian system with an 8-dimensional supermanifold as the configuration space. The supermanifold is constructed using the Hopf fibration, which naturally embeds the sphere S^3 within a 4-dimensional Euclidean space R^4. We demonstrate that the supersymmetric mechanics on S^3 can be formulated in terms of a set of 16 first-class constraints, which generate the supertranslation and superrotation symmetries of the system. The constraints are used to construct a supercharge operator, which plays a crucial role in the derivation of the supersymmetric Hamiltonian and the evaluation of the supersymmetric partition function. Our provide a deep understanding of the supersymmetric mechanics on S^3 and have significant implications for the study of supersymmetric systems in higher-dimensional spaces. The supersymmetric mechanics on S^3 offers a novel framework for exploring the interplay between supersymmetry and geometry, and our work lays the foundation for further investigation into the properties and applications of these systems.

Text: Our understanding of the behavior of matter in extreme environments, such as near black holes or neutron stars, is crucial for advancing our knowledge of general relativity and its applications. We employed a geometric approach to derive the geodesic equation for test particles in exact bumpy spacetimes. Utilizing the Petrov classification, we identified a class of spacetimes that exhibit a range of observable properties, including gravitational lensing, frame-dragging, and orbital precession. We then solved the geodesic equation numerically to obtain the orbits of test particles in these spacetimes. Our indicate that the observable properties of orbits in exact bumpy spacetimes are sensitive to the specific parameters of the spacetime, including the mass, spin, and quadrupole moment of the compact object. We found that the orbital precession of test particles in these spacetimes can be significant, with effects that are detectable through observations of gravitational waves or electromagnetic radiation. Text: This paper develops a extensive Galois theory for iterated endomorphisms, a class of transcendental dynamical systems that arise from repeated application of endomorphisms to a given algebraic variety. We establish the foundations of this theory by introducing a Galois group associated with a particular iterated endomorphism, which encodes the symmetries of the dynamical system. Our main result shows that the Galois group is a profinite group, thereby providing a topological structure that enables the investigation of the fundamental group of the dynamical system. We then demonstrate that the Galois group acts faithfully on the algebraic closure of the original field, establishing a Galois correspondence between the Galois group and the intermediate fields of the dynamical system. This correspondence offers a powerful tool for studying the dynamical properties of iterated endomorphisms, including the behavior of periodic points and the structure of the dynamical system's invariant subvarieties. Our work lays the groundwork for a deeper understanding of the algebraic and geometric properties of iterated endomorphisms, and has far-reaching implications for the work of transcendental dynamical systems.

Text: We present a comprehensive investigation of the next-to-next-to-leading order (NNLO) vertex corrections in charmless hadronic B decays, focusing specifically on the imaginary part of the decay amplitudes. Our calculations are performed in the context of the Standard Model, with particular emphasis on the imaginary part of the decay amplitudes, which plays a crucial role in determining the CP-violating asymmetries in these decays. Our study provides valuable insights into the underlying dynamics of charmless hadronic B decays and offers a crucial step towards a more accurate determination of the Cabibbo-Kobayashi-Maskawa (CKM) matrix elements. Text: This paper presents a comprehensive examination of the necessary conditions underpinning Schur-positivity, a fundamental property in the representation theory of the general linear group. We establish that a partition-weighted polynomial is Schur-positive if and only if it satisfies a set of algebraic and combinatorial constraints, which can be distilled into three primary conditions. Firstly, the polynomial must be invariant under the action of the symmetric group, thereby ensuring its irreducibility. Secondly, the polynomial must exhibit positivity modulo the ideal generated by the hook Schur polynomials, thereby establishing a connection to the fundamental representation theory of the general linear group. Thirdly, the polynomial must satisfy a specific set of divisibility conditions, which are derived from the combinatorial properties of the partition lattice. Our demonstrate that these three conditions are both necessary and sufficient for Schur-positivity, thereby providing a unified framework for understanding this crucial property. The implications of our are far-reaching, with applications in various areas of algebraic and combinatorial representation theory.

Text: The rapid neutron capture process (r-process) is a critical nucleosynthesis mechanism responsible for the production of heavy elements in the universe. However, observational evidence for r-process elements in the Milky Way and nearby galaxies has been inconsistent, with some studies suggesting a decline in r-process yields over cosmic time. We conducted a comprehensive analysis of publicly available spectroscopic data for a sample of 500 metal-poor stars in the Milky Way, using the Sloan Digital Sky Survey (SDSS) and the Apache Point Observatory Galactic Evolution Experiment (APOGEE). Our sample was selected to have [Fe/H] < -2.0, ensuring a high probability of r-process enrichment. Our analysis reveals a significant decline in the abundance of r-process elements (Ba, Eu, and U) in metal-poor stars of the Milky Way, with a median [Eu/Fe] ratio decreasing by ~30% over the past 13 Gyr. This trend is consistent across multiple r-process-sensitive elements and is statistically significant at the 2.5σ level. Our suggest that the r-process may have played a less significant role in the enrichment of the Milky Way's metal-poor halo over cosmic time.

Text: We present a comprehensive investigation into the critical fluctuations of the superconducting phase transition in magnesium diboride (MgB2) confined to magnetic field-tuned cylinders; utilizing a combination of scanning tunneling spectroscopy and theoretical modeling, we show the influence of spatial confinement on the superconducting state of MgB2. Taken together, by carefully tuning the magnetic field strength, we create cylindrical domains of varying diameters, effectively isolating the superconducting material from the surrounding environment. The resulting critical fluctuations are probed through analysis of the local density of states, revealing a distinct dependence on the cylinder diameter. Our findings indicate that the superconducting critical temperature (Tc) is enhanced in smaller diameter cylinders, while the central fluctuations exhibit a non-monotonic behavior with respect to the cylinder diameter. These results provide valuable understanding into the role of spatial confinement on the superconducting phase transition and shed light on the complex interplay between superconducting fluctuations and the underlying material structure. At the same time, the implications of our work are far-reaching, with potential applications in the development of distinctive superconducting devices and materials.

Text: Observational studies of planetary nebulae and supernova remnants reveal spatially confined, metal‑enriched condensations that may serve as conduits for newly nucleosynthesized elements into the interstellar medium; in the present investigation we examine the influence of oxygen‑rich droplets—compact, high‑density condensations enriched in O, C, and N—on the chemical evolution of the ISM, employing a synergistic approach that integrates high‑resolution optical spectroscopy, infrared imaging, and hydrodynamic simulations to identify and characterize these droplets within the planetary nebula NGC 7027 and the supernova remnant Cassiopeia A. Spectroscopic diagnostics disclose electron temperatures ranging from 8 to 10 kK and electron densities exceeding 10^5 cm^−3, while oxygen abundances reach up to an order of magnitude above the ambient medium. Hydrodynamic simulations suggest that these droplets persist for several ×10^4 years prior to homogenization, during which they liberate their constituent metals via conductive interfaces and turbulent entrainment. The aggregate mass of oxygen released by these droplets throughout a star‑forming epoch is found to be commensurate with that injected by stellar winds and supernova ejecta, implying that droplets constitute a substantial, hitherto underappreciated channel for ISM enrichment; consequently, these necessitate the inclusion of metal‑rich clumps within galactic chemical evolution models in order to faithfully reproduce observed abundance gradients.

Our results provide a clear insight into of the role of edge spin accumulation in modulating the spin transport properties of lateral spin valves, and highlight the potential for manipulating spin-dependent phenomena in mesoscopic structures. Text: This work presents a theoretical and experimental investigation into the generation of capillary-gravity waves by a slow-moving object in a liquid medium. We consider a scenario where a submerged or floating object is slowly translated through the fluid with a velocity that is much smaller than the characteristic wave speed, thereby allowing the application of a low-Reynolds-number approximation. Via a combination of linear and nonlinear theories, we derive a set of equations that describe the evolution of the wave field in response to the object's movement. Our outcomes uncover that the wave pattern exhibits a complex interplay between capillary and gravity forces, with the former dominating at shorter wavelengths and the latter governing the behavior at larger scales. Experimental data obtained through a high-speed camera and particle image velocimetry are also presented, demonstrating excellent agreement with the theoretical predictions. The investigation contributes to our grasp of of the fundamental physics underlying wave generation by slowly moving objects and has implications for various fields, including oceanography, hydraulics, and surface science. The findings can be applied to model and predict wave behavior in a range of natural and engineered systems.

Text: The detection of intact forward protons in proton–proton collisions provides a unique laboratory for probing rare exclusive processes and for accessing kinematic regimes where Standard Model (SM) s are suppressed. Tagging these protons with dedicated near‑beam detectors (e.g., AFP and CT‑PPS) enables precise reconstruction of the central system’s mass and quantum numbers, thereby opening new avenues for the discovery of physics beyond the SM, such as anomalous gauge couplings, heavy resonances, and extra‑dimensional signatures. We present a comprehensive analysis framework that combines Monte‑Carlo event generation (MadGraph5_aMC@NLO, Pythia 8) with a realistic simulation of the forward proton spectrometers, including beam optics, detector acceptance, and timing resolution. Signal processes—central exclusive production of diphoton, dilepton, and dijet final states mediated by photon‑photon and gluon‑gluon fusion—are contrasted against dominant SM s using a multivariate classifier trained on kinematic variables (ξ₁, ξ₂, Δφ, rapidity gaps). Systematic uncertainties from proton transport, pile‑up mitigation, and luminosity are incorporated via a profile‑likelihood approach. With an integrated luminosity of 300 fb⁻¹ at √s = 13 TeV, the forward‑proton tagging strategy yields a 5σ sensitivity to anomalous quartic gauge couplings |a₀⁽W⁾/Λ²| ≈ 2 × 10⁻⁶ GeV⁻² and to scalar resonances up to 1.5 TeV with cross sections as low as 0.2 fb. The technique also provides competitive limits on large‑extra‑dimension models (M_D > 5 TeV). These demonstrate that tagged forward protons constitute a powerful, complementary probe for new physics at the LHC.

Text: We yield an in-depth exploration of the contributions of Leonid Vitaliyevich Kantorovich to the development of linear programming, a fundamental area of operations research. His work laid the groundwork for the subsequent development of the simplex technique by George Dantzig in the 1940s. we examine the pivotal role of Kantorovich's research in the evolution of linear programming, highlighting the significance of his contributions to the field. Through a critical analysis of Kantorovich's original publications and contemporary reviews, we illustrate the extent to which his work influenced the development of linear programming as a distinct area of study. Furthermore, we discuss the implications of Kantorovich's research for the broader field of operations research, underscoring its continued relevance in modern applications of linear programming. Text: Modified gravity theories, such as f(R) acceleration models, have been proposed as alternative explanations for the observed accelerating expansion of the universe, bypassing the need for dark energy. These models modify the Einstein-Hilbert action by introducing a function of the Ricci scalar, R. We utilize a combination of cosmological observations, including Type Ia supernovae, baryon acoustic oscillations, and cosmic microwave radiation data, to constrain the parameters of several popular f(R) models. We employ a Markov Chain Monte Carlo algorithm to sample the parameter space and determine the best-fit values. Our analysis reveals that the Hu-Sawicki and Starobinsky models are consistent with the observational data, while the Tsujikawa model is disfavored. We find that the f(R) models can provide a good fit to the data, with a slight deviation from the standard ΛCDM model. The constraints on the model parameters, such as the amplitude of the modification and the scale factor at which it becomes significant, are tightened, providing valuable insights into the viability of f(R) theories as an alternative to dark energy.

Text: We present a novel combinatorial framework for analyzing the structural properties of random planar maps with faces of arbitrary degrees, a class of objects that have garnered significant attention in recent years due to their ubiquity in statistical physics, computer science, and mathematics. Leveraging a combination of probabilistic and algebraic techniques, we derive a precise characterization of the radius and profile of these maps, two key geometric invariants that capture the distribution of distances from the origin to the periphery of the map. Our show that the radius of the map exhibits a power-law scaling behavior with respect to the number of faces, while the profile of the map can be approximated by a Gaussian random variable. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the distribution of face degrees in these maps exhibits a striking pattern, with certain degrees emerging as preferred values in the large map limit. Text: We report the discovery of superconductivity without electron-electron attraction in a quasi-one-dimensional metal, challenging the conventional understanding of superconductivity mechanisms. The material in question is a carefully synthesized and characterized organic compound, featuring a chain-like structure with a high degree of electronic correlation. Through a combination of experimental and theoretical approaches, including angle-resolved photoemission spectroscopy, scanning tunneling microscopy, and density functional theory calculations, we demonstrate that superconductivity arises from the interplay between electronic correlations and the quasi-one-dimensional band structure. Specifically, we find that the superconducting state is mediated by a new mechanism involving the formation of a gapless, excitonic-like collective mode, which arises from the coupling of electrons to the lattice vibrations. This mode, in turn, enables the formation of Cooper pairs without the need for electron-electron attraction, providing a paradigmatic example of a non-conventional superconducting state. Our outcomes have marked implications for the insight into of superconductivity in low-dimensional systems and the development of new superconducting materials.

Text: This paper investigates the properties and behavior of the group of Hamiltonian homeomorphisms in the L^\infty-norm, a metric space that has garnered significant attention in recent years due to its connections to symplectic geometry and topological dynamics. We establish a comprehensive framework for understanding this group, which we denote by \text{Ham}_\infty(X,\omega), where X is a compact symplectic manifold and \omega is a symplectic form on X. Our main result is the characterization of the group's structure in terms of a certain type of topological equivalence, which we refer to as \omega-equivalence. Specifically, we prove that two Hamiltonian homeomorphisms are \omega-equivalent if and only if they are conjugate via a Hamiltonian isotopy, providing a fundamental connection between the group's algebraic structure and its geometric properties. Furthermore, we derive a number of key consequences from this characterization, including the existence of a finite generating set for the group and a criterion for a Hamiltonian homeomorphism to be \omega-equivalent to the identity map. These shed new light on the complex interplay between symplectic geometry, topology, and dynamics in this context.

Text: The pseudospin degree of freedom, emerging from the layer index in semiconductor bilayers, supports collective excitations analogous to ferromagnetic spin waves but governed by interlayer Coulomb coherence rather than exchange interactions. Here we develop a microscopic theory of the pseudospin resonance (PSR) by extending the random‑phase approximation to a bilayer Hamiltonian that includes interlayer tunneling, bias‑induced asymmetry, and realistic screened Coulomb potentials. By diagonalizing the coupled charge‑density response matrices we derive analytic expressions for the resonance frequency, linewidth, and oscillator strength as functions of carrier density, layer separation, and external electric fields. The theory predicts a non‑monotonic dispersion, with a pronounced softening near the critical imbalance where the system undergoes a transition from a coherent excitonic condensate to a compressible state. Comparison with recent terahertz spectroscopy and inelastic light‑scattering measurements on GaAs double‑quantum‑well structures shows quantitative agreement without adjustable parameters. Our establish the PSR as a sensitive probe of interlayer phase coherence and provide design criteria for exploiting pseudospin dynamics in novel quantum‑electronic devices.

Text: Recent studies of dense clumps/cores in a number of regions of low-mass star formation have shown that the mass distribution of these clumps closely resembles the initial mass function (IMF) of field stars. In this paper, we highlight a potential difficulty in this interpretation, namely that clumps of varying mass are likely to have systematically varying lifetimes. This timescale problem can effectively destroy the similarity bewteen the clump and stellar mass functions, such that a stellar-like clump mass function (CMF) in a much steeper stellar IMF. Text: We examine the habitat segregation between Lyman Break Galaxies (LBGs) and Lyman-alpha Emitters (LAEs) in the vicinity of a quasar (QSO) at redshift z~5, a critical epoch in the early universe. Our results reveal a significant spatial segregation between LBGs and LAEs, with LBGs preferentially located in the vicinity of the QSO, while LAEs reside in regions with lower QSO radiation flux. This segregation implies that the QSO radiation has a profound impact on the formation and evolution of these galaxies, suppressing star formation in LBGs due to the ionizing radiation and heating of the surrounding intergalactic medium. Text: In a groundbreaking feat of experimental innovation, we successfully engineered an efficient one-way quantum computing paradigm leveraging two-photon four-qubit cluster states generated via spontaneous parametric down-conversion (SPDC) within the confines of type-II β-barium borate (BBO) crystals. The efficacy of this novel approach to quantum information processing was amply demonstrated by our , wherein a two-photon four-qubit cluster state was reliably created and manipulated with an impressively high fidelity of 88.3%, corroborated by tomographic reconstruction. To realize this milestone, we harnessed a state-of-the-art down-conversion apparatus to produce two-photon entangled states, which were subsequently reconfigured through the intermediacy of polarization beamsplitters (PBS) and a programmable optical network, thus giving rise to a four-qubit cluster state. A carefully optimized series of optical transformations enabled the highly efficient production of a one-way quantum information processor, thereby facilitating the implementation of quantum circuits that showcased the remarkable capabilities of cluster state quantum computing. Text: Being motivated by John Tantalo's Planarity Game, we consider straight line plane drawings of a planar graph $G$ with edge crossings and wonder how obfuscated such drawings can be. We define $obf(G)$, the obfuscation complexity of $G$, to be the maximum number of edge crossings in a drawing of $G$. Relating $obf(G)$ to the distribution of vertex degrees in $G$, we show an efficient way of constructing a drawing of $G$ with at least $obf(G)/3$ edge crossings. We prove bounds $(\delta(G)^2/24-o(1))n^2 < \obf G <3 n^2$ for an $n$-vertex planar graph $G$ with minimum vertex degree $\delta(G)\ge 2$. The shift complexity of $G$, denoted by $shift(G)$, is the minimum number of vertex shifts sufficient to eliminate all edge crossings in an arbitrarily obfuscated drawing of $G$ (after shifting a vertex, all incident edges are supposed to be redrawn correspondingly). If $\delta(G)\ge 3$, then $shift(G)$ is linear in the number of vertices due to the known fact that the matching number of $G$ is linear. However, in the case $\delta(G)\ge2$ we notice that $shift(G)$ can be linear even if the matching number is bounded. As for computational complexity, we show that, given a drawing $D$ of a planar graph, it is NP-hard to find an optimum sequence of shifts making $D$ crossing-free.

Utilizing the Green's function method, we have derived the spectral function of nucleons in nuclear matter, which embodies the self-consistent nature of the many-body system, thereby furnishing a detailed understanding of the complex interplay between the constituent nucleons. Our rigorous calculations have consistently demonstrated significant modifications to the EOS and single-particle spectra when three-body forces are included, particularly at intermediate to high densities, yielding a softer EOS and a broader single-particle spectrum, which collectively indicate a more pronounced quenching of the nucleon spectral function. Our results confirm that F_q(x,a,b) functions are resistant to linear and differential cryptanalysis, making them suitable for use in secure cryptographic applications. Text: We study linear and nonlinear development of relativistic and ultrarelativistic current sheets of pair plasmas with antiparallel magnetic fields. Two types of two-dimensional problems are investigated by particle-in-cell simulations. First, we present the development of relativistic magnetic reconnection, whose outflow speed is an order of the light speed c. It is demonstrated that particles are strongly accelerated in and around the reconnection region, and that most of magnetic energy is converted into "nonthermal" part of plasma kinetic energy. Second, we present another two-dimensional problem of a current sheet in a cross-field plane. In this case, the relativistic drift kink instability (RDKI) occurs. Particle acceleration also takes place, but the RDKI fast dissipates the magnetic energy into plasma heat. We discuss the mechanism of particle acceleration and the theory of the RDKI in detail. It is important that properties of these two processes are similar in the relativistic regime of T > mc^2, as long as we consider the kinetics. Comparison of the two processes indicates that magnetic dissipation by the RDKI is more favorable process in the relativistic current sheet. Therefore the striped pulsar wind scenario should be reconsidered by the RDKI.

Text: This paper addresses the construction of a maximum matching in trees under a set of additional structural constraints that arise in network design and phylogenetic reconstruction, where the matched edges must satisfy prescribed adjacency or weight‑selection rules. We introduce two deterministic polynomial‑time algorithms that exploit the hierarchical decomposition inherent to tree graphs. The first algorithm performs a bottom‑up dynamic programming traversal, computing for each vertex a compact state vector that encodes the optimal matching size for each admissible local configuration; this yields an overall time complexity of \(O(n)\) for trees with \(n\) vertices. The second algorithm leverages a greedy augmentation scheme guided by a novel “critical‑edge” ordering, which guarantees that each augmentation step preserves feasibility with respect to the imposed constraints and terminates after at most \(n/2\) iterations, resulting in \(O(n\log n)\) runtime. Formal correctness proofs are provided, establishing that both procedures produce a globally optimal constrained matching. Extensive computational experiments on synthetic and real‑world tree instances corroborate the theoretical bounds and demonstrate superior practical performance compared with existing unconstrained matching algorithms. The results expand the toolkit for exact combinatorial optimization on tree structures and suggest avenues for extending the framework to broader graph families.

By incorporating a derivatively-coupled inflaton field, our model provides a novel framework for understanding the dynamics of preheating, a phase transition that occurs at the end of inflation, where the energy stored in the inflaton field is transferred to other fields, leading to the formation of perturbations. We analyze the effects of preheating on the evolution of the inflaton and the perturbation spectrum, focusing on the interplay between the inflaton's self-interactions and its couplings to other fields. Our indicate that preheating can significantly impact the amplitude and spectral index of primordial perturbations, as well as the dynamics of the inflaton field itself. Furthermore, we find that the derivatively-coupled model provides a natural explanation for the observed amplitude of scalar perturbations, while also predicting a distinctive signature in the tensor-to-scalar ratio. These have important implications for our understanding of the early universe and the origins of structure in the cosmos.

Text: It is well known that Pfaffian formulas for eigenvalue correlations are useful in the analysis of real and quaternion random matrices. Moreover the parametric correlations in the crossover to complex random matrices are evaluated in the forms of Pfaffians. In this article, we review the formulations and applications of Pfaffian formulas. For that purpose, we first present the general Pfaffian expressions in terms of the corresponding skew orthogonal polynomials. Then we clarify the relation to Eynard and Mehta's determinant formula for hermitian matrix models and explain how the evaluation is simplified in the cases related to the classical orthogonal polynomials. Applications of Pfaffian formulas to random matrix theory and other fields are also mentioned.

Text: This investigation examines the conditions under which stepwise algorithms, a widely employed for variable selection in statistical regression models, concomitantly satisfy subset selection criteria, thereby ensuring the identification of the most efficacious model. A stepwise algorithm iteratively appends or deletes variables from a model based on their contributory effect to the goodness of fit, until a predetermined stopping criterion is fulfilled. Notwithstanding the algorithm's stopping rule, it may not invariably coincide with the optimal subset selection criteria, thereby potentially resulting in suboptimal model selection. In an effort to rectify this issue, we derive a necessary and sufficient condition for a stepwise algorithm to meet the D-optimality criterion, a widely utilized subset selection criterion in statistical regression, by demonstrating that the algorithm meets the D-optimality criterion if and only if the step size of the algorithm is commensurate with the optimal model size. Moreover, we demonstrate that this condition is also sufficient for the algorithm to meet other subset selection criteria, including the A-optimality and E-optimality criteria, thereby underscoring the significance of the derived condition. Our research provide invaluable insight into the behavior of stepwise algorithms and have far-reaching implications for the employment of these algorithms in statistical modeling and data analysis.

Text: On large angular scales, the polarization of the CMB contains information about the evolution of the average ionization during the epoch of reionization. Interpretation of the polarization spectrum usually requires the assumption of a fixed functional form for the evolution, e.g. instantaneous reionization. We develop a model-independent method where a small set of principal components completely encapsulate the effects of reionization on the large-angle E-mode polarization for any reionization history within an adjustable range in redshift. Using Markov Chain Monte Carlo , we apply this approach to both the 3-year WMAP data and simulated future data. WMAP data constrain two principal components of the reionization history, approximately corresponding to the total optical depth and the difference between the contributions to the optical depth at high and low redshifts. The optical depth is consistent with the constraint found in previous analyses of WMAP data that assume instantaneous reionization, with only slightly larger uncertainty due to the expanded set of models. Using the principal component approach, WMAP data also place a 95% CL upper limit of 0.08 on the contribution to the optical depth from redshifts z>20. With improvements in polarization sensitivity and foreground modeling, approximately five of the principal components can ultimately be measured. Constraints on the principal components, which probe the entire reionization history, can test models of reionization, provide model-independent constraints on the optical depth, and detect signatures of high-redshift reionization.

Text: The Kondo effect, a fundamental phenomenon in condensed matter physics, has been extensively studied in various systems, including graphene, due to its unique electronic properties. In this study, we demonstrate the tuning of Kondo physics in graphene using gate voltage, which enables precise control over the Fermi level and electron density. By applying a gate voltage, we modulate the strength of the Kondo coupling between localized impurity spins and the itinerant electrons in graphene, leading to a pronounced variation in the Kondo temperature. Our experimental , supported by theoretical modeling, reveal a clear dependence of the Kondo resonance on the gate voltage, allowing for the manipulation of the Kondo effect in a controlled manner. The observed behavior is attributed to the gate-voltage-induced shift of the Fermi level, which alters the density of states and thereby influences the Kondo interaction. This study not only provides new insights into the Kondo physics in graphene but also opens up opportunities for the development of novel graphene-based devices, where the Kondo effect can be exploited for potential applications in quantum computing and spintronics. The ability to tune the Kondo effect in graphene using gate voltage paves the way for further exploration of this phenomenon in other two-dimensional materials.

Text: We investigate the dynamical evolution of trans-Neptunian objects (TNOs) in typical scattered disk orbits (scattered TNOs) by performing simulations using several thousand particles lying initially on Neptune-encountering orbits. We explore the role of resonance sticking in the scattered disk, a phenomenon characterized by multiple temporary resonance captures ('resonances' refers to external mean motion resonances with Neptune, which can be described in the form r:s, where the arguments r and s are integers). First, all scattered TNOs evolve through intermittent temporary resonance capture events and gravitational scattering by Neptune. Each scattered TNO experiences tens to hundreds of resonance captures over a period of 4 Gyr, which represents about 38% of the object's lifetime (mean value). Second, resonance sticking plays an important role at semimajor axes a < 250 AU, where the great majority of such captures occurred. It is noteworthy that the stickiest (i.e., dominant) resonances in the scattered disk are located within this distance range and are those possessing the lowest argument s. This was evinced by r:1, r:2 and r:3 resonances, which played the greatest role during resonance sticking evolution, often leading to captures in several of their neighboring resonances. Finally, the timescales and likelihood of temporary resonance captures are roughly proportional to resonance strength. The dominance of low s resonances is also related to the latter. In sum, resonance sticking has an important impact on the evolution of scattered TNOs, contributing significantly to the longevity of these objects.

Text: Although one-loop calculations provide a realistic description of bulk and single-particle nuclear properties, it is necessary to examine loop corrections to develop a systematic finite-density power-counting scheme for the nuclear many-body problem when loops are included. Moreover, it is imperative to study exchange and correlation corrections systematically to make reliable predictions for other nuclear observables. One must also verify that the natural sizes of the one-loop parameters are not destroyed by explicit inclusion of many-body corrections. The loop expansion is applied to a chiral effective hadronic lagrangian; with the techniques of Infrared Regularization, it is possible to separate out the short-range contributions and to write them as local products of fields that are already present in our lagrangian. (The appropriate field variables must be re-defined at each order in loops.) The corresponding parameters implicitly include short-range effects to all orders in the interaction, so these effects need not be calculated explicitly. The remaining (long-range) contributions that must be calculated are nonlocal and resemble those in conventional nuclear-structure calculations. Calculations at the two-loop level are carried out to illustrate these techniques at finite densities and to verify that the coupling parameters remain natural when fitted to the empirical properties of equilibrium nuclear matter.

Text: Recent theoretical and phenomenological investigations have been undertaken to determine the lower mass limit of the lightest neutralino (χ), a hypothetical supersymmetric particle purported to exist within the Minimal Supersymmetric Standard Model (MSSM). Predicted to be the lightest superpartner particle, the χ is postulated to constitute a substantial component of the universe's enigmatic dark matter. Utilizing a judicious amalgamation of theoretical and experimental constraints, a lower mass bound for the lightest neutralino has been derived, wherein various parametrizations of the MSSM are taken into account. These include, notably, the gaugino mass unification scenario, the gravity-mediated supersymmetry breaking scenario, and the anomaly-mediated supersymmetry breaking scenario. A thorough examination of the phenomenological consequences of diverse supersymmetry-breaking patterns reveals that the most stringent lower mass bound is dictated by electroweak precision data, specifically the Z boson's invisible decay width and the Higgs boson's mass measurement. Our indicate that the lightest neutralino mass is necessitated to exceed a minimum value of approximately 45 GeV to evade current experimental constraints. This lower mass bound exercises a critical constraint upon the MSSM parameter space, particularly for the gaugino mass unification scenario. A thorough discussion of the implications of this result is forthcoming, encompassing future searches of supersymmetry at colliders and prospects for the direct and indirect detection of the lightest neutralino. The Minimal Supersymmetric Standard Model, neutralino, dark matter, electroweak precision data, and supersymmetry-breaking patterns are central concepts underlying this theoretical framework.

Text: Certain aspects of the AdS/CFT correspondence are studied in detail. We investigate the one-loop mass shift to certain two-impurity string states in light-cone string field theory on a plane wave . We find that there exist logarithmic divergences in the sums over intermediate mode numbers which cancel between the cubic Hamiltonian and quartic "contact term". We argue that generically, every order in intermediate state impurities contributes to the mass shift at leading perturbative order. The same mass shift is also computed using an improved 3-string vertex proposed by Dobashi and Yoneya. The result is found to agree with gauge theory at leading order and is close but not quite in agreement at subleading order. We extend the analysis to include discrete light-cone quantization, considering states with up to three units of p+. We study the (apparently) first-order phase transition in the weakly coupled plane-wave matrix model at finite temperature. We analyze the effect of interactions by computing the relevant parts of the effective potential for the Polyakov loop operator to three loop order. We show that the phase transition is indeed of first order. We also compute the 2-loop correction to the Hagedorn temperature. Finally, correlation functions of 1/4 BPS Wilson loops with the infinite family of 1/2 BPS chiral primary operators are computed in N=4 super Yang-Mills theory by summing planar ladder diagrams. The correlation functions are also computed in the strong-coupling limit using string theory; the result is found to agree with the extrapolation of the planar ladders. The result is related to similar correlators of 1/2 BPS loops by a simple re-scaling of the coupling constant, discovered by Drukker for the case of the 1/4 BPS loop VEV.

Text: A spectral method is described for solving coupled elliptic problems on an interior and an exterior domain. The method is formulated and tested on the two-dimensional interior Poisson and exterior Laplace problems, whose solutions and their normal derivatives are required to be continuous across the interface. A complete basis of homogeneous solutions for the interior and exterior regions, corresponding to all possible Dirichlet boundary values at the interface, are calculated in a preprocessing step. This basis is used to construct the influence matrix which serves to transform the coupled boundary conditions into conditions on the interior problem. Chebyshev approximations are used to represent both the interior solutions and the boundary values. A standard Chebyshev spectral method is used to calculate the interior solutions. The exterior harmonic solutions are calculated as the convolution of the free-space Green's function with a surface density; this surface density is itself the solution to an integral equation which has an analytic solution when the boundary values are given as a Chebyshev expansion. Properties of Chebyshev approximations insure that the basis of exterior harmonic functions represents the external near-boundary solutions uniformly. The method is tested by calculating the electrostatic potential resulting from charge distributions in a rectangle. The resulting influence matrix is well-conditioned and solutions converge exponentially as the resolution is increased. The generalization of this approach to three-dimensional problems is discussed, in particular the magnetohydrodynamic equations in a finite cylindrical domain surrounded by a vacuum.

Text: Most industrial machine tools have a serial kinematic architecture, which means that each axis has to carry the following one, including its actuators and joints. High Speed Machining highlights some drawbacks of such architectures: heavy moving parts require from the machine structure high stiffness to limit bending problems that lower the machine accuracy, and limit the dynamic performances of the feed axes. That is why PKMs attract more and more researchers and companies, because they are claimed to offer several advantages over their serial counterparts, like high structural rigidity and high dynamic capacities. Text: This investigation elucidates the decomposition numbers for finite Coxeter groups, a pivotal concept in the representation theory of these groups, and their intricate association with generalised non-crossing partitions, thereby facilitating a profound comprehension of the underlying combinatorial dynamics. By virtue of a meticulous examination of the Kazhdan-Lusztig basis elements and their symbiotic relationship with generalised non-crossing partitions, a novel combinatorial interpretation of decomposition numbers emerges, wherein these numbers can be expressed as weighted enumerations of these partitions, thereby enabling a computationally efficient calculation of their properties. Notably, this connection between decomposition numbers and generalised non-crossing partitions is predicated upon a recursive formula, which underscores the profound implications of this association for the representation theory of finite Coxeter groups, including the derivation of canonical bases and the elucidation of their properties. Text: This study presents an analysis of AKARI infrared observations of the globular clusters NGC104 (47 Tucanae) and NGC362, with a focus on the properties of their circumstellar dust populations. Utilizing the AKARI space telescope's mid-infrared photometric data, we identified and characterized a total of 24 candidate asymptotic giant branch (AGB) stars and 17 candidate post-AGB stars in each cluster. Our analysis revealed that the circumstellar dust in both clusters exhibits a range of characteristics, including dust mass, temperature, and optical depth, which can be used to constrain models of dust formation and evolution. We found that the dust populations in the two clusters differ significantly, with NGC104 exhibiting a larger fraction of warm dust and NGC362 showing a greater presence of cold dust. These provide new insights into the processes governing the formation and evolution of circumstellar dust in globular clusters, with implications for our understanding of the chemical and dynamical evolution of these ancient stellar systems. Text: Quantum phase transitions (QPTs) in correlated electron systems are critical phenomena where a continuous change in a control parameter leads to a sudden and dramatic change in the system's ground state. The periodic Anderson model (PAM) has been extensively used to study QPTs in heavy fermion systems, where the interplay between localized and itinerant electrons drives the transition. However, the PAM is a simplified model that neglects certain important interactions, such as the extended periodic Anderson model (EPAM), which includes additional hybridization and Coulomb repulsion terms. Using a combination of analytical and numerical , including the Lanczos algorithm and the density matrix renormalization group (DMRG), we have studied the QPTs in the EPAM. We have focused on the effects of the additional interactions on the phase diagram and the critical behavior of the system. Interestingly, we observed that the EPAM exhibits a rich phase diagram, with multiple QPTs and a complex interplay between the different phases. We have identified a novel critical regime, characterized by a non-Fermi liquid behavior, which arises from the interplay between the hybridization and Coulomb interactions. Our have significant implications for the understanding of QPTs in heavy fermion systems and highlight the importance of considering the extended interactions in the PAM.

Text: In this work, we investigate the fundamental mechanisms of dissipation in graphene and nanotube resonators, which have garnered significant attention in the field of nanomechanics and nanotechnology. Utilizing a combination of experimental and theoretical approaches, we have elucidated the dominant sources of energy loss in these systems, including material defects, phonon-phonon interactions, and environmental influences such as air damping and temperature fluctuations. Our results reveal that the intrinsic dissipation in graphene resonators is significantly lower than that of carbon nanotube resonators, attributed to the higher mobility and lower density of defects in graphene. Furthermore, we illustrate that the dissipation in these systems can be effectively mitigated through the implementation of surface modification techniques, such as chemical functionalization and nanostructuring, which reduce the impact of environmental influences and improve the mechanical quality factor. These results have important implications for the design and optimization of graphene and nanotube-based devices, including nanoscale sensors, actuators, and energy harvesting systems, where minimization of energy loss is essential for achieving considerable performance and efficiency.

Text: Interstate conflict remains a pervasive and complex phenomenon, posing significant threats to global stability and security. The intricate dynamics of such conflicts necessitate a comprehensive understanding of the underlying factors and mechanisms that drive escalation and de-escalation. This study employs a multi- approach, combining statistical analysis of historical conflict data with agent-based modeling and game-theoretic frameworks. A dataset of 500 interstate conflicts between 1945 and 2020 is analyzed to identify key predictors of conflict onset and duration. An agent-based model is then developed to simulate the interactions between states, incorporating variables such as power asymmetry, economic interdependence, and diplomatic engagement. The indicate that a combination of economic sanctions, diplomatic mediation, and strategic military deterrence can effectively reduce the likelihood of conflict escalation. The agent-based model simulations reveal that the introduction of a third-party mediator can decrease conflict duration by up to 30%, while targeted economic sanctions can reduce the probability of conflict onset by 25%. These provide valuable insights for policymakers and scholars seeking to develop effective strategies for mitigating and resolving interstate conflicts.

Text: The Fibonacci Hamiltonian, a quasi-periodic operator, has been extensively studied in the context of quantum mechanics and condensed matter physics, exhibiting unique properties that distinguish it from periodic and random systems. In this study, we investigate the spectral properties of the Fibonacci Hamiltonian, focusing on the fractal dimension of its spectrum. By employing a combination of analytical and numerical techniques, we demonstrate that the spectrum of the Fibonacci Hamiltonian exhibits a fractal structure, characterized by a non-integer fractal dimension. Our show that the fractal dimension of the spectrum is related to the golden mean, a fundamental constant in the Fibonacci sequence, and that it exhibits a universal behavior, independent of the specific parameters of the Hamiltonian. Furthermore, we find that the fractal dimension is connected to the transport properties of the system, with implications for the understanding of quantum localization and delocalization in quasi-periodic systems. Our work provides new insights into the intricate relationships between the spectral properties of the Fibonacci Hamiltonian and the underlying mathematical structure of the Fibonacci sequence, shedding light on the complex behavior of quasi-periodic systems.

Text: In the study of celestial mechanics, the classification of orbits has been a long-standing problem. Current frameworks, such as the Hill's lunar theory and the Lie series expansion, have limitations in describing the complex dynamics of multi-body systems. This study introduces a novel approach, the incidence class, to categorize orbits based on their topological properties. Using a combination of computational and analytical , we investigated the incidence class of a large set of orbits in a three-body problem. Our approach employed a graph-theoretic framework to identify the incidence relations between orbits, which were then used to construct a hierarchy of orbits. This hierarchy was validated through numerical simulations and compared with existing classifications. We demonstrate that the incidence class provides a more comprehensive and robust framework for classifying orbits than existing . The hierarchy of orbits revealed a previously unknown structure, where orbits are organized in a nested, tree-like configuration. Our have implications for the understanding of complex systems in astronomy and physics, and highlight the potential of the incidence class in describing hierarchical structures in various fields. This study opens avenues for further research into the topological properties of orbits and their applications in celestial mechanics and beyond.

Text: This work investigates the phenomenon of Gaussian departure in turbulent flows, where the statistical distribution of velocity fluctuations deviates from a Gaussian distribution. By leveraging a combination of analytical and numerical techniques, we establish a sufficient condition for the onset of Gaussian departure, which is characterized by a specific threshold in the mean-square vorticity. Specifically, we demonstrate that for a turbulent flow with a given energy spectrum and a specified mean-square vorticity, the probability distribution of velocity fluctuations will depart from a Gaussian distribution when the ratio of the mean-square vorticity to the mean-square velocity exceeds a critical value. This central value is shown to be a function of the energy spectrum and the Reynolds number, and is found to be steady with previous numerical simulations and experimental observations. Our results offer a quantitative framework for grasp of the mechanisms underlying Gaussian departure in turbulent flows, and have implications for the modeling and prediction of turbulent phenomena in a wide range of physical systems.

Text: This investigation undertakes a comprehensive elucidation of the spatial dispersion of Riemann zeros, thereby introducing a paradigmatic shift in their characterization through the implementation of extended fractal approximations. Leveraging the foundational research of Newman and Odlyzko, who initially substantiated the fractal nature of the distribution of prime numbers, this study extends the scope of their to the non-trivial zeros of the Riemann zeta function. By utilizing an adapted version of the Newman-Keane algorithm, a substantial dataset of Riemann zeros was generated, to which a diverse array of fractal analysis techniques, including the box-counting method and the correlation dimension, were applied in order to divulge the underlying topological structure of their distribution. The indicate that the Riemann zeros exhibit a multifaceted, self-similar pattern, which can be accurately encapsulated within the framework of an extended fractal model. Specifically, it was found that the distribution of Riemann zeros can be adequately described by a fractal dimension of approximately 1.52, thereby furnishing novel insights into the nature of the Riemann hypothesis, with profound implications for our comprehension of the distribution of prime numbers and the behavior of the Riemann zeta function, and suggesting potential avenues for further investigation into the properties of fractal systems.

Text: Work-life balance is one of the most talked-about yet least-achieved ideals of modern professional life. The increasing pace of technology, the culture of constant connectivity, and the blurring of physical boundaries between office and home have made it harder than ever to truly disconnect. Yet the evidence is clear: sustained overwork leads to diminishing returns. Productivity drops, creativity suffers, health deteriorates, and relationships erode. Genuine balance is not about spending equal hours on work and personal life - it is about ensuring that neither dimension of your existence is permanently sacrificed for the other. It requires intentional boundaries: designated times for deep work, designated times for rest and relationship, and the discipline to honor both. It also requires organizational cultures that value output over presence, and that normalize recovery as part of performance. On an individual level, learning to say no, to delegate, and to rest without guilt are essential skills for sustainable professional and personal wellbeing.

Text: This study investigates the application of Central and Local Limit Theorems to the analysis of RNA structures, providing novel insights into the thermodynamic and kinetic properties of these complex biological molecules. Our demonstrate that the Central Limit Theorem can be effectively employed to describe the distribution of free energy changes associated with RNA folding and melting, while the Local Limit Theorem offers a more refined characterization of the structural ensembles at the transition state. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the Local Limit Theorem can be used to predict the kinetic rates of RNA folding and unfolding, providing a quantitative understanding of the underlying dynamical processes. Text: The integration of Code Division Multiple Access (CDMA) technology in Intelligent Transportation Systems (ITS) has shown significant potential in enhancing the efficiency, safety, and reliability of transportation infrastructure. By leveraging the capabilities of CDMA, ITS can support a wide range of applications, including vehicle-to-vehicle and vehicle-to-infrastructure communications, traffic management, and incident response. CDMA technology enables the simultaneous transmission of multiple signals over a single communication channel, thereby increasing the overall bandwidth and reducing interference. This is particularly beneficial in ITS, where a large number of vehicles and infrastructure components need to communicate with each other in real-time. Furthermore, CDMA's inherent security features, such as encryption and authentication, can help protect against cyber threats and ensure the integrity of critical transportation data. The application of CDMA technology in ITS has been demonstrated through various pilot projects and simulations, which have shown promising in terms of improved traffic flow, reduced congestion, and enhanced safety. Overall, the use of CDMA technology in ITS has the potential to revolutionize the way transportation systems operate, making them more efficient, safe, and sustainable. Text: This study presents a comprehensive analysis of the optical variability of infrared power law-selected galaxies and X-ray sources in the GOODS-South field, a deep, multi-wavelength survey of the universe. Applying photometric observations from the Hubble Space Telescope and Spitzer Space Telescope, we identified a sample of 120 infrared power law-selected galaxies, which are known to harbor buried active galactic nuclei (AGN). By combining these data with X-ray observations from Chandra and NuSTAR, we detected a statistically significant correlation between infrared luminosity and optical variability, indicating that more luminous AGN exhibit greater variability in their optical emission. Furthermore, we found that X-ray-selected active galactic nuclei in the sample exhibit a higher fraction of variability compared to infrared power law-selected galaxies, suggesting that the X-ray emission is a more sensitive probe of AGN variability. Our outcomes offer new perspective into the physics of AGN and their host galaxies, and highlight the importance of monitoring the optical variability of AGN to disentangle the contributions of stellar and AGN activity in the infrared emission of galaxies. These results have implications for understanding the growth and evolution of galaxies.

Text: Flocking behavior, characterized by the coordinated movement of individuals in a group, is a ubiquitous phenomenon observed in various animal species. However, in real-world scenarios, animals often face noisy environments that can disrupt their ability to communicate and maintain group cohesion. This noisy environment can arise from various sources, including sound pollution, visual distractions, or even the presence of predators. To investigate the impact of noise on flocking behavior, we conducted a series of experiments using a custom-built simulation platform and a large-scale robotic flocking system. We simulated various noisy environments with different levels of intensity and frequency characteristics, and analyzed the resulting flocking behavior in terms of cohesion, alignment, and separation. We also compared the performance of our robotic flocking system with and without noise exposure. Interestingly, we observed that noisy environments can significantly disrupt flocking behavior, leading to decreased cohesion and increased variability in movement patterns. However, we also found that certain types of noise can actually enhance group coordination, particularly when the noise frequency matches the natural communication frequency of the flocking individuals.

Text: Investigating the spontaneous emergence of atom-radiation entanglement in two-level atomic ensembles reveals a intricate interplay between the atomic system and the electromagnetic field. Our findings indicate that interactions between the atoms and the radiation field autonomously generate entanglement, a fundamental quantum mechanical phenomenon, in the absence of external coherent driving or precise control over the system. Spontaneous entanglement arises from inherent fluctuations within the radiation field and the atomic ensemble, characterized by non-zero quantum discord. A theoretical framework based on a master equation approach was devised to describe this process, accounting for both the collective behavior of the atomic ensemble and the radiation field. The results demonstrate that entanglement in the system is highly sensitive to various parameters, including atomic density, radiation field intensity, and detuning between atomic and radiation frequencies, with the potential for control and manipulation through adjustments to these parameters, rendering it a promising platform for quantum information processing and quantum optics applications.

Text: This paper presents a novel ZF-equivalent expression to the Axiom of Choice (AC), formulated in the language of set theory with five quantifiers. The proposed expression, denoted as (AC5), employs the membership relation (∈) and equality (=) as its sole primitive relations. We demonstrate that (AC5) is equivalent to the standard Axiom of Choice in Zermelo-Fraenkel set theory (ZF) by establishing a series of bi-implications between the two. Specifically, we prove that (AC5) implies the well-ordering principle, which in turn implies the standard Axiom of Choice. Conversely, we show that the Axiom of Choice implies the satisfaction of (AC5). This equivalence is achieved through a sequence of well-founded recursion steps, leveraging the properties of (AC5) to derive a set-theoretic representation of the axiom's key properties. Our provide a new perspective on the Axiom of Choice and its relationship to ZF set theory, offering insights into the robustness and expressiveness of five-quantifier expressions in set theory.

Text: The D_{s0}^+(2317) meson has been a subject of interest in hadron physics due to its unusual properties, and its internal structure remains a topic of debate. In this study, we explore the possibility of the D_{s0}^+(2317) being an iso-triplet four-quark meson, consisting of a combination of two quarks and two antiquarks. This interpretation is motivated by the meson's mass and decay modes, which can be naturally explained by a tetraquark configuration. We investigate the implications of this scenario, including the predicted existence of neutral and doubly charged partners, D_{s0}^0 and D_{s0}^{++}, which would complete the iso-triplet. Using a constituent model approach, we estimate the masses and production rates of these hypothetical mesons, and discuss potential experimental signatures for their detection. Our suggest that the D_{s0}^+(2317) and its predicted partners could be produced in high-energy collisions, such as those at LHC or future electron-positron colliders, providing a unique opportunity to test the tetraquark hypothesis and shed light on the nature of exotic hadrons. This research contributes to the ongoing effort to understand the structure and properties of mesons beyond the traditional quark-antiquark picture.

Text: This study focuses on automorphisms of a polynomial ring R = k[x_1, x_n] over an algebraically closed field k, which admit reductions of type I. Specifically, we investigate the class of automorphisms σ of R that can be reduced to the identity automorphism when composed with a suitable automorphism τ of the polynomial ring R', where R' is obtained from R by setting the leading coefficients of some variables equal to zero. In particular, we prove that σ admits a reduction of type I if and only if σ(x_i) is of the form x_i + f_i(x_{i+1}, ..., x_n) for some polynomial f_i in k[x_{i+1}, ..., x_n] with a certain degree condition. We further demonstrate that this condition is equivalent to the condition that the automorphism σ is a birational map with a specific type of singular locus. Our provide a new characterization of automorphisms of the polynomial ring that admit reductions of type I and shed light on the relationship between birational maps and automorphisms of polynomial rings.

Text: This investigation undertakes a comprehensive, multi-wavelength examination of a quiescent solar region, thereby furnishing novel, profound insights into the intricate dynamics governing the solar atmosphere. Leveraging a concerted amalgamation of ground-based and space-based observatories, specifically the Solar Dynamics Observatory (SDO) and the Atmospheric Imaging Assembly (AIA), we have procured high-resolution observational data encompassing multiple wavelengths, including ultraviolet (UV), extreme ultraviolet (EUV), and X-rays, pertaining to a stable quiescent solar region. Our in-depth analysis reveals a complex synergy between magnetic field lines, thermal energy, and plasma flows, which are pivotal for grasping the underlying mechanisms governing the quiescent solar region. Through the meticulous examination of time-series data, we have identified periodic oscillations in the magnetic field lines and plasma flows, indicative of magnetohydrodynamic (MHD) waves, which are a crucial manifestation of the dynamic interplay between magnetic and thermal processes. Moreover, our suggest that these oscillations are attenuated by the interaction with magnetic reconnection events, culminating in the dissipation of thermal energy and the establishment of a stable equilibrium state. These discoveries possess significant implications for our comprehension of the quiescent solar region and its pivotal role in the solar cycle, thereby underscoring the importance of multi-wavelength observations in unraveling the complex dynamics of the solar atmosphere.

Text: We present a systematic examination of the changes in semi-major axis caused by the mutual interactions of a group of massive bodies orbiting a central star in the presence of eccentricity dissipation. For parameters relevant to the oligarchic stage of planet formation, dynamical friction keeps the typical eccentricities small and prevents orbit crossing. Interactions at impact parameters greater than several Hill radii cause the protoplanets to repel each other; if the impact parameter is instead much less than the Hill radius, the protoplanets shift slightly in semi-major axis but remain otherwise unperturbed. If the orbits of two or more protoplanets are separated by less than a Hill radius, they are each pushed towards an equilibrium spacing between their neighbors and can exist as a stable co-orbital system. In the shear-dominated oligarchic phase of planet formation we show that the feeding zones contain several oligarchs instead of only one. Growth of the protoplanets in the oligarchic phase drives the disk to an equilibrium configuration that depends on the mass ratio of protoplanets to planetesimals, $\Sigma/\sigma$. Early in the oligarchic phase, when $\Sigma/\sigma$ is low, the spacing between rows of co-orbital oligarchs are about 5 Hill radii wide, rather than the 10 Hill radii cited in the literature. It is likely that at the end of oligarchy the average number of co-orbital oligarchs is greater than unity. In the outer solar system this raises the disk mass required to form the ice giants. In the inner solar system this lowers the mass of the final oligarchs and requires more giant impacts than previously estimated. This result provides additional evidence that Mars is not an untouched leftover from the oligarchic phase, but must be composed of several oligarchs assembled through giant impacts.

Text: The Josephson effect, a fundamental phenomenon in superconductivity, describes the tunnelling of Cooper pairs between two superconductors separated by a thin insulating barrier. Recent research has led to the investigation of granular carbon films, which exhibit intriguing properties reminiscent of superconductivity. Our study aims to explore the possibility of Josephson-like behaviour in these materials. We fabricated granular carbon films using a combination of pulsed laser deposition and thermal annealing techniques. The films were characterized using scanning tunnelling microscopy (STM), X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS), and electrical transport measurements. We examined the influence of film thickness, annealing temperature, and substrate material on the observed Josephson-like behaviour. Our demonstrate the emergence of Josephson-like behaviour in granular carbon films, characterized by the appearance of zero-bias conductance peaks and Josephson currents in the presence of a superconducting counter-electrode. Notably, the Josephson current was found to depend on the film thickness and annealing temperature, suggesting a correlation between the granular carbon structure and the observed superconducting-like phenomena. These open up new avenues for research into the properties of granular carbon materials and their potential applications in quantum electronics.

Text: This study presents an in-depth analysis of the fundamental parameters of He-weak and He-strong stars, focusing on their helium abundance, surface gravity, and effective temperature. He-weak and He-strong stars are a subset of chemically peculiar stars characterized by anomalies in their helium abundance, with the former exhibiting reduced helium surface abundance and the latter displaying enhanced helium surface abundance. These provide new insights into the evolution and structure of He-weak and He-strong stars, shedding light on the underlying physical mechanisms responsible for their helium abundance anomalies.

Text: .** Lie antialgebras, introduced in the late 1990s, form a hybrid class of graded algebras that interpolate between Lie algebras and Jordan superalgebras. Their defining identities combine antisymmetry with a "half-derivation" property, yielding a rich representation theory and unexpected links to symplectic geometry and conformal field theory. Despite their early promise, a systematic study of their basic algebraic structure and classification remains incomplete. .** We develop a uniform framework for finite-dimensional Lie antialgebras over an algebraically closed field of characteristic zero. By exploiting the graded commutator and the anticommutative product, we construct the universal enveloping algebra and establish a PBW-type theorem. Cohomological techniques are employed to classify central extensions and deformations, while a detailed analysis of the associated derivation algebras yields a complete list of simple components. Computational tools (SageMath) are used to verify the Jacobi-like identities for low-dimensional examples and to explore the representation theory of the newly identified simple algebras. .** We prove that every finite-dimensional Lie antialgebra decomposes into a direct sum of a simple algebra of type (K_3) and a nilpotent ideal. Three new simple Lie antialgebras of dimensions four and six are discovered, together with their full automorphism groups. Cohomology computations reveal a one-parameter family of non-trivial deformations of (K_3), suggesting a moduli space structure. Crucially, finally, we establish a correspondence between these deformations and symplectic actions on supermanifolds, thereby extending the known geometric realizations of Lie antialgebras.

Text: In this paper we advance the simple analytic photometric redshift estimator for Type Ia supernovae (SNe Ia) proposed by Wang (2007), and use it to study simulated SN Ia data. We find that better than 0.5% accuracy in z_phot (with RMS[(z_phot-z_spec)/(1+z_spec)]<0.005) is possible for SNe Ia with well sampled lightcurves in three observed passbands (riz) with a signal-to-noise ratio of 25 at peak brightness, if the extinction by dust is negligible. The corresponding bias in z_phot (the mean of (z_phot-z_spec)) is 5.4\times 10^{-4}. If dust extinction is taken into consideration in the riz observer-frame lightcurves, the accuracy in z_phot deteriorates to 4.4%, with a bias in z_phot of 8.0\times 10^{-3}. Adding the g band lightcurve improves the accuracy in z_phot to 2.5%, and reduces the bias in z_phot to -1.5\times 10^{-3}. Our have significant implications for the design of future photometric surveys of SNe Ia from both ground and space telescopes. Accurate and precise photometric redshifts boost the cosmological utility of such surveys.

Text: We present a comprehensive investigation into the role of natural dark matter in supersymmetric grand unified theories (SUSY GUTs) with non-universal gaugino masses. By incorporating a non-universal gaugino mass spectrum, we demonstrate that the viable dark matter candidates in these models can be significantly enhanced, thereby alleviating the stringent constraints imposed by direct and indirect detection experiments. Moreover, our analysis reveals that the lightest neutralino, a common dark matter candidate in SUSY GUTs, can be naturally stabilized against radiative corrections, leading to a more stable and predictive framework — we identify a novel region of parameter space that satisfies the conditions for natural dark matter, characterized by a large mass gap between the lightest neutralino and the next-to-lightest neutralino, and a gaugino mass hierarchy that is consistent with the observed electroweak symmetry breaking scale. Our results demonstrate that SUSY GUTs with non-universal gaugino masses offer a promising avenue for resolving the dark matter puzzle, and we discuss the implications of our findings for future experimental searches and theoretical investigations.
