Text: Admission control as a mechanism for providing QoS requires an accurate description of the requested flow as well as already admitted flows. Since 802.11 WLAN capacity is shared between flows belonging to all stations, admission control requires knowledge of all flows in the WLAN. Further, estimation of the load-dependent WLAN capacity through analytical model requires inputs about channel data rate, payload size and the number of stations. These factors combined point to a centralized admission control whereas for 802.11 DCF it is ideally performed in a distributed manner. The use of measurements from the channel avoids explicit inputs about the state of the channel described above. BUFFET, a model based measurement-assisted distributed admission control scheme for DCF proposed in this paper relies on measurements to derive model inputs and predict WLAN saturation, thereby maintaining average delay within acceptable limits. Being measurement based, it adapts to a combination of data rates and payload sizes, making it completely autonomous and distributed. Performance analysis using OPNET simulations suggests that BUFFET is able to ensure average delay under 7ms at a near-optimal throughput.

Text: We investigate the age constraints that can be placed on the double pulsar system using models for the spin-down of the first-born 22.7-ms pulsar A and the 2.77-s pulsar B with characteristic ages of 210 and 50 Myr respectively. Formation 80 Myr ago, closer to B's characteristic age, would result in the contribution from J0737-3039 to the inferred coalescence rates for double neutron star binaries increasing by 40%. The 180 Myr age is closer to A's characteristic age and would be consistent with the most recent estimates of the coalescence rate. Text: In a seminal contribution to the burgeoning field of quantum information science, this investigation elucidates the intricacies of controlled teleportation of arbitrary multi-qubit states in a generalised form, leveraging d-dimensional Greenberger-Horne-Zeilinger (GHZ) states as the paradigmatic basis for facilitating such a process. Text: Hundreds of substellar companions to solar-type stars will be discovered with the Kepler satellite. We discuss in detail the periodic flux modulations arising from the tidal force on the star due to a substellar companion. An analytic expression for the variability is derived in the equilibrium-tide approximation. We demonstrate analytically and through numerical solutions of the linear, nonadiabatic stellar oscillation equations that the equilibrium-tide formula works extremely well for stars of mass <1.4 Msun with thick surface convection zones. More massive stars with largely radiative envelopes do not conform to the equilibrium-tide approximation and can exhibit flux variations $\ga$10 times larger than naive estimates. Over the full range of stellar masses considered, we treat the oscillatory response of the convection zone by adapting a prescription that A. J. Brickhill developed for pulsating white dwarfs. Compared to other sources of periodic variability, the ellipsoidal lightcurve has a distinct dependence on time and system parameters. We suggest that ellipsoidal oscillations induced by giant planets may be detectable from as many as ~100 of the 10^5 Kepler target stars. (Abridged)

Text: We put forward a search for the Standard Model Higgs boson in the WW decay channel via vector boson fusion (VBF) in data collected by the Compact Muon Solenoid (CMS) experiment at the Sizable Hadron Collider (LHC). Text: The operation of MOSFET‑type nanostructures under intense high‑frequency (HF) electric fields is increasingly relevant for terahertz‐enabled electronics. In such regimes, the tunneling coupling between the channel and source/drain reservoirs is dynamically renormalized, yet the conventional symmetric treatment of photon‑assisted tunneling fails to capture the observed bias‑dependent asymmetries. Understanding the unbalanced renormalization of tunneling amplitudes is essential for predicting device performance and for engineering field‑controlled transport. We employ a non‑perturbative Floquet‑Keldysh formalism to derive effective tunneling Hamiltonians for a prototypical MOSFET geometry subjected to a linearly polarized HF field (frequency 0.5–5 THz, amplitude up to 10 MV m⁻¹). The approach incorporates side‑band generation, field‑induced dressing of the electronic states, and a self‑consistent treatment of the gate‑oxide capacitance. Numerical simulations of the resulting master equations yield time‑averaged current–voltage characteristics, while analytical scaling laws are extracted for the renormalized tunneling rates as functions of field strength and frequency. The analysis reveals a pronounced unbalance: tunneling from source to channel is enhanced by a factor ∝ J₀²(α) + J₁²(α), whereas the reverse process is suppressed by J₀²(α) − J₁²(α), with α the dimensionless field amplitude. This asymmetry leads to a rectification of the HF‑induced current and a shift of the subthreshold swing by up to 30 mV/decade. The derived scaling predicts a crossover from photon‑assisted to field‑dominated regimes, offering design guidelines for THz‑modulated MOSFETs.

For bias energies significantly larger than Omega_0 the quasiparticles have short lifetimes due to this coupling, and the FT-LDOS is featureless if the electron-impurity scattering is treated within the Born approximation. In this regime it is important to include boson exchange for the electron-impurity scattering which provides a `step down' in energy for the electrons and allows for long lifetimes. This many-body effect produces qualitatively different , namely the presence of peaks in the FT-LDOS which are mirrors of the quasiparticle interference peaks which occur at bias energies smaller than ~ Omega_0. The experimental observation of these quasiparticle mirages would be an important step forward in elucidating the role of many-body effects in FT-LDOS measurements.

Text: A pond is a body of standing water, either natural or human-made, that is usually smaller than a lake. Text: We present a novel comprehensive first-principles theoretical study of the electronic properties and relative stabilities of edge-oxidized zigzag graphene nanoribbons. The stable oxidized configurations maintain a spin-polarized ground state with antiferromagnetic ordering localized at the edges, similar to the fully hydrogenated counterparts. More important, edge oxidation is found to lower the onset electric field required to induce half-metallic behavior and extend the overall field range at which the systems remain half-metallic. Once the half-metallic state is reached, further increase of the external electric field intensity produces a rapid decrease in the spin magnetization up to a point where the magnetization is quenched completely. Text: We present a novel approach to probing the fundamental nature of space-time by examining the implications of noncommutativity on the renormalizable gauge sector of the theta-expanded Noncommutative Scalar Model (NCSM). This modification arises from the noncommutative geometry-induced mixing between the Z boson and the gamma-gamma pair, which is a direct consequence of the noncommutative space-time structure. Our demonstrate that the Z -> gamma gamma decay process can serve as a sensitive probe of noncommutative effects, and that the observation of such effects would provide strong evidence for space-time noncommutativity. Text: This study explores the age problem in the holographic dark energy model, a theoretical framework that attempts to explain the accelerating expansion of the universe. Our results indicate that the age problem persists even when incorporating a non-zero equation of state parameter, which is often used to alleviate the issue. We also examine the consequences of modifying the holographic dark energy model to include a non-trivial scale factor dependence, which leads to a more accurate match with observational data. Our outcomes suggest that the age problem remains a significant challenge for the holographic dark energy model, and further modifications or refinements are necessary to reconcile the model's predictions with observational evidence.

Text: We present a precise measurement of the e+e- -> K+K- cross section via data collected with the SND detector at the VEPP-2M e+e- collider, operating in the center-of-mass energy range of 1.04 to 1.38 GeV. The analysis is based on a total integrated luminosity of 2.9 pb^-1, yielding approximately 2.6 million K+K- events, which were reconstructed from the charged kaon and pion decay modes. The cross section is determined using an unbinned maximum likelihood fit to the energy dependence of the K+K- production, incorporating a detailed simulation of the detector response and background processes. The measured cross section values are found to vary between 0.7 and 3.1 nb, with an average uncertainty of around 4%. The distribution of eigenvalues and eigenvectors outside of the RMT bounds displays prominent and systematic deviations from the RMT predictions. Moreover, these deviations are stable in time. Text: In the realm of infinitary combinatorics, specifically within descriptive set theory, a novel class of infinite combinatorial structures emerges in the form of Long Borel Hierarchies (LBH), whose intricate nature warrants a thorough investigation. This research endeavors to contribute to a deeper comprehension of the complex relationships between infinite combinatorial structures and definability, ultimately shedding light on the inherent properties of LBHs and their far-reaching implications. LBHs are characterized by an inductive progression of Borel sets, denoted as ${\cal A}_0 \subset {\cal A}_1 \subset \ldots$, each of which is a subset of the space of infinite binary sequences, $\omega^{\omega}$. A rigorous framework is established to analyze LBHs, focusing on their intrinsic properties, such as a novel conception of Borel rank. This metric gauges the complexity of LBHs by quantifying the number of iterations necessary to attain a given member of the hierarchy. Furthermore, the intricate relationships between LBHs and other well-established classes of sets within descriptive set theory, including $G_\delta$ sets and $F_\sigma$ sets, are meticulously examined. The present study also delves into the definability of LBHs, utilizing an array of formulaic paradigms, including second-order and higher-order logic. The pivotal of this research include a characterization of LBHs in terms of their Borel rank and hierarchical complexity, underscoring the intricate connections between these properties. Moreover, it is demonstrated that every LBH can be effectively described by a sequence of Borel sets with uniformly bounded complexity, thereby providing a tangible representation of their intrinsic structure. Conversely, an illustrative example of a LBH exhibits a pronounced degree of non-determinacy, underscoring the limitations of higher-order logic in accurately describing these structures. The outcomes of this research collectively provide novel insights into the configuration of infinite combinatorial structures and have far-reaching implications for our comprehension of the symbiotic relationship between infinitary combinatorics and definability. The developed framework and methodologies can be applied to an expansive array of problems within descriptive set theory and infinite combinatorics, ultimately enriching our understanding of these interconnected fields. Text: Fermi gases, composed of fermionic atoms, exhibit unique quantum properties due to the Pauli exclusion principle. Cooling these systems to near-degeneracy temperatures is a fundamental challenge in the study of strongly correlated many-body systems. Conventional evaporative cooling techniques often fail due to the Fermi gas's tendency to undergo phase separation. In this work, we employ a novel pairing-based cooling approach to systematically cool ultracold Fermi gases of 40K atoms. By utilizing Feshbach resonances to create a population of quasi-bound pairs, we demonstrate a highly efficient cooling mechanism. The pair population is dynamically balanced with the unpaired atoms through a series of controlled phase transitions. Our experimental setup includes a magneto-optical trap and a magnetic field-controlled Feshbach resonance. We achieve a record-low temperature of 20 nK in a Fermi gas, exceeding the degeneracy temperature by a factor of 10. The pairing-based cooling enables the creation of a highly degenerate Fermi gas with a Fermi energy exceeding 10 μK. Our open new avenues for the study of strongly correlated Fermi systems, including the investigation of superfluid behavior and the exploration of non-equilibrium dynamics in quantum many-body systems.

Text: Bluffing is a fundamental strategic behavior that allows agents to influence opponents' beliefs and actions. In human decision-making, bluffing underlies many economic and social interactions, yet the mechanisms by which artificial systems acquire and deploy deceptive strategies remain poorly understood. Human participants played repeated rounds of a no-limit Texas Hold'em variant while an AI agent learned to bluff through self-play and adversarial training. The AI achieved a 27 % higher win rate against human opponents compared to a non-deceptive baseline. Human subjects exhibited significant adjustments in calling frequencies after observing AI bluffing, evidencing belief manipulation. Moreover, the learned bluffing policy converged to a mixture of high-variance bet sizing and contextual signal exploitation, mirroring patterns documented in human expert play. Crucially, our demonstrate that reinforcement learning can endow artificial agents with nuanced bluffing capabilities, offering insights into the cognitive and computational underpinnings of strategic deception.

Text: After Hurricane Sandy, some libraries in New Jersey became places of refuge. And in the Queens Library's Far Rockaway branch, which didn't have heat or light, the librarians set up shop in the parking lot to continue children's story hours." In calmer times, public library systems offer a staggering array of programming that goes well beyond the books-and-story-time model many of us remember from our childhoods. Ziesenhenne rattles off a list of some of Palo Alto's offerings: a seed-lending library, home-brewing tutorials, a "Knack 4 Knitting" club, bilingual story hours, programs designed to help immigrants learn how to live in the United States. Keeping up with a national trend, the library recently created a makerspace with 3-D printers. In July, one branch hosted a workshop on how to use "graywater" from inside a house to sustain native-plant landscaping in the yard. The list goes on and on. There's something for almost everyone at the local library, whether you're a parent who needs literacy support for your preschooler, an immigrant working on language skills or bureaucratic forms, a mystery fan in search of the latest whodunit by a favorite author, or someone experiencing homelessness who needs assistance with social services or access to a computer and the Internet.

Text: Backward stochastic differential equations (BSDEs) constitute a versatile tool for representing nonlinear expectations, stochastic control, and probabilistic solutions of partial differential equations. While the theory is well-developed for deterministic horizons and integrable terminal data, many applications-e.g., optimal stopping, default risk, and stochastic target problems-lead naturally to a random stopping time as the horizon and to terminal conditions that may be merely measurable or even singular (unbounded or taking the value +∞ on a set of positive probability). A rigorous treatment of such BSDEs is still lacking. We consider BSDEs driven by a Brownian motion on a filtered probability space equipped with a finite stopping time (tau). The generator (f(t,omega,y,z)) satisfies a standard monotonicity-Lipschitz structure, while the terminal condition (xi) is allowed to belong only to the extended space (L{0}(mathcal{F}_{tau})) and may be singular. By introducing a sequence of truncated terminal data (xi{n}=xiwedge n) and employing a penalisation scheme together with a priori estimates derived from BMO-martingale techniques, we establish uniform integrability of the associated solution processes. The limit of the approximating solutions is shown to solve the original BSDE in a minimal-solution sense. Uniqueness is proved under an additional convexity condition on the generator. We prove existence of a minimal adapted solution ((Y,Z)) on ([0,tau]) for BSDEs with random horizon and singular terminal condition, together with a comparison principle and stability under perturbations of the data. As a corollary, we obtain probabilistic representations for viscosity solutions of semilinear parabolic PDEs with Dirichlet data prescribed on a random boundary and possibly infinite boundary values. Crucially, the extend the BSDE framework to a broad class of problems in finance and stochastic control where default times and unbounded payoffs naturally arise.

These two assertions collectively encapsulate the essential geometric properties of the curvature tensor $\mathcal{R}$ and, by extension, the strongly local form $\mathcal{F}$. The proof of Sch'nol's Theorem has far-reaching implications for the theoretical study of strongly local forms and their applications in various disciplines. The underpinning the proof of Sch'nol's Theorem hinges on a judicious integration of geometric and analytical techniques, including the employment of the curvature tensor and its associated invariants, as well as advanced tools from differential geometry, such as the theory of connections and curvature forms. In , Sch'nol's Theorem for Strongly Local Forms represents a significant advancement in the theoretical understanding of this class of geometric objects, with far-reaching consequences for the study of their structure and behavior. A regularized least-squares optimization yields the potential parameters, with cross-validation against a hold-out set to prevent overfitting. Text: This study presents an in-depth analysis of the acoustic spectrum of the metal-poor subgiant nu Indi, focusing on the characterization of its solar-like oscillations. Utilizing high-cadence spectroscopic observations gathered from the HARPS and HARPS-N instruments at the ESO La Silla and La Palma observatories, we have extracted a rich set of oscillation modes spanning a wide frequency range of approximately 1.4-4.2 mHz. The acoustic spectrum reveals a complex pattern of modes, including a prominent dipole mode (l=1) and a multitude of higher-order modes (l=2-5) with varying degree of multiplet structure. Our analysis suggests that the observed mode lifetimes are significantly shorter than those predicted by standard models, indicating the presence of turbulent mixing in the star's interior. The derived mode lifetimes exhibit a clear dependence on the mode frequency and degree, suggesting that the turbulent mixing is more pronounced in the higher-frequency and higher-degree modes. These have important implications for our understanding of the internal dynamics of metal-poor subgiants and the role of turbulent mixing in shaping their internal structure.

Text: In this work we undertake a comprehensive classification, up to equivalence, of all \(G\)-gradings on the simple Lie algebras of type \(A_{n}\) defined over an algebraically closed field of characteristic \(p>3\); by exploiting the well‑known bijective correspondence between such gradings and rational cocharacters of the linear algebraic group \(\mathrm{SL}_{n+1}\), the problem is effectively reduced to an investigation of toral subalgebras and the attendant weight space decompositions, wherein we demonstrate that every admissible grading is in fact induced by a diagonalizable torus, and moreover that one may always select the grading group to be a finite abelian group whose rank does not exceed \(n\). More concretely, we furnish an explicit parametrization of the resulting isomorphism classes via pairs \((\Lambda,\varphi)\), where \(\Lambda\) is a sublattice of \((\mathbb{Z}/p\mathbb{Z})^{\,n+1}\) that is orthogonal to the root lattice of type \(A_{n}\) and \(\varphi\) is a group homomorphism into the chosen grading group; this description not only reproduces the established classification in characteristic zero but also extends it to the modular setting, thereby uncovering novel phenomena such as the emergence of nontrivial \(p\)-torsion within the grading group. Finally, we discuss the implications of this classification for the structural theory of graded simple Lie algebras and for the construction of graded simple modules, highlighting both theoretical insights and potential avenues for further research.

Text: In this treatise, we introduce a novel paradigm for constructing a family of solutions to the quantum Yang-Baxter equation, denominated rime R-matrices, which interpolate between the paradigmatic rational, trigonometric, and elliptic families while preserving a hitherto unexplored "rime" symmetry. By imposing a graded permutation constraint and a generalized spectral-parameter dependence, we elucidate an explicit parametrization in terms of a singular deformation parameter and an auxiliary spectral variable, thereby providing a unified framework for the derivation of these rime R-matrices. Subsequently, we demonstrate that these R-matrices conform to the braid relation, unitarity, and crossing symmetry, and that they reduce to the well-known Hecke-type solutions in specific limits, thereby underscoring the pertinence of our approach. Furthermore, we establish that the associated quantum algebras exhibit a non-standard coproduct structure, yielding novel integrable spin chains with long-range interactions, and employing explicit transfer-matrix constructions, we reveal that the rime models possess a comprehensive set of commuting charges. Utilizing algebraic Bethe ansatz techniques, we compute the spectrum of these charges in the thermodynamic limit, thereby providing a comprehensive understanding of the underlying dynamics. Lastly, we discuss the potential applications of the rime deformation to quantum affine algebras and the AdS/CFT spectral problem, highlighting how this deformation offers a flexible framework for generating novel integrable structures and underscoring the significance of this work in opening a new direction for the systematic exploration of Yang-Baxter solutions beyond conventional classification schemes.

Our strategy relies on the identification of the Regge poles in the anomalous dimension of the reliable action and the subsequent application of a generalized form of the Regge expansion. Through a in-depth assessment of the Regge trajectories, we identify the key points that lead to the Reggeization of the theories, and show the emergence of the predicted Regge poles in the scattering amplitudes. Our outcomes offer a quantitative description of the Regge behavior in these supersymmetric theories, and shed light on the underlying dynamics that govern their high-energy behavior. Text: We present photometry with the Advanced Camera for Surveys (ACS) on the Hubble Space Telescope (HST) of stars in the Magellanic starburst galaxy NGC 4449. The galaxy has been imaged in the F435W (B), F555W (V) and F814W (I) broad-band filters, and in the F658N (Halpha) narrow-band filter. Our photometry includes 300,000 objects in the (B, V) color-magnitude diagram (CMD) down to V < 28, and 400,000 objects in the (V, I) CMD, down to I < 27 . A subsample of 200,000 stars has been photometrized in all the three bands simultaneously. The features observed in the CMDs imply a variety of stellar ages up to at least 1 Gyr, and possibly as old as a Hubble time. The spatial variation of the CMD morphology and of the red giant branch colors point toward the presence of an age gradient: young and intermediate-age stars tend to be concentrated toward the galactic center, while old stars are present everywhere. The spatial variation in the average luminosity of carbon stars suggests that there is not a strong metallicity gradient (< 0.2 dex). Also, we detect an interesting resolved star cluster on the West side of the galaxy, surrounded by a symmetric tidal or spiral feature consisting of young stars. The positions of the stars in NGC 4449 younger than 10 Myr are strongly correlated with the Halpha emission. We derive the distance of NGC 4449 from the tip of the red giant branch to be D=3.82 pm 0.27 Mpc. This result is in agreement with the distance that we derive from the luminosity of the carbon stars.

Text: Andi Ashworth Learning to Cook, and Why it Matters More than just a reflection of domesticity, cooking plays a role in the flourishing of human life and in the service of others. The first meal Chuck and I made together after we married in May of 1975 was a dinner of orange Jell-O and canned asparagus. We'd decided to be vegetarians, but had no idea how to go about it in a healthy way. At the ages of eighteen and nineteen, we knew very little about good nutrition and even less about whole foods. As a result, on our first food gathering trip to Albertson's, we simply left the meat out of the grocery cart and came home with foods that were familiar to us. I left my mother's home knowing almost nothing about cooking, nor why it would matter to learn. Other than making cookie dough or occasionally starting the meatloaf before my mom got home from work, I was largely ignorant of the culinary arts. My mom did her serious cooking on the weekends, and on special occasions she made perfect apple pies, mouth-watering fried chicken, and many other delights. I could have learned a great deal from her, but growing up I wasn't really interested. As a teenager, even one about to be married, I didn't give much thought to domestic life except as a place to work against sexual stereotypes and bring my budding 1970s feminist agenda to bear. Text: **Mechanical Proof of the Second Law of Thermodynamics Based on Volume Entropy** .** The Second Law of Thermodynamics, traditionally formulated in terms of entropy increase, lacks a rigorous mechanical derivation that directly links microscopic dynamics to macroscopic irreversibility. This quantity offers a natural bridge between Hamiltonian mechanics and thermodynamic entropy. .** We consider a closed Hamiltonian system of (N) particles with interparticle potentials satisfying standard regularity conditions. By constructing a coarse-grained partition of the energy hypersurface into cells of equal Liouville volume, we derive an exact expression for the time evolution of the volume entropy under Liouville's theorem. Employing a perturbative expansion in the small parameter (epsilon = Delta E / E) (where (Delta E) is the energy fluctuation within a cell), we show that the coarse-grained entropy obeys a non-negative entropy production rate. Numerical simulations of a Lennard-Jones gas confirm that the volume entropy monotonically increases toward its equilibrium value, while the fine-grained Liouville entropy remains constant. .** The analysis yields a mechanical proof that the coarse-grained volume entropy of an isolated Hamiltonian system is a non-decreasing function of time, thereby providing a first-principles derivation of the Second Law. This result clarifies the role of phase-space coarse-graining in generating macroscopic irreversibility and establishes volume entropy as a robust mechanical analogue of thermodynamic entropy.

Text: Massive star formation in the nuclear disk of galaxies is a complex and poorly understood process. The nuclear disk, a region of high density and intense star formation, is thought to be the birthplace of many high-mass stars. However, the formation mechanisms of these stars remain unclear due to the lack of observational evidence. We have conducted a survey of maser emission in the nuclear disk of the galaxy NGC 1068 using the Atacama Large Millimeter/submillimeter Array (ALMA). Maser emission is a signpost of shock-induced star formation and provides a unique probe of the physical conditions in the interstellar medium. By analyzing the maser emission spectra and spatial distributions, we aim to investigate the relationship between maser activity and massive star formation. Our observations reveal a high incidence of maser emission in the nuclear disk of NGC 1068, particularly in regions of intense star formation. The maser spectra show a range of velocities and spatial distributions that suggest the presence of multiple shock fronts and turbulent flows. Crucially, these suggest that masers are an effective probe of massive star formation in the nuclear disk, providing valuable insights into the complex processes that govern the formation of high-mass stars.

Text: The classical sewing lemma is a cornerstone of rough‑path theory, providing a deterministic construction of integrals from increment maps that satisfy suitable Hölder‑type control estimates. Its standard formulation assumes a commutative target space, limiting applicability to scalar‑valued or abelian vector‑valued signals. Many contemporary problems—in quantum stochastic analysis, non‑abelian gauge theory, and operator‑valued differential equations—require integration in non‑commutative Banach algebras, where the lack of commutativity obstructs a direct transfer of the classical result. We develop a non‑commutative sewing framework on a complete normed algebra \((\mathcal{A},\|\cdot\|)\). Starting from a two‑parameter map \(\delta: [0,T]^2\to\mathcal{A}\) satisfying a generalized Chen‑type relation \(\delta_{s,t}= \delta_{s,u}+\delta_{u,t}+R_{s,u,t}\) with a remainder \(R\) controlled by a super‑additive function \(\omega\), we introduce a non‑commutative control norm that respects the algebra product. By constructing dyadic partitions and employing a Banach‑fixed‑point argument on the space of increment families, we prove convergence of the discrete sewing procedure to a unique limit \(\mathcal{I}(\delta)\). Explicit estimates are derived: \[ \|\mathcal{I}(\delta)_{s,t}-\delta_{s,t}\|\le C\,\omega(s,t)^{\beta}, \] for any \(\beta>1\) determined by the Hölder regularity of \(\delta\). The non‑commutative sewing lemma holds under the same Hölder exponents as its commutative counterpart, provided the algebra norm is sub‑multiplicative. This yields a robust construction of operator‑valued rough integrals and enables the formulation of differential equations driven by non‑commutative rough signals. Applications to quantum stochastic differential equations demonstrate that solutions obtained via the new lemma coincide with those derived from Hudson‑Parthasarathy calculus, thereby bridging deterministic rough‑path techniques and quantum stochastic analysis.

Text: Neutron stars are known to possess intense magnetic fields, playing a crucial role in their evolution and observational characteristics. We employed a numerical magnetohydrodynamic (MHD) simulation to investigate the emergence of toroidal magnetic fields in Type II superconducting neutron stars. Interestingly, we observed that toroidal magnetic fields can emerge in Type II superconducting neutron stars through the interaction between the star's internal dynamics and the superconducting state. The toroidal field component was found to be significant, reaching up to 10% of the poloidal field strength in some cases. This finding has important implications for our understanding of neutron star magnetism and the associated observational signatures, such as X-ray and gamma-ray emission.

Text: We report on our second-epoch VLBI and VLA observations of the Type Ib/c supernova 2001em, five years after the explosion. It was suggested that SN 2001em might be a jet-driven gamma ray burst (GRB), with the jet oriented near the plane of the sky, which would entail relativistic expansion or motion. Our VLBI image shows that SN 2001em is still unresolved five years after the explosion. For a distance of 83 Mpc (H_0 = 70 km/s/Mpc), the nominal expansion velocity is 5800 +/- 10,000 km/s, and the proper motion is 33,000 +/- 34,000 km/s. Our values are inconsistent with either relativistic expansion or motion, but are consistent with the non-relativistic expansion speeds and small proper motions seen in other supernovae. In particular these values are consistent with radio emission from SN 2001em being due to normal, non-relativistic supernova ejecta interacting with the circumstellar medium. Our VLA observations show a power-law decay in flux density since the time of the peak in the 8.4 GHz radio lightcurve in ~2003.

Text: The Casimir effect, arising from quantum vacuum fluctuations between closely spaced conductors, is traditionally regarded as a static, attractive force. Recent theoretical proposals suggest that temporal modulation of material properties or boundary conditions can induce a dynamic, “pulsating” component to the Casimir interaction, potentially enabling novel actuation mechanisms in micro‑ and nano‑electromechanical systems (MEMS/NEMS). However, experimental verification of such time‑dependent forces remains elusive due to the stringent requirements on modulation speed, amplitude, and detection sensitivity. We employed a high‑Q micro‑resonator fabricated from doped silicon, incorporating a suspended gold plate separated from a planar gold substrate by a sub‑micron vacuum gap. The optical conductivity of the plate was modulated at frequencies up to 10 GHz using ultrafast laser pulses (pump–probe scheme), thereby varying its dielectric response on timescales shorter than the cavity round‑trip time. A phase‑locked heterodyne interferometer measured the resulting oscillatory displacement of the resonator, while finite‑difference time‑domain simulations provided quantitative predictions for the pulsating Casimir pressure under the experimental parameters. The measurements reveal a clear periodic modulation of the Casimir force with an amplitude of 0.45 % of the static value, in agreement with theoretical expectations within experimental uncertainty (±0.07 %). The observed phase relationship confirms that the force follows the imposed dielectric modulation rather than thermal or photothermal effects. These constitute the first direct observation of a dynamically tunable Casimir interaction, opening pathways for controllable quantum‑fluctuation‑driven actuation in nanoscale devices.

This paradigmatic innovation, predicated on the principles of Szemerédi's theory, not only generalizes the original framework but also extends its applicability to a vast array of combinatorial objects, encompassing graphs, hypergraphs, and matroids. The proposed regularity lemma posits the existence of a partition of the vertex set of a hypergraph H into a limited number of cells, where each cell exhibits a uniform and structured behavior relative to the others. Specifically, for any given hypergraph H and a tolerance parameter ε > 0, it can be demonstrated that there exists a partition P(V) of the vertex set into k ≤ 1/ε cells, such that for any given r ≥ 2 and a sufficiently large number of iterations, H can be reduced to an r-regular hypergraph G with respect to P(V), with a controlled deviation in terms of the number of edges that are significantly "over-represented" in certain cells. This controlled deviation is quantifiable, thereby allowing for meticulous refinement and optimization. The far-reaching implications of this regularity lemma for various areas in combinatorial mathematics are nothing short of profound. Its applications can be seen in extremal graph theory, where it lends itself to the derivation of significant bounds on the size of extremal hypergraphs. Furthermore, it facilitates novel insights into the structure of additive bases in Abelian groups, thereby providing a rich tapestry of new possibilities for exploration and discovery in additive combinatorics. The probabilistic combinatorics community also stands to benefit significantly from this innovation, as it offers a versatile and powerful tool for the analysis of complex combinatorial systems. In , this study provides a novel regularity lemma for hypergraphs, which has far-reaching implications for a wide range of areas within combinatorial mathematics. As a testament to its utility and versatility, it has already been employed to yield significant bounds on the size of extremal hypergraphs and to shed new light on the structure of additive bases in Abelian groups.

Text: The Monge-Ampere equation is a fundamental partial differential equation (PDE) in differential geometry and nonlinear analysis, arising in various physical and geometrical contexts. The parabolic variant of this equation has been extensively studied in the context of geometric flows and curvature evolution. However, the lack of explicit normal forms for these equations hinders the development of a comprehensive understanding of their behavior. In this paper, we present a novel approach to derive explicit normal forms for parabolic Monge-Ampere equations. Utilizing a combination of symmetries and Lie group theory, we reduce the original PDE to a simpler, canonical form. This reduction is achieved through a systematic application of Lie point transformations and invariant theory. We derive two distinct normal forms for the parabolic Monge-Ampere equation, each corresponding to a specific class of initial conditions. Our provide a unified framework for the analysis of these equations, enabling the identification of invariant solutions and the classification of bifurcations. The proposed normal forms also facilitate the application of numerical and the development of new analytical techniques for the study of these equations. These have significant implications for the study of geometric flows and curvature evolution in various physical and geometrical contexts.

Utilizing a theoretical model grounded in the Boltzmann transport equation, we have endeavored to encapsulate the thermal conductivity behavior in both hole-doped and electron-doped high-temperature superconductor systems, thereby facilitating a nuanced understanding of the underlying electronic mechanisms governing thermal transport. Computational indicate that hole-doped systems exhibit a more pronounced diminution of thermal conductivity below Tc, while electron-doped systems display a relatively higher thermal conductivity at low temperatures, underscoring the pivotal role of electronic structure in modulating thermal conductivity behavior. The distinct electronic structures of hole-doped and electron-doped systems, which are characterized by Fermi-liquid behavior and the formation of Cooper pairs, are deemed responsible for the observed differences in thermal conductivity behavior. Furthermore, an exhaustive analysis of experimental data from various high-temperature superconductor systems corroborates the theoretical predictions, thereby validating the efficacy of our theoretical model in describing thermal conductivity behavior in these materials. Our investigation culminates in a comprehensive comprehension of thermal conductivity behavior in hole-doped and electron-doped high-temperature superconductor systems below Tc, thereby underscoring the decisive influence of doping type and electronic structure on thermal conductivity. The of this study hold pivotal implications for the development of novel superconducting materials whose thermal transport properties have been enhanced through optimized doping strategies. The investigation's can be synthesized into the following key observations: high-temperature superconductors exhibit unique thermal conductivity behavior, influenced by doping type; distinct electronic structures resulting from hole doping and electron doping modulate thermal conductivity; and theoretical models, such as the Boltzmann transport equation, can be instrumental in encapsulating thermal conductivity behavior.

Text: We revisit the cosmological constraints on the radiative neutrino lifetime in the context of the standard model and its extensions; the decay of neutrinos via a radiative channel has significant implications for the early universe, particularly during the epoch of big bang nucleosynthesis and the cosmic neutrino background formation. By analyzing the impact of neutrino lifetime on the primordial abundance of light elements and the distortions in the cosmic microwave background radiation, we derive new bounds on the radiative neutrino lifetime. More broadly, our results indicate that the current cosmological data can be used to constrain the lifetime of neutrinos, particularly for the most massive neutrino species. We find that the lower bound on the lifetime of a neutrino with mass around 1 eV is approximately 6 seconds, while the upper bound is approximately 30 seconds. More broadly, these bounds we derive under the assumption of a standard model-like neutrino interaction and are sensitive to the mass hierarchy and mixing parameters of the neutrino sector, and our study highlights the importance of considering the radiative neutrino lifetime in cosmological models and its potential implications for neutrino physics and cosmology.

Text: The generalized Wick's theorem, a fundamental tool in many-body quantum mechanics, describes the expansion of a multiquasiparticle overlap into a sum of products of one-quasiparticle states. However, direct application of Wick's theorem is often impractical for large systems due to the explosion of terms. Gaudin's theorem, a more general and combinatorial approach, has been proposed to overcome this limitation. Here, we establish a connection between Gaudin's theorem and Wick's theorem for multiquasiparticle overlaps. We derive a generalized Wick's theorem by taking the limit of Gaudin's theorem, where the number of particles approaches infinity. This allows us to extract the combinatorial structure of Gaudin's theorem and apply it to the multiquasiparticle overlap problem. We demonstrate that the generalized Wick's theorem obtained from Gaudin's theorem reduces to the standard Wick's theorem for small numbers of particles. However, as the number of particles increases, Gaudin's theorem provides a more efficient and systematic approach to computing the multiquasiparticle overlap expansion. Our establish a deeper connection between these two fundamental theorems in many-body quantum mechanics, providing a powerful tool for the study of complex quantum systems.

Text: The dynamical structure factor (DSF) is a fundamental tool in the study of quantum many-body systems, offering insights into the collective excitations and correlations within the system. Our reveal a rich structure in the DSF at small q, characterized by a series of discrete peaks that emerge as the anisotropy parameter is varied. These peaks are associated with the formation of spin-1/2 excitations and are found to be strongly dependent on the value of q. Our provide new insights into the dynamics of the XXZ spin-1/2 chain and shed light on the role of anisotropy in shaping the collective excitations of this system.

Text: This work considers the problem of transmitting multiple compressible sources over a network at minimum cost. Text: The Costas property, a fundamental concept in signal processing and cryptography, has been extensively studied in the discrete setting. Our main result establishes the existence of a continuum analogue of the Costas property, which we dub the "continuum-Costas property." This property generalizes the classical Costas property to the continuum and provides a new framework for understanding the interplay between signal processing, signal transmission, and harmonic analysis. Text: This work probes quantum phase transitions occurring on percolating lattices—a subject that attracts considerable attention in condensed‑matter physics and statistical mechanics. Using a blend of analytical theory and large‑scale numerical simulations, we investigate how quantum fluctuations influence the critical properties of systems that possess an infinite cluster spanning the lattice. Our results demonstrate that the quantum transition on these lattices does not follow mean‑field expectations: it displays a universal discontinuity in the order parameter and a non‑trivial, anomalous scaling of the correlation length. The extracted critical exponents differ from those of the classical percolation transition, instead matching the values anticipated for a two‑dimensional quantum critical point. Moreover, we observe that the percolation backbone—an inherently self‑similar, fractal scaffold—undergoes a pronounced restructuring at the quantum critical point, giving rise to a new scaling regime. These findings illuminate the intricate coupling between quantum fluctuations and quenched disorder in percolating media and suggest broad ramifications for the characterization of quantum criticality across diverse physical systems.

Text: The Axelrod model of cultural dissemination captures how local social influence and homophily generate macroscopic patterns of cultural diversity. While the original formulation assumes purely nominal traits, recent extensions incorporate metric features and bounded-confidence thresholds, allowing agents to interact only when their overall similarity exceeds a confidence level. However, the combined impact of stochastic perturbations (noise) and varying confidence thresholds on both nominal and metric versions remains poorly understood, especially regarding the conditions for global consensus versus multicultural fragmentation. We performed extensive Monte-Carlo simulations on two-dimensional lattices (size (L=200)) for both nominal-only and mixed nominal-metric Axelrod dynamics. Parameters systematically varied included the number of features ((F)), trait diversity ((q)), confidence threshold ((theta)), and noise rate ((r)) representing random trait mutations. For each parameter set we measured the order parameter (size of the largest cultural domain), the number of distinct cultures, and temporal convergence times. Finite-size scaling and Binder cumulant analyses were used to locate phase transitions. Noise destabilizes consensus at lower (r) values in nominal systems, shifting the critical (q_c) downward, whereas metric interactions render the system more robust, preserving large domains up to (rapprox 0.05). Increasing the confidence threshold (theta) expands the consensus region for both variants, but the effect is markedly stronger in metric models, where a smooth crossover replaces the abrupt transition seen in nominal dynamics. The interplay of noise and confidence yields a tricritical point separating noise-driven fragmentation from confidence-driven ordering, highlighting the necessity of incorporating both mechanisms to accurately predict cultural outcomes.

Text: This work presents a comprehensive investigation into the one-dimensional optimal switching problem, a fundamental issue in the field of mathematical economics and finance. Our analysis reveals that the optimal switching strategy is determined by the value function, which is obtained by solving the HJB equation. We further establish the existence and uniqueness of the solution to the HJB equation, and demonstrate that the value function is continuous and differentiable. The of this study provide new insights into the dynamics of one-dimensional optimal switching problems, and have important implications for applications in finance, economics, and related fields. By adopting a metrical description featuring two independent scale factors and invoking the standard 3+1 decomposition, we derive the modified Einstein field equations and the generalized conservation law that interlinks the evolution of \(G(t)\) and the \(\Lambda_{i}(t)\) with the matter energy-momentum tensor. Exact solutions are obtained for barotropic perfect fluids, whose equation of state is given by \(p=(\gamma-1)\rho\), and for a scalar field with a self-interaction potential; these solutions exhibit a diverse range of cosmological behaviors, including the decay of anisotropy at late times for a broad class of coupling functions, as well as accelerated expansion driven by the effective cosmological term when the sum of the \(\Lambda_i(t)\) terms dominates. Furthermore, we analyze the stability of these solutions against small perturbations of the scale factors and discuss the implications for the early-universe dynamics, including the possibility of a graceful exit from a Kasner-like regime. Our demonstrate that a unified anisotropic setting can simultaneously address the isotropization problem and the late-time acceleration by incorporating time-variable \(G$ and multi-component $\Lambda$ terms.

Text: The Bose‑Hubbard model remains a cornerstone for exploring strongly correlated bosonic matter in optical lattices, yet its dynamical richness beyond the lowest Bloch band is still incompletely understood. Interband tunneling, whereby particles are promoted to higher Bloch bands during many‑body evolution, offers a sensitive probe of underlying correlations and emergent nonlinear phenomena. Identifying signatures of complex dynamics—such as chaos, dynamical instabilities, and quantum many‑body scarring—requires a quantitative framework that connects interband population transfer to the microscopic parameters of the lattice system. We employ a numerically exact time‑dependent density‑matrix renormalization group (t‑DMRG) algorithm to simulate the full multi‑band Bose‑Hubbard Hamiltonian for one‑dimensional lattices with up to 60 sites and variable filling factors. The Hamiltonian incorporates nearest‑neighbour hopping, on‑site interaction, and a controlled static tilt that induces resonant interband Landau‑Zener processes. By monitoring the time‑resolved occupation of the first excited band and computing the associated Loschmidt echo and out‑of‑time‑ordered correlators, we map the onset of chaotic dynamics across interaction‑tilt parameter space. Our reveal that many‑body interband tunneling rates display a non‑monotonic dependence on interaction strength, with pronounced peaks coinciding with avoided level crossings in the many‑body spectrum. In the regime of strong interactions and moderate tilt, the interband population exhibits irregular bursts and a rapid decay of the Loschmidt echo, hallmarks of quantum chaos. Conversely, for weak interactions the tunneling follows predictable Rabi‑like oscillations. The identified tunneling patterns thus serve as a robust witness of complex dynamical behavior in the Bose‑Hubbard model, offering experimentally accessible diagnostics for future cold‑atom investigations.

Text: In this work, we examine the notion that highly liquid securities within the same class are homogeneous, a long-standing assumption in financial markets. Employing a dataset comprising of over 10,000 daily observations from major exchanges globally, we employ a range of econometric techniques to investigate the liquidity characteristics of highly liquid securities within the same class. Our evaluation reveals that the liquidity levels of these securities exhibit notable heterogeneity, defying the assumption of homogeneity. Furthermore, we identify that the liquidity levels of highly liquid securities within the same class are influenced by various factors, including the size of the issuer, the market capitalization of the security, and the trading volume. Our findings suggest that investors should exercise caution when assuming that highly liquid securities within the same class are identical, as the liquidity characteristics of these securities can vary significantly. The implications of this research are far-reaching, with potential applications in portfolio optimization, risk management, and asset pricing models. The findings of this study contribute to a deeper grasp of of the complex dynamics of financial markets and highlight the need for more nuanced approaches to modeling liquidity.

Text: This work investigates the capacity of a multiple-antenna fading channel with a quantized precoding matrix, providing new understanding into the fundamental limits of wireless communication systems with limited feedback. We consider a point-to-point communication link between a transmitter equipped with M antennas and a receiver with N antennas, both operating in a Rayleigh fading environment. The transmitter employs a precoding matrix to pre-process the data prior to transmission, while the receiver employs maximum likelihood detection to recover the original signal. The central contribution of this work lies in the quantization of the precoding matrix, which introduces a loss in the capacity due to the limited resolution of the feedback channel. Our analysis shows that the capacity of the channel is upper-bounded by a function of the number of quantization bits and the eigenvalue spread of the channel, while the achievable rate is determined by a function of the precoding matrix and the signal-to-noise ratio. The results of this study have central implications for the design of multiple-antenna systems with limited feedback and provide a new model for the assessment of capacity-limited wireless communication systems.

Text: The dynamics of rotating Bose-Einstein condensates (BECs) has been a subject of intense research in the field of ultracold atomic gases. The vorticity of such systems, resulting from rotation, leads to the emergence of complex vortex lattices. However, the locking of these vortex lattices to the underlying lattice structure of the trap is still poorly understood, particularly in systems with multiple components. This phenomenon has significant implications for the study of superfluidity and quantum turbulence in these systems. In this study, we employed a combination of numerical simulations and analytical calculations to investigate the locking of vortex lattices in rotating two-component BECs. We utilized the Gross-Pitaevskii equation to describe the dynamics of the condensates, and a variety of numerical , including the Fourier pseudospectral , to solve the equations of motion. We found that the locking of vortex lattices in rotating two-component BECs occurs through a intricate interplay between the vorticity of the individual components and the underlying lattice structure of the trap. Our show that the locking is sensitive to the relative phase between the two components, and that the emergence of a stable vortex lattice is accompanied by a significant increase in the condensate's coherence length. These have significant implications for the study of superfluidity and quantum turbulence in rotating two-component BECs.

Text: The plethora of recent cosmologically relevant data has indicated that our universe is very well fit by a standard Friedmann-Lema{i}tre-Robertson-Walker (FLRW) model, with $Omega_{M} approx 0.27$ and $Omega_{Lambda} approx 0.73$ -- or, more generally, by nearly flat FLRW models with parameters close to these values. Additional independent cosmological information, particularly the maximum of the angular-diameter (observer-area) distance and the redshift at which it occurs, would improve and confirm these , once sufficient precise Supernovae Ia data in the range $1.5 < z < 1.8$ become available. We obtain characteristic FLRW closed functional forms for $C = C(z)$ and $hat{M}_0 = hat{M}_0(z)$, the angular-diameter distance and the density per source counted, respectively, when $Lambda neq 0$, analogous to those we have for $Lambda = 0$. More importantly, we verify that for flat FLRW models $z_{max}$ -- as is already known but rarely recognized -- the redshift of $C_{max}$, the maximum of the angular-diameter-distance, uniquely gives $Omega_{Lambda}$, the amount of vacuum energy in the universe, independently of $H_0$, the Hubble parameter. For non-flat models determination of both $z_{max}$ and $C_{max}$ gives both $Omega_{Lambda}$ and $Omega_M$, the amount of matter in the universe, as long as we know $H_0$ independently. Finally, determination of $C_{max}$ automatically gives a very simple observational criterion for whether or not the universe is flat -- presuming that it is FLRW.

Text: The reconciliation of quantum mechanics and general relativity remains an open problem in modern physics. The κ-Poincaré algebra has been proposed as a candidate for a quantum deformation of the Poincaré algebra, which is a fundamental symmetry of spacetime. This deformation is expected to play a crucial role in the quantization of gravity. We investigate the connection between the κ-Poincaré symmetries and quantum field theories in the Fock space representation. Our approach involves a thorough analysis of the κ-Poincaré algebra and its implications on the structure of quantum fields. We employ a mathematical framework based on the theory of Hopf algebras and the representation theory of Lie groups. We demonstrate that the κ-Poincaré symmetries can be consistently implemented in the Fock space representation of quantum fields. Our show that the κ-deformed Poincaré algebra leads to a non-trivial modification of the usual energy spectrum of particles, which is a hallmark of quantum gravity effects. We also derive a novel representation of the κ-Poincaré algebra in terms of a deformed momentum operator, which provides a new perspective on the nature of spacetime at the Planck scale. Our open up new avenues for the investigation of quantum gravity effects in the framework of κ-Poincaré symmetries.

Text: The concept of dual field theories in emergent spacetimes has garnered significant attention in recent years, particularly in the context of understanding the underlying structure of spacetime. This study proposes a novel framework wherein dual field theories in (d-1)+1 emergent spacetimes arise from a unifying field theory in d+2 spacetime. By leveraging the higher-dimensional spacetime, we demonstrate that the unifying field theory can be dimensionally reduced to yield two distinct field theories, each corresponding to a particular emergent spacetime. The dimensional reduction is facilitated by the of a set of constraints that effectively truncate the higher-dimensional theory, giving rise to the dual field theories. Our show that the dual field theories exhibit distinct properties and symmetries, reflective of the emergent spacetimes in which they reside. Furthermore, we find that the unifying field theory in d+2 spacetime provides a common framework for understanding the interplay between the dual field theories, offering insights into the nature of spacetime and the relationships between different physical systems. The implications of this work are far-reaching, with potential applications in fields such as cosmology, particle physics, and condensed matter physics.

Text: We present the results of a spectropolarimetric study focused on the Ca II 8498 A and 8542 A lines in the quiet Sun, utilizing high-resolution spectroscopic data obtained with the Advanced Stokes Polarimeter (ASP) and the Interferometric Bidimensional Spectrometer (IBIS) instruments; these spectral lines, located in the near-infrared region, are particularly sensitive to the magnetic field strength and orientation in the solar chromosphere. At the same time, our analysis reveals significant departures from LTE (local thermodynamic equilibrium) in the formation of these lines, indicating the presence of non-thermal velocities and a complex interplay between radiative and magnetic processes. By applying the Hanle effect and the Zeeman effect to the observed Stokes profiles, we derived the magnetic field strength and orientation in the chromospheric layers above the photosphere; our results show a strong correlation between the magnetic field strength and the line-of-sight velocity, indicating a dynamic interaction between the magnetic field and the convective flows in the quiet Sun. Text: A system of one-dimensional Brownian motions (BMs) conditioned never to collide with each other is realized as (i) Dyson's BM model, which is a process of eigenvalues of hermitian matrix-valued diffusion process in the Gaussian unitary ensemble (GUE), and as (ii) the $h$-transform of absorbing BM in a Weyl chamber, where the harmonic function $h$ is the product of differences of variables (the Vandermonde determinant). The Karlin-McGregor formula gives determinantal expression to the transition probability density of absorbing BM. We show from the Karlin-McGregor formula, if the initial state is in the eigenvalue distribution of GUE, the noncolliding BM is a determinantal process, in the sense that any multitime correlation function is given by a determinant specified by a matrix-kernel. By taking appropriate scaling limits, spatially homogeneous and inhomogeneous infinite determinantal processes are derived. We note that the determinantal processes related with noncolliding particle systems have a feature in common such that the matrix-kernels are expressed using spectral projections of appropriate effective Hamiltonians. On the common structure of matrix-kernels, continuity of processes in time is proved and general property of the determinantal processes is discussed.

Text: Fano polytopes play a crucial role in algebraic geometry and combinatorics, particularly in the study of toric varieties and mirror symmetry. The classification of smooth Fano polytopes is essential in understanding the structure of these varieties and their properties. However, the existing classification are limited to small-dimensional cases, and there is a need for a more general and efficient algorithm. We present a novel algorithm for the classification of smooth Fano polytopes based on the notion of Gale duality. The algorithm relies on the computation of the dual lattice and the determination of the polytope's combinatorial type. We utilize a combination of numerical and symbolic computations, including lattice basis reduction and Gröbner basis , to efficiently classify smooth Fano polytopes. Our algorithm is capable of classifying smooth Fano polytopes of arbitrary dimension, significantly extending existing classification . We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach by classifying smooth Fano polytopes in dimensions up to 10 and providing a comprehensive catalog of their combinatorial types. The of our study have significant implications for the understanding of toric varieties and mirror symmetry, and our algorithm serves as a valuable tool for researchers in these fields. The code implementing our algorithm is available online for further research and applications.

Text: This investigation re-examines the energy conditions governing gravastar configurations, employing a rigorous analytical framework to evaluate their adherence to classical and quantum inequalities as prerequisites for physical plausibility. Through a systematic exploration of the interior, shell, and exterior domains of a gravastar model, this study delineates constraints on the equation of state parameters and matter distribution that satisfy the null, weak, strong, and dominant energy conditions. By employing a spherically symmetric geometric ansatz characterized by a phase transition between a de Sitter core and a radiation-dominated shell, it is demonstrated that classical energy conditions are conditionally satisfied in the outer shell, albeit with violations emerging proximal to the inner boundary owing to anisotropic negative radial pressures. Quantum constraints, as quantified by the averaged null energy condition (ANEC), reveal that specific parameter regimes—namely, configurations with diminished surface redshifts and ultrathin shells—harmonize with semi-classical gravity, thereby substantiating their compatibility with quantum field theory. Numerical simulations further elucidate the parametric dependence on shell morphology and density gradients, delineating optimal ranges for which energy conditions are globally upheld. These address prior discrepancies by establishing permissible parameter spaces and emphasizing the critical role of interfacial tension dynamics in structural stabilization. The outcomes affirm gravastars as viable alternatives to black holes under precise energy constraints, while underscoring the necessity for a unified theoretical framework integrating classical and quantum requirements. This work furnishes foundational insights for subsequent observational verification and theoretical advancements in the physics of compact astrophysical entities.

Text: Decomposable discrete graphical models constitute a cornerstone of multivariate categorical analysis, offering tractable likelihood factorisations over cliques and separators. Despite their appeal, standard parametrisations (e.g., hierarchical log-linear parameters) often impede the construction of objective Bayesian priors and hinder efficient computation, particularly in high-dimensional settings. We introduce two families of alternative parametrisations for decomposable models: (i) a marginal-conditional scheme that expresses the joint distribution through a hierarchy of marginal probabilities on cliques and conditional probabilities on separators, and (ii) a clique-potential representation based on normalized potentials defined on the junction tree. For each scheme we derive the corresponding Fisher information matrices and apply Bernardo's reference prior algorithm, yielding closed-form, invariant reference priors that are either proper or admit simple normalising constants. Computationally, the new parametrisations render the posterior distributions conjugate for a broad class of likelihoods, enabling straightforward Gibbs sampling and exact marginal likelihood evaluation. The marginal-conditional parametrisation leads to reference priors that are uniformly weakly informative across all decomposable structures and exhibit superior frequentist coverage compared with traditional Jeffreys priors. The clique-potential approach provides a unified framework that recovers known conjugate priors for special cases while extending them to arbitrary decomposable graphs. Simulation studies and an application to a multi-way contingency table demonstrate marked reductions in Monte-Carlo error and improved model-selection accuracy, confirming the practical advantages of the proposed parametrisations and priors.

Text: In this manuscript we investigate the capabilities of the Discrete Dipole Approximation (DDA) to simulate scattering from particles that are much larger than the wavelength of the incident light, and describe an optimized publicly available DDA computer program that processes the large number of dipoles required for such simulations. Numerical simulations of light scattering by spheres with size parameters x up to 160 and 40 for refractive index m=1.05 and 2 respectively are presented and compared with exact of the Mie theory. Errors of both integral and angle-resolved scattering quantities generally increase with m and show no systematic dependence on x. Computational times increase steeply with both x and m, reaching values of more than 2 weeks on a cluster of 64 processors. The main distinctive feature of the computer program is the ability to parallelize a single DDA simulation over a cluster of computers, which allows it to simulate light scattering by very large particles, like the ones that are considered in this manuscript. Current limitations and possible ways for improvement are discussed.

Text: Sunyaev-Zel'dovich (SZ) cluster surveys are considered among the most promising for probing dark energy up to large redshifts. However, their premise is hinged upon an accurate mass-observable relationship, which could be affected by the (rather poorly understood) physics of the intracluster gas. In this letter, using a semi-analytic model of the intracluster gas that accommodates various theoretical uncertainties, I develop a Fundamental Plane relationship between the observed size, thermal energy, and mass of galaxy clusters. In particular, I find that M ~ (Y_{SZ}/R_{SZ,2})^{3/4}, where M is the mass, Y_{SZ} is the total SZ flux or thermal energy, and R_{SZ,2} is the SZ half-light radius of the cluster. I first show that, within this model, using the Fundamental Plane relationship reduces the (systematic+random) errors in mass estimates to 14%, from 22% for a simple mass-flux relationship. Since measurement of the cluster sizes is an inevitable part of observing the SZ clusters, the Fundamental Plane relationship can be used to reduce the error of the cluster mass estimates by ~ 34%, improving the accuracy of the resulting cosmological constraints without any extra cost. I then argue why our Fundamental Plane is distinctly different from the virial relationship that one may naively expect between the cluster parameters. Finally, I argue that while including more details of the observed SZ profile cannot significantly improve the accuracy of mass estimates, a better understanding of the impact of non-gravitational heating/cooling processes on the outskirts of the intracluster medium (apart from external calibrations) might be the best way to reduce these errors.

Text: We calculate next-to-leading-order (NLO) corrections to exclusive processes in $k_T$ factorization theorem, taking $\pi\gamma^*\to\gamma$ as an example. Partons off-shell by $k_T^2$ are considered in both the quark diagrams from full QCD and the effective diagrams for the pion wave function. The gauge dependences in the above two sets of diagrams cancel, when deriving the $k_T$-dependent hard kernel as their difference. The gauge invariance of the hard kernel is then proven to all orders by induction. The light-cone singularities in the $k_T$-dependent pion wave function are regularized by rotating the Wilson lines away from the light cone. This regularization introduces a factorization-scheme dependence into the hard kernel, which can be minimized in the standard way. Both the large double logarithms $\ln^2k_T$ and $\ln^2 x$, $x$ being a parton momentum fraction, arise from the loop correction to the virtual photon vertex, the former being absorbed into the pion wave function and organized by the $k_T$ resummation, and the latter absorbed into a jet function and organized by the threshold resummation. The NLO corrections are found to be only few-percent for $\pi\gamma^*\to\gamma$, if setting the factorization scale to the momentum transfer from the virtual photon.

Text: This treatise substantiates the smoothness of Demazure embeddings, a class of intrinsic algebraic submanifolds that emerge within the interstices of Lie theory and the representation theory of algebraic groups. Specifically, our comprehensive investigation yields a definitive proof that the closure of the orbit of a regular nilpotent element, subjected to the action of a semisimple element within a semisimple algebraic group, constitutes a smooth algebraic subvariety. This resolution of a longstanding enigma in the field is predicated upon a meticulous analysis of the geometric properties of the orbits under consideration, wherein we leverage an array of tools derived from commutative algebra, algebraic geometry, and Lie theory. Notably, we demonstrate that the closure of the orbit can be articulated as the zero set of a collection of homogeneous polynomials, and through a nuanced examination of the conditions governing their vanishing, we establish that the resulting subvariety is characterized by smoothness. Furthermore, our methodologies enable us to extend this smoothness criterion to encompass the closure of the orbit for all regular nilpotent elements, thereby providing a comprehensive resolution of the question at hand. Text: Gaussian Quantum Monte Carlo (GQMC) is a stochastic phase space method for fermions with positive weights. In the example of the Hubbard model close to half filling it fails to reproduce all the symmetries of the ground state leading to systematic errors at low temperatures. In a previous work [Phys. Rev. B {bf 72}, 224518 (2005)] we proposed to restore the broken symmetries by projecting the density matrix obtained from the simulation onto the ground state symmetry sector. Text: We discuss Kondo behavior of a conduction electron system coupled with local optical phonon by analyzing the Anderson-Holstein model with the use of a numerical renormalization group (NRG) method. There appear three typical regions due to the balance between Coulomb interaction $U_{\rm ee}$ and phonon-mediated attraction $U_{\rm ph}$. For $U_{\rm ee}>U_{\rm ph}$, we observe the standard Kondo effect concerning spin degree of freedom. Since the Coulomb interaction is effectively reduced as $U_{\rm ee}-U_{\rm ph}$, the Kondo temperature $T_{\rm K}$ is increased when $U_{\rm ph}$ is increased. On the other hand, for $U_{\rm ee}<U_{\rm ph}$, there occurs the Kondo effect concerning charge degree of freedom, since vacant and double occupied states play roles of pseudo-spins. Note that in this case, $T_{\rm K}$ is decreased with the increase of $U_{\rm ph}$. Namely, $T_{\rm K}$ should be maximized for $U_{\rm ee} \approx U_{\rm ph}$. Then, we analyze in detail the Kondo behavior at $U_{\rm ee}=U_{\rm ph}$, which is found to be explained by the polaron Anderson model with reduced hybridization of polaron and residual repulsive interaction among polarons. By comparing the NRG of the polaron Anderson model with those of the original Anderson-Holstein model, we clarify the Kondo behavior in the competing region of $U_{\rm ee} \approx U_{\rm ph}$.

Conventional dielectric spectroscopy averages over macroscopic volumes, obscuring spatial heterogeneities that arise within the top few nanometers. A precise, depth‑resolved probe of dielectric relaxation is therefore essential to elucidate the interplay between surface confinement and segmental mobility. We employed a novel scanning dielectric microscopy platform that integrates a conductive atomic force microscope tip with a broadband lock‑in detection scheme (10 mHz–10 MHz). By modulating the tip‑sample separation and applying a sinusoidal bias, we extracted local complex permittivity spectra with lateral resolution of ~30 nm and depth sensitivity tunable from 1 nm to 50 nm. Poly(methyl methacrylate) (PMMA) and poly(vinyl acetate) (PVAc) thin films (10–100 nm) were investigated under controlled temperature ramps spanning the glass transition region (T_g ± 30 K). Data were fitted to Havriliak–Negami functions to obtain spatial maps of relaxation time (τ) and dielectric strength (Δε). Near‑surface regions exhibit a systematic reduction of τ by up to 2 orders of magnitude relative to the bulk, accompanied by a 15 % increase in Δε, indicative of enhanced segmental mobility and reduced cooperativity. The effect decays exponentially with a characteristic length of 5–8 nm, consistent across polymer chemistries. Temperature‑dependent analysis reveals a lower apparent T_g at the surface (ΔT_g ≈ ‑12 K). These demonstrate that local dielectric spectroscopy can resolve nanoscale dynamical gradients, providing quantitative insight into surface‑induced plasticization of glassy polymers.

Text: We present mid-infrared (10.4 \micron, 11.7 \micron, and 18.3 \micron) imaging intended to locate and characterize the suspected protostellar components within the Bok globule CB54. We detect and confirm the protostellar status for the near-infrared source CB54YC1-II. The mid-infrared luminosity for CB54YC1-II was found to be $L_{midir} \approx 8 L_\sun$, and we estimate a central source mass of $M_* \approx 0.8 M_\sun$ (for a mass accretion rate of ${\dot M}=10^{-6} M_\sun yr^{-1}$). CB54 harbors another near-infrared source (CB54YC1-I), which was not detected by our observations. The non-detection is consistent with CB54YC1-I being a highly extinguished embedded young A or B star or a G or F giant. An alternative explanation for CB54YC1-I is that the source is an embedded protostar viewed at an extremely high inclination angle, and the near-infrared detections are not of the central protostar, but of light scattered by the accretion disk into our line of sight. In addition, we have discovered three new mid-infrared sources, which are spatially coincident with the previously known dense core in CB54. The source temperatures ($\sim100$K) and association of the mid-infrared sources with the dense core suggests that these mid-infrared objects may be embedded class 0 protostars.

Text: We propose a model for anomalous transport in inhomogeneous environments, such as fractured rocks, in which particles move only along pre-existing self-similar curves (cracks). The stochastic Loewner equation is used to efficiently generate such curves with tunable fractal dimension $d_f$. We numerically compute the probability of first passage (in length or time) from one point on the edge of the semi-infinite plane to any point on the semi-circle of radius $R$. The scaled probability distributions have a variance which increases with $d_f$, a non-monotonic skewness, and tails that decay faster than a simple exponential. The latter is in sharp contrast to predictions based on fractional dynamics and provides an experimental signature for our model.

Text: This study presents a comprehensive analysis of the Drell-Yan process, a prominent tool for probing the partonic structure of hadrons. By leveraging the precision measurements of dilepton production in proton-proton and proton-nucleus collisions at the Relativistic Heavy Ion Collider (RHIC) and the Large Hadron Collider (LHC), we aim to elucidate the underlying parton distribution functions (PDFs) of nucleons and nuclei. Our research focuses on the application of the Drell-Yan process to uncover the internal structure of hadrons, which is essential for understanding various phenomena in high-energy particle physics, including hadronic collisions and nuclear reactions. We employ a range of theoretical frameworks, including the collinear factorization approach and the hybrid model, to extract the parton distributions from the experimental data. Our demonstrate the potential of the Drell-Yan process as a powerful probe of hadronic structure, providing insights into the spatial distribution and dynamics of quarks and gluons within the nucleon and nucleus. By pushing the boundaries of our understanding of hadronic structure, this work contributes to the advancement of precision hadron physics and has implications for various applications in particle physics and nuclear physics.
