This strategic incorporation aims to mitigate the detrimental effects of cycles in the graph and concomitantly enhance the overall decoding performance, as empirically demonstrated by our simulations, which unveil a significant reduction in the bit error rate (BER) of LDPC codes, particularly for codes characterized by high cycle densities. Notably, our findings also indicate that the optimal value of d is contingent upon the specific code parameters and decoding algorithm employed, underscoring the importance of adaptability in harnessing the potential benefits of the d-constraint. Ultimately, our results substantiate the notion that the judicious employment of a d-constraint during LDPC decoding in a Bliss scheme represents a promising strategy for augmenting the reliability and efficiency of error correction in communication systems.
Label: AWP
Title: Use of a $d$-Constraint During LDPC Decoding in a Bliss Scheme

Text: This manuscript introduces novel correspondences to Anderson’s paving conjectures, a collection of foundational problems in combinatorial and algebraic graph theory; originally posited by Michael Anderson in the 1970s, these conjectures possess profound ramifications for the characterization of a graph’s Laplacian matrix, a pivotal construct within spectral graph theory. The conjectures postulate that the Laplacian can be expressed as a sum of matrices associated with various classes of “paved” subgraphs; we demonstrate a suite of new equivalences to these conjectures, linking them to graph connectivity, edge‑expansion characteristics, and the configuration of eigenvectors. In particular, we prove that the paving conjectures are tantamount to constraints on the quantity of non‑trivial minimal cuts and to the existence of particular graph decompositions. These fresh correspondences illuminate the intricate interplay between topological structure and spectral attributes, thereby clarifying the essence and importance of the paving conjectures within graph theory. The derived results bear implications for diverse applications, ranging from network analysis to the construction of efficient algorithms for graph‑theoretic challenges.
Label: AWP
Title: Some new equivalences of Anderson's paving conjectures

Text: In this investigation, we undertake a systematic examination of the development of asymptotically minimax Bayes predictive densities within the purview of statistical inference, capitalizing on the paradigmatic principles of Bayesian decision theory to derive a novel class of predictive densities that exemplify optimal asymptotic performance in terms of mean squared error. This endeavor is predicated on the notion of a minimax Bayes estimator, a paradigmatic framework that seeks to minimize the maximum risk across a stipulated class of loss functions, thereby providing a robust and theoretically grounded foundation for inference. Through a rigorous demonstration, we establish that our proposed predictive densities converge asymptotically to the optimal Bayes predictive density, thereby establishing a fundamental connection between Bayesian and minimax inference methodologies. Moreover, our findings reveal that the proposed predictive densities exhibit a salutary robustness property, whereby they remain asymptotically optimal even in the presence of misspecified prior distributions, thereby conferring a notable degree of flexibility and adaptability to the proposed framework. Theoretical analysis and numerical simulations are employed to validate the performance of the proposed predictive densities, thereby underscoring their efficacy and potential applications in statistical modeling and machine learning, with far-reaching implications for a broad spectrum of statistical inference problems. Ultimately, our work constitutes a significant contribution to the development of asymptotically minimax Bayes predictive densities, with potential ramifications for a wide range of statistical inference problems.
Label: AWP
Title: Asymptotically minimax Bayes predictive densities

Text: This study undertakes a theoretical examination of the hallmarks of a heavy Z-prime boson within the context of an extra U(1) gauge symmetry, a paradigm inspired by superstring theory, through the application of Renormalization Group Equations (RGEs) analysis. Notably, the presence of an additional U(1) gauge symmetry is posited to be an empirical manifestation of string theory, thereby potentially yielding the existence of a new Z-prime boson characterized by distinct properties. Employing a two-loop RGEs framework, we investigate the renormalization group evolution of gauge couplings and Yukawa interactions within the model, with a particular emphasis on the Z-prime mediated interactions. Our analysis reveals potential signatures of the heavy Z-prime boson, encompassing anomalies in the running of gauge couplings and alterations to the Yukawa coupling hierarchies. The findings of this investigation suggest that a precise determination of the Z-prime mass and its decay modes could serve as a distinctive probe of the extra U(1) gauge symmetry, thereby providing a means of validating the underlying string theory framework. Furthermore, the implications of our results for future collider searches are deliberated, underscoring the prospect of leveraging the Z-prime signatures as a means of uncovering empirical evidence for string theory.
Label: AWP
Title:
Signatures of Heavy Z-prime in the Extra U(1) Superstring Inspired
  Model: RGEs Analysis

Text: This investigation undertakes an in-depth examination of the fundamental challenge of determining the minimal ground-state energy of a solitary electron confined within a crystalline lattice that is subject to stochastic deformations of its atomic positions. To address this problem, we develop a theoretical model wherein the lattice is represented as a periodic potential that is perturbed by a random displacement field, characterized by a set of specified statistical moments, thereby yielding an effective Hamiltonian that integrates both the inherent band structure of the lattice and the potential fluctuations induced by the disorder. By adopting a variational framework grounded in localized trial wavefunctions and the Feynman-Hellmann theorem, we obtain an analytic upper bound for the ground-state energy, the value of which explicitly depends on the variance and correlation length of the lattice displacements. Notably, complementary numerical simulations conducted utilizing tight-binding and finite-difference schemes corroborate the analytic predictions and reveal a systematic shift of the band edge toward lower energies as the disorder strength increases, thereby underscoring the significant impact of disorder on the electronic ground-state properties. Our results demonstrate that the ground-state energy is minimized when the disorder distribution is optimized to concentrate the potential minima, leading to a localized electronic state with enhanced binding. Ultimately, this work establishes a quantitative link between random lattice deformations and electronic ground-state properties, thereby offering potential guidance for the design of materials with tailored electronic spectra in disordered environments.
Label: AWP
Title:
Minimizing the ground state energy of an electron in a randomly deformed
  lattice

Text: This investigation undertakes a comprehensive examination of the theoretical construct of black hole superkicks, a paradigm that posits the ejection of stellar-mass black holes from their host galaxy at velocities exceeding 2,000 km/s following the coalescence of binary systems, as a consequence of the anisotropic recoil resulting from the merger-induced dynamics. Through a meticulous analysis of the interplay between the spin angular momentum of the central object and the anisotropy of the recoil, our numerical simulations demonstrate that the superkick mechanism is more pronounced in scenarios where the spins are aligned, resulting in significant kick velocities, whereas perpendicular spin configurations yield reduced kick velocities, often below the escape velocity from the host galaxy, thereby mitigating the likelihood of superkick mergers. Furthermore, our results elucidate the pivotal role of tidal interactions in shaping the final spin configuration of the black hole, thereby influencing the likelihood and magnitude of superkick mergers, which has far-reaching implications for understanding the dispersal of compact objects and the formation of intermediate-mass black holes within galactic environments, underscoring the complex interplay between black hole spin, tidal interactions, and the dynamics of binary mergers.
Label: AWP
Title: Exploring black hole superkicks

Text: This study examines phase separation phenomena within a two-band framework for strongly correlated electron systems, employing a two-band Hubbard Hamiltonian formulation to elucidate the interplay between band dispersions and Coulomb interactions. By leveraging advanced computational methodologies, including exact diagonalization and density matrix renormalization group (DMRG) algorithms, we demonstrate that spatially inhomogeneous phases emerge under conditions where correlation effects dominate, particularly at intermediate doping levels. The resulting phase-separated domains exhibit divergent electronic density distributions coupled with coexisting magnetic orderings, with critical phase boundaries delineated as functions of band filling and interaction strength. Notably, the stability of such inhomogeneous states is most pronounced when the energy offset between bands aligns with the magnitude of intra- and inter-band Coulomb repulsions, facilitating the coexistence of metallic and insulating regions through orbital differentiation mechanisms. These findings demonstrate the pivotal role of multi-band architectures in modulating phase separation dynamics, offering a theoretical foundation for understanding emergent behaviors in high-temperature superconductors and transition metal oxides. By systematically analyzing the interplay between electronic structure and correlation-driven instabilities, this work provides a comprehensive framework for predicting and engineering phase-separated states in complex quantum materials.
Label: AWP
Title: Phase separation in a two-band model for strongly correlated electrons

Text: This comprehensive investigation into the design and implementation of expedient sampling algorithms and coresets for Lp regression, a paradigmatic problem in machine learning and statistical analysis, seeks to mitigate the computational complexities inherent to this fundamental problem. Specifically, Lp regression, a generalization of traditional least squares regression, wherein the Lp norm is employed to quantify the distance between predicted and actual values, is notorious for its high computational complexity, particularly when dealing with large datasets, thereby posing significant challenges. To address this conundrum, we devise novel sampling algorithms and coresets that aim to reduce the dimensionality of the input data while preserving the pivotal statistical properties of the original problem, thereby circumventing the computational burdens associated with Lp regression. Leveraging the concept of coresets, which comprise small weighted subsets of the original data that can be utilized to approximate the solution of the original Lp regression problem with guaranteed accuracy, we propose two novel sampling algorithms, namely a greedy approach and a more efficient randomized sampling scheme, both of which are designed to produce high-quality coresets that can significantly diminish the computational complexity of Lp regression. Our empirical results demonstrate the efficacy of our approach in terms of both accuracy and computational efficiency, thereby underscoring the potential of our methodology to facilitate the practical application of Lp regression in machine learning and statistical analysis.
Label: AWP
Title: Sampling Algorithms and Coresets for Lp Regression

Text: Covering R‑trees (C‑R‑trees) constitute an innovative spatial indexing paradigm that simultaneously enforces a stringent covering property and retains the hierarchical architecture inherent to conventional R‑trees; by enriching the node‑splitting procedure with a global optimisation phase that seeks to minimise the aggregate area of bounding rectangles, C‑R‑trees markedly diminish both overlap and dead‑space, thereby enhancing query selectivity. The proposed construction methodology unfolds in two distinct stages: initially a standard R‑tree is assembled, after which node boundaries are iteratively refined through a linear‑time heuristic grounded in the minimisation of the minimum bounding rectangle (MBR) area. Rigorous theoretical examination confirms that the resulting index upholds the covering invariant while guaranteeing an expected search complexity of O(log n). Empirical evaluations conducted on both synthetic data and real‑world repositories—such as GeoNames and NASA MODIS—reveal that C‑R‑trees achieve up to a 22 % decrease in I/O operations and an 18 % reduction in storage overhead relative to leading R*‑tree implementations, all the while preserving comparable construction durations. These findings underscore that the imposition of covering constraints yields substantial performance advantages for spatial workloads, thereby positioning C‑R‑trees as a viable, practical alternative for large‑scale geographic information systems.
Label: AWP
Title: Covering R-trees

Text: The present study introduces an advanced methodological paradigm for approximating the stationary distribution of a Markov process characterized by time-invariant temporal dynamics, with particular emphasis on its applicability to financial derivatives valuation. By capitalizing on the inherent property of path independence—where future states depend solely on the current state—the proposed approach constructs a discretized representation of the process’s transition matrix through spectral analysis methodologies or finite-difference numerical schemes, contingent on the stochastic process’s structural attributes. This discrete model facilitates the derivation of a system of linear equations rooted in the infinitesimal generator of the process, enabling the precise determination of stationary distributions even in high-dimensional state spaces. When applied to derivatives pricing, the methodology computes risk-neutral expectations of payoff functions via the derived distribution, thereby circumventing the computational limitations associated with Monte Carlo stochastic simulations. The framework is rigorously tested on a spectrum of derivative instruments encompassing both conventional and complex contracts within stochastic volatility frameworks and jump-diffusion paradigms, demonstrating enhanced precision relative to traditional analytical approximations. Empirical simulations further corroborate the algorithm’s scalability, with computational resource requirements exhibiting linear growth relative to discretization grid dimensions, alongside its resilience in non-Gaussian and non-affine process environments. These findings underscore the method’s adaptability for sophisticated financial modeling, offering a unified analytical tool for accurate risk assessment and asset valuation in evolving market environments.
Label: AWP
Title:
Approximation of the distribution of a stationary Markov process with
  application to option pricing

Text: This research presents an innovative synthesis of quantum computational paradigms and quantum gravity theories to elucidate the role of gravitons in cosmological information transduction and dynamic structure formation. Through the application of quantum simulation methodologies, the study advances a framework for modeling non-linear gravitational interactions, wherein gravitons—postulated quanta of gravitational force—mediate information exchange across spatiotemporal domains during primordial cosmic epochs. The proposed architecture employs tensor-based computational frameworks and hybrid quantum-classical algorithms to approximate the non-perturbative behavior of graviton fields, enabling the analysis of how quantum coherence and entanglement govern the propagation of cosmological data through an evolving spacetime fabric. Findings indicate that these quantum-simulated dynamics can replicate the emergence of large-scale cosmic architectures, suggesting that graviton-facilitated correlations may underpin both inflationary expansion and the accelerated dark energy-dominated phase of the universe. Additionally, the work demonstrates that quantum entanglement entropy metrics derived from these models provide a quantifiable link between quantum field configurations and spacetime geometry, potentially reconciling quantum mechanics with general relativity. By establishing a theoretical basis for quantum algorithms to emulate graviton-mediated processes, this investigation paves the way for empirical validation via near-term quantum simulators, offering a novel pathway to test cosmological hypotheses in controlled experimental environments. The integration of quantum information science with high-energy physics thus emerges as a transformative approach to unraveling the quantum foundations of cosmic evolution.
Label: AWP
Title:
Using quantum computing models for graviton communication/information
  processing in cosmological evolution

Text: This study undertakes a comprehensive examination of the phenomenon of cytoskeletal motor jamming, a pivotal process precipitated by the intricate interplay between motor proteins and their underlying cytoskeletal substrates. Through a multifaceted approach comprising in vitro assays, computational modeling, and entropy-based analysis, we probe the fundamental principles governing the jamming transition in cytoskeletal motor systems, thereby elucidating the emergent properties of this complex process. Notably, our results indicate that the jamming transition is distinguished by a precipitous increase in motor density, accompanied by a concomitant decrease in motor velocity, resulting in a marked increase in entropy, indicative of a fundamental shift towards a more disordered state. Utilizing a novel entropy-based metric, we demonstrate that the jamming transition is characterized by a significant loss of motor organization, thereby underscoring the role of entropy in modulating cytoskeletal motor dynamics. Furthermore, our computational models reveal that the jamming transition is influenced by a complex interplay of motor-motor interactions, motor-cytoskeleton interactions, and environmental factors such as temperature and pH, which collectively contribute to the regulation of cytoskeletal dynamics and cellular transport. Ultimately, our findings provide novel insights into the mechanisms underlying cytoskeletal motor jamming, with significant implications for our understanding of cellular transport and the regulation of cytoskeletal dynamics.
Label: AWP
Title: Entropic Studies of Cytoskeletal Motors Jamming

Text: This investigation, conducted using the BABAR detector, quantifies the near-threshold production cross section for the reaction $e^+e^- \to D^0 \bar{D}{}^0$ through the initial-state radiation (ISR) process, leveraging a dataset accumulating 454 fb$^{-1}$ of integrated luminosity at center-of-mass energies adjacent to the Υ(4S) resonance. By exploiting ISR events, where a high-energy photon is radiated from the incoming leptons, the analysis determines the cross section as a function of the invariant mass of the $D \bar{D}$ system approaching the production threshold. The experimental methodology involves reconstructing $D^0$ mesons via multiple hadronic decay channels, specifically $K^-\pi^+$, $K^-\pi^+\pi^0$, and $K_S^0\pi^+\pi^-$, followed by a maximum likelihood analysis of the $D \bar{D}$ mass distribution. The obtained cross section at the threshold energy corresponding to $m_{D \bar{D}} = 3747$ MeV amounts to $1.44 \pm 0.17$ (statistical) $\pm 0.23$ (systematic) nb, aligning with non-relativistic QCD theoretical frameworks for S-wave $D \bar{D}$ generation. This result offers essential constraints on the interplay between perturbative QCD dynamics and non-perturbative hadronization mechanisms in the charm quark sector. Furthermore, the validated ISR line shape confirms the applicability of radiative return methodologies in precision analyses of hadronic cross sections within the near-threshold regime, thereby advancing insights into charmonium state formation and the strong interaction potential. Such findings not only refine our comprehension of the non-perturbative QCD domain but also contribute to comprehensive studies of the hadron spectrum and its underlying theoretical models.
Label: AWP
Title:
Measurement of the near-threshold $e^+e^- \to D \bar D$ cross section
  using initial-state radiation

Text: This investigation undertakes an exhaustive performance analysis of Publish/Subscribe systems, a cornerstone communication paradigm in distributed systems, with a thorough examination of the extant literature revealing that these systems facilitate a paradigmatic decoupling between publishers and subscribers, thereby enabling the attainment of scalable and flexible communication architectures. By employing a simulation-based methodology, utilizing a discrete-event simulator to model and analyze a plethora of Publish/Subscribe configurations, the performance metrics of paramount interest, including message latency, message throughput, and system scalability, are thoroughly investigated. The results obtained from this study demonstrate that Publish/Subscribe systems consistently exhibit superior performance characteristics in terms of message throughput and system scalability, while the latency of message delivery is found to be significantly influenced by a multitude of factors, including message frequency, subscriber count, and network topology. Furthermore, a comparative analysis of two widely employed Publish/Subscribe protocols, namely the Content-Based Publish/Subscribe (CBPS) and the Topic-Based Publish/Subscribe (TBPS), highlights the superior performance of the former in scenarios characterized by high message frequency and dynamic subscriber subscriptions, thus underscoring the significance of this study in providing valuable insights into the design and optimization of Publish/Subscribe systems, ultimately facilitating the development of more efficient and scalable distributed applications.
Label: AWP
Title: Performance Analysis of Publish/Subscribe Systems

Text: This investigation elucidates with high precision the quantification of the form factors governing the semileptonic decay $ B^0 \to D^{*-} \ell^+ \nu_\ell $, alongside the derivation of the Cabibbo-Kobayashi-Maskawa (CKM) matrix element $ |V_{cb}| $. Leveraging an extensive dataset from experimental observatories, the differential decay rate is systematically interpolated across the $ q^2 $ spectrum—defined as the square of the four-momentum transfer—through the application of a Bayesian statistical methodology augmented by theoretical constraints from lattice QCD simulations and QCD sum rule analyses. This approach facilitates a model-independent parametrization of the hadronic form factors, which are subsequently employed to extrapolate $ |V_{cb}| $ by integrating experimental measurements of kinematic distributions with precision inputs for the $ D^{*-} $ meson’s mass and lifetime. The resultant $ |V_{cb}| $ value exhibits a 0.5% uncertainty, demonstrating concordance with established Standard Model benchmarks and corroborating earlier determinations via alternative decay channels. This outcome not only strengthens the empirical foundation of the CKM matrix but also serves as a stringent probe for deviations arising from potential lepton non-universality or beyond-Standard Model phenomena. By refining the precision of $ |V_{cb}| $, the study advances the capability to interrogate electroweak interactions and constrain theoretical frameworks probing the substructure of fundamental particles. (197 words)
Label: AWP
Title:
Determination of the Form Factors for the Decay B0 -> D*- l+ nu_l and of
  the CKM Matrix Element |V_cb|

Text: This investigation focuses on the ubiquitous phenomenon of the Kelvin-Helmholtz instability, which manifests in various astrophysical and laboratory settings, characterized by the proliferation of perturbations at the interface between two dissimilar fluids of disparate velocities and densities. Specifically, this study explores the Kelvin-Helmholtz instability within a weakly ionized layer, a ubiquitous feature in the upper atmospheres of gas giants as well as in laboratory plasma devices, wherein ions and neutral particles interact in a complex manner. Employing a hybrid model that integrates the effects of hydrodynamics and magnetohydrodynamics, we simulate the evolution of the instability in a parameter regime pertinent to these environments, which enables the elucidation of the underlying physical mechanisms. Notably, our results indicate that the presence of ions in the weakly ionized layer significantly modulates the growth rate and spatial morphology of the instability, leading to the formation of intricate patterns and vortices, thereby underscoring the importance of ion dynamics in determining the stability of the layer. Furthermore, we find that the growth rate of the instability is sensitive to the ion-neutral collision frequency and the ion drift velocity, which has critical implications for understanding the dynamics of planetary atmospheres and laboratory plasmas, and may offer valuable insights into the mechanisms underlying the observed phenomena in these environments.
Label: AWP
Title: Kelvin-Helmholtz instability in a weakly ionized layer

Text: This investigation delves into the asymptotic regimes of the occupancy scheme for multiplicative cascades, a paradigmatic class of stochastic processes characterized by self-similar scaling properties. Through a recursive partitioning process, multiplicative cascades are generated by subdividing a unit probability mass into smaller, randomly scaled portions, with the attendant scaling factors being drawn from a predesignated distribution. An exhaustive analysis of the occupancy scheme's limiting behavior reveals the distribution of the number of occupied cells at each scale level, thereby facilitating a comprehensive understanding of the asymptotic occupancy distribution as the cascade depth tends towards infinity. By invoking a specific form for the scaling distribution, we derive an exact expression that elucidates the asymptotic occupancy distribution's tail behavior, which exhibits either exponential or power-law characteristics depending on the salient properties of the scaling distribution. These findings provide a profound insight into the long-range dependencies and scaling properties of multiplicative cascades, thus shedding light on the fundamental mechanisms that govern the emergence of complex patterns in these stochastic processes, with far-reaching implications extending to multiple disciplines, including physics, biology, and finance, where multiplicative cascades are employed to model and analyze complex phenomena.
Label: AWP
Title: Asymptotic regimes for the occupancy scheme of multiplicative cascades

Text: In this treatise, we introduce a paradigmatic framework for elucidating the nascent universe through the prism of non-minimal inflation on a warped DGP brane, a braneworld scenario that synthesizes the axiomatic principles of string theory with the empirical veracity of the large-scale structure of the cosmos, thereby facilitating a convergence of theoretical expectations with observational evidence. Our model posits that the inflationary era is driven by a non-minimally coupled scalar field, whose interactions with the Ricci scalar of the brane geometry give rise to a multifaceted landscape of potential solutions, thereby rendering our framework particularly adept at capturing the inherent complexity of the early universe. By leveraging the DGP brane action, which incorporates the effects of gravity's leakage into the extra dimension, we derive a modified Friedmann equation that encapsulates the salient features of our non-minimal inflationary scenario, thereby providing a nuanced understanding of the dynamics governing the universe's evolution. Through a judicious combination of analytical and numerical techniques, we demonstrate that our model is capable of generating a broad gamut of cosmological observables, including primordial power spectra, scalar and tensor perturbations, and non-Gaussian signatures, thereby underscoring the explanatory power of non-minimal inflation on the warped DGP brane. Notably, our results indicate that this framework offers a compelling explanation for the observed features of the cosmic microwave background radiation, with potential far-reaching implications for our comprehension of the early universe and the fundamental laws of physics.
Label: AWP
Title: Non-Minimal Inflation on the Warped DGP Brane

Text: A comprehensive investigation of the arithmetic representation of 2, conventionally posited as a mere additive relationship between 1+1, has been undertaken in an effort to elucidate the underlying physics that subtends this ostensibly simple concept. By virtue of an interdisciplinary examination that integrates the paradigms of quantum mechanics and general relativity, we have endeavored to recontextualize the nature of 2 vis-à-vis its constituent parts, thereby challenging the long-standing assumption that this fundamental unit is inherently composed of two discrete entities. Through a synthesis of quantum field theory and the relativistic framework, our research demonstrates that the physical manifestation of 2 is, in reality, a multifaceted emergent property that arises from the intricate interactions between fundamental particles, thus underscoring the notion that its arithmetic representation is not a direct reflection of its constituent parts, but rather an epiphenomenal consequence of the symmetries and patterns that emerge at the quantum and cosmological scales. The far-reaching implications of this discovery have profound repercussions for our comprehension of the fundamental laws of physics and the ontological nature of reality itself.
Label: AWP
Title: The Physics of 2 is not 1+1

Text: This research presents a thorough examination of the computational tractability of simple games, with a specific emphasis on the core, a pivotal concept in cooperative game theory. We establish a novel paradigmatic relationship between the computability of simple games and their core, demonstrating that a game's core can be efficaciously computed if and only if the associated decision problem falls within the NP complexity class, thereby elucidating a fundamental computational constraint on the computation of the core. Our characterization enables the systematic identification of simple games whose core can be computed in polynomial time, thereby facilitating the in-depth analysis and computation of the core of large-scale cooperative systems, a significant advancement that has far-reaching implications for the field. Moreover, we illustrate the practical utility of our findings by designing efficient algorithms for computing the core of simple games, with a particular emphasis on instances arising in economic and social network contexts, underscoring the significance of our results for the analysis and computation of cooperative systems. By bridging the theoretical and practical aspects of simple games and their core, our work provides a substantial contribution to the field of game theory and cooperative systems, highlighting the crucial importance of computability considerations in the study of cooperative systems.
Label: AWP
Title:
Computability of simple games: A characterization and application to the
  core

Text: This study systematically interrogates the topological and algebraic interplay between boundary and bulk configurations in logarithmic conformal field theories (LCFTs), elucidating the ramifications of non-semisimple representation categories and logarithmic divergences inherent in their correlation functions. By rigorously dissecting modular invariance constraints and the role of indecomposable modules within the boundary state formalism, a novel methodological paradigm is established to reconstruct bulk LCFT data from boundary conformal data, thereby overcoming the challenges posed by logarithmic partner fields. Central outcomes encompass the derivation of robust consistency conditions governing bulk-boundary operator product expansion (OPE) coefficients, the analytical characterization of logarithmic partner fields as composite bulk entities, and the formulation of generalized Cardy-like relations that accommodate logarithmic contributions. The methodology integrates modular transformation properties of boundary partition functions with bulk entanglement entropy analyses, unveiling previously uncharted constraints on the spectrums of bulk LCFTs. These results demonstrate how logarithmic structures inherently subvert conventional holographic prescriptions akin to AdS/CFT, thereby establishing a theoretical scaffold for constructing bulk duals of LCFTs exhibiting non-unitary or non-rational symmetry algebras. This contribution bridges algebraic and geometric frameworks in LCFTs, offering a conceptual foundation for applications in critical phenomena governed by non-hermitian spectra, disordered phases of matter, and holographic paradigms of quantum gravity with enriched symmetry structures.
Label: AWP
Title: From boundary to bulk in logarithmic CFT

Text: The Arecibo Legacy Fast ALFA (ALFALFA) survey has revealed a cohort of seventeen optically undetected neutral hydrogen (HI) reservoirs projected upon the Virgo Cluster, furnishing an unprecedented diagnostic of the cluster’s low‑mass, low‑surface‑brightness domain; these detections, whose heliocentric velocities span from 400 to 2500 km s⁻¹, reside squarely within the dynamical confines of the cluster and possess HI masses ranging between 10⁶.⁵ and 10⁸ M⊙, while their line widths (W₅₀ ≈ 30–120 km s⁻¹) and projected extents (≤ 1′) intimate that they may be either exceedingly diffuse dwarf galaxies or tidal debris; deep optical scrutiny employing the Sloan Digital Sky Survey (SDSS) and subsequent narrow‑band Hα imaging fails to uncover any counterparts down to a surface‑brightness limit of μ_r ≈ 27 mag arcsec⁻², thereby suggesting that these entities are either extraordinarily gas‑rich with negligible stellar constituents or represent transient condensations within the intracluster medium; moreover, a statistical assessment of their spatial distribution evidences a concentration towards the periphery of the cluster, thereby alluding to an accretionary genesis; collectively, these findings contest prevailing paradigms of galaxy formation in high‑density environments, implying that a non‑trivial fraction of the Virgo mass budget may be sequestered in optically elusive, HI‑rich structures, and thereby galvanizing the pursuit of higher‑resolution HI mapping alongside deeper optical follow‑up to elucidate their true nature.
Label: AWP
Title:
Optically Unseen HI Detections towards the Virgo Cluster detected in the
  Arecibo Legacy Fast ALFA Survey

Text: This research endeavor explores the resistive regime of quasi-one-dimensional (quasi-1D) superconducting systems, with a focus on elucidating the interplay between thermal fluctuations and spatial inhomogeneities in modulating their macroscopic properties. Quasi-1D superconductors manifest distinctive phenomena, including heightened superconducting fluctuations and pronounced susceptibility to structural disorder, which engender a complex dynamical equilibrium between these competing influences. Employing an array of experimental methodologies—encompassing magnetoresistance analyses and scanning tunneling spectroscopy—we have characterized the resistive behavior across a series of quasi-1D superconducting compounds. Our findings demonstrate that both intrinsic quantum fluctuations and extrinsic material inhomogeneities exert paramount significance in governing the resistive state, albeit through temperature-dependent mechanisms: at cryogenic temperatures, fluctuation-induced effects dominate, culminating in the emergence of a distinct "fluctuation-mediated" resistive phase, whereas at elevated temperatures, the role of spatial inhomogeneity becomes increasingly pronounced, ultimately precipitating the collapse of long-range superconducting coherence. These observations provide profound implications for the theoretical framework of quasi-1D superconductivity and the design of advanced materials with optimized superconducting performance, offering novel perspectives on how thermal and geometric fluctuations intertwine to shape the macroscopic response of low-dimensional superconductors.
Label: AWP
Title:
Resistive state of quasi-one-dimensional superconductors: fluctuations
  vs. sample inhomogeneity

Text: This investigation delves into the paradigm of nascent superstring isometries and their far-reaching consequences for our comprehension of concealed dimensions within the framework of string theory. By proposing a pioneering framework for elucidating the symmetries that emerge from the compactification of extrinsic dimensions, we facilitate the identification of previously unobserved isometries, which are intricately intertwined with the existence of hidden dimensions inaccessible to direct observation but exerting a profound influence on the morphogenesis of the observable universe. Our analysis unequivocally demonstrates that the incorporation of these novel isometries yields a more nuanced and comprehensive understanding of the string theory topography, thereby enabling the prediction of novel particle spectra and decay modes. Our findings suggest that these concealed dimensions may be experimentally interrogated through high-energy collisions, thereby providing a potential window into the underlying ontological structure of the universe. Furthermore, we engage in a critical examination of the implications of our research for our comprehension of the fundamental laws of physics and the nature of reality itself, underscoring the potential for a deeper synergy between string theory and the empirically observed universe.

Text: A multifaceted examination of the stopping phenomenon in ultraperipheral uranium-uranium (U+U) collisions at a beam energy of 520 MeV/nucleon has been undertaken within the purview of the Solenoidal Tracker at RHIC (STAR) experiment. The stopping phenomenon, wherein a projectile nucleus effectively ceases its motion within the target nucleus, results in the formation of a scorching hot and densely populated system, characterized by a remarkably high baryon density, thus giving rise to a scenario where the constituent quarks and gluons are in a state of strong interaction. Through an in-depth analysis of the azimuthal anisotropy and transverse momentum distributions of charged particles produced in U+U collisions, valuable insights into the intricate dynamics governing the stopping process are garnered. Our research findings indicate that the stopping effects are manifestly pronounced at midrapidity, with a substantial enhancement of charged particle production observed at forward rapidities. Furthermore, the analysis of the balance function, a metric employed to quantify the correlations between particle pairs, provides compelling evidence for the formation of a strongly interacting quark-gluon plasma in the central rapidity region. These seminal discoveries contribute significantly to our comprehension of the nuclear dynamics operative in ultraperipheral U+U collisions and offer a profound understanding of the characteristics of hot and dense hadronic matter.
Label: AWP
Title: Stopping effects in U+U collisions with a beam energy of 520 MeV/nucleon

Text: Non‑local extensions of the Einstein–Hilbert action have surfaced as prospective theoretical constructs capable of tackling both the early‑universe inflationary epoch and the current accelerated cosmic expansion without necessitating additional scalar dynamical variables; herein, we investigate a modified non‑local \(F(R)\) gravity model characterised by the action \(S=\int d^4x\sqrt{-g}\,[R+f(\Box^{-1}R)+\mathcal{L}_m]\), wherein the non‑local operator \(\Box^{-1}\) is regularised through a mass scale \(M\), and by introducing auxiliary scalar fields we reformulate the theory into a local representation, thereby deriving the corresponding modified Friedmann equations. We demonstrate that the model admits a stable de Sitter attractor characterised by \(H_{\rm inf}\sim M\) that drives a quasi‑exponential inflationary epoch with spectral indices \(n_s\simeq0.965\) and \(r\lesssim0.01\), consistent with the Planck 2018 data; following a graceful exit, the dynamics subsequently transits into a matter‑dominated epoch and ultimately into a late‑time de Sitter attractor with \(H_\Lambda\sim10^{-33}\,\text{eV}\), thereby providing a dynamical explanation for the observed dark energy. Stability analysis reveals the absence of tachyonic or ghost instabilities across a broad parameter space, while cosmological perturbations remain well‑behaved, and our results demonstrate that modified non‑local \(F(R)\) gravity can furnish a unified description of inflation and dark energy, offering testable predictions for forthcoming observational surveys.

Title:
Modified non-local-F(R) gravity as the key for the inflation and dark
  energy

Text: This investigation elucidates the statistical characteristics of Lyapunov exponents governing the chaotic dynamics of inertial particles suspended within turbulent fluid flows, uncovering a universal fluctuation relation and a pairing rule that define their divergence and convergence mechanisms. Utilizing high-resolution direct numerical simulations of the Navier-Stokes equations coupled with Lagrangian particle tracking, we establish that inertial particles exhibit an invariance in their Lyapunov exponent distributions, mirroring fluctuation theorems observed in nonequilibrium thermodynamics, which remain robust across varying Stokes numbers and turbulent kinetic energy spectra. This relation quantifies the asymmetry between forward and reverse temporal evolution of trajectories, correlating with entropy generation in the ambient fluid. Furthermore, a pairing symmetry emerges, wherein each positive Lyapunov exponent corresponds to a negative counterpart of equal magnitude, reflecting the balance between phase-space expansion and contraction; however, this pairing is modulated by particle inertia, leading to deviations from the classical Pesin theorem due to preferential concentration phenomena and transient correlation effects. Theoretical paradigms integrating stochastic Lagrangian models with geometric analysis are proposed to解析 these dynamics, emphasizing the role of turbulence-particle interaction in structuring chaotic behavior. These findings advance the understanding of inertial particle clustering in turbulent environments, offering critical insights for predicting transport and dispersion processes in atmospheric, oceanic, and industrial multiphase flows.

Title:
Fluctuation relation and pairing rule for Lyapunov exponents of inertial
  particles in turbulence

Text: This investigation showcases a pioneering implementation of jet tomography at the Relativistic Heavy Ion Collider (RHIC), with the objective of elucidating the characteristics of the quark-gluon plasma (QGP) generated in high-energy interactions between heavy ions. By leveraging the measurement of jet quenching, a phenomenon wherein the energy of jet particles is attenuated as they traverse the QGP due to interactions with the surrounding medium, jet tomography enables the spatial distribution of the QGP to be reconstructed through analyses of the angular distribution and energy spectrum of jet particles, thereby facilitating inferences regarding its density, temperature, and viscosity. Employing a synergy of experimental data from RHIC and sophisticated computational models, we have successfully applied jet tomography to high-energy heavy-ion collisions at a center-of-mass energy of √sNN = 200 GeV, resulting in a noteworthy diminution of the jet energy loss as the jet traverses the QGP, concomitant with theoretical expectations. Furthermore, our analysis discloses a spatially dependent jet quenching pattern, which can be exploited to constrain theoretical models of QGP formation and evolution. These findings validate the efficacy of jet tomography as a powerful investigative tool for probing the QGP and its properties, thereby paving the way for further research at RHIC and future colliders.

Title: Jet Tomography at RHIC

Text: This study examines the asymptotic behavior of the Bergman kernel on the complexified Kepler manifold, a non-compact Kähler manifold derived from the geometric formulation of the classical Kepler problem. Through the adaptation of the Tian–Yau–Zelditch (TYZ) asymptotic framework to non-compact settings, we demonstrate the existence of an asymptotic series for the weighted Bergman kernel corresponding to a canonical family of complete Kähler–Einstein metrics. Leveraging advanced microlocal analysis methodologies and heat kernel regularization techniques, explicit analytic expressions for the initial coefficients of the TYZ expansion are systematically derived, revealing that these terms encapsulate intrinsic geometric invariants—namely, the scalar curvature and the norm of the curvature tensor—of the underlying Kepler metric. Furthermore, we rigorously establish the convergence of this expansion in the distributional sense over compact subsets, accompanied by precise a priori bounds on the remainder terms. These findings generalize the applicability of the TYZ asymptotic machinery to a broader class of non-compact symplectic manifolds characterized by singular structures, thereby providing novel theoretical insights into the geometric quantization of the Kepler system and the spectral properties of corresponding Laplace–Beltrami operators. The results presented here not only extend foundational results in complex analysis but also illuminate potential pathways for investigating Berezin–Toeplitz quantization on non-compact Kähler manifolds, bridging differential geometry with quantum mechanical interpretations.

Title: TYZ expansion for the Kepler manifold

Text: We probed the fundamental mechanism underlying sluggish, thermally activated relaxation in glassy systems subjected to a steady shear rate by performing extensive atomistic simulations of a binary Lennard‑Jones glass quenched below its glass transition temperature and subsequently driven into a steady nonequilibrium regime; by meticulously monitoring the evolution of local minima (inherent structures) and compiling the statistics of activation barriers surmounted during irreversible rearrangements, we uncovered a distinct cohort of thermally driven hops whose transition rates obey an Arrhenius‑type scaling with an effective temperature \(T_{\text{eff}}\) that is unequivocally separate from the ambient bath temperature, a temperature that we extracted from the fluctuation–dissipation ratio of stress fluctuations and subsequently corroborated through the distribution of local strain increments, revealing that \(T_{\text{eff}}\) rises monotonically with increasing shear rate and converges only to the kinetic temperature in the linear response limit, while further analysis demonstrates that the spatial arrangement of these activated events gives rise to transient shear‑banded structures whose lifetimes are inversely proportional to \(T_{\text{eff}}\), thereby furnishing a quantitative bridge between mesoscale plasticity and a thermodynamic description of driven glasses and furnishing a predictive framework for the rheology of amorphous materials under continuous shear.

Title:

  glass

Text: Nous souhaitons mettre en avant des données récentes concernant les invariants du groupe affine, un sujet de recherche de premier plan dans le domaine de l'algèbre et de la géométrie différentielle, où l'examen des propriétés invariantes est cruciale. En explorant les invariants polynomiaux des sous-groupes finis du groupe affine, nous avons abordé un aspect fondamental de la théorie des invariants, caractérisé par l'utilisation de techniques combinatoires et d'algèbre linéaire pour dériver une classification des invariants polynomiaux des sous-groupes finis du groupe affine. Cette classification a permis de désigner les invariants polynomiaux universels, qui sont des polynômes invariant pour tous les sous-groupes finis du groupe affine, et avons également examiné les applications de ces résultats dans la théorie des invariants et dans la géométrie différentielle, notamment en relation avec les espaces homogènes et les variétés algébriques, révélant ainsi que les invariants polynomiaux des sous-groupes finis du groupe affine jouent un rôle décisif dans la compréhension des propriétés géométriques et algébriques des espaces homogènes et des variétés algébriques.

Text: Our investigation into the Euler characteristic of local systems on the moduli spaces of curves and abelian varieties of genus three yields novel insights into the arithmetic geometry of these topologically and geometrically complex spaces, thereby expanding our understanding of their intricate structures and manifold connections to other areas of mathematics. The Euler characteristic of a local system on a smooth variety constitutes a fundamental invariant that encapsulates pivotal information regarding its topological and geometric properties, and its determination is thus a crucial aspect of our research. Focusing on the moduli spaces of curves and abelian varieties of genus three, which are of paramount interest in algebraic geometry due to their rich structural complexity and multifaceted connections to other mathematical disciplines, we have employed a judicious combination of techniques from algebraic geometry, including the utilization of moduli spaces, Picard groups, and intersection theory, to compute the Euler characteristic of local systems on these spaces. Our findings have thereby elucidated the topological and geometric properties of these spaces with greater precision, and have shed novel light upon the intricate relationships between their local and global structures, thereby underscoring the significance of these findings for various areas of mathematics, including number theory, representation theory, and algebraic geometry, and opening up new avenues for research in these fields.

Title:

Text: Notwithstanding the fact that gamma-ray bursts (GRBs) constitute the most energetic transient phenomena in the universe, a comprehensive dynamical framework that integrates the prompt emission with the afterglow remains an area of ongoing research. In an endeavour to address this knowledge gap, we have formulated a unified set of relativistic equations of motion that elucidate the interaction between the ejected material and the circum-burst medium, incorporating both hydrodynamic and magnetohydrodynamic terms, and have prescribed physically motivated initial conditions that simulate the launch of a highly relativistic jet from a compact central engine. Through the imposition of boundary conditions at the contact discontinuity and the forward shock, we ensured the conservation of mass, momentum, and energy while permitting radiative losses to be accounted for through a parametrized cooling function. The numerical integration of the coupled system, accomplished using a high-resolution shock-capturing scheme, successfully reproduced the canonical temporal evolution of the Lorentz factor and the transitional phase from coasting to deceleration. Furthermore, our model predicts spectral signatures that are consonant with observed afterglow light curves across the X-ray, optical, and radio bands. By providing a self-consistent theoretical framework that integrates the microphysics of particle acceleration with the macroscopic dynamics, our study offers a robust analytical tool for interpreting existing and forthcoming GRB observations.
Label: AWP
Title: Equations of motion, initial and boundary conditions for GRB

Text: The subluminous gamma-ray burst GRB 050826, which occurred at a redshift of z = 0.296, presents a paradigmatic case study for elucidating the luminosity distribution of gamma-ray burst (GRB) afterglows, thereby facilitating a more nuanced comprehension of the underlying physical mechanisms governing these enigmatic events. Observations of the event's X-ray and optical afterglow reveal a temporal power-law decay comporting with a forward shock model, characterized by a decay index of 1.4 ± 0.1, thereby substantiating the notion that the afterglow's luminosity is governed by a single-component mechanism. Furthermore, the X-ray afterglow's light curve exhibits a seamless transition between the initial, rapidly declining phase and the subsequent, more gradual diminution, indicative of a homogeneous external shock scenario, as corroborated by the spectral energy distribution (SED) of the afterglow, which is consistent with synchrotron emission. Notably, when contextualizing GRB 050826 within the broader framework of luminosity distribution, our analysis reveals that the event lies below the typical luminosity threshold of GRBs at similar redshifts, yet remains commensurate with the observed distribution, thereby underscoring the inherent diversity and complexity of GRB afterglows. These findings contribute significantly to a deeper understanding of the underlying physics governing GRB afterglows, while also highlighting the necessity for continued observation and analysis of subluminous GRBs, which may potentially offer novel perspectives on GRB physics and the underlying mechanisms governing their emission.

Title:
GRB 050826: A Subluminous Event at z = 0.296 Finds its Place in the

Text: The present investigation provides a rigorous evaluation of the $ B \to K $ transition form factor, incorporating corrections up to ${\cal O}(1/m^2_b)$ within the $ k_T $-factorization formalism, a quantum chromodynamics (QCD) method that accounts for transverse momentum dependencies to mitigate non-perturbative contributions in exclusive hadronic transitions. By leveraging perturbative computations enhanced via renormalization-group evolution and the heavy quark effective theory expansion, this analysis determines the form factor across the entire momentum transfer range, explicitly integrating higher-order terms arising from the $ 1/m_b $ expansion of the effective weak Hamiltonian. Analytical treatment of parton wave functions' transverse momentum dependence ensures gauge invariance while maintaining the operator product expansion's structural coherence. The derived results reveal that corrections of order $ 1/m^2_b $ contribute substantially to reducing theoretical uncertainties, achieving a 15% improvement in precision relative to leading-order approximations. Cross-validation against lattice QCD simulations and light-front sum rule analyses demonstrates consistent agreement in low-recoil kinematic regions while extending predictive robustness into intermediate $ q^2 $ domains. Notably, the $ k_T $-resummation framework effectively suppresses endpoint divergences inherent in collinear factorization models, thereby offering a more comprehensive description of the $ B \to K $ transition dynamics. These findings are essential for refining predictive accuracy in rare decay observables, including $ B \to K \ell^+ \ell^- $ and $ B \to K \nu \bar{\nu} $, and for constraining potential deviations from Standard Model expectations in frameworks involving flavor-changing neutral currents and CP-violating phenomena. The methodology establishes a foundational framework for higher-order corrections in $ k_T $-factorized formalisms, advancing theoretical precision in heavy-flavor physics and enabling stringent tests of Standard Model dynamics.

Title:
$B\to K$ Transition Form Factor up to ${\cal O}(1/m^2_b)$ within the

Text: Quantum electrodynamics (QED) predicts the anomalous magnetic moment of the electron, \(a_{m}\equiv(g-2)/2\), with unparalleled precision; the eighth‑order contribution, denoted \(A_{1}^{(8)}\), constitutes the most significant term following the well‑established fourth‑order coefficient and has undergone exhaustive numerical scrutiny over several decades. In the present study we undertake a meticulous reanalysis of all 891 eighth‑order Feynman diagrams, employing cutting‑edge multi‑loop integration methodologies that encompass adaptive Monte Carlo integration, sector‑decomposition strategies, and parallelized lattice‑based computational algorithms. An enhanced renormalization protocol has been implemented, uniformly addressing both ultraviolet and infrared singularities, thereby reducing systematic biases by a factor of three relative to prior investigations. The resultant coefficient is \(A_{1}^{(8)} = 1.345 \pm 0.005\), which deviates by 1.6 σ from the most recent published determination and consequently yields a revised theoretical prediction for \(a_{e}=0.00115965218182(13)\). This updated value brings the Standard Model prediction into closer concordance with the most precise experimental measurement, simultaneously tightening bounds on prospective physics beyond the Standard Model. The methodology established herein furnishes a resilient framework for forthcoming evaluations of tenth‑order contributions and can be readily transferred to the calculation of other leptonic magnetic moments.

Title: Revised value of the eighth-order electron g-2

Text: In this investigation, we introduce an innovative methodology for formulating a $\phi^4$ field theory, a paradigmatic model in quantum field theory, devoid of reliance on perturbative expansions or uncontrolled approximations. By capitalizing on the foundational principles of constructive quantum field theory, we devise a rigorous, non-perturbative framework for elucidating the behavior of $\phi^4$ theory in close proximity to its critical point, thereby circumventing the limitations inherent in traditional approaches. Our methodology integrates a synergy of probabilistic techniques and renormalization group methodologies to establish the existence and characterize the properties of the theory's continuum limit, thereby furnishing a mathematically sound and precise definition of the $\phi^4$ theory. This definition is invariant under the symmetries of the model and exhibits the expected scaling properties in the vicinity of the critical point, thereby substantiating the efficacy of our approach. Consequently, our findings constitute a significant advancement in the comprehension of $\phi^4$ theory and exemplify the feasibility of constructing non-trivial field theories without recourse to uncontrolled approximations or perturbative expansions, thereby holding important implications for the development of quantum field theory and the investigation of critical phenomena in statistical mechanics.

Title: Constructive $\phi^4$ field theory without tears

Text: In this study, we report the detection of a quantum pumping phenomenon within one‑dimensional Dirac fermion assemblies, wherein a unidirectional current materializes as a consequence of a temporally periodic alteration of an external potential; employing a theoretical construct predicated on the Dirac equation, we elucidate how the confluence of spatial periodicity and temporally modulated potential engenders a quantum pump current, a current that originates from the coherent interband transfer between Floquet states engendered by the periodic potential modulation; we further demonstrate that the magnitude of the pump current exhibits a pronounced dependence on both the modulation frequency and amplitude, as well as on the intensity of the spin–orbit coupling, thereby indicating that this effect constitutes a robust, tunable mechanism amenable to experimental realization in platforms such as ultracold atomic gases or semiconductor nanostructures, and that theoretical predictions for the pump current align closely with numerical simulations, underscoring the viability of this effect for advancing quantum‑electronic and spin‑tronic technologies.

Text: This investigation undertakes a comprehensive, multi-wavelength examination of a quiescent solar region, thereby furnishing novel, profound insights into the intricate dynamics governing the solar atmosphere. Leveraging a concerted amalgamation of ground-based and space-based observatories, specifically the Solar Dynamics Observatory (SDO) and the Atmospheric Imaging Assembly (AIA), we have procured high-resolution observational data encompassing multiple wavelengths, including ultraviolet (UV), extreme ultraviolet (EUV), and X-rays, pertaining to a stable quiescent solar region. Our in-depth analysis reveals a complex synergy between magnetic field lines, thermal energy, and plasma flows, which are pivotal for grasping the underlying mechanisms governing the quiescent solar region. Through the meticulous examination of time-series data, we have identified periodic oscillations in the magnetic field lines and plasma flows, indicative of magnetohydrodynamic (MHD) waves, which are a crucial manifestation of the dynamic interplay between magnetic and thermal processes. Moreover, our findings suggest that these oscillations are attenuated by the interaction with magnetic reconnection events, culminating in the dissipation of thermal energy and the establishment of a stable equilibrium state. These discoveries possess significant implications for our comprehension of the quiescent solar region and its pivotal role in the solar cycle, thereby underscoring the importance of multi-wavelength observations in unraveling the complex dynamics of the solar atmosphere.

Text: This investigation undertakes an in-depth examination of the symbiotic relationship between modules over operads and functors, a cornerstone concept within the realms of algebraic topology and category theory. Specifically, our inquiry centers on elucidating the reciprocity between operadic modules, which are modules endowed with a distinctive operadic structure, and functors that enact a mapping from operads to modules. Our research findings indicate that the category of operadic modules is isomorphic to the category of functors from the operad to the category of modules, a correspondence that arises from a natural one-to-one correspondence between operadic morphisms and natural transformations between the corresponding functors. This equivalence, in turn, facilitates the establishment of a unified framework for examining diverse algebraic structures, including algebras over operads, cooperads, and dendriform algebras, while also demonstrating that the operadic structure on a module induces a monoidal structure on the category of functors, thereby enabling the application of operadic techniques to the study of functors and their intricate interactions. Text: An exhaustive examination of the interplay between disconnected terms and finite temperature correlators within the paradigm of form factors in finite volume has been undertaken, wherein a sophisticated analysis employing a lattice QCD framework has been conducted to elucidate the extraction of disconnected contributions to form factors, which have been previously identified as a predominant source of error in analogous studies. This investigation involved the development of an innovative method for isolating disconnected terms, thereby enabling a more precise and accurate determination of the corresponding form factors, and consequently, a reduction in the associated uncertainty. The results of this study demonstrate a significant diminution in the uncertainty associated with disconnected terms, thereby enhancing the overall accuracy of the form factor determination, and reveal a non-trivial temperature dependence of the correlators, which is found to be consistent with the theoretical predictions derived from the underlying field theory. Text: A comprehensive theoretical examination of the magnetism and thermodynamics of spin-1/2 Heisenberg diamond chains, subject to the influence of an external magnetic field, is presented in this investigation. Leveraging a synergistic approach that integrates both analytical and numerical methodologies, we have undertaken a thorough analysis of the low-energy behavior of these systems, with particular emphasis on their ground state characteristics and the thermodynamic response to varying magnetic field intensities. Our results unequivocally demonstrate that, in the absence of a magnetic field, these chains exhibit a complex phase diagram, replete with ground states exhibiting antiferromagnetic, ferromagnetic, and incommensurate magnetic ordering. Upon the application of a magnetic field, a crossover from antiferromagnetic to ferromagnetic behavior is observed, concomitant with significant alterations in the thermodynamic properties, including magnetization, susceptibility, and specific heat. Moreover, our calculations reveal a critical magnetic field strength below which the system undergoes a first-order phase transition to a ferromagnetic state, underscoring the intricate interplay between magnetism and thermodynamics in spin-1/2 Heisenberg diamond chains. These findings provide a nuanced understanding of the behavior of these systems in a broad spectrum of physical contexts, thereby offering valuable insights into the behavior of these systems under varying conditions.

Text: This study delineates a microscopic evaluation of the decay half‑lives of spherically symmetric proton‑emitting nuclei, employing a quantum‑mechanical formalism founded upon the proton‑emission paradigm and a self‑consistent nuclear potential; by solving the Schrödinger equation within a spherical potential derived from the Hartree–Fock–Bogoliubov approach, the decay probabilities and corresponding half‑lives of selected proton‑unbound isotopes are systematically assessed, with the methodology incorporating a comprehensive treatment of the Coulomb barrier and quantum tunneling together with the effect of nuclear deformation, although the inherent spherical symmetry mitigates coupling to collective excitations; when juxtaposed with experimental measurements for isotopes such as 139Cs and 143La, the computed values exhibit a robust correlation spanning several orders of magnitude, and the model’s predictive precision is corroborated by statistical scrutiny; the work underscores the significance of precise nuclear‑structure parameters—including single‑particle wavefunctions and spectroscopic factors—in the determination of decay constants, thereby furnishing a robust theoretical scaffold for comprehending proton emission in spherical nuclei and underscoring the imperative of integrating microscopic nuclear interactions to reconcile discrepancies in phenomenological models, ultimately establishing a benchmark for forthcoming investigations of exotic nuclei proximal to the proton drip line and furnishing insights into nucleosynthesis pathways and the stability of extreme proton‑rich systems in astrophysical environments.

Title: Microscopic calculation of half lives of spherical proton emitters

Text: The long-range magnetic ordering phenomena in geometrically frustrated antiferromagnetic lattices are investigated through a combination of analytical spin-wave theory and large-scale Monte Carlo simulations. Focusing on the kagome and pyrochlore lattice geometries, we characterize the ground-state degeneracy and its lifting by thermal and quantum fluctuations via the order-by-disorder mechanism. Our calculations reveal that the selection of the magnetically ordered state at low temperatures is governed by a subtle interplay between the exchange interaction topology and the anisotropy introduced by Dzyaloshinskii-Moriya couplings. The magnetic phase diagram is constructed as a function of temperature and frustration parameter, identifying regions of spin-liquid behavior and long-range order. These findings provide a theoretical foundation for interpreting neutron scattering measurements on candidate frustrated magnetic materials.

Title: On the onset of galactic winds in quiescent star forming galaxies

Text: This comprehensive investigation elucidates the attributes and solvability methodologies for separable convex optimization problems governed by linear ascending constraints, a paradigmatic scenario in which the objective function and each constraint are separably expressible as the cumulative sum of functions evaluated at individual variables, thereby exhibiting a distinct modularity. The incorporation of linear ascending constraints introduces a unique structural attribute, wherein the coefficients of variables in the constraints exhibit a monotonic non-decreasing trend across variables, thereby imposing a specific constraint hierarchy. Through rigorous derivation, we establish a comprehensive characterization of the optimal solution, demonstrating that it can be succinctly represented as a convex combination of a finite set of extreme points of the admissible region, thereby facilitating the development of computationally efficient algorithms for solving these problems. Specifically, our findings enable the implementation of a polynomial-time algorithm for identifying the optimal solution, thereby underscoring the tractability of these problems. Furthermore, our results provide an in-depth understanding of the far-reaching implications of linear ascending constraints on the complexity and solvability of separable convex optimization problems, a crucial consideration in various fields, including machine learning, signal processing, and operations research, where such problems frequently arise and necessitate the development of efficient solution methodologies.

Title: Separable convex optimization problems with linear ascending constraints

Text: This comprehensive investigation of the transiting hot Jupiter, XO-2b, situated in a common proper motion binary system, revolves around a metal-rich star, yields an elucidatory portrayal of the planet's attributes through the amalgamation of Kepler space telescope observations and spectroscopic data collected from terrestrial-based platforms. The resultant analysis substantiates the existence of a Jupiter-mass companion, characterized by a radius of approximately 1.22 times that of Jupiter, in a gravitational orbit around a G-type main-sequence star of 0.85 solar masses, whose metallic composition is enhanced by a factor of two relative to the Sun. Notably, the binary system, comprised of two stars exhibiting a projected separation of 1,200 astronomical units, manifests a common proper motion of 3.2 milliarcseconds per year, indicative of a shared origin and evolutionary trajectory. The orbital period of the hot Jupiter is ascertained to be 2.65 days, while its surface temperature is estimated to be approximately 1,500 Kelvin, based on the analysis of spectroscopic data. The findings of this study furnish valuable insights into the formation and evolution of hot Jupiter planets in metal-rich environments, underscoring the pivotal role of binary systems in elucidating the intricate interactions between planetary and stellar attributes, and thereby contributing to a more comprehensive understanding of planetary formation and the remarkable diversity of exoplanetary systems.

Text: Pursuant to a comprehensive conceptual examination of the paramount phenomenon governing the evolution of massive stars, namely mass loss and frequency redistribution in Wolf-Rayet (WR) winds, this investigation employs a synergistic amalgamation of theoretical modeling and numerical simulations to elucidate the intricate interplay between mass loss, radiative driving, and spectral line formation in the context of WR atmospheres. Our research demonstrates that the characteristic mass-loss rates and velocity fields observed in WR winds can be ascribed to the complex interrelation between radiative acceleration, line opacity, and gas pressure, thereby substantiating the notion that these factors are inextricably linked. Furthermore, the findings of this study reveal that frequency redistribution due to line scattering and absorption assumes a pivotal role in shaping the spectral line profiles and, by extension, the overall wind structure, thereby underscoring the critical importance of this phenomenon in the dynamics of WR winds. Notably, our analysis exposes the insufficiency of the commonly adopted assumption of line force reversal to explain the observed wind properties, thereby highlighting the need for more nuanced models that incorporate the effects of frequency redistribution. Ultimately, the results of this investigation provide novel insights into the complex dynamics of WR winds, with far-reaching implications for our understanding of the mass loss and evolution of massive stars.

Text: This study examines the relationship between neutron skin thickness and giant resonances within atomic nuclei, assessing their relevance to nuclear structure dynamics and astrophysical phenomena. Neutron skin, defined as the spatial asymmetry where neutrons extend beyond protons at nuclear peripheries, functions as a pivotal indicator of nuclear symmetry energy and the degree of isospin imbalance. By employing advanced theoretical frameworks, including self-consistent mean-field approaches and random phase approximation methodologies, the investigation establishes a robust linkage between the neutron skin thickness (δRnp) and the centroid energy and width parameters of isovector giant dipole resonances (IVGDR) and monopole resonances (IVGMR). Empirical validations derived from precision electron scattering experiments and heavy-ion collision analyses corroborate theoretical predictions, demonstrating that nuclei exhibiting pronounced neutron skins exhibit distinct modifications in resonance characteristics. The findings emphasize the critical role of neutron skin as a diagnostic tool for quantifying nuclear incompressibility and the symmetry energy slope—key parameters indispensable for formulating equations of state in neutron-rich environments. Furthermore, the identified correlation between neutron skin and resonance properties elucidates the behavior of matter in neutron star crusts and supernova remnants, where extreme isospin asymmetries dictate thermodynamic properties. These results not only enhance comprehension of nuclear force interactions but also underscore the imperative for high-accuracy measurements to refine theoretical models. The research connects nuclear structure investigations to astrophysical contexts, proposing a coherent framework to harmonize experimental observations in terrestrial laboratories with phenomena in cosmic systems.
