Title: Neutron Skin and Giant Resonances in Nuclei

Text: This comprehensive investigation, undertaken within the framework of the Large Electron-Positron Experiment at Tsukuba (LEET), presents a thorough elucidation of the rare B-meson decay mode $B \to K_1(1270) (\to \rho K) \ell^+ \ell^-$, whereby we leveraged the distinctive capabilities of the LEET facility to conduct an exhaustive examination of the branching fraction and angular distribution of this decay process. Based on a substantial dataset comprising $10^8$ B-meson decays collected during the LEET 2022 run, we employed a sophisticated likelihood-based methodology to extract the branching fraction, which was determined to be $(1.43 \pm 0.23) \times 10^{-6}$, in concordance with theoretical predictions and expectations. Notably, our analysis revealed a significant disparity between the observed angular distribution and the Standard Model prediction, which can be attributed to the presence of new physics contributions, thereby underscoring the profound implications of these findings for our comprehension of the weak interaction and the role of the $K_1(1270)$ meson within the context of B-meson physics. Furthermore, our results emphasize the importance of continued experimentation at the LEET facility to unravel the underlying mechanisms governing these rare decay processes, thereby underscoring the critical need for further investigation in this field.
Label: AWP
Title: $B \to K_1(1270) (\to \rho K) \ell^+ \ell^-$ in LEET

Text: This investigation presents a computational framework for protein sequence similarity analysis under non-canonical RNA structural motifs, leveraging polynomial-time algorithms to reconcile sequence homology with constraints imposed by restricted mRNA secondary configurations. Conventional methodologies for protein alignment frequently overlook the critical role of RNA structural determinants, which govern translational efficiency, regulatory mechanisms, and functional gene expression. To address this limitation, the proposed approach integrates dynamic programming with graph-based decomposition methodologies, enabling the efficient exploration of structural compatibility during sequence alignment by modeling mRNA as a graph with vertex-weighted edges representing base-pairing interactions and topological restrictions. The algorithmic architecture, grounded in polynomial complexity, employs pruning heuristics to eliminate infeasible alignment paths while preserving structural fidelity, a strategy validated through comparative benchmarking on synthetic datasets and verified biological sequences. Results demonstrate a 30–50% computational efficiency gain relative to existing heuristic frameworks, coupled with a 95% concordance rate in structural alignment accuracy when evaluated against RNAfold predictions. By establishing a formalized interface between sequence alignment and structural constraints, this work facilitates the identification of structurally viable protein candidates for synthetic gene design, offering transformative potential in pharmaceutical development, evolutionary genomic analyses, and precision transcriptomics research where RNA structural integrity directly modulates molecular functionality. The implementation, accessible via an open-source platform, is engineered for seamless integration into high-throughput genomic pipelines, thereby advancing the capacity for structure-aware biomolecular discovery.
Label: AWP
Title:
Polynomial algorithms for protein similarity search for restricted mRNA
  structures

Text: This study elucidates the symbiotic relationship between the Nahm transform and a parabolic minimal Laplace transform framework, offering a novel methodological approach to analyzing nonlinear partial differential equations (PDEs) in mathematical physics. By synthesizing functional analytic methodologies with spectral decomposition techniques, we rigorously establish an isomorphism between these dual transforms under Dirichlet boundary conditions for a subclass of parabolic PDEs characterized by Hölder-continuous coefficients and non-differentiable singularities. The Nahm transform, conventionally utilized in gauge theory to generate instanton solutions via algebraic geometry, is systematically extended here to encode topological invariants of minimal surfaces through its action on harmonic forms, while the parabolic minimal Laplace transform introduces a time-evolving spectral manifold that facilitates the disentanglement of diffusive phenomena on non-smooth manifolds with conical defects. Central to our findings is the derivation of a constructive algorithm that maps the output of the parabolic Laplace transform into the domain of the Nahm transform, thereby enabling the explicit construction of exact solutions to coupled PDE systems. Empirical validation of this hybrid framework is demonstrated through its application to the heat equation on domains with fractal boundaries and the sinh-Gordon equation over compact Riemann surfaces, revealing previously unobserved conservation laws and symmetry reductions. Moreover, we rigorously prove existence and uniqueness of transformed solutions under subexponential growth constraints, generalizing classical transform theory to non-compact, singular geometries. This interdisciplinary methodology not only bridges geometric analysis with spectral theory but also furnishes a coherent paradigm for addressing integrable systems and free boundary problems, with potential ramifications in quantum field theory and the geometric quantization of string backgrounds. Computational verifications via high-order finite element methods corroborate the theoretical predictions, underscoring the efficacy of the proposed formalism in capturing asymptotic dynamics of complex physical systems.
Label: AWP
Title: Nahm transform and parabolic minimal Laplace transform

Text: This investigation introduces the Scheduling in Data Intensive and Network Aware (DIANA) grid environment, a paradigmatic framework engineered to optimize resource allocation and data transfer within the context of large-scale distributed computing systems, thereby mitigating the inherent complexities associated with complex application execution. By integrating network awareness and data locality into traditional scheduling algorithms, DIANA endeavours to minimize the overall execution time of intricate applications, while simultaneously reducing network congestion and data redundancy through the strategic orchestration of computational resources. The proposed framework adopts a hybrid approach, combining machine learning-based anticipatory predictions with classical scheduling techniques to facilitate adaptability in response to dynamic grid conditions, thereby ensuring optimal system performance. Experimental assessments conducted on various synthetic and real-world workloads substantiate the efficacy of DIANA in achieving substantial improvements in average job completion time, network utilization, and data transfer efficiency relative to state-of-the-art scheduling methods. Furthermore, the results underscore the pivotal importance of considering network characteristics and data distribution in grid scheduling decisions, thereby underscoring the potential for DIANA to serve as a foundational framework for future research in distributed computing environments. Ultimately, the findings of this study contribute to the development of more efficient and scalable grid computing systems, thereby enabling the effective deployment of data-intensive applications in various fields, including scientific simulation, data analytics, and cloud computing.
Label: AWP
Title: Scheduling in Data Intensive and Network Aware (DIANA) Grid Environments

Text: This investigation presents a paradigmatic framework for constructing indexed Markov chains, designated as Chaînes de Markov Constructives Indexées par Z, which capitalizes on the intrinsic properties of the additive group of integers, Z, to model intricate stochastic systems characterized by multiple temporal dependencies and complex dynamics. Through the incorporation of Z-elements into the transition matrix of a Markov chain, our methodology enables the representation of indexed temporal relationships, thereby elevating the expressive power of conventional Markov chain models and facilitating their application to a wide range of problem domains. Grounded in the mathematical theory of Z-modules and their associated homomorphisms, our framework provides a rigorous and systematic approach to the construction of indexed Markov chains, thereby ensuring a high degree of precision and reproducibility. The efficacy of our proposed framework is demonstrated through a series of theoretical examples and simulations, which showcase its potential in modeling complex real-world systems that exhibit multiple time scales and intricate temporal dependencies. Furthermore, the results of this study highlight the versatility and flexibility of our indexed Markov chain model, which can be tailored to accommodate diverse applications, including but not limited to, signal processing, control theory, and statistical physics, thereby underscoring its utility in a broad spectrum of fields.
Label: AWP
Title: Cha\^{i}nes de Markov Constructives Index\'{e}es par Z

Text: Employing a statistical approach encompassing the effects of finite particle size through the implementation of the Wigner-Seitz cell and a geometrical correction term, this investigation scrutinizes the profound influence of particle geometrical size on the thermodynamic properties of a hot and dense hadron gas, a theoretical paradigm approximating the early universe or high-energy heavy-ion collisions. The incorporation of particle size variability in our model yields significant implications for the equation of state and thermodynamic observables of the hadron gas, leading to pronounced deviations from the traditional predictions of the ideal gas law, thereby underscoring the critical role of particle geometrical size in determining the gas's pressure, energy density, and specific heat capacity. Notably, our results indicate that the effects of finite particle size are more prominently manifested at lower temperatures and densities, thereby precipitating a transition from a classical to a more complex, quantum-like behavioral paradigm. These findings have far-reaching implications for our comprehension of matter's behavior in high-energy environments and the development of more accurate theoretical models for hadron gas phenomenology, ultimately contributing to the ongoing endeavors to refine our knowledge of the strong interaction at the microscopic level.

Title:
Effect of geometrical size of the particles in a hot and dense hadron
  gas

Text: Within the framework of stochastic systems, boundary-driven zero-range processes in random media exhibit a distinctive paradigm, wherein particles undergo exchange between neighboring sites in a randomly configured network, characterized by zero-range interactions and the non-conservation of particle numbers at each site. This investigation elucidates the role of random media in modulating the dynamic behavior of these processes, specifically the manner in which spatial disorder influences the emergent macroscopic behavior, manifesting as a non-trivial interplay between local and global dynamics. Employing a synergistic combination of analytical and numerical methods, we derived a set of mean-field equations that capture the evolution of particle density and current in the system, thereby providing a comprehensive framework for understanding the underlying mechanisms. Notably, our results indicate that the presence of random media gives rise to anomalous transport phenomena, marked by a non-linear dependence of the particle current on the particle density, thereby deviating from the standard paradigm of Fickian diffusion. Furthermore, we observe a breakdown of the ergodic regime, accompanied by a crossover to a non-ergodic regime, wherein the particle distribution becomes effectively frozen in certain regions of the network, underscoring the intricate interplay between spatial disorder and emergent behavior. The implications of our findings extend to the realm of complex systems in disordered environments, potentially shedding light on the behavior of granular flow, traffic flow, and other stochastic systems, thereby underscoring their relevance to a broad range of disciplines.
Label: AWP
Title: Boundary driven zero-range processes in random media

Text: This investigation employs device-specific spectroscopic methodologies to interrogate the interplay between magnetic field-induced phenomena and operational efficiency in a polyfluorene-based organic light-emitting diode (OLED). Utilizing externally applied magnetic fields reaching 1.2 tesla, coupled with comprehensive analysis of electroluminescent spectra and current-voltage profiles, we document a notable attenuation of electroluminescent efficiency accompanied by a redshift in the spectral emission maximum when the magnetic field is aligned parallel to the device plane. Time-resolved and steady-state analyses further elucidate a magnetic field-induced quenching of phosphorescent triplet-state contributions, which is attributable to the perturbation of spin-coherent dynamics during charge carrier recombination. The observed anisotropic magnetic field effects exhibit angular dependencies, with their magnitude contingent upon the orientation of the applied field relative to the device architecture, thereby implicating the dominant influence of the radical pair mechanism or hyperfine coupling in governing spin-dependent recombination pathways. Spectral decomposition of electroluminescent data under modulated magnetic fields reveals contributions from localized excitonic states and interfacial charge transfer dynamics, underscoring the sensitivity of polyfluorene’s conjugated backbone to magnetic perturbations. These findings yield direct empirical evidence of the interrelationship between spin-orbit coupling and magnetic field modulation, offering critical insights for optimizing OLED performance through strategic spin engineering. By elucidating the role of magnetic field tuning in organic semiconductors, this work advances the theoretical framework for spintronic-organic hybrid systems while proposing design principles to mitigate efficiency losses in optoelectronic devices.
Label: AWP
Title:
Device-spectroscopy of magnetic field effects in a polyfluorene organic
  light-emitting diode

Text: Exchangeable stochastic networks, whose vertex labellings are inherently arbitrary and whose probability laws remain unchanged under any permutation of node indices, naturally arise in the statistical interrogation of relational data. In the present work we formulate an all‑encompassing theoretical construct that generalizes the Aldous–Hoover representation to sparse network regimes, thereby delineating the asymptotic limits of exchangeable graphs through graphon‑based processes endowed with edge‑density scaling. Moreover, we introduce a novel multilevel exchangeable family that simultaneously encapsulates community structure and degree heterogeneity while preserving the exchangeability property. By amalgamating probabilistic coupling techniques with empirical process theory, we rigorously establish the consistency of the empirical graphon estimator under modest moment constraints and furnish explicit finite‑sample error bounds. Extensive simulation studies reveal that our proposed models more accurately reconstruct latent block structure and degree distributions than traditional stochastic block models whenever exchangeability is satisfied. Finally, we demonstrate the practical applicability of our methodology on a large‑scale social network dataset, uncovering interpretable community structures that are congruent with known demographic attributes. These findings supply a solid theoretical foundation for statistical inference in exchangeable network models and pave the way toward scalable Bayesian inference for massive relational data.
Label: AWP
Title: Exchangeable Random Networks

Text: This investigation introduces a paradigm-shifting theoretical framework for inflationary scalar electrodynamics, thereby reconciling the universally observed homogeneity and isotropy of the cosmos with the inherently turbulent dynamics of the primordial universe. In this framework, a stochastic inflationary scalar electrodynamics model is formulated, which generalizes conventional electrodynamics by incorporating a stochastic scalar field responsible for driving inflationary expansion. This stochastic scalar field is posited to be coupled to the electromagnetic field, with its fluctuations governed by a Fokker-Planck equation that encapsulates the stochastic dynamics. By deriving the corresponding action functional and performing a perturbative expansion, we obtain the stochastic electrodynamics equations of motion, which elucidate the intricate interplay between the stochastic scalar field and the electromagnetic field. Our results unequivocally demonstrate that the stochastic scalar field can generate a scale-invariant power spectrum of scalar perturbations, which is consonant with empirical observational data. Moreover, we find that the stochastic electrodynamics framework provides a self-consistent explanation for the emergence of the observed homogeneity and isotropy of the universe during the inflationary era, thereby resolving a longstanding paradox in cosmological theory. Ultimately, our findings offer a novel and nuanced perspective on the early universe, underscoring the pivotal role of stochastic fluctuations in shaping the evolution of the cosmos.
Label: AWP
Title: Stochastic Inflationary Scalar Electrodynamics

Text: This longitudinal investigation into the Turkish Journal of Chemistry's (TJC) Hirsch index over a 20-year period, from 2000 to 2020, endeavors to elucidate the profound implications of this metric on research productivity and citation patterns within the field of chemistry, thereby contributing to the ongoing debate surrounding its limitations and potential biases. Predicated on the premise that the Hirsch index, a paradigmatic metric employed to evaluate a researcher's or journal's output and impact, warrants a more comprehensive examination, this study undertakes an in-depth analysis of the TJC's Hirsch index trajectory, thereby furnishing insights into the journal's research trajectory and citation dynamics. Notably, the results indicate a statistically significant escalation in the Hirsch index, suggesting a sustained augmentation in the journal's impact and citation potential, a finding consonant with the theoretical underpinnings of this metric. Furthermore, this analysis underscores the salience of article type, author collaboration, and institutional affiliation on the Hirsch index, thereby underscoring the need for a more nuanced understanding of citation metrics and their inherent complexities. Consequently, this case study provides a novel contribution to the ongoing discourse on the role of citation metrics in evaluating research output and offers a framework for future investigations into the Hirsch index's utility and limitations, thus facilitating a more informed understanding of the latter's implications for research evaluation and citation analysis.
Label: AWP
Title:
What does Hirsch index evolution explain us? A case study: Turkish
  Journal of Chemistry

Text: The discovery of diffuse cosmic gamma-rays within the energy spectrum of 1-20 MeV has precipitated a plethora of interest amongst the scientific community, with far-reaching implications for our comprehension of the universe's intricate composition and evolutionary trajectory. Notably, recent observations conducted by space-based gamma-ray telescopes have unveiled a persistent and diffuse gamma-ray flux in this energy range, characterized by a complex spectral morphology that poses significant challenges to interpretation within the conventional framework of astrophysical sources. A particularly intriguing hypothesis posits that this anomaly may be correlated with dark matter, a ubiquitous yet enigmatic form of matter thought to account for approximately 27% of the universe's mass-energy budget, which is believed to interact with normal matter through feeble interactions. This interaction may manifest as the observed gamma-ray flux, thereby underscoring the potential significance of dark matter as an explanatory mechanism. Although conventional astrophysical sources, such as supernovae remnants and active galactic nuclei, are well-documented to produce gamma-rays within this energy range, the diffuse nature of the observed flux and its spectral characteristics suggest that an alternative, more unconventional explanation may be requisite to fully elucidate the phenomenon. Consequently, further investigation is deemed necessary to ascertain whether the observed gamma-ray flux indeed constitutes a signature of dark matter, or whether it can be attributed to other, more conventional astrophysical processes.
Label: AWP
Title: Diffuse cosmic gamma-rays at 1-20 MeV: A trace of the dark matter?

Text: In this treatise, we posit the existence of a magnetized string cosmological paradigm situated within a cylindrically symmetric inhomogeneous universe characterized by a variable cosmological constant, $\Lambda$, thereby amalgamating topological attributes inherent to a string framework with the dynamic properties of a magnetized plasma in the nascent cosmos. Our proposed model assumes a spatially inhomogeneous and anisotropic metric, thereby facilitating the presence of a cosmic string, while the variable $\Lambda$ is modeled using a dynamical equation of state, which efficaciously captures the evolving nature of dark energy. The ensuing formulation enables the derivation of the Einstein field equations, taking into account the effects of a magnetic field and the variable $\Lambda$, resulting in a rich tapestry of analytical solutions that elucidate a diverse array of cosmological behaviors, including accelerated expansion, cyclic evolution, and the emergence of complex topological structures. Notably, these findings possess profound implications for our comprehension of the early universe, dark energy, and the intricate interplay between gravity, electromagnetism, and topology, thereby providing a novel framework for exploring the dynamics of these fundamental forces and shedding light on the enigmatic evolution of the universe.
Label: AWP
Title:
Magnetized String Cosmological Model in Cylindrically Symmetric
  Inhomogeneous Universe with Variable Cosmological-Term $\Lambda$

Text: This investigation showcases a pioneering realization of the quantum NAND algorithm leveraging quantum dots as a paradigmatic candidate for the development of scalable quantum computing architectures. By ingeniously integrating quantum dots into a nanoscale framework, we substantiate the feasibility of a quantum NAND gate, a foundational component essential for the implementation of quantum logic operations. The intrinsic ability of quantum dots to exhibit quantum coherence at ambient temperatures significantly facilitates the efficient execution of quantum algorithms, thereby obviating the necessity for cryogenic cooling protocols. Our experimental methodology entails the fabrication of a nanocavity-based quantum dot structure, which is subsequently optically coupled to a superconducting resonator, thereby forming a quantum circuit that enables the execution of the quantum NAND algorithm, a pivotal gate crucial for the realization of quantum computations. Notably, our experimental results demonstrate a high-fidelity implementation of the quantum NAND gate, boasting a fidelity of 93.2% and an operation time of 20 nanoseconds, underscoring the potential of quantum dots as a viable platform for large-scale quantum computing applications. This research highlights the prospect of quantum dots as a scalable and practical solution for the implementation of quantum algorithms, thereby rendering significant implications for the advancement of quantum computing technologies and potentially paving the way for the practical realization of quantum computers.
Label: AWP
Title: A quantum dot implementation of the quantum NAND algorithm

Text: This investigation delves into the intrinsic properties of PT symmetric non-selfadjoint operators, with a particular focus on their diagonalizability and spectral characteristics, thereby elucidating the paradigmatic relationship between these operators and their PT symmetry. Specifically, a PT symmetric operator is thereby defined as an operator that commutes with the composition of the parity operator P and the time reversal operator T, thereby underscoring the fundamental role of these symmetries in the operator's behavior. Notably, our analysis encompasses both the diagonalizable and the non-diagonalizable cases, with a resultant demonstration that the real discrete spectrum of these operators constitutes a pivotal aspect of their PT symmetry, wherein the real or complex conjugate pair spectra represent a direct consequence of the operator's PT symmetry. Furthermore, we establish conditions under which the operator is diagonalizable, and demonstrate that such diagonalization is accompanied by a basis transformation that preserves the operator's PT symmetry, thereby underscoring the intricate interplay between the operator's spectral properties and PT symmetry. Through the judicious application of both analytical and numerical methods, we validate the efficacy of these results, thereby highlighting the distinctive features of PT symmetric non-selfadjoint operators with real discrete spectrum, and thereby underscoring the profound implications of these findings for the comprehension of PT symmetric quantum systems and their potential applications in quantum mechanics and quantum field theory.
Label: AWP
Title:
$PT$ symmetric non-selfadjoint operators, diagonalizable and
  non-diagonalizable, with real discrete spectrum

Text: By leveraging the comprehensive temperature, polarization, and gravitational lensing datasets obtained through the Planck satellite mission, we execute a combined likelihood-based analysis of cosmological parameters within extended ΛCDM frameworks, incorporating the total neutrino mass (Σmν) and additional neutrino–neutrino or neutrino–dark-sector interactions. The high-precision cosmic microwave background power spectra constrain the acoustic damping tail and the late-universe integrated Sachs–Wolfe phenomenon, whereas the gravitational lensing reconstruction directly examines the suppression of large-scale structure formation induced by massive neutrinos. By integrating Planck observations with baryon acoustic oscillation measurements, degeneracies between the summed neutrino mass (Σmν) and the Hubble constant (H0) are effectively resolved, yielding an upper bound of Σmν < 0.12 eV at 95% confidence level within the minimal theoretical framework. Within scenarios incorporating neutrino self-interactions mediated by a light scalar particle, the collision rate at recombination epochs is constrained to Γν < 10⁻³ eV, which corresponds to a coupling parameter g ≲ 10⁻⁴. These constraints demonstrate parity with, and offer supplementary insights to, terrestrial neutrino oscillation and beta-decay investigations, effectively excluding a broad category of low-energy neutrino-mediated dark matter hypotheses. Our findings underscore the sustained efficacy of Planck's observational data in elucidating the intrinsic characteristics of neutrinos and their cosmological implications, thereby reinforcing the satellite's instrumental role in advancing our understanding of fundamental particle physics and cosmic structure evolution.
Label: AWP
Title:
Constraining Models of Neutrino Mass and Neutrino Interactions with the
  Planck Satellite

Text: This investigation introduces a paradigmatic mathematical framework for dissecting the hypermetric cone, a pivotal object in the discipline of metric geometry, into a collective set of L-domains, thereby mitigating the aforementioned object's notorious complexity and facilitating the efficient computation of hypermetric distances and metrics. As a convex cone encompassing all conceivable hypermetric functions on a finite set of points, the hypermetric cone has far-reaching applications in geometry, physics, and computer science, underscoring its inherent significance; however, its unwieldy complexity has hitherto hindered the development of expedient algorithms for computing these metrics. By capitalizing on the properties of L-domains and their intrinsic relationships to hypermetric functions, our research establishes a constructive methodology for decomposing the hypermetric cone into a finite union of L-domains, each of which corresponds to a specific subset of points, thereby enabling the efficacious computation of hypermetric distances and metrics, and yielding profound implications for a diverse range of applications, including geometric analysis, machine learning, and data analysis. The proposed framework represents a significant advancement in our comprehension of the hypermetric cone and serves as a foundational precursor to the development of novel algorithms and techniques in these fields.
Label: AWP
Title: The decomposition of the hypermetric cone into L-domains

Text: Our research endeavor, an innovative cavity experiment, endeavours to investigate the existence of hypothetical hidden sector photons, a theoretical prediction posited by various modifications to the paradigmatic Standard Model of particle physics. This novel experimental approach leverages a highly sensitive photonic cavity to detect the faint electromagnetic signatures potentially emitted by hidden sector particles interacting with the Standard Model sector, an occurrence that would have profound implications for our understanding of the fundamental forces governing particle physics. The experimental apparatus comprises a high-quality factor optical cavity, synergistically coupled to a microwave cavity, thereby augmenting its sensitivity to the weak electromagnetic signals that would be indicative of such interactions. To facilitate the extraction of these faint signals from the omnipresent background noise, a meticulously calibrated system of lasers and microwave sources is employed in conjunction with a sophisticated data acquisition and analysis system. By operating the cavity at cryogenic temperatures, a regime that minimizes thermal noise, our experiment achieves an unprecedented level of sensitivity, thereby rendering it capable of detecting hidden sector photons with energies that lie beneath the electroweak scale, a threshold that heretofore has been considered inaccessible to experimental detection. Initial results from this experiment are encouraging, and further upgrades and extensions are contemplated to systematically explore the parameter space of hidden sector theories, thereby elucidating the underlying dynamics governing these enigmatic particles.
Label: AWP
Title: A Cavity Experiment to Search for Hidden Sector Photons

Text: This investigation into the emergence of chaotic traveling rolls in Rayleigh-Bénard convection, a paradigmatic model for elucidating the intricacies of fluid dynamics and thermal convection, reveals the existence of ephemeral, spatially periodic patterns exhibiting long-range correlations and intricate dynamics through the application of numerical simulations and analytical methodologies. These chaotic traveling rolls emerge from the nonlinear interaction between the fluid's buoyancy-driven convective motion and the thermal boundary conditions imposed upon the system, thereby giving rise to a complex interplay of fluid dynamics and thermodynamics. Notably, our results indicate that the system's chaotic behavior is characterized by a continuous spectrum of wave numbers, thereby substantiating the presence of a non-equilibrium statistical steady state that deviates from thermodynamic equilibrium. Furthermore, the chaotic traveling rolls exhibit scale-invariant properties, suggesting a profound connection to the concept of universality in complex systems, where the emergence of patterns is governed by underlying symmetries and scaling laws. Our findings provide novel insights into the underlying physics of Rayleigh-Bénard convection and shed light on the pivotal role of chaotic dynamics in the emergence of complex spatiotemporal patterns in fluid systems, with far-reaching implications for our comprehension of heat transfer, fluid mixing, and pattern formation in various natural and industrial processes.
Label: AWP
Title: Chaotic traveling rolls in Rayleigh-B\'enard convection

Text: This investigation into the rational homotopy type of a blow-up in the stable scenario undertakes a multifaceted analysis of the resultant topological space's algebraic and topological characteristics, thereby elucidating the underlying properties that govern its behavior. Specifically, the stable case pertains to a particular instance wherein the blow-up operation is executed on a manifold or variety boasting an adequately elevated dimensionality, thereby yielding a space whose rational homotopy type can be precisely defined. By leveraging the paradigmatic framework of Sullivan's minimal models, our research reveals that the rational homotopy type of the blow-up is inextricably linked to the minimal models of both the original space and the exceptional divisor, with the ensuing rational homotopy type of the blow-up being isomorphic to that of the original space, albeit accompanied by the incorporation of a specific rational homotopy group associated with the exceptional divisor. Moreover, our findings establish a precise algebraic correlation between the minimal models of the blow-up and the original space, thereby furnishing a concrete, algebraic description of the resultant space's rational homotopy type. These significant outcomes have far-reaching implications for the study of algebraic and topological invariants of topological spaces, while underscoring the pivotal importance of the stable case in the blow-up operation.
Label: AWP
Title: The rational homotopy type of a blow-up in the stable case

Text: This comprehensive study undertakes a thorough examination of the thermodynamic properties of first-order phase transitions in classical lattice gas spin models, a paradigmatic class of statistical mechanical systems that have been extensively utilized to model phase transitions in a myriad of physical and chemical contexts, thereby underscoring their profound relevance to the underlying mechanisms governing this phenomenon. Through a synergistic integration of numerical simulations and analytical techniques, our investigation unequivocally demonstrates the occurrence of first-order phase transitions in these models, characterized by the manifestation of discontinuous changes in the order parameter and concomitant variations in thermodynamic quantities, thereby elucidating the fundamental distinction between these transitions and their continuous counterparts. Notably, our results reveal a qualitative disparity in the critical behavior of these systems, whereby the order parameter exhibits a pronounced discontinuous jump at the transition temperature, and we further establish that the associated latent heat is non-zero, thereby underscoring the thermodynamic distinctiveness of the phase boundary. By scrutinizing the phase diagram and critical exponents of these models, our investigation provides profound insights into the underlying mechanisms driving these transitions and sheds light on the intricate interplay between lattice structure and spin interactions in determining the phase behavior of these systems, thereby yielding valuable implications for the theoretical understanding of phase transitions in a vast array of systems, ranging from condensed matter physics to biology.
Label: AWP
Title: First order phase transitions in classical lattice gas spin models

Text: This comprehensive investigation, undertaken through an exhaustive quantum Monte Carlo analysis, elucidates the intricacies of ring-shaped polariton parametric luminescence in a semiconductor microcavity, wherein a rigorously numerical approach was employed to simulate the behavior of exciton-polaritons within a microcavity structure specifically engineered to incorporate a ring-shaped resonant cavity and an embedded semiconductor gain medium. The resultant calculations reveal that the ring-shaped cavity configuration precipitates a substantial enhancement of the parametric gain of the polariton system, thereby increasing the efficiency of the parametric luminescence process. Moreover, our results demonstrate that the ring-shaped cavity configuration induces a pronounced spatial modulation of the polariton modal distribution, thereby yielding a distinct ring-shaped emission pattern, which is found to be in excellent concordance with experimental observations, thereby offering valuable insights into the underlying physical mechanisms governing the dynamics of polariton parametric luminescence in semiconductor microcavities. Consequently, our findings provide novel avenues for optimizing the design of microcavity structures for enhanced polariton parametric luminescence applications, with far-reaching implications for the development of novel optoelectronic devices and quantum information processing technologies.
Label: AWP
Title:
Quantum Monte Carlo study of ring-shaped polariton parametric
  luminescence in a semiconductor microcavity

Text: This investigation develops an encompassing framework that converges computational simulation and three-dimensional virtual reality (VR) engineering tools to facilitate the dynamical modeling and imaging of composite nanomaterials, thereby yielding a comprehensive paradigm for the simulation and visualization of their structural and mechanical behavior. A multiscale modeling approach was employed to simulate the structural and mechanical behavior of various nanocomposite systems, encompassing polymer and ceramic matrices reinforced with carbon nanotubes (CNTs) and graphene nanoplatelets (GNPs), which enabled the prediction of their mechanical properties and thermal stability under diverse loading conditions. Computational simulations were conducted using finite element methods (FEM) and molecular dynamics (MD), and the resultant data were further visualized and analyzed using 3D VR tools, thereby facilitating real-time exploration of the material's microstructure and dynamic behavior. The validity of the computational simulations was subsequently validated through experimental characterization of the nanocomposites using transmission electron microscopy (TEM), scanning electron microscopy (SEM), and Raman spectroscopy, thereby establishing a robust correlation between simulation and experimental results. This integrated approach provides a powerful platform for the design, development, and optimization of composite nanomaterials with tailored properties, thereby opening up new avenues for potential applications in energy storage, biomedical devices, and advanced aerospace engineering. The findings of this study have significant implications for the development of next-generation nanomaterials with enhanced performance and functionality.
Label: AWP
Title:
Computational Simulation and 3D Virtual Reality Engineering Tools for
  Dynamical Modeling and Imaging of Composite Nanomaterials

Text: A comprehensive analysis of the nucleon's weak structure, facilitated by atmospheric neutrinos, enables us to probe the vector and axial form factors that govern quasi-elastic, resonance, and deep-inelastic scattering regimes pertinent to contemporary and prospective atmospheric neutrino detectors. Through the development of a duality-constrained parameterization, which subsumes quark-hadron duality relations at intermediate momentum transfers and adheres to lattice QCD and electron-scattering data at low and high momentum transfers, respectively, we derive smooth, physically informed functional forms that seamlessly interpolate between the elastic, resonance, and scaling domains. This parameterization, implemented within a Monte-Carlo framework, is juxtaposed against an exhaustive corpus of experimental data, encompassing MINERvA, T2K, and IceCube atmospheric flux analyses, thereby enabling a rigorous evaluation of its efficacy. Notably, the duality-constrained model exhibits a reduction in systematic uncertainty on the predicted charged-current cross sections of up to 15% relative to conventional dipole or phenomenological fits, thereby enhancing the precision of neutrino oscillation parameter extraction. Furthermore, this development has significant implications for the interpretation of atmospheric neutrino data within the context of next-generation detectors, such as Hyper-Kamiokande and the Deep Underground Neutrino Experiment.
Label: AWP
Title:
Modeling Atmospheric Neutrino Interactions: Duality Constrained
  Parameterization of Vector and Axial Nucleon Form Factors

Text: This investigation undertakes a rigorous examination of the derivation of quantum theory from the foundational concept of Hamilton's Principle, a fundamental postulate in classical mechanics, under the auspices of incomplete information. By seamlessly integrating principles of information theory and uncertainty into the Hamiltonian framework, we devise a novel approach to quantum theory that effectuates a harmonious reconciliation of classical and quantum descriptions of physical phenomena, thereby transcending traditional dichotomies. Rooted in the paradigm of optimal control theory, our formulation endeavors to minimize the discrepancy between the classical Hamiltonian and a quantum-inspired Hamiltonian, thus generating a quantum-like description of particle behavior that is predicated on the principles of minimal deviation. The resultant quantum theory is demonstrated to reproduce the salient features of the standard quantum theory, including wave-particle duality and the Heisenberg uncertainty principle, while also exhibiting novel characteristics that arise from the presence of incomplete information. This framework offers a paradigmatic shift in our understanding of the origins of quantum theory and its relationship to classical mechanics, with potential implications for the development of novel quantum technologies and a deeper comprehension of the fundamental nature of reality. Furthermore, a thorough analysis and experimentation are warranted to fully elucidate the predictive power and physical significance of this novel quantum theory, thereby facilitating a more nuanced understanding of its implications and potential applications.
Label: AWP
Title: Quantum theory from Hamilton's Principle with imperfect information

Text: Deception, particularly bluffing, constitutes an essential strategic element in competitive gaming and bargaining contexts; nevertheless, a rigorous formalization of such behaviour has proven difficult. In this study we present a reinforcement‑learning architecture that endows artificial agents with the capacity to acquire bluffing tactics within a partially observable Markov decision process that abstracts the mechanics of simplified poker. The experimental setup involves a zero‑sum duel, wherein a deep Q‑network is trained in conjunction with an auxiliary reward signal that reflects the adversary’s posterior belief state, and the policy is further enriched by a stochastic exploration schedule explicitly designed to promote deceptive maneuvers. Over the course of 200 000 training episodes the agents are evaluated against both rule‑based heuristics and perfect‑information baselines. Empirical results indicate that the resulting policy resorts to bluffing roughly 35 % of the time, yielding a 12 % increase in victory frequency relative to a non‑bluffing counterpart and surpassing a deterministic strategy by 8 %. A detailed examination of belief‑state updates reveals that the adversary is successfully misled in 22 % of encounters, thereby corroborating the efficacy of the learned bluffing behaviour. These outcomes demonstrate that deep reinforcement learning is capable of internalizing sophisticated deceptive strategies, thereby opening new perspectives for the investigation of human‑AI interactions and for the engineering of resilient AI systems that are adept at both detecting and executing bluffing.
Label: AWP
Title: Learning to Bluff

Text: This research undertakes a comprehensive examination of the algebraic paradigm governing crossed products, with a particular emphasis on the intricate interplay between locally C*-algebras and the notion of Morita equivalence. By engaging in a thorough analysis of the implications of this relationship on the intrinsic structural properties of the crossed product, our investigation elucidates its topological and algebraic characteristics, thereby shedding novel light on the underlying dynamics. Notably, our exploration of the Morita equivalence of locally C*-algebras reveals a profound extension of this equivalence to their respective crossed products, thereby establishing a fundamental and far-reaching connection between these two disparate frameworks. Furthermore, our investigation into the consequences of this equivalence on the existence and uniqueness of the crossed product yields significant insights into its salient characteristics, underscoring its paramount importance in the context of C*-algebra theory. Our findings demonstrate that the crossed product of locally C*-algebras can be regarded as a Morita equivalent object, thereby facilitating a more profound understanding of the algebraic structure of these algebras and their manifold applications in operator algebras and non-commutative geometry, and accordingly, contribute significantly to the advancement of our knowledge in this field, providing innovative methodologies and perspectives for the study of crossed products and their properties.
Label: AWP
Title: Crossed products of locally C*-algebras and Morita equivalence

Text: The bulk viscosity of superfluid neutron stars exerts a fundamental influence on their thermodynamic evolution, oscillatory stability, and susceptibility to gravitational wave emission. Within these astrophysical entities, the cores are characterized by superfluid neutrons coexisting with superconducting protons, with their interplay governed by neutrino-driven interactions and non-equilibrium Cooper pair formation and dissociation processes. By analyzing the thermal and compositional gradients inherent to the stellar interior, this study quantifies the bulk viscosity contributions stemming from these superfluid phases, emphasizing how temperature- and density-dependent microphysical mechanisms, such as Cooper pair thermal fluctuations and phonon-mediated energy dissipation, modulate macroscopic fluid behavior. The results demonstrate a marked suppression of bulk viscosity in superfluid domains relative to conventional fluid configurations, resulting in extended damping timescales for non-radial oscillations and modified thresholds for r-mode instability onset. Furthermore, the synergistic effects of bulk viscosity and neutrino emissivity govern the core’s thermal relaxation dynamics, thereby impacting observed surface cooling profiles. These findings not only highlight the imperative role of quantum coherence in governing macroscopic stellar behavior but also underscore the necessity of integrating precision microphysical modeling to bridge laboratory nuclear physics with astrophysical observations. By advancing our comprehension of how superfluidity regulates neutron star dynamics, this work provides a foundation for interpreting phenomena such as millisecond pulsar spin-down kinetics and transient thermal emissions while offering novel constraints for equations of state in extreme dense matter regimes.
Label: AWP
Title: Bulk viscosity of superfluid neutron stars

Text: In this study we formulate and scrutinize BIon configurations within the context of topological string theory, emphasizing their function as non‑perturbative probes of the underlying Calabi–Yau geometry; by incorporating D‑brane sources into the A‑model and leveraging the topological vertex formalism, we obtain exact expressions for the world‑volume gauge fields that support spike‑like solutions bridging distinct Lagrangian submanifolds, and these BIons are demonstrated to encode information concerning open string moduli and mirror symmetry, with their profiles dictated by holomorphic curves calibrated by the ambient Kähler form; moreover, we establish that the tension of the BIon is quantized in units of the topological string coupling and that their interactions reproduce the anticipated fusion rules of the associated boundary operators, while our analysis uncovers a novel correspondence between BIon junctions and the algebra of open‑closed string amplitudes, thereby suggesting a deeper connection between brane dynamics and the enumerative invariants of the target space; numerical verifications against established Gromov–Witten invariants confirm the validity of the construction, and the formalism furnishes a systematic method to generate higher‑order corrections, thereby opening new avenues for probing non‑local effects in topological string theory and for exploring the interplay among geometry, gauge dynamics, and duality symmetries.

Title: BIons in topological string theory

Text: The advent of gravitational wave detection from merging binaries has profoundly transformed our comprehension of strong-field gravity in binary systems, necessitating a meticulous examination of various factors, including the precision of waveform models, the repercussions of instrumental noise, and the influence of astrophysical uncertainties, in order to accurately interpret these results. Within this framework, our investigation focuses on elucidating the impact of waveform model errors on the extraction of binary parameters from gravitational wave observations, revealing that current waveform models, although satisfactory for numerous applications, can yield systematic errors in parameter estimation, particularly for high-mass or highly eccentric binaries, which underscores the imperative of continued waveform model refinement. Additionally, our analysis demonstrates that the incorporation of additional astrophysical uncertainties, such as tidal interactions and black hole spin, can significantly enhance the accuracy of parameter recovery, thereby underscoring the importance of more comprehensive treatments of astrophysical uncertainties in gravitational wave data analysis. Ultimately, by addressing these challenges, we can optimize the extraction of scientific information from future gravitational wave observations and further our understanding of the intricate astrophysical processes governing binary coalescence, thus facilitating a more sophisticated comprehension of strong-field gravity in binary systems.

Title:
Interpreting the results of searches for gravitational waves from
  coalescing binaries

Text: This investigation introduces a pioneering framework for the fabrication of relatively diminutive polyhedra via the judicious amalgamation of Sonobé modules, a class of three-dimensional origami paper constructs capable of forming a diverse array of polyhedral geometries through interconnected configurations. Our modular system comprises a standardized assortment of connectors, each tailored to a particular Sonobé module configuration, which can be systematically combined to generate a wide gamut of polyhedral structures, thereby underscoring the system's versatility. Text: This study presents an innovative framework for the reduction of linear time-periodic (LTP) systems, designated as snapshot-driven balanced truncation, facilitating the derivation of compact dynamical models while maintaining essential structural attributes. Conventional approaches to balanced truncation for LTP systems rely on the resolution of operator-valued Lyapunov equations to synthesize time-varying controllability and observability gramians, a process that becomes computationally infeasible for systems with high-dimensional state spaces. The proposed methodology circumvents this limitation by harnessing temporally sampled data—specifically, input-output responses captured at discrete intervals across a single period—to numerically approximate these gramians. Through projection of the collected snapshots into a reduced subspace and subsequent resolution of a sequence of compact, time-varying Lyapunov-inspired equations, the method generates balanced realizations wherein states are hierarchically ranked by their contribution to system dynamics, enabling the selective elimination of less influential components. The framework ensures the preservation of asymptotic stability in the reduced-order model and formulates a priori error bounds contingent on the singular values of the balanced gramians, thereby providing quantifiable guarantees on the fidelity of the approximation. Empirical evaluations conducted on canonical LTP systems—such as a mechanically oscillating system subjected to periodic forcing and an electrical network with temporally modulated components—demonstrate significant computational efficiency compared to established techniques without compromising accuracy. The snapshot-driven approach is particularly efficacious for systems exhibiting rapidly evolving dynamics or expansive state representations, where direct gramian computation is impractical. This research establishes a conceptual bridge between data-centric model reduction paradigms and classical Lyapunov-based methodologies, offering a robust analytical tool for the analysis and control of complex time-periodic systems in domains including power grid networks, aerospace engineering, and vibrational isolation technologies.
Label: AWP
Title: Snapshot-based Balanced Truncation for Linear Time-periodic Systems

Text: The present investigation examines the propagation characteristics of solitary and shock waves within discretized double power-law (DDPL) media, a category of granular systems distinguished by bimodal power-law distributions in particulate dimensions. Employing computational modeling and analytical frameworks, we elucidate the emergence of distinctive wave dynamics inherent to DDPL configurations, wherein the interplay between interparticle forces and size-dependent dissipative mechanisms governs the emergence of nonlinear wave phenomena. Our findings reveal that solitary waves, defined by localized nonlinear displacement profiles, are capable of formation and sustained propagation within DDPL matrices, with their velocity and morphological characteristics contingent upon the exponent parameters of the power-law distributions and the heterogeneity of particulate sizes. Conversely, shock waves, which emerge from the disintegration of solitary wave structures, exhibit divergent behavior, wherein their propagation rates and amplitude magnitudes are modulated by the interplay between interparticle forces and size-dependent dissipative mechanisms. This research contributes to the comprehension of granular system dynamics across diverse geological and engineered contexts, such as sedimentary processes, rockfall mechanics, and slope failure mechanisms, by demonstrating the critical role of particulate size heterogeneity in mediating wave behavior. The outcomes of this inquiry offer novel perspectives on the intricate wave dynamics within DDPL media and underscore the criticality of incorporating size-dependent material properties in the analysis of granular media.
Label: AWP
Title: Solitary and shock waves in discrete double power-law materials

Text: This study examines the interdependence of charge conservation and the equivalence principle within the formalism of noncommutative geometry, characterized by canonical commutator relations among spatial coordinates. By extending classical electrodynamics to incorporate noncommutative structures, we derive altered Maxwell equations that encapsulate spacetime noncommutativity and scrutinize their ramifications for charge conservation. Leveraging Noether's theorem and symmetry analysis, we demonstrate that the noncommutative parameter introduces perturbations to the continuity equation, yielding a recalibrated conservation law contingent on the commutator structure of the underlying spacetime. Concurrently, the validity of the equivalence principle is reassessed by evaluating how noncommutative geometry modulates the coupling between gravitational and electromagnetic fields. Applying a minimal coupling prescription to curved noncommutative spacetime, we discern that the equivalence principle persists only under stringent constraints on noncommutative parameters, thereby preserving the universality of free-fall. Our findings elucidate a conflict between charge conservation and the equivalence principle in noncommutative regimes, manifesting as discrepancies in energy-momentum tensor components and gravitational redshift phenomena. Furthermore, a consistency criterion is established, correlating the noncommutative scale with observational constraints on charge conservation anomalies, thereby constructing an empirical validation framework. These insights underscore the imperative of harmonizing quantum spacetime paradigms with foundational tenets of general relativity and electromagnetism, offering novel perspectives on the coexistence of noncommutative geometry with fundamental conservation laws and gravitational invariance.
Label: AWP
Title:
On Charge Conservation and The Equivalence Principle in the
  Noncommutative Spacetime

Text: The present investigation introduces a hybrid formalism wherein a saturation model is embedded within the non-Glauber framework to elucidate the dynamics of high-energy nuclear collisions, thereby diverging from conventional Glauber-based methodologies. Departing from the conventional fixed nucleon-nucleon interaction framework, the non-Glauber paradigm incorporates stochastic fluctuations in participant nucleon numbers and spatial configurations, thereby offering a more nuanced representation of collision geometry. By integrating saturation physics, governed by the Balitsky-Kovchegov evolution equation, the model accounts for density-dependent suppression of gluon interactions at elevated momentum scales—a critical mechanism for characterizing the initial state of heavy-ion collisions. Computational analyses reveal that this hybrid formalism effectively reconciles with empirical data from collisions at the Large Hadron Collider (LHC) and Relativistic Heavy Ion Collider (RHIC), particularly in high-gluon-density regimes, with enhanced concordance observed in pseudorapidity distributions and transverse momentum spectra. The results further emphasize the pivotal role of saturation scales in modulating phenomena such as energy loss and jet quenching, thereby establishing a bridge between non-linear QCD dynamics in the initial state and the subsequent emergence of collective hydrodynamic behavior in the quark-gluon plasma. Comparative analyses with hydrodynamic simulations demonstrate improved alignment in elliptic flow metrics, underscoring the indispensable interplay between saturation effects and non-Glauber fluctuations in elucidating the genesis of collective motion. This study not only advances the theoretical underpinnings of high-energy nuclear collisions but also underscores the necessity of a saturation-aware non-Glauber framework for probing the intricate interplay between non-linear QCD evolution and the macroscopic properties of strongly interacting matter under extreme thermodynamic conditions.
Label: AWP
Title: Saturation model in the non-Glauber approach

Text: This investigation introduces an innovative paradigm for determining the state of large-scale, spatiotemporally chaotic systems, which are distinguished by their intricate and unpredictable behavior, characterized by an intricate interplay of complex dynamics and nonlinear interactions. By integrating a synergy of machine learning algorithms and numerical modeling methodologies, the proposed approach identifies and extracts key patterns and correlations that underlie the system's dynamics, thereby facilitating the development of a robust and accurate framework for reconstructing the system's state from limited and noisy observational data. Through the application of this integrated methodology to a diverse array of exemplary systems, including fluid turbulence, climate modeling, and population dynamics, we demonstrate its efficacy in accurately predicting the system's state, thereby underscoring the significance of this innovative approach in elucidating the underlying physics that govern these complex systems. Underpinned by a profound understanding of the underlying physical principles and leveraging the inherent symmetries and self-similarity present in chaotic systems, the developed methodology enables the efficient capture of the intricate structures and patterns that govern the behavior of these complex systems, thereby facilitating the estimation of their state with remarkable precision. The far-reaching implications of this research extend to a diverse range of fields, including climate prediction, weather forecasting, and the study of complex biological systems, where the reliable estimation of the system's state is crucial for understanding and mitigating the effects of chaos, thereby informing evidence-based interventions and policy decisions.

Title: Estimating the State of Large Spatiotemporally Chaotic Systems

Text: This investigation pertains to the current flowing through non-equilibrium steady states (NESS), a topic of considerable interest within the framework of stochastic processes, particularly in systems that deviate significantly from equilibrium. Our research endeavors to elucidate the cumulants and large deviations of the current through NESS, wherein the system's dynamics is orchestrated by an external bias. By integrating analytical and numerical methodologies, we derive explicit formulae for the cumulants of the current in terms of the system's parameters and the strength of the external bias, thus facilitating a comprehensive understanding of the relationships between these variables. Notably, our findings are consonant with the Fluctuation Theorem, a foundational principle that establishes a reciprocal relationship between the probability of observing a given current in the forward and backward directions. Furthermore, we undertake an in-depth analysis of the large deviation characteristics of the current, revealing that the associated rate function exhibits a complex structure that is contingent upon the underlying system's dynamics. The implications of our research are far-reaching, contributing significantly to the comprehension of non-equilibrium systems and the behavior of currents in such settings, thereby shedding light on the intricate interplay between the system's parameters, the external bias, and the emergent current statistics. Ultimately, the results of this study offer novel insights into the behavior of non-equilibrium systems and hold the potential to inform both theoretical and experimental research within this field.

Title:
Cumulants and large deviations of the current through non-equilibrium
  steady states

Text: This comprehensive investigation undertakes a multifaceted examination of the spectroscopic properties of mesons comprising heavy quarks, thereby elucidating the salient characteristics and intrinsic features of these enigmatic entities. Leveraging cutting-edge experimental methodologies and sophisticated data analytical techniques, we have conducted an in-depth investigation of the energy spectra of mesons comprised of charm and bottom quarks in conjunction with light quarks, thereby furnishing a wealth of knowledge regarding the internal structure and dynamic behavior of these hadrons. Notably, our empirical findings provide valuable insight into the fundamental principles governing the behavior of these particles, thereby significantly enhancing our comprehension of Quantum Chromodynamics (QCD), the underlying theoretical framework of strong interactions. Specifically, our results reveal deviations from perturbative predictions, indicating the presence of non-perturbative effects, which are pivotal in the context of hadron spectroscopy, and are consonant with lattice QCD calculations. Furthermore, the implications of our findings have far-reaching consequences for the development of more accurate theoretical models, underscoring the significant contributions that this research will make towards the ongoing endeavors in high-energy physics to elucidate the properties of heavy quark mesons and the underlying forces governing their behavior.

Title: Spectroscopy of Mesons with Heavy Quarks

Text: This comprehensive study undertakes a meticulous examination of the complex dynamics exhibited by the wet granular gas, a multifaceted system characterized by the intricate interplay of frictional and cohesive forces governing the interactions amongst its constituent particles. Through the employment of cutting-edge numerical simulations and experimental methodologies, we have thoroughly investigated the dynamic properties of the wet granular gas under a range of conditions, encompassing disparate particle sizes, velocities, and surface tensions. Notably, our findings reveal a multifaceted array of complex behavior, including the spontaneous emergence of self-organized patterns, intermittent fluctuations, and a transition to chaotic dynamics as the system's kinetic energy and particle interactions escalate, thereby underscoring the system's propensity for unpredictable behavior. Moreover, we observe that the observed chaoticity is strongly contingent upon the system's dimensionality, with higher-dimensional systems manifesting more pronounced chaotic behavior. Furthermore, we have identified a critical threshold beneath which the system exhibits a more ordered, harmonic motion, whereas above this threshold, the system's behavior becomes increasingly erratic and complex, exhibiting characteristics of a non-linear system. These novel findings have far-reaching implications for our comprehension of the behavior of granular systems in various industrial and natural contexts, including powder processing, sediment transport, and geological phenomena, thereby underscoring the significance of this research in the fields of materials science and geophysics.

Text: This research examines the characteristics and consequences of Accardi complementarity within the interval $-\frac{1}{2} < \mu < 0$, building upon prior investigations that predominantly addressed non-negative domains of $\mu$. Through the application of analytical frameworks and structural methodologies within the domain of quantum probability theory, we establish that the complementarity paradigm—defined by the coexistence of incompatible quantum measurements in mutually exclusive yet experimentally verifiable configurations—exhibits a qualitative metamorphosis in this parameter regime. Key findings include the demonstration that for $-\frac{1}{2} < \mu < 0$, the classical constraints governing measurement compatibility dissolve, giving rise to non-classical entanglements and the violation of classical bounds, as quantified by newly formulated constraints demarcating the thresholds of quantum phenomena. These conditions are underpinned by $\mu$-dependent symmetric properties and the algebraic architecture of the associated Hilbert space, which are rigorously delineated through operator-theoretic analysis. Further related results encompass the derivation of novel criteria for joint measurability, wherein the interplay between $\mu$ and the non-commutative geometry of quantum observables is elucidated. Theoretical ramifications extend to foundational inquiries in quantum information processing paradigms and the characterization of the demarcation between quantum and classical regimes. By synthesizing mathematical formalism with empirical pertinence, this work offers a nuanced perspective on the role of structural parameters in modulating quantum coherence and measurement incompatibility.

Title: Accardi complementarity for -1/2 < mu < 0 and related results

Text: We introduce a paradigm-shifting approach to fabricating a lattice of microtraps for ultracold atoms by harnessing the magnetic properties of patterned films, thereby circumventing the limitations of traditional trapping methodologies. Utilizing a synergy of lithographic techniques and thin-film deposition, we successfully engineer a magnetic lattice comprising periodically arranged micro-magnets with bespoke magnetic moments, thereby yielding an array of microtraps for ultracold atoms that are delineated by the localized magnetic fields generated by the patterned film. By judiciously adjusting the magnetic moment and lattice geometry, we achieve a high degree of precision in manipulating the trap potential, thereby facilitating the confinement of atoms within individual microtraps. Our experimental findings unequivocally substantiate the viability of leveraging patterned magnetic films as a platform for ultracold atom trapping, offering several salient advantages over conventional trapping methods, including scalability, flexibility, and negligible background noise. The proposed lattice of microtraps harbors significant potential applications in the investigation of quantum many-body physics, quantum information processing, and precision spectroscopy, and could serve as a versatile instrument for the exploration of ultracold atomic gases in artificial micro-structures.

Title:
A lattice of microtraps for ultracold atoms based on patterned magnetic
  films

Text: Within the theoretical framework of Quantum Chromodynamics (QCD), the neutral color-flavor-locked (CFL) phase has attracted considerable scholarly interest owing to its profound implications for the dynamics of strong interactions, particularly in regimes characterized by extreme matter density. This phase, distinguished by concurrent phenomena of chiral symmetry breaking and non-perturbative color confinement, is hypothesized to manifest under conditions of asymptotically high baryonic density. The present investigation advances a diagrammatic formalism to analytically derive the effective masses of mesons within the CFL phase, employing a methodical perturbative expansion of the effective action in terms of mesonic field amplitudes, followed by an iterative summation of dominant logarithmic contributions to refine the theoretical predictions. The resultant effective action serves as a foundational tool for quantifying the mass parameters of key mesonic states, including the lowest-lying pseudoscalar and vector mesons, revealing a distinct scaling relationship wherein the pseudoscalar meson mass is substantially suppressed relative to its vector counterpart. Comparative analysis with prior computational methodologies yields consistent meson mass estimates, thereby validating the robustness of the diagrammatic approach. These findings not only corroborate existing theoretical frameworks but also offer critical quantitative benchmarks for elucidating the phenomenological landscape of the CFL phase in dense QCD matter.
Label: AWP
Title:
A diagrammatic derivation of the meson effective masses in the neutral
  color-flavor-locked phase of Quantum Chromodynamics

Text: DNA nanorobotics amalgamates the intrinsic programmability of nucleic‑acid self‑assembly with the exquisite precision of nanomechanical actuation, thereby engendering autonomous molecular machines capable of sensing, transporting, and manipulating nanoscale cargo; in the present investigation, we engineered a DNA‑based walker that traverses a one‑dimensional track composed of single‑stranded DNA footholds, propelled via toehold‑mediated strand displacement and powered by ATP‑mimicking fuel strands, and, through the concurrent application of time‑resolved Förster resonance energy transfer and atomic force microscopy, we quantified its stepwise translocation, achieving an average velocity of 2.3 nm s⁻¹ and a processivity of 45 successive steps before dissociation; by coupling this walker to a DNA origami cargo platform, we accomplished selective delivery of fluorescently labelled quantum dots to predefined sites on a microfluidic chip, thereby demonstrating on‑chip routing with 92 % accuracy, while the integration of a hairpin‑based sensor module endowed the system with autonomous responsiveness to the presence of a target microRNA, triggering cargo release solely upon detection, and collectively these results establish a versatile framework for DNA‑based nanorobotics that can be programmed for complex, multi‑step tasks, offering a promising route toward programmable drug delivery, nanoscale assembly, and biosensing.

Title: DNA Nanorobotics

Text: This investigation elucidates the formulation of an innovative non-perturbative time-dependent configuration within the framework of string theory, offering a paradigm shift in analyzing transient phenomena that transcend perturbative methodologies. By employing sophisticated topological constructs and algebraic-geometric techniques, a precise analytical model is derived for a temporally evolving multi-brane ensemble, distinguished by intricate flux compactifications and moduli field stabilization mechanisms. The proposed configuration demonstrates resilience against quantum fluctuations, adhering to stringent energy constraints dictated by the supergravity action, thereby ensuring physical consistency. Through the application of dualistic frameworks—including T-duality transformations and holographic correspondence—this model facilitates the mediation of transitions between divergent vacuum states, thereby providing a theoretical scaffold for cosmological evolution scenarios rooted in string-theoretic principles. The time-dependent nature of the configuration engenders emergent interactions between closed and open string sectors, engendering ephemeral non-geometric backgrounds that challenge conventional static compactification paradigms. Furthermore, the configuration’s inherent stability against perturbative instabilities suggests its applicability in modeling primordial cosmological epochs or elucidating gravitational effects in evolving spacetime geometries.
